items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for three days before the festivals of gentiles, it is forbidden to engage in business transactions with them. Rabbi Yehuda permits collecting debts from them because it causes them distress, but the Sages counter that even if distressed now, they will be happy later.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שלפני חגי הגויים אסור לשאת ולתת עמם, להשאיל ולשאול, להלוות וללוות, לפרוע ולהיפרע. רבי יהודה מתיר להיפרע מהם משום צערם, וחכמים דוחים ששמחתם תשוב לאחר זמן.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that for three days before gentile festivals, business transactions with them are forbidden.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת באיסור משא ומתן עם גויים לפני חגיהם, ומביאה מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לחכמים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda permits collecting debts from them because it causes them distress.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת באיסור משא ומתן עם גויים לפני חגיהם, ומביאה מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לחכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object that even if distressed now, the gentile will be happy later.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת באיסור משא ומתן עם גויים לפני חגיהם, ומביאה מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לחכמים.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ושמואל בגרסת 'אידיהן' או 'עידיהן'
items.text_en: Gemara's debate on the vocalization of 'eideihen'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree on whether to read 'eideihen' (their festivals) or 'eideihen' (their witnesses). Each reading is supported by a biblical verse: 'eideihen' from 'ki karov yom eidam' (their calamity), and 'eideihen' from 'yitnu eideihem veyitzdaku' (their witnesses). The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each preference.
items.desc: רב ושמואל נחלקו: אחד גורס 'אידיהן' מלשון איד (אסון), ואחד גורס 'עידיהן' מלשון עדות. כל אחד מביא ראיה מפסוקים: 'אידיהן' מפסוק 'כי קרוב יום אידם', ו'עידיהן' מפסוק 'יתנו עדיהם ויצדקו'. הטעם לגרסת 'אידיהן' הוא שתברא (שבר) עדיף, ולגרסת 'עידיהן' – העדות שגורמת לתברא עדיפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel over the vocalization of the Mishnah's word: one reads 'eideihen' (their festivals) and the other reads 'eideihen' (their witnesses), and both readings are stable.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת רב ושמואל בגרסת 'אידיהן' או 'עידיהן', וקובע ששתי הגרסאות אינן משובשות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports each reading with a biblical verse: 'eideihen' from 'כי קרוב יום אידם' (their calamity) and 'eideihen' from 'יתנו עדיהם ויצדקו' (their witnesses).
sub.desc: מביא ראיה לגרסת 'אידיהן' מפסוק 'כי קרוב יום אידם', ולגרסת 'עידיהן' מפסוק 'יתנו עדיהם ויצדקו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why each authority did not adopt the alternative reading.
sub.desc: מסביר את טעם כל גרסה: גרסת 'אידיהן' מעדיפה את השבר עצמו, וגרסת 'עידיהן' מעדיפה את העדות שגורמת לשבר.

sub.desc_en: The advocate of 'eideihen' answers that the concept of 'calamity' (תברא) is more direct and preferable.
sub.desc: מסביר את טעם כל גרסה: גרסת 'אידיהן' מעדיפה את השבר עצמו, וגרסת 'עידיהן' מעדיפה את העדות שגורמת לשבר.

sub.desc_en: The advocate of 'eideihen' answers that what causes their calamity is the testimony they gave against themselves, so 'testimony' is the more fundamental concept.
sub.desc: מסביר את טעם כל גרסה: גרסת 'אידיהן' מעדיפה את השבר עצמו, וגרסת 'עידיהן' מעדיפה את העדות שגורמת לשבר.

items.text: Refutation and alternative proof for 'eideihen'
items.text_en: Refutation and alternative proof for 'eideihen'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the proof from 'yitnu eideihem veyitzdaku', noting that the verse refers to Israel, not the nations. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that Israel's mitzvot testify for them in the World to Come. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua then provides an alternative proof for 'eideihen' from the verse 'yotzrei fesel kulam tohu vachamudeihem bal yo'ilu ve'eideihem hema'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'יִתְּנוּ עֵדֵיהֶם וְיִצְדָּקוּ' (let them bring their witnesses and be justified) is written about Israel, not the nations, undermining the proof for the reading 'עֵידֵיהֶן' (their witnesses).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that the verse indeed refers to Israel: the mitzvot (commandments) that Israel performs in this world come and testify for them in the World to Come, while the nations hear and admit the truth.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's alternative proof
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's alternative proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua provides an alternative proof for the reading 'עֵידֵיהֶן' (their witnesses) from the verse 'יֹצְרֵי פֶסֶל כֻּלָּם תֹּהוּ וַחֲמוּדֵיהֶם בַּל יוֹעִילוּ וְעֵדֵיהֶם הֵמָּה' (the makers of idols are all vanity, and their cherished objects are worthless, and their witnesses are they themselves).

items.text: מדרש על עתיד אומות העולם
items.text_en: Aggadic narrative: the nations' judgment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa (or Rabbi Simlai) teaches that in the future, God will bring a Torah scroll and invite those who engaged with it to receive their reward. The nations will gather in confusion, but God will tell them to enter one by one.
items.desc: רבי חנינא בר פפא (או רבי שמלאי) דורש שלעתיד לבוא הקב"ה מביא ספר תורה ואומר למי שעסק בה יבוא ויטול שכרו. אומות העולם מתקבצים בערבוביה, והקב"ה אומר להם להיכנס כל אומה ואומה בפני עצמה.

sub.text: רבי חנינא בר פפא (או רבי שמלאי)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa (or Rabbi Simlai)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa (or Rabbi Simlai) teaches that in the future, God will bring a Torah scroll and invite those who engaged with it to receive their reward.
sub.desc: רבי חנינא בר פפא (או רבי שמלאי) דורש שלעתיד לבוא הקב"ה מביא ספר תורה ואומר למי שעסק בה יבוא ויטול שכרו.

sub.desc_en: The nations gather in confusion, and God tells them to enter one by one.
sub.desc: אומות העולם מתקבצים בערבוביה, והקב"ה אומר להם להיכנס כל אומה ואומה בפני עצמה.

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: איסוף האומות לדין
items.text_en: Introduction: The gathering of nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the nations are gathered before God, and the term 'le'umim' refers to kingdoms. God ensures they do not mix so they can hear His words.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את הפסוק 'ויאספו לאמים' ומפרשת ש'לאום' הוא מלכות, ושואלת מדוע הקב"ה מפריד ביניהן – כדי שלא יתערבבו וישמעו את דבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the gathering of nations, interpreting 'le'umim' as kingdoms, and explains that God prevents their mixing so they can hear His words.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בפסוק ומפרשת ש'לאום' הוא מלכות, ושואלת מדוע הקב"ה מפריד בין האומות.

items.text: מלכות רומי נכנסת ראשונה לדין
items.text_en: Rome enters first due to its importance
items.desc_en: The kingdom of Rome enters first because it is the most important, as derived from a verse. Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Chisda provide support for this principle.
items.desc: מלכות רומי נכנסת ראשונה משום חשיבותה, כפי שנלמד מפסוקים ומדברי רבי יוחנן ורב חסדא. מוסבר שהחשוב נכנס ראשון לדין.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the kingdom of Rome enters first for judgment because it is the most important.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שמלכות רומי נכנסת ראשונה לדין.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proves Rome's importance from the verse describing a beast that devours and tramples the whole earth.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שמלכות רומי נכנסת ראשונה לדין.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the beast as wicked Rome, whose coinage spread throughout the world.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שמלכות רומי נכנסת ראשונה לדין.

sub.desc_en: The gemara invokes Rav Chisda's principle that the more important party enters judgment first, citing a verse about the king entering before the nation.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מניין שהחשוב נכנס ראשון לדין.

sub.desc_en: The gemara offers two reasons for the king entering first: either it is improper for the king to wait outside, or to prevent the intensification of divine anger.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מניין שהחשוב נכנס ראשון לדין.

items.text: טענת רומי ודחייתה
items.text_en: Rome's claim and God's rejection
items.desc_en: Rome claims they built markets, bathhouses, and amassed wealth for Israel's sake. God rebukes them, saying these were for their own benefit, and challenges them to produce the Torah.
items.desc: רומי טוענת שתיקנה שווקים ומרחצאות והרביתה כסף וזהב למען ישראל. הקב"ה דוחה את טענותיה ואומר שהכל נעשה לצורכה, ושואל אם יש בה מגיד תורה. רומי יוצאת בפחי נפש.

sub.desc_en: God asks Rome what they occupied themselves with.
sub.desc: הקב"ה שואל את מלכות רומי במה עסקו.

sub.desc_en: Rome claims they built markets, bathhouses, and amassed wealth for Israel's sake so that Israel could engage in Torah study.
sub.desc: הקב"ה שואל את מלכות רומי במה עסקו.

sub.desc_en: God rebukes Rome, saying all their works were for their own benefit — markets for prostitution, bathhouses for self-indulgence, and the silver and gold are His.
sub.desc: הקב"ה דוחה את טענת רומי ואומר שהכל נעשה לצורכה.

sub.desc_en: God challenges Rome to produce the Torah, and they depart in shame.
sub.desc: הקב"ה שואל אם יש ברומי מגיד תורה, והם יוצאים בפחי נפש.

items.text: מלכות פרס נכנסת לדין
items.text_en: Persia enters and its claim is rejected
items.desc_en: Persia enters after Rome, described as a bear. They claim to have built bridges, conquered cities, and waged wars for Israel. God rejects their claim, saying these were for their own purposes, and they leave disappointed.
items.desc: מלכות פרס נכנסת אחרי רומי, וטוענת שגשרה גשרים, כבשה כרכים וערכה מלחמות למען ישראל. הקב"ה דוחה את טענותיה באותו אופן, ופרס יוצאת בפחי נפש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that after Rome leaves, the kingdom of Persia enters, identified as the bear-like beast, and Rav Yosef describes their gluttonous and restless nature.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתארת את כניסת מלכות פרס לדין לאחר רומי, ומסבירה את חשיבותה באמצעות דברי רב יוסף.

sub.desc_en: God asks Persia what they occupied themselves with, and they claim to have built bridges, conquered cities, and waged wars for Israel's sake.
sub.desc: הקב"ה שואל את מלכות פרס במה עסקו, והם משיבים שבנו גשרים, כבשו כרכים וערכו מלחמות למען ישראל.

sub.desc_en: God rejects their claim, stating their bridges were for tolls, cities for garrisons, and wars were His own, and they leave disappointed.
sub.desc: הקב"ה דוחה את טענות פרס, ומראה שמעשיהם היו למען עצמם, ולכן הם יוצאים בפחי נפש.

items.text: שאלות על כניסת האומות לדין
items.text_en: Why other nations enter despite seeing failure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Persia and other nations enter after seeing Rome's failure. They reason that they built the Temple or did not subjugate Israel, but ultimately they are not important enough to enter earlier.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע פרס נכנסה לדין לאחר שראתה שרומי לא הועילה, ומדוע שאר האומות נכנסות. התשובה: פרס חשבה שבנתה את בית המקדש, ושאר האומות סברו שלא שעבודו בישראל כמו הראשונים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Persia enters judgment after seeing Rome's failure.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע מלכות פרס נכנסה לדין לאחר שראתה שרומי לא הועילה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that each nation enters thinking it has a merit the previous one lacked.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע מלכות פרס נכנסה לדין לאחר שראתה שרומי לא הועילה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why later nations enter after seeing the failure of all previous ones.
The Gemara explains that later nations claim they did not subjugate Israel.
The Gemara asks why some nations are considered important and enter first while others are not.
The Gemara answers that important nations are those whose kingdoms endure until the Messiah comes.

items.text: טענת האומות: לא קיבלו את התורה
items.text_en: Nations challenge Israel's acceptance of Torah
items.desc_en: The nations argue that they were never offered the Torah, but Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God offered it to all nations and only Israel accepted. They then claim they would have kept it, but God notes they did not keep the seven Noahide laws.
items.desc: האומות טוענות שלא קיבלו את התורה, אך הגמרא מביאה מדברי רבי יוחנן שהקב"ה הציע את התורה לכל האומות והן לא קיבלוה. האומות מתקנות טענתן: קיבלו אך לא קיימו, ושואלות מדוע לא נכפה עליהן הר כגיגית כמו על ישראל.

sub.desc_en: The nations ask God whether they were ever offered the Torah and then rejected it, citing verses that God appeared at Seir and Paran.
sub.desc: האומות טוענות שלא קיבלו את התורה מעולם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God offered the Torah to every nation and language, and only Israel accepted it.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר שהקב"ה הציע את התורה לכל אומה ולשון, והן לא קיבלוה.

sub.desc_en: The nations shift their argument, claiming they would have kept the Torah if they had accepted it, and complain that God coerced Israel with a mountain held over them like a tub.
sub.desc: האומות משנות את טענתן: קיבלו את התורה אך לא קיימוה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Chama cites the verse 'they stood at the foot of the mountain' to prove that God held the mountain over Israel like a tub, threatening burial if they refused the Torah.
sub.desc: רב דימי בר חמא מביא ראיה שכפה הר כגיגית על ישראל.

items.text: דחיית טענת האומות: קיום שבע מצוות בני נח
items.text_en: God's response and the nations' failure
items.desc_en: God asks the nations where they kept the seven commandments they accepted. Rav Yosef explains they did not keep them, so God permitted them. The Gemara questions if this rewards sinners, and Mar brei d'Ravina begins to answer.
items.desc: הקב"ה משיב שהאומות לא קיימו את שבע מצוות בני נח שקיבלו, כפי שנלמד מדברי רב יוסף. הגמרא מקשה שאם התיר להן, נמצא חוטא נשכר, ומביאה את דברי מר בריה דרבינא.

sub.desc_en: God asks the nations where they fulfilled the seven Noahide commandments they accepted.
sub.desc: הקב"ה דורש מהאומות להציג את קיום שבע מצוות בני נח שקיבלו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a verse to prove the nations did not keep the seven commandments, so God permitted them.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מביא ראיה מהפסוק שהאומות לא קיימו את שבע מצוות בני נח, ולכן הקב"ה התירן להן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if God permitted the nations for not keeping the commandments, then a sinner would be rewarded.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מביא ראיה מהפסוק שהאומות לא קיימו את שבע מצוות בני נח, ולכן הקב"ה התירן להן.

sub.desc_en: Mar brei d'Ravina begins to answer the objection.
sub.desc: מר בריה דרבינא מתחיל לתרץ את הקושיה.

items.text: Reward for non-Jews who observe Torah
items.text_en: Reward for non-Jews who observe Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that non-Jews who observe Torah do receive reward, but not as much as those commanded, citing Rabbi Chanina that one commanded and does is greater than one not commanded and does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that non-Jews who observe the Torah receive no reward.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir proves from the verse 'אשר יעשה אתם האדם' that a non-Jew who studies Torah is like a High Priest.
The Gemara resolves that non-Jews do receive reward, but not as much as one commanded; rather like one not commanded.
Rabbi Chanina supports this with the principle that one commanded and does is greater than one not commanded and does.

items.text: The nations' claim and God's response
items.text_en: The nations' claim and God's response
items.desc_en: The nations argue before God that Israel did not keep the Torah. God says He testifies for them, but the nations object that a father cannot testify for his son. God then offers heaven and earth as witnesses, but the nations counter that heaven and earth are biased due to the condition set at creation.

sub.desc_en: The nations argue before God that Israel, who accepted the Torah, did not actually fulfill it.
God responds that He Himself testifies that Israel fulfilled the entire Torah.
The nations object that a father cannot testify for his son, citing the verse 'בני בכורי ישראל' (My firstborn son Israel).
God offers heaven and earth as witnesses that Israel fulfilled the Torah.
The nations counter that heaven and earth are biased witnesses, citing the verse that God conditioned creation on Israel's acceptance of the Torah, as taught by Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

items.text: Witnesses from history
items.text_en: Witnesses from history
items.desc_en: God proposes that historical figures testify for Israel: Nimrod for Abraham, Laban for Jacob, Potiphar's wife for Joseph, Nebuchadnezzar for Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, Darius for Daniel, and Job's friends for all Israel, citing the verse 'Let them bring their witnesses and be justified.'

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah introduces a verse about heaven and earth fearing and being silent, explaining that initially they feared (that Israel would not accept the Torah) and ultimately were silent (when Israel accepted it).
God proposes that historical figures testify for Israel: Nimrod for Abraham, Laban for Jacob, and Potiphar's wife for Joseph.

God continues proposing witnesses: Nebuchadnezzar for Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, Darius for Daniel, and Job's friends for all Israel, citing the verse 'Let them bring their witnesses and be justified.'

items.text: The test with sukkah
items.text_en: The test with sukkah
items.desc_en: The nations ask to start anew, but God rebukes them, saying one who did not prepare on Shabbat eve cannot eat on Shabbat. Nevertheless, He offers them the 'easy mitzvah' of sukkah. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that mitzvot are for today, not for reward, and explains that God does not act with unfairness, and sukkah is called easy because it costs nothing.

sub.desc_en: The nations ask God to give them the Torah anew so they can observe it.
God rebukes the nations, comparing their request to one who did not prepare on Shabbat eve and cannot eat on Shabbat.
God offers the nations the 'easy mitzvah' of sukkah (סוכה) as a test.
The Gemara objects, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that mitzvot are for today, not for reward, implying God's offer is inconsistent.
The Gemara resolves that God does not act with unfairness (טרוניא), and sukkah is called 'easy' because it involves no financial loss (חסרון כיס).

items.text: The nations fail the test
items.text_en: The nations fail the test
items.desc_en: Each nation builds a sukkah on their roof, but God intensifies the sun in the summer solstice, causing them to kick their sukkah and leave, fulfilling the verse 'Let us break their bonds.' The Gemara questions how God can do this if He does not act with unfairness, and answers that Israel also sometimes suffers from the heat.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes how each nation builds a sukkah on their roof, but God intensifies the sun at the summer solstice, causing them to kick their sukkah and leave, citing the verse 'Let us break their bonds.'
The Gemara questions how God can intensify the sun if He does not act with unfairness (טרוניא) toward His creatures.
The Gemara answers that this is not unfair because Israel also sometimes suffers from the heat at that time.

items.text: Gemara's question on the nations' suffering
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the nations' suffering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the nations would be exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah due to suffering, yet still be punished for not observing it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the nations, who are exempt from sukkah due to suffering, should still be punished for not observing it.

items.text: God's laughter and Rabbi Yitzchak's limitation
items.text_en: God's laughter and Rabbi Yitzchak's limitation
items.desc_en: God laughs at the nations, but Rabbi Yitzchak says this laughter only occurs on that specific day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that God immediately sits and laughs at the nations, citing the verse 'He who sits in heaven laughs.'
Rabbi Yitzchak limits God's laughter to that specific day only.

items.text: Alternative version: Rabbi Yossi on future converts
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbi Yossi on future converts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi says the nations will convert in the future, but the Gemara objects that converts are not accepted in the messianic era. The converts are described as wearing mitzvot, but when war comes, they abandon them, leading to God's laughter.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement, now applied to a baraita about Rabbi Yossi.
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Yossi states that in the future the nations will convert.
Objects that converts are not accepted in the messianic era, citing a baraita that no converts were accepted in the days of David and Solomon.
Answers that these are not genuine converts but 'dragged converts' who superficially adopt mitzvot like תפילין (phylacteries), ציצית (fringes), and מזוזה (mezuzah).
Describes how the converts abandon their mitzvot when war comes, leading God to laugh, and Rabbi Yitzchak limits this laughter to that day alone.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's description of God's daily schedule
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's description of God's daily schedule
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda describes the twelve hours of the day: God studies Torah, judges the world, sustains it, and plays with the Leviathan. Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that God plays with His creations, not at them, and only on that day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier statement that God only laughs on one day, citing Rav Yehuda's description of God's daily schedule which includes playing with the Leviathan in the fourth quarter.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that God plays with His creations (the Leviathan), not at them, and this playfulness occurs only on that specific day.

items.text: No laughter after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: No laughter after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rav Acha tells Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak that since the Temple's destruction, there is no laughter for God. The Gemara attempts to prove this from verses but concludes that only forgetfulness is absent, not laughter.

sub.text: Rav Acha to Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Acha to Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha states that since the Temple's destruction, there is no laughter for God.
The Gemara asks: from where do we know that there is no laughter?
The Gemara suggests proving it from the verse calling for weeping, but rejects it as possibly only for that day.
The Gemara suggests proving it from the verse about not forgetting Jerusalem, but rejects it as only proving no forgetfulness, not no laughter.
The Gemara concludes with the verse 'I have been silent from of old, I will be silent, I will restrain myself' as proof that God no longer laughs.

items.text: God's activities in the fourth quarter and at night
items.text_en: God's activities in the fourth quarter and at night
items.desc_en: In the fourth quarter, God teaches Torah to children. Originally, Metatron taught them. At night, God either does similar activities, rides a cherub through worlds, or listens to the song of the Chayot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what God does during the fourth quarter of the day.
The Gemara answers that God sits and teaches Torah to young children, citing a verse about teaching those weaned from milk.
The Gemara asks who originally taught the children before God took over.
The Gemara offers two alternatives: either Metatron taught them, or God always did both.
The Gemara asks what God does at night.
The Gemara offers three alternatives: God does similar activities as by day, rides a cherub through eighteen thousand worlds, or listens to the song of the Chayot.

items.text: Reward for Torah study at night
items.text_en: Reward for Torah study at night
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi says one who abandons Torah for idle talk is fed coals. Resh Lakish says one who studies Torah at night has a thread of kindness drawn over him by day, with an alternative version referring to the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi states that one who abandons Torah study for idle conversation is fed coals of broom, citing a verse.
Resh Lakish says that one who studies Torah at night has a thread of kindness drawn over him by day, explaining the verse.
An alternative version attributes to Resh Lakish that one who studies Torah in this world, which is like night, has a thread of kindness drawn over him in the World to Come, which is like day.

items.text: Analogy of humans to fish and the fate of the wicked
items.text_en: Analogy of humans to fish and the fate of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says humans are compared to fish: when they leave Torah and mitzvot, they die. The Gemara explains this refers to this world (cold and heat) or the World to Come (the sun's heat for punishment or healing).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel introduces the analogy of humans to fish: just as fish die when they leave water, so humans die when they abandon Torah and mitzvot.
The Gemara offers one interpretation: the analogy refers to this world, where cold and heat (צִנִּים פַּחִים) are the only things not in Heaven's hands, per Rabbi Chanina.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: the analogy refers to the World to Come, where the sun's heat punishes the wicked and heals the righteous, per Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

items.text: The dual effect of the future day on wicked and righteous
items.text_en: The dual effect of the future day on wicked and righteous
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the future day described in Malachi will destroy the wicked entirely (root and branch) but heal and delight the righteous, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse about the future day that burns the wicked like stubble, destroying both root and branch, and interprets that the wicked have no root in this world and no branch in the world to come.

The Gemara adds that the righteous are healed and delighted by that day, citing the verse about the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings and the righteous leaping like calves from the stall.

items.text: The necessity of governmental authority
items.text_en: The necessity of governmental authority
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares humans to fish, where the larger swallows the smaller, and notes that without fear of government, people would devour each other. It cites Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim's teaching to pray for the government's peace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara compares humans to fish, where the larger swallows the smaller, and states that without fear of government, people would devour each other.
Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim teaches to pray for the peace of the government, for without its fear, people would swallow each other alive.

items.text: Resolving contradictions in verses about God's power and anger
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions in verses about God's power and anger
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa resolves a contradiction between verses describing God's power as limited and great, attributing the former to judgment and the latter to war. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina resolves a contradiction about God's anger, applying one verse to Israel and the other to the nations. Rav Chinana bar Pappa further explains that 'I have no wrath' means God has already sworn not to destroy Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa raises a contradiction between verses that describe God's power as limited and as great.
Rav Chinana bar Pappa resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to the time of judgment, the other to the time of war.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's contradiction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's contradiction
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina raises a contradiction between verses that say God has no wrath and that He is vengeful and wrathful.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's resolution
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina resolves: one verse applies to Israel, the other to the nations of the world.
Rav Chinana bar Pappa explains that 'I have no wrath' means God has already sworn not to destroy Israel, and the other phrase refers to His regret over not having sworn earlier.

items.text: God's search for merit among the nations
items.text_en: God's search for merit among the nations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri explains that when God seeks to destroy the nations, He examines their merit; if they have any, He redeems them, otherwise He destroys them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri explains the verse 'And it shall come to pass on that day that I will seek to destroy all the nations' — God seeks their merit; if they have merit He redeems them, otherwise He destroys them.

items.text: God's lenient judgment of Israel and their ingratitude
items.text_en: God's lenient judgment of Israel and their ingratitude
items.desc_en: Rava explains that God judges Israel differently from the nations, exacting a small penalty like a chicken's peck. Rabbi Abba and Rav Papi in Rava's name add that God redeems Israel with worldly wealth and disciplines them with minor sufferings to strengthen them for the World to Come, but Israel responds with falsehood and evil.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that God judges Israel leniently, exacting only a minor penalty like a chicken's peck, unlike the harsh judgment of the nations.
The gemara offers an alternative interpretation: even a small mitzvah (מצוה) like a chicken's peck is counted by God toward a great account, and through their prayer (שוע) He saves them.
Rabbi Abba adds that God redeems Israel with their worldly wealth so they may merit the World to Come, but Israel responds with falsehood.
Rav Papi in Rava's name states that God disciplines Israel with minor sufferings in this world to strengthen them for the World to Come, but Israel repays with evil.

items.text: The story of Rav Safra, the minim, and Rabbi Avahu
items.text_en: The story of Rav Safra, the minim, and Rabbi Avahu
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu praised Rav Safra to the minim, who then questioned him about a verse implying that God punishes those He loves. Rav Safra was silent, and the minim tormented him. Rabbi Avahu intervened, explaining that Rav Safra was expert in tannaitic matters, not biblical interpretation. He then gave a parable: a creditor collects from a friend little by little, but from an enemy all at once.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that Rabbi Avahu praised Rav Safra to the minim, leading them to exempt him from tax for thirteen years.
The minim confront Rav Safra with a verse (Amos 3:2) implying that God punishes those He loves, and ask rhetorically whether a creditor who loves his debtor would demand payment.
Rav Safra remains silent, and the minim torment him by wrapping a scarf around his neck.
Rabbi Avahu arrives, asks why they are tormenting Rav Safra, and explains that his praise was limited to tannaitic expertise, not biblical interpretation.
The minim ask Rabbi Avahu why he himself knows the answer, and he responds that he and his colleagues study diligently, whereas Rav Safra does not.
Rabbi Avahu answers the minim's original question with a parable: a creditor collects from a friend little by little, but from an enemy all at once, explaining why God punishes Israel gradually.

items.text: The distinction between complete and incomplete righteous
items.text_en: The distinction between complete and incomplete righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana explains Abraham's plea that God not kill the righteous with the wicked. The Gemara questions this from a verse that mentions cutting off both righteous and wicked, and resolves that it refers to an incomplete righteous person. Even a complete righteous person can be punished if they failed to protest wrongdoing, as derived from the verse 'from My sanctuary begin'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana introduces Abraham's plea to God not to kill the righteous with the wicked, citing the verse from Genesis.
The Gemara objects that a verse says God will cut off both righteous and wicked, contradicting Abraham's plea.
The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to an incomplete righteous person, not a complete one.
The Gemara questions whether a complete righteous person is never punished, citing the verse 'from My sanctuary begin'.
Rav Yosef teaches that the verse should be read as 'from My sanctified ones', referring to those who fulfilled the entire Torah.
The Gemara resolves that even a complete righteous person who failed to protest wrongdoing is treated like an incomplete righteous person and punished.

items.text: The duration of God's daily anger
items.text_en: The duration of God's daily anger
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves a contradiction between verses about God's anger, applying one to an individual and the other to the community. The Sages then teach that God's anger lasts only a moment, a precise fraction of an hour, which only Balaam could discern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a contradiction between two verses about God's anger and resolves it by applying one to an individual and the other to the community.
The Sages teach in a baraita that God's anger lasts only a moment, a precise fraction of an hour, which only Balaam could discern.

items.text: Balaam's ignorance of his donkey's knowledge
items.text_en: Balaam's ignorance of his donkey's knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Balaam could know God's mind if he didn't even understand his donkey. It recounts a story where Balaam's donkey rebukes him for riding her and hints at inappropriate behavior.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Balaam could know God's mind if he did not even understand his donkey.
The Gemara recounts a story where Balaam's donkey rebukes him for riding her and hints at inappropriate behavior, showing Balaam's ignorance.

items.text: Balaam's true knowledge: timing God's anger
items.text_en: Balaam's true knowledge: timing God's anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Balaam knew the exact moment of God's anger, which is brief. Rabbi Elazar says God told Israel that He refrained from anger during Balaam's time, as Balaam himself noted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Balaam's true knowledge was knowing the exact moment of God's anger.
Rabbi Elazar explains that God refrained from anger during Balaam's time, as Balaam himself noted.

items.text: Duration and timing of God's wrath
items.text_en: Duration and timing of God's wrath
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how long God's anger lasts (a moment) and when it occurs (the first three hours of the day, when a rooster's comb turns white). Abaye describes the sign of that hour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how long God's wrath lasts and answers that it is a moment, citing Amemar or Ravina's definition.
The Gemara provides two scriptural proofs that God's anger lasts only a moment, from Psalms and Isaiah.
The Gemara asks when God becomes angry, and Abaye answers that it is during the first three hours of the day, when a rooster's comb turns white without red streaks.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's attempt to curse a heretic
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's attempt to curse a heretic
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tried to curse a heretic at the moment of God's anger but fell asleep, learning that it is not proper to do so, as God's mercy extends to all.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was troubled by a heretic and planned to curse him at the moment of God's anger, placing a rooster between his legs to watch for the sign.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi fell asleep at the critical moment and concluded from the verses that it is not proper to curse, as God's mercy extends to all creatures.

items.text: Prayer at the time of divine anger
items.text_en: Prayer at the time of divine anger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says God is angry when kings bow to the sun. Rav Yosef rules that one should not pray the Musaf prayer alone on Rosh Hashanah during the first three hours, but communal prayer is fine due to merit.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: A Tanna states in the name of Rabbi Meir that God becomes angry at the moment when kings bow to the sun.
Rav Yosef rules that one should not pray the Musaf prayer alone on Rosh Hashanah during the first three hours, lest the court examine his deeds and reject him.
The Gemara objects that if the concern applies to an individual, it should also apply to the community, and answers that the community's merit is greater.
The Gemara objects that if so, the individual's morning prayer should also be prohibited, and answers that since the community is praying, the individual is not rejected.

items.text: Reconciling God's anger with His study of Torah
items.text_en: Reconciling God's anger with His study of Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: God studies Torah (truth) in the first three hours, yet also judges. It resolves that Torah is truth and God acts beyond the letter of the law in judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if God studies Torah (truth) in the first three hours, how can He also judge at that time? It proposes to reverse the earlier statement.
The Gemara resolves: Torah is truth, so God judges strictly; but in judgment He acts לפנים משורת הדין (beyond the letter of the law), reconciling the two activities.

items.text: Mitzvot as witnesses and the sin of the Golden Calf
items.text_en: Mitzvot as witnesses and the sin of the Golden Calf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that mitzvot done in this world testify for Israel in the next, and that the sin of the Golden Calf was allowed to provide an opening for repentance, as Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse 'אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם' to mean that the mitzvot are to be done today, not tomorrow, and their reward is not taken today.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that all mitzvot Israel performs in this world come and testify for them in the World to Come, citing the verse 'יִתְּנוּ עֵדֵיהֶם וְיִצְדָּקוּ'.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that the mitzvot also strike the nations of the world in the face in the World to Come, based on the verse 'לְעֵינֵי הָעַמִּים'.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that Israel sinned with the Golden Calf only to provide an opening for penitents, citing the verse 'מִי יִתֵּן וְהָיָה לְבָבָם זֶה'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that neither David nor Israel were inherently suited for their sins, but they sinned to provide a model for repentance.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why mention both individual and communal sin?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why mention both individual and communal sin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse needed to mention both an individual sinner and a communal sinner, as each case alone might have been insufficient to teach the other. The individual's sin is less public, while the community's prayer is more powerful.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse teaches about repentance for both an individual sinner and a communal sinner, directing each to a corresponding example.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: the individual's sin is less public, while the community's prayer is more powerful, so each alone might have been insufficient to teach the other.

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Elazar on repentance and sin
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Elazar on repentance and sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that David established the 'yoke of repentance.' He further teaches that a mitzvah precedes a person to the World to Come, while a sin leads him to judgment. Rabbi Elazar adds that sin clings to a person like a dog, both in this world and the next.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that David established the yoke of repentance.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani further teaches that a mitzvah precedes a person to the World to Come, while a sin leads him to judgment, citing verses.
Rabbi Elazar adds that a sin clings to a person like a dog, both in this world and the next, citing the story of Joseph.

items.text: Resh Lakish: Gratitude to the ancestors for sinning
items.text_en: Resh Lakish: Gratitude to the ancestors for sinning
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says we should thank our ancestors for sinning, because had they not sinned, we would not have been born. He cites the verse 'I said you are gods' to show that their sin led to mortality and thus to future generations.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that we should be grateful to our ancestors for sinning with the Golden Calf, because had they not sinned we would not have been born, citing the verse that they would have been like gods but were reduced to mortality.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Would there be no birth without sin?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Would there be no birth without sin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the ancestors had not sinned, would they not have procreated? It cites verses commanding procreation and marital intimacy. It resolves that the command was for the generation at Sinai, but the promise of eternal life was conditional. Rabbi Yosei adds that the son of David will not come until all souls in the 'body' are exhausted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the ancestors would not have procreated had they not sinned, citing verses commanding procreation and marital intimacy.
The Gemara raises another objection from a verse promising goodness to children, and answers that it refers to those standing at Sinai.
The Gemara objects with Reish Lakish's statement that God showed Adam all future generations, implying procreation was always intended.
Rabbi Yosei adds that the Messiah will not come until all souls in the body are exhausted, supporting the necessity of future generations.

items.text: Refined statement: 'As if we did not come to the world'
items.text_en: Refined statement: 'As if we did not come to the world'
items.desc_en: The Gemara rephrases Resh Lakish's statement: not that we would not have come, but as if we had not come. It then questions whether the Torah's laws of levirate marriage and inheritance imply mortality, and answers that they were conditional, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that creation was conditional on Israel accepting the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines Reish Lakish's statement: not that we would not have come into the world, but that we would be as if we had not come.
The Gemara questions whether the refined statement implies that without sin they would not have died, citing the Torah's laws of levirate marriage and inheritance that presuppose death.
The Gemara answers that those passages were written conditionally.
The Gemara objects: Are verses written conditionally?
The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that creation itself was conditional on Israel accepting the Torah.

items.text: Debate: Did Israel accept the Torah to abolish the Angel of Death?
items.text_en: Debate: Did Israel accept the Torah to abolish the Angel of Death?
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that it is impossible to abolish the Angel of Death because the decree was already made. Another baraita states that Israel accepted the Torah so that no nation would rule over them. Rabbi Yosei says they accepted it so that the Angel of Death would not rule over them. The Gemara reconciles the verses: 'death' in the verse refers to poverty, blindness, leprosy, or childlessness, as these are considered like death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that it is impossible to abolish the Angel of Death because the decree was already made.
The Tanna Kamma explains that Israel accepted the Torah only so that no nation or tongue would rule over them.
Rabbi Yosei states that Israel accepted the Torah so that the Angel of Death would not rule over them, citing the verse 'I said: You are godlike beings'.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yosei: the verse 'that it might be good for them' implies there is still death.
Rabbi Yosei answers that since there is no death, there is no greater good than this.
The Gemara asks the Tanna Kamma: what does 'death' in the verse mean?
The Gemara answers that 'death' refers to poverty, as the Master said four are considered as dead: a pauper, a blind person, a leper, and one who has no children.

sub.text: Gemara's support for poverty as death
sub.text_en: Gemara's support for poverty as death
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports that a pauper is considered dead by citing the verse 'for all the men are dead' referring to Dathan and Abiram who became impoverished.
The Gemara supports that a blind person, a leper, and one without children are considered dead, each with a verse.

items.text: The word 'if' as a language of supplication and Moses' rebuke
items.text_en: The word 'if' as a language of supplication and Moses' rebuke
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that 'if' in the Torah is a language of supplication, not condition, citing verses. Moses rebukes Israel as 'ingrates, children of ingrates' for not responding to God's wish with 'You give it.' The text breaks off mid-verse.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that the word 'if' in the Torah is a language of supplication, not condition, and support this with verses from Psalms and Isaiah.
The Tannaim cite Moses' rebuke to Israel as 'ingrates, children of ingrates' for not responding to God's wish with 'You give it.'
The Gemara begins to support the charge of ingratitude by citing a verse about Israel's complaint against the manna, but the text breaks off.

items.text: Rebuke delayed forty years
items.text_en: Rebuke delayed forty years
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even Moses did not rebuke Israel until after forty years in the desert, as derived from verses. Rabba deduces that a person does not fully grasp their teacher's intent until forty years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept of ingratitude (כְּפוּיֵי טוֹבָה) by citing Adam's blame of Eve.
The Gemara deduces that even Moses did not rebuke Israel until after forty years in the desert, as derived from the verses about the manna and the giving of the heart.
Rabba concludes from this that a person does not fully grasp their teacher's intent until forty years.

items.text: Praise for Israel engaged in Torah and charity
items.text_en: Praise for Israel engaged in Torah and charity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah interprets a verse to praise Israel when they engage in Torah and charity, as their evil inclination is under their control. The school of Elijah adds that one should submit to Torah like an ox to the yoke and a donkey to its burden.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Bena'ah interpreting the verse 'אשריכם זורעי על כל מים' to praise Israel when they engage in Torah and charity, as their evil inclination is under their control.
The school of Elijah adds that one should submit to Torah like an ox to the yoke and a donkey to its burden.

items.text: Question on the three-day prohibition
items.text_en: Question on the three-day prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that business with idolaters is forbidden for three days before their festival, asking if such a long period is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that business with idolaters is forbidden for three days before their festival, asking if such a long period is necessary.

items.text: Mishnah on four times for informing about animal sale
items.text_en: Mishnah on four times for informing about animal sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that on four specific occasions a seller must inform the buyer if he sold the mother or daughter for slaughter, implying that one day suffices for informing about meat consumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing four times a year when a seller must inform the buyer if he sold the mother or daughter for slaughter, including Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's addition of Yom Kippur eve in the Galilee.

items.text: Distinction between consumption and sacrifice
items.text_en: Distinction between consumption and sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that for consumption one day suffices, but for sacrifice three days are needed. It then questions whether three days are enough for sacrifice, citing a Mishnah that one asks about Passover laws thirty days prior. The Gemara resolves that for Jews, who have disqualifying blemishes even in the eye, thirty days are needed; for Noahides, who only have missing limbs, three days suffice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the Mishnah's one-day requirement for consumption and the three-day requirement for sacrifice.
The Gemara objects that three days seems insufficient for sacrifice, citing a Mishnah that one asks about Passover laws thirty days prior, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel saying two weeks.
The Gemara resolves that for Jews, who have disqualifying blemishes even in the eye, thirty days are needed; for Noahides, who only have missing limbs, three days suffice.

items.text: Source for prohibition of missing limb for Noahides
items.text_en: Source for prohibition of missing limb for Noahides
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from a verse that a missing limb is forbidden for Noahides. The Gemara questions whether the verse is needed for this, suggesting it might exclude a tereifah, but concludes that tereifah is derived from another verse, and this verse indeed teaches about missing limbs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'וּמִכׇּל הָחַי' that a missing limb (מחוסר אבר) is forbidden for Noahides, as the Torah requires bringing an animal whose limbs' heads are alive.
The Gemara objects that this verse is needed to exclude a טריפה (animal with a fatal condition) from being offered, not to teach about missing limbs.

The Gemara answers that the exclusion of a טריפה is derived from the phrase 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע' (to keep seed alive), since a טריפה does not give birth, so this verse remains available to teach about missing limbs.

items.text: Defense of the derivation from 'itach' for treifah animals
items.text_en: Defense of the derivation from 'itach' for treifah animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara defends the view that a treifah cannot give birth, using the verse 'itach' to require animals similar to Noah. It rejects the possibility that Noah himself was a treifah, citing 'tamim' and 'tzaddik', and explains that 'lehachyot zera' excludes the old and sterile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that a treifah can give birth, what can be said to defend the derivation from 'itach'?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'itach' requires animals similar to Noah, i.e., whole and capable of reproduction.
The Gemara objects: perhaps Noah himself was a treifah, but the verse 'tamim' is written about him.
The Gemara rejects the objection: perhaps 'tamim' refers to his ways, but 'tzaddik' is also written about him, implying physical wholeness.
The Gemara objects further: perhaps both terms refer to moral qualities, not physical wholeness, but then God would not command Noah to bring only treifot like himself.
The Gemara resolves: now that the derivation from 'itach' is established, the verse 'lehachyot zera' excludes the old and sterile, teaching that only animals capable of reproduction were taken.

items.text: The inquiry: Are the festival days included in the three-day prohibition?
items.text_en: The inquiry: Are the festival days included in the three-day prohibition?
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether the three days of prohibition before a festival include the festival days themselves or exclude them.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an inquiry: does the phrase 'three days' in the Mishnah include the festival days themselves or exclude them?

items.text: First attempted proof from Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.text_en: First attempted proof from Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that the festival days are not included, because Rabbi Yishmael counts three before and three after, which would be redundant if the festival days themselves were counted. The Gemara deflects by suggesting the tanna simply mirrored the phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that the festival days are not included (הן בלא אידיהן) by citing Rabbi Yishmael's statement that three days before and three days after are forbidden, arguing that if the festival days themselves were counted, Rabbi Yishmael would have counted them redundantly.
The Gemara deflects the proof by suggesting that the tanna simply mirrored the phrasing 'three before' with 'three after' without intending to exclude the festival days themselves.

items.text: Second attempted proof from Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi quoting Shmuel states that for Rabbi Yishmael, Christians are always forbidden, which would be impossible if the festival days were included. The Gemara clarifies that the question is only for the Rabbis, not for Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi quotes Shmuel that for Rabbi Yishmael, Christians are always forbidden, which would be impossible if the festival days included their own days.

The Gemara clarifies that the question about 'הן ואידיהן' (the festival days including their own days) is only relevant for the Rabbis, not for Rabbi Yishmael, who holds 'הן בלא אידיהן' (the festival days without their own days).

items.text: Third attempted proof from the list of festivals
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from the list of festivals
items.desc_en: Ravina cites a baraita listing the festivals: Kalenda, Saturnalia, and Kratesim. Rav Chanin bar Rava explains Kalenda is eight days after the solstice and Saturnalia eight days before. If the festival days were included, there would be ten days, but the tanna counts Kalenda as one day.

sub.desc_en: Ravina cites a baraita listing the festivals of gentiles (Kalenda, Saturnalia, Kratesim) and Rav Chanin bar Rava explains that Kalenda is eight days after the solstice and Saturnalia eight days before.
The Gemara objects that if the festival days themselves were included, there would be ten days, but the tanna counts Kalenda as only one day.

items.text: Fourth proof from the Mishnah's phrasing and conclusion
items.text_en: Fourth proof from the Mishnah's phrasing and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's wording 'before their festivals' that the festival days are not included, otherwise it would say 'their festivals three days'. The Gemara concludes definitively that the prohibition is for the days without the festival days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that if the festival days were included, the Mishnah would have said 'their festivals three days' rather than 'before their festivals three days'.
The Gemara raises a possible counterargument: perhaps the Mishnah says 'before their festivals' only to exclude the days after, but could still include the festival days themselves.
The Gemara concludes definitively that the prohibition applies to the days without the festival days, as the Mishnah's wording cannot be explained otherwise.

items.text: Inquiry into the reason for the prohibition: profit or stumbling block?
items.text_en: Inquiry into the reason for the prohibition: profit or stumbling block?
items.desc_en: A new inquiry asks whether the prohibition is due to profit or the verse 'before a blind person do not place a stumbling block'. The practical difference is when one has his own animal: if profit, it is forbidden; if stumbling block, it is permitted. The Gemara then questions whether having one's own animal exempts one from the stumbling block prohibition, citing a baraita from Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: is the prohibition of selling an animal to a gentile three days before their festival due to the concern of profit (הרווחה) or due to the verse 'before a blind person do not place a stumbling block' (לפני עור לא תתן מכשול)?

The Gemara asks what practical difference arises between the two reasons: if the prohibition is due to profit, then even when the seller has his own animal it is forbidden; if due to the stumbling block, it is permitted because the buyer already has his own animal.

The Gemara objects: does having one's own animal truly exempt one from the prohibition of 'before a blind person do not place a stumbling block'? It cites a baraita from Rabbi Natan that suggests otherwise.

items.text: Source for the prohibition of giving a stumbling block
items.text_en: Source for the prohibition of giving a stumbling block
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for not handing a cup of wine to a nazirite or a limb from a living animal to a Noahide, citing 'before a blind man do not place a stumbling block'. It then clarifies that the case is where the recipient cannot reach it himself, e.g., across a river, as indicated by the term 'reach out' rather than 'give'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for not handing a cup of wine to a nazirite or a limb from a living animal to a Noahide, citing 'before a blind man do not place a stumbling block', and notes the difficulty that the recipient could take it himself.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the recipient cannot reach it himself, e.g., across a river, as indicated by the term 'reach out' rather than 'give'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on business dealings before their festival
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on business dealings before their festival
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether business dealings (nasa v'natan) with an idolater before his festival are forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan forbids it, while Reish Lakish permits it. Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita about their festival days being forbidden, but Reish Lakish limits it to the festival day itself. An alternative version has Reish Lakish citing the baraita against Rabbi Yochanan, but the Tanna calls both 'their festival'.

items.text: Baraita supporting Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Reish Lakish: the prohibition of business dealings applies only to items that last, but for non-lasting items it is permitted; even for lasting items, if one already transacted, it is permitted. Rav Zevid adds that non-lasting items may be sold to them but not bought from them.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Reish Lakish: the prohibition of business dealings applies only to lasting items, but for non-lasting items it is permitted; even for lasting items, if one already transacted, it is permitted.
Rav Zevid adds that non-lasting items may be sold to them but not bought from them.

items.text: Story of the heretic's gift to Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a
items.text_en: Story of the heretic's gift to Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a
items.desc_en: A heretic sent a dinar to Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a on his festival. Reish Lakish advised him to take it and throw it into a pit in front of him, but Rabbi Yehuda worried about enmity. Reish Lakish clarified he meant indirectly, not in the heretic's presence.

sub.desc_en: The storyteller introduces the case: a heretic sent a Caesarean dinar to Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a on his festival, with Reish Lakish sitting before him.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a asks what to do: taking the dinar would cause the heretic to thank his idol, but refusing would create enmity.
Reish Lakish advises taking the dinar and throwing it into a pit in front of the heretic; Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a objects that this would cause even more enmity.
Reish Lakish clarifies that he meant to throw it indirectly, not in the heretic's presence, to avoid enmity.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of borrowing, lending, and repayment
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of borrowing, lending, and repayment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits lending to and borrowing from idolaters before their festival. The Gemara questions why borrowing is prohibited since it reduces the idolater's assets. Abaye says it is a decree due to lending, while Rava says all cases are because the idolater will give thanks. The Gemara explains why each case is necessary to teach, as each has a unique reason for the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why borrowing from idolaters is prohibited, since it reduces their assets rather than benefiting them.
Abaye answers that borrowing is prohibited as a decree due to the concern that one might come to lend to them.
Rava answers that all cases are prohibited because the idolater will go and give thanks to his idol.
The Gemara questions why borrowing money from idolaters is prohibited, since it reduces their assets.
Abaye answers that borrowing money is prohibited as a decree due to the concern that one might come to lend to them.
Rava answers that borrowing money is prohibited because the idolater will go and give thanks.
The Gemara questions why collecting payment from idolaters is prohibited, since it reduces their assets.
Abaye answers that collecting payment is prohibited as a decree due to the concern that one might come to repay them.
Rava answers that collecting payment is prohibited because the idolater will go and give thanks.
The Gemara explains why the case of engaging in business needed to be taught separately, as one might have thought borrowing is permitted since it reduces the idolater's assets.
The Gemara explains why borrowing items needed to be taught separately, as one might have thought borrowing money is permitted since the idolater fears the money will not be returned.
The Gemara explains why borrowing money needed to be taught separately, as one might have thought collecting payment is permitted since the idolater is distressed and will not give thanks.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling and the principle of eventual joy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling and the principle of eventual joy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda permits repayment from them because they are distressed now. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a woman may not plaster her oven on the holiday because she is distressed now but happy later. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that in holiday laws, all cases involve eventual joy, but Ravina says an idolater is always distressed about repayment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda rejects the principle that even though the gentile is distressed now, he will be happy afterward.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yehuda does apply the principle of eventual joy in the context of holiday laws.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing holiday laws, where all cases involve eventual joy.
Ravina offers an alternative resolution: a gentile is always distressed about repayment, so the principle of eventual joy does not apply.

items.text: Comparison with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and ruling
items.text_en: Comparison with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is contrasted with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who distinguishes between a loan with a document (not collected) and an oral loan (collected, as it is like saving from them). Rav Yosef reports that the halakha follows both Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Yehuda, and explains the latter with a baraita about a dyer who changes the color.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who distinguishes between a loan with a document (not collected) and an oral loan (collected, as it is like saving from them).
Rav Yosef, sitting behind Rabbi Abba before Rav Huna, reports that the halakha follows both Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha regarding the distinction between loans, and follows Rabbi Yehuda as per a baraita about a dyer who changes the color.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding payment for wool when a shearer improves an animal. Rabbi Meir requires payment for the wool's value, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between cases where the improvement exceeds the expense and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding payment for wool when a shearer improves an animal.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Why state halakha as Rabbi Yehuda?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Why state halakha as Rabbi Yehuda?
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions why the Mishnah needs to state the halakha as Rabbi Yehuda, given the principle that a dispute followed by an anonymous ruling is decided according to the anonymous ruling. Rav Huna counters that there is no order in the Mishnah, but Rav Yosef argues that all of Nezikin is one tractate. An alternative answer is given that the anonymous ruling is a definitive halakha.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef turns the discussion to explain why the Mishnah needed to state the halakha as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, since one might have thought the majority opinion prevails.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah also states the halakha as Rabbi Yehuda, since the principle of a dispute followed by an anonymous ruling should make it obvious.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah in Bava Metzia to show that the dispute is in Bava Kamma and the anonymous ruling is in Bava Metzia, supporting the principle.

items.text: Baraita: Saying 'Let us see if you will stand with me this evening'
items.text_en: Baraita: Saying 'Let us see if you will stand with me this evening'
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses whether one may say to another 'Let us see if you will stand with me this evening' (a conditional commitment). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa permits it, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rules in accordance with him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute about whether one may say 'see if you will stand with me this evening,' and Rabbi Yochanan rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
A baraita opens by stating the prohibition against saying 'Let us see if you will stand with me this evening,' and then records Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's dissenting opinion that it is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana citing Rabbi Yoḥanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana citing Rabbi Yoḥanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Ḥana reports in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's lenient position.

items.text: Baraita: Seeking a second ruling from a sage
items.text_en: Baraita: Seeking a second ruling from a sage
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that one who receives a ruling of impurity or prohibition from a sage should not seek a lenient ruling from another sage. If two sages disagree, follow the greater one, or if equal, follow the stringent opinion. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa distinguishes between Torah and scribal matters, and Rav Yosef rules in accordance with him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a general rule: one who receives a ruling of impurity or prohibition from a sage should not seek a contrary ruling from another sage.

The baraita continues with a case of two conflicting rulings: follow the greater sage, or if equal, the stringent opinion; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa distinguishes between Torah and scribal matters, and Rav Yosef rules in accordance with him.

items.text: Baraita: Repentant sinners and acceptance
items.text_en: Baraita: Repentant sinners and acceptance
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses whether those who repent from sinful practices are accepted back. Rabbi Meir says they are never accepted, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between secret and public repentance. An alternative version states that if they made their deeds secret, they are accepted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether those who retract their rulings are accepted back, with Rabbi Yehuda distinguishing between secret and public retractions.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: if they repented in secret they are not accepted, but if they repented publicly they are accepted.
An alternative version states that if they made their deeds secret (i.e., repented discreetly), they are accepted.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: dispute about accepting penitents
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: dispute about accepting penitents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites a dispute about accepting those who worship idols in private versus public. Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha accept them in both cases, citing the verse 'Return, wayward children.' Rabbi Yitzchak of Kfar Akko reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in accordance with that pair.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling that those who worship idols in public (בפרהסיא) are not accepted as penitents.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha dispute the Tanna Kamma, ruling that penitents are accepted in both cases, citing the verse 'Return, wayward children' (שובו בנים שובבים).

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of Kfar Akko citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of Kfar Akko citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of Kfar Akko reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the הלכה (binding law) follows that pair (Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha).

items.text: Mishnah: three days before and after their festivals
items.text_en: Mishnah: three days before and after their festivals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says it is forbidden to transact with gentiles three days before and three days after their festivals; the Sages say it is forbidden only before, but permitted after.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael forbids transactions with gentiles three days before and three days after their festivals, while the Sages forbid only before but permit after.

items.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi citing Shmuel: a Christian is always forbidden according to Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi citing Shmuel: a Christian is always forbidden according to Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi quotes Shmuel: according to Rabbi Yishmael, transacting with a Christian (a 'Notzri') is always forbidden, presumably because every day is like a festival for them.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi reports in Shmuel's name that according to Rabbi Yishmael, transacting with a Christian is always forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: identifying the anonymous Sages – four possible distinctions
items.text_en: Gemara: identifying the anonymous Sages – four possible distinctions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Sages' ruling in the Mishnah seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, and proposes four distinctions between them: (1) whether the prohibition applies to the festivals themselves without their surrounding days; (2) whether transacting after the fact is permitted; (3) whether Shmuel's leniency for the Diaspora is accepted; (4) whether Nachum HaMadi's one-day-before rule is accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the anonymous Sages of the Mishnah differ from the Tanna Kamma since their rulings appear identical.

The first answer suggests the distinction is whether the prohibition extends to the festivals themselves without their surrounding days; the Tanna Kamma prohibits only the festivals themselves, while the later Sages prohibit the festivals plus their surrounding days.
The second answer proposes that the distinction lies in whether transacting business after the fact (בדיעבד) is permitted; the Tanna Kamma permits it, while the later Sages forbid it.

The third answer suggests that the distinction is whether to accept Shmuel's leniency that for the Diaspora only the festival day itself is forbidden; the Tanna Kamma accepts it, while the later Sages reject it.

The fourth answer proposes that the distinction is whether to accept Nachum HaMadi's rule that only one day before their festivals is forbidden; the Tanna Kamma rejects it, while the later Sages accept it.

items.text: Nachum HaMadi's ruling and its rejection
items.text_en: Nachum HaMadi's ruling and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita where Nachum HaMadi says only one day before their festivals is forbidden, but the Sages rejected his statement. The Gemara then asks: but the later Sages (Rabbanan Batra'ei) seem to agree with him? It answers: those 'Sages' are actually Nachum HaMadi himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita where Nachum HaMadi rules that only one day before their festivals is forbidden.
The Sages reject Nachum HaMadi's statement, saying it was suppressed and never said.
The Gemara objects: but the later Sages (Rabbanan Batra'ei) seem to agree with Nachum HaMadi's position.
The Gemara resolves: those 'Sages' are actually Nachum HaMadi himself, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Another baraita of Nachum HaMadi: selling horses
items.text_en: Another baraita of Nachum HaMadi: selling horses
items.desc_en: Another baraita: Nachum HaMadi permits selling an old male horse for war. The Sages rejected this too. The Gemara notes that Ben Beteira also permits selling horses, but he does not distinguish between males and females, whereas Nachum does, so Nachum aligns with the Sages, yet his statement was rejected.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Nachum HaMadi's opinion that one may sell an old male horse for war, but the Sages rejected this statement.

The Gemara questions why Nachum's opinion was rejected, given that Ben Beteira also permits selling horses, and notes that Ben Beteira does not distinguish between males and females, whereas Nachum does, aligning him with the Sages.
The Gemara concludes that despite the alignment, the Sages still rejected Nachum's statement, and it was not accepted.

items.text: Third baraita: tithing shevet produce
items.text_en: Third baraita: tithing shevet produce
items.desc_en: A third baraita: Nachum HaMadi says that shevet (a type of produce) is tithed as seed, vegetables, and zirim. The Sages rejected this. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer holds a similar view, but the case there is different (involving a garden bed).

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Nachum HaMadi's ruling that shevet (a type of produce) is tithed as seed, vegetables, and zirim (a type of seed).
The Sages reject Nachum HaMadi's statement, saying it was suppressed and never said.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer holds a similar view, so why was Nachum's statement suppressed?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer's case is different, involving a garden bed (דגינוניתא), not the general rule of shevet.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's question to Abaye: one ruling of Nachum that is accepted
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's question to Abaye: one ruling of Nachum that is accepted
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi asks Abaye: a great man from our place (Nachum HaMadi) had every statement rejected with 'the matter was suppressed and not said' – is there any ruling of his that we follow? Abaye answers: yes, one – that one may ask personal needs in the 'Shomea Tefillah' blessing. The Gemara adds that this is related to a dispute about the order of prayer.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi asks Abaye whether any ruling of Nachum HaMadi is accepted, given that all his statements were suppressed.
Abaye answers that there is one ruling they follow: one may ask personal needs in the 'Shomea Tefillah' blessing.
The Gemara notes that this ruling is related to a dispute about the order of prayer (the 'great chains' of the blessings).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the order of prayer
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the order of prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says one should ask personal needs before praying, citing 'A prayer of the afflicted when he faints and pours out his complaint before God.' Rabbi Yehoshua says one should pray first, then ask needs, citing 'I pour out my complaint before Him, I declare my trouble before Him.' The Gemara resolves the verses and explains the real dispute via Rabbi Simlai's teaching: one should always arrange praise of God before praying, as Moses did.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that one should ask personal needs and then pray, citing the verse 'A prayer of the afflicted when he faints and pours out his complaint before God' and interpreting 'complaint' as prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua states that one should pray first and then ask personal needs, citing the verse 'I pour out my complaint before Him, I declare my trouble before Him.'
The Gemara asks Rabbi Eliezer about the verse 'I pour out my complaint before Him' and explains that he interprets it as 'when my trouble is before Him, I declare it' (i.e., after prayer).
The Gemara asks Rabbi Yehoshua about the verse 'A prayer of the afflicted when he faints' and explains that he interprets it as 'when before God he pours out his complaint' (i.e., prayer first).

sub.text: Gemara's question: what is the real dispute?
sub.text_en: Gemara's question: what is the real dispute?
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the verses are not interpreted definitively by either side, what is the actual basis of their dispute?

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Simlai's teaching
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Simlai's teaching
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by citing Rabbi Simlai's teaching that one should always arrange praise of God before praying, as demonstrated by Moses who first praised God and then asked to enter the land.

items.text: Dispute about when to ask personal needs in prayer
items.text_en: Dispute about when to ask personal needs in prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer regarding whether one can learn from Moses' prayer. The Sages rule that one asks personal needs in the blessing 'Shome'a Tefillah'. Various Amoraim add qualifications: one may add requests at the end of each blessing, or in the appropriate blessing for the need, or even after the Amidah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua learns from Moses' prayer, Rabbi Eliezer rejects it because Moses was exceptional, and the Sages rule that one asks personal needs in the blessing 'Shome'a Tefillah'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, and Rav's qualification
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, and Rav's qualification
