sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the halacha follows the Sages, and Rav adds that one may also add requests at the end of each blessing relevant to that blessing.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi cites Rav that one may insert specific needs in the appropriate blessing: a sick person in the blessing for the sick, and a request for sustenance in the blessing of the years.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that even after the Amidah, one may recite requests as lengthy as the Yom Kippur service.

items.text: Mishnah: Festivals of gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: Festivals of gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the festivals of gentiles that are prohibited: Kalenda, Saturnalia, Kratesis, the king's accession day, birthday, and death day. Rabbi Meir adds more, while the Sages distinguish based on whether the death involves burning. Other personal celebrations are only prohibited on that day and for that individual.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the gentile festivals that are prohibited: Kalenda, Saturnalia, Kratesis, the king's accession day, birthday, and death day, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages distinguish: a death involving burning indicates idolatry, while one without burning does not.
The Mishnah adds that personal celebrations like shaving, returning from sea or prison, or a son's wedding feast are only prohibited on that day and for that individual.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of Kalenda and Saturnalia
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of Kalenda and Saturnalia
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava defines Kalenda as eight days after the winter solstice and Saturnalia as eight days before, citing a verse as a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava defines Kalenda as eight days after the winter solstice and Saturnalia as eight days before, citing a verse as a mnemonic.

items.text: Origin of Kalenda and Saturnalia from Adam's mistake
items.text_en: Origin of Kalenda and Saturnalia from Adam's mistake
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Adam, seeing the days shorten after creation, feared it was punishment for his sin and fasted eight days. When the days lengthened, he realized it was natural and made eight festive days. The next year he made both periods festive. He intended them for Heaven, but later generations turned them into idolatry. A difficulty is raised for the opinion that the world was created in Nisan.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Adam, seeing the days shorten after creation, feared it was punishment for his sin and fasted eight days.

The baraita continues that when the days lengthened, Adam realized it was natural and made eight festive days; the next year he made both periods festive, intending them for Heaven, but later generations turned them into idolatry.

The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the opinion that the world was created in Nisan, Adam would have already seen short and long days, so why would he have been surprised by the shortening days?

items.text: Adam's sacrifice on the first day and the horned ox
items.text_en: Adam's sacrifice on the first day and the horned ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that on the day Adam was created, he saw the sun set and feared darkness, fasting and weeping all night. When dawn came, he realized it was natural and offered a sacrifice of an ox whose horns preceded its hooves. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the ox had one horn on its forehead, citing a verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the spelling indicates one horn.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts Adam's fear at sunset on his first day, his fasting and weeping all night, and Eve weeping opposite him.
When dawn came, Adam realized the pattern of nature and offered a sacrifice of an ox whose horns preceded its hooves, citing the verse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that Adam's ox had a single horn on its forehead, citing the same verse.
The Gemara objects that the word 'מקרן' (with a full letter yod) implies two horns, not one.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verse is written defectively as 'מקרן' (without the yod), indicating a single horn.

items.text: Dispute: Is Kalenda prohibited for all or only for its worshippers?
items.text_en: Dispute: Is Kalenda prohibited for all or only for its worshippers?
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana asks whether towns subject to Rome are prohibited from Kalenda. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it is prohibited for all, while Rabbi Yochanan says only for its worshippers. A baraisa supports Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana asks whether towns subject to Rome are prohibited from Kalenda or permitted.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that Kalenda is prohibited for all, including non-worshippers.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that Kalenda is prohibited only for its worshippers.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's position, stating that even Rome itself is prohibited only for its worshippers.

items.text: Halakha of Saturnalia, Kratesis, and other festivals
items.text_en: Halakha of Saturnalia, Kratesis, and other festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that for Saturnalia, Kratesis, and the king's accession day, the prohibition applies only before the festival, not after. For a gentile's son's wedding feast, only that day and that person are prohibited. Rav Ashi supports this from the Mishnah. The Gemara explains that 'that person' excludes his servants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that for Saturnalia, Kratesis, and the king's accession day, the prohibition applies only before the festival, not after.
Rav Ashi supports the ruling by citing the Mishnah's list of festivals where only that day and that person are prohibited.
The Gemara explains that 'that person' excludes his servants, confirming the ruling.

items.text: Jews in the diaspora and gentile feasts
items.text_en: Jews in the diaspora and gentile feasts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael says that Jews outside Israel are considered pure idolaters if they attend a gentile's feast for his son, even if they eat their own food, as the verse equates the invitation to eating from sacrifices to the dead. Rava explains that the prohibition begins from the invitation itself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that Jews in the diaspora who attend a gentile's feast for his son are considered pure idolaters, even if they eat their own food, as the verse equates the invitation to eating from sacrifices to the dead.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the prohibition only applies if the Jew actually eats from the gentile's food, not merely from the invitation.
Rava answers that the verse uses 'וְקָרָא לְךָ' (and he invites you) rather than 'וְאָכַלְתָּ' (and you eat), proving the prohibition begins from the invitation itself.

items.text: Duration of prohibition for items used in idolatrous festivals
items.text_en: Duration of prohibition for items used in idolatrous festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's ruling: for the first thirty days, any item from an idolater's festival is forbidden regardless of whether the owner says it was for the festival. After thirty days, it is forbidden only if the owner says it was for the festival. Rav Pappa defines the time limits: the prohibition lasts up to twelve months, and the initial period begins when they hang barley in the threshing baskets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Mishnah's ruling: for the first thirty days, any item from an idolater's festival is forbidden regardless of the owner's statement; after thirty days, it is forbidden only if the owner says it was for the festival.
The Gemara asks: until when does the prohibition last if the owner says it was for the wedding celebration?
Rav Pappa answers: the prohibition lasts up to twelve months of the year.
The Gemara asks: from when initially is it prohibited?

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa says in the name of Rava: the initial period begins when they cast barley into the mortars to prepare beer for the wedding.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Yitzchak's practice
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Yitzchak's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's ruling by citing an incident where Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya encountered an idolater after twelve months, heard him admit the item was for the festival, and refrained from eating. The Gemara deflects by noting that Rav Yitzchak was an important person who acted stringently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's ruling by citing an incident where Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya encountered an idolater after twelve months, heard him admit the item was for the festival, and refrained from eating.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by noting that Rav Yitzchak was an important person who acted stringently.

items.text: Identity of the festival 'Kratesis'
items.text_en: Identity of the festival 'Kratesis'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'Kratesis' refers to the day Rome seized power. A baraita mentions both Kratesis and the day Rome seized power, leading Rav Yosef to explain that Rome seized power twice: once in the days of Queen Cleopatra and once in the days of the Greeks. Rav Dimi adds that the Romans fought 32 battles against the Greeks, eventually forming a coalition with Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the festival 'Kratesis' refers to.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that Kratesis is the day Rome seized power.
The Gemara objects that a baraita lists both Kratesis and the day Rome seized power, implying they are distinct.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rome seized power on two separate occasions: once in the days of Queen Cleopatra and once in the days of the Greeks.

Rav Dimi provides supporting evidence: the Romans fought 32 battles against the Greeks until they formed a partnership with Israel, stipulating that if the kings come from one side, the governors come from the other.

items.text: The dispute between Rome and Greece and its resolution
items.text_en: The dispute between Rome and Greece and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Romans proposed a legal dispute to the Greeks: which is more important, a pearl or a precious stone? The Greeks answered that the pearl is subordinate to the stone, and so on, until the Torah scroll is supreme. The Romans then claimed that since they have the Torah scroll and Israel is with them, they are superior. The Greeks were subjugated for 26 years, and the Gemara explains the verses that were interpreted to justify this.

sub.desc_en: The Romans propose a legal dispute to the Greeks, asking whether a pearl or a precious stone should serve as a base for the other, and the Greeks answer that the pearl is subordinate to the precious stone.
The Romans ask whether a precious stone or an onyx should serve as a base, and the Greeks answer that the precious stone is subordinate to the onyx.
The Romans ask whether an onyx or a Torah scroll should serve as a base, and the Greeks answer that the onyx is subordinate to the Torah scroll.
The Romans claim superiority because they have the Torah scroll and Israel with them, forcing the Greeks to submit; they remain faithful for 26 years and then subjugate the Jews.

The Gemara asks what verses the Romans interpreted initially and ultimately, and answers that initially they interpreted 'Let us take our journey... I will go before you' and ultimately 'Let my lord pass over before his servant'.

items.text: The 26 years of subjugation and the story of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
items.text_en: The 26 years of subjugation and the story of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know about the 26 years, and cites Rav Kahana's account of Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's teaching: 180 years before the Temple's destruction, the evil kingdom spread over Israel; 80 years before, impurity was decreed on foreign lands and glass vessels; 40 years before, the Sanhedrin went into exile. The Gemara explains that this meant they stopped adjudicating fines, due to a decree that anyone who ordains or is ordained will be killed. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained five elders between Usha and Shfar'am, and was martyred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we know about the twenty-six years of faithful partnership.
Rav Kahana cites the story of Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's illness and the request for teachings from his father.

Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei reports three chronological milestones: 180 years before the destruction, the evil kingdom spread; 80 years before, impurity was decreed on foreign lands and glass; 40 years before, the Sanhedrin was exiled.
The Gemara asks what halakhic significance the Sanhedrin's exile has.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi answers that the exile meant they no longer adjudicated cases of fines.
The Gemara objects, citing Rav Yehuda's statement that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava preserved the laws of fines, and questions whether they could have been forgotten.
The Gemara resolves that the laws of fines ceased to be implemented due to the Roman decree against ordination.
The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained five elders between Usha and Shfar'am, with Rav Avya adding Rabbi Nechemya.
The Gemara describes the martyrdom of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava after the ordination.

items.text: Correction: the Sanhedrin stopped adjudicating capital cases
items.text_en: Correction: the Sanhedrin stopped adjudicating capital cases
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects the earlier statement: the Sanhedrin did not stop adjudicating fines but rather capital cases. The reason is that murderers were so numerous that the court could not judge them, so they moved from place to place to avoid liability, as the verse teaches that the place causes judgment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects the earlier statement: the Sanhedrin stopped adjudicating capital cases, not cases of fines.
The Gemara explains the reason: since murderers were numerous and the court could not judge them, they moved from place to place to avoid liability.

The Gemara cites the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עַל פִּי הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יַגִּידוּ לְךָ מִן הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא' (and you shall do according to the sentence they declare to you from that place), teaching that the place causes the judgment.

items.text: Opening baraita on Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Herodian rule
items.text_en: Opening baraita on Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Herodian rule
items.desc_en: The baraita lists the durations of Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Herodian rule while the Temple stood, then instructs to calculate the years after its destruction. The Gemara notes a discrepancy: the total of the listed years is 206, but the baraita says Greek rule was 180 years; it explains that 26 years of Greek rule were not counted because the Greeks did not subjugate Israel during that time.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the durations of Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Herodian rule while the Temple stood, then instructs to calculate the years after its destruction.
The Gemara questions the baraita's total: the listed years sum to 206, but the baraita says Greek rule was only 180 years.
The Gemara explains that 26 years of Greek rule were not counted because the Greeks did not subjugate Israel during that time.

items.text: Rav Pappa's advice for correcting scribal and tanna errors
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's advice for correcting scribal and tanna errors
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa advises that if a tanna errs in the details of years, one should ask the scribe how many years are written and add twenty years to find the correct number. Conversely, if the scribe errs, one should ask the tanna how many years he counts and subtract twenty years. The mnemonic is that the scribe is deficient and the tanna adds.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa advises that if a tanna errs in the details of years, one should ask the scribe how many years are written and add twenty years to find the correct number.
Rav Pappa advises that if the scribe errs, one should ask the tanna how many years he counts and subtract twenty years, with the mnemonic that the scribe is deficient and the tanna adds.

items.text: Baraita of the school of Elijah on the six millennia
items.text_en: Baraita of the school of Elijah on the six millennia
items.desc_en: The baraita of the school of Elijah teaches that the world lasts six thousand years: two thousand years of chaos, two thousand years of Torah, and two thousand years of the Messianic era, but due to our many sins, some years of the Messianic era have already passed.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Elijah
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Elijah
sub.desc_en: The baraita of the school of Elijah teaches that the world lasts six thousand years: two thousand years of chaos, two thousand years of Torah, and two thousand years of the Messianic era, but due to our many sins, some years of the Messianic era have already passed.

items.text: Determining the start of the Torah period
items.text_en: Determining the start of the Torah period
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions when the two thousand years of Torah begin. It cannot be from the giving of the Torah, as that would be too few years. Instead, it begins from the verse 'the souls they made in Haran' when Abraham was 52 years old. The calculation shows that from that point to the giving of the Torah is 448 years, which matches the baraita's count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the two thousand years of Torah begin, noting that from the giving of the Torah to the present is less than two thousand years.
The Gemara answers that the Torah period begins from the verse 'the souls they made in Haran' (בראשית יב:ה), when Abraham was 52 years old.
The Gemara calculates that from Abraham's 52nd year to the giving of the Torah is 448 years, matching the baraita's count.

items.text: Rav Pappa's second correction rule for the Torah period
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's second correction rule for the Torah period
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa gives a similar rule for the Torah period: if a tanna errs in the details, ask the scribe how many years are written and add 48 years to find the correct number. The mnemonic is incomplete in the text.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states a rule: if a tanna errs in the details, ask the scribe how many years are written and add 48 years to find the correct number, with a mnemonic.

items.text: Clarification of the scribe's error
items.text_en: Clarification of the scribe's error
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if a scribe errs in counting the forty-eight cities, one can ask the Tanna how many he taught, subtract forty-eight, and find the discrepancy. A mnemonic is given: the scribe is deficient, the Tanna adds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the scribe's error by suggesting to ask the Tanna how many cities he taught, subtract forty-eight, and find the discrepancy, with a mnemonic that the scribe is deficient and the Tanna adds.

items.text: Rav Huna's method for calculating years in a week
items.text_en: Rav Huna's method for calculating years in a week
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua teaches that if one does not know how many years have passed in the current Sabbatical cycle, he should add one year, calculate the Jubilee cycles and the Sabbatical cycles, and then subtract two from each hundred and apply the remainder to the Sabbatical cycles. The mnemonic is from the verse about the famine in Joseph's time.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua teaches the method for calculating the current year in the Sabbatical cycle: add one year, then compute the Jubilee cycles and the Sabbatical cycles.
Rav Huna completes the calculation: subtract two from each hundred, apply the remainder to the Sabbatical cycles, and provides the mnemonic from the verse about the famine in Joseph's time.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's warning about buying land after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's warning about buying land after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that after four hundred years from the destruction of the Temple, one should not buy a field worth a thousand dinars for one dinar. A baraita adds that after 4231 years from Creation, one should not buy such a field. The difference between the two calculations is three years.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina warns that after four hundred years from the destruction of the Temple, one should not buy a field worth a thousand dinars for one dinar.
A baraita adds a parallel warning based on the year from Creation: after 4231 years from Creation, one should not buy such a field.
The Gemara asks what difference exists between the two calculations.
The Gemara answers that the difference between them is three years, as the baraita's calculation adds three years.

items.text: Introduction of a document with a date
items.text_en: Introduction of a document with a date
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic about a document that had a certain date written on it, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a document that had a certain date written on it, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Initial question about the document's dating
items.text_en: Initial question about the document's dating
items.desc_en: The rabbis initially suspect that a document with an extra six years is post-dated (מאוחר) and should be invalid until its time. Rav Nachman defends the scribe, arguing that he counts the six years of Median rule, which the rabbis do not count, so the document is actually written on time.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis suspect the document is post-dated (מאוחר) and propose delaying its collection until its stated time.
Rav Nachman defends the scribe, arguing he counts the six years of Median rule that the rabbis omit, so the document is written on time.
A baraita citing Rabbi Yosei confirms that the Medes ruled for six years before their empire expanded, supporting Rav Nachman's explanation.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and Rav Nachman's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and Rav Nachman's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps we count years from the Exodus, not from Greek kings, making the document post-dated. Rav Nachman responds that in the diaspora, we only count by Greek kings. Rav Acha initially thinks Rav Nachman is deflecting, but then finds a supporting baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps we count from the Exodus, not Greek kings, making the document post-dated by a millennium.
Rav Nachman responds that in the diaspora, only Greek kings are used for dating documents.
Rav Acha initially thinks Rav Nachman is deflecting, but then finds a supporting baraita.

items.text: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof from the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah) that years for kings are counted from Nisan for Jewish kings and from Tishrei for non-Jewish kings. Since we currently count from Tishrei, it must be that we count by Greek kings, not the Exodus (which would be Nisan).

sub.desc_en: Ravina opens by citing the Mishnah that Nisan is the new year for kings and festivals, and asks what halachic purpose the counting for kings serves.
Rav Chisda answers that the counting for kings is used for dating documents (שטרות).
The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah also says Tishrei is the new year for years and shemittah, and Rav Chisda says that too is for documents, creating a conflict between the two rulings.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the Nisan-based counting is for Jewish kings, while the Tishrei-based counting is for non-Jewish kings.
Ravina concludes: since we currently count from Tishrei, we must be counting by Greek kings, not by the Exodus (which would be Nisan).

items.text: First explanation of 'יום גינוסיא'
items.text_en: First explanation of 'יום גינוסיא'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'the day of their kings' גינוסיא'. Rav Yehudah explains it as the day when gentiles appoint their king. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that lists both 'יום גינוסיא' and 'יום שמעמידין בו את מלכם', and is resolved by distinguishing between the king's own day and his son's day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'יום גינוסיא' (coronation day) means, and Rav Yehuda answers it is the day they appoint their king.
The Gemara objects that a baraita lists both 'coronation day' and 'appointment day' separately, and resolves that one refers to the king's own day, the other to his son's.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that lists both 'יום גינוסיא' and 'יום שמעמידין בו את מלכם' as separate items.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the king's own day and his son's day.

items.text: Objection and alternative explanation: birthday
items.text_en: Objection and alternative explanation: birthday
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: do they appoint a son to succeed his father? A baraita says they do not. So 'גינוסיא' must mean birthday. But another baraita lists both 'גינוסיא' and 'לידה', leading to a resolution: the distinction is between the king's own day and his son's day. A third baraita lists both for the king and his son, forcing the original explanation (appointment) to stand, with the same distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: do they actually appoint a son to succeed his father? Rav Yosef's baraita says they do not, citing the verse 'הנה קטן נתתיך בגוים' (Behold, I have made you small among the nations) to prove that a son is not appointed king after his father.
The Gemara proposes that 'גינוסיא' must mean birthday, not appointment day.
The Gemara objects: a baraita lists both 'גינוסיא' and 'לידה' as separate categories, implying they are distinct.
The Gemara resolves: the distinction is between the king's own day (לידה) and his son's day (גינוסיא).

sub.text: Gemara's objection from a third baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from a third baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a third baraita that lists both 'גינוסיא' and 'לידה' for the king and his son, undermining the previous resolution.

The Gemara reverts to the original explanation that 'גינוסיא' means appointment day, and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the king's own appointment (גינוסיא) and his son's appointment (לידה).

items.text: Resolution: appointment through consultation
items.text_en: Resolution: appointment through consultation
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: a son can be appointed king through consultation (שאלה), as in the case of Asverus son of Antoninus who became king.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection about king's sons: they can be appointed through a request (שאלה), as in the case of Asverus son of Antoninus who reigned.

items.text: Antoninus's request to Rabbi and the parable
items.text_en: Antoninus's request to Rabbi and the parable
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi that his son Asverus reign and that Tiberias be made a colony, but fears the Romans won't agree to both. He demonstrates through a parable with a man and a dove. Rabbi understands the hint. Later, Antoninus complains that the Roman nobles trouble him, and Rabbi advises him to remove them one by one, as shown by uprooting radishes.

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi that his son Asverus reign and that Tiberias be made a colony, but fears the Romans won't agree to both.
Antoninus demonstrates through a parable with a man riding another and a dove that only one request can be fulfilled at a time.
Rabbi understands the hint: Antoninus wants Asverus to reign and then for Asverus to make Tiberias a colony.
Antoninus complains that the Roman nobles trouble him.
Rabbi demonstrates by uprooting one radish at a time from the garden bed that Antoninus should remove the nobles one by one.
Antoninus understands the hint: he should kill the nobles one by one and not provoke them all at once.

items.text: Secret communication between Antoninus and Rabbi
items.text_en: Secret communication between Antoninus and Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Antoninus communicated with Rabbi through hints rather than openly or in a whisper, citing the verse about birds carrying the matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Antoninus did not simply tell Rabbi openly or whisper to him.
The Gemara answers that Antoninus feared Roman eavesdroppers, citing the verse that a bird may carry the matter.

items.text: Antoninus's gifts and Rabbi's response
items.text_en: Antoninus's gifts and Rabbi's response
items.desc_en: Antoninus sends various items to Rabbi, including gold and wheat, but Rabbi declines, instructing that the wheat be given to those who come after him.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Antoninus's daughter Gira, who engaged in forbidden behavior, and lists the symbolic items Antoninus sent to Rabbi.
Antoninus daily sent Rabbi crushed gold and wheat, but Rabbi declined the wheat, instructing that it be given to future generations who would come after him.

items.text: Antoninus's request for privacy and the incident with Rabbi Chanina bar Chama
items.text_en: Antoninus's request for privacy and the incident with Rabbi Chanina bar Chama
items.desc_en: Antoninus has a secret passage to Rabbi's house and kills servants who are present. He asks that no one be there when he comes. Rabbi Chanina bar Chama is found there, and Antoninus objects. Rabbi Chanina revives a dead servant, demonstrating his power.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Antoninus's secret passage to Rabbi's house and his practice of killing servants who witness his arrival.
Antoninus finds Rabbi Chanina bar Chama with Rabbi and objects that his request for privacy was violated.
Rabbi Chanina bar Chama revives the dead servant through prayer, demonstrating his power, and Antoninus acknowledges it.

items.text: Antoninus serves Rabbi and expresses humility
items.text_en: Antoninus serves Rabbi and expresses humility
items.desc_en: Antoninus serves Rabbi daily, even bowing for him to step on him to get into bed, and Rabbi expresses that this will earn Antoninus a place in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Antoninus's daily service to Rabbi, including bowing for Rabbi to step on him to get into bed, and Rabbi's blessing that this will earn Antoninus a place in the World to Come.

items.text: Theological debate: Will Antoninus merit the World to Come?
items.text_en: Theological debate: Will Antoninus merit the World to Come?
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks if he will enter the World to Come, citing verses that seem to exclude Edom. Rabbi responds that the verses refer only to those who act like Esau, and a baraita supports this, specifically excluding Antoninus and Ketiah bar Shalom.

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi whether he will enter the World to Come.
Rabbi answers affirmatively that Antoninus will enter the World to Come.
Antoninus objects by citing the verse 'No survivor shall remain for the house of Esau' (Obadiah 1:18), implying that all Edomites are excluded.
Rabbi resolves that the verse applies only to one who acts like Esau, not to Antoninus who acts righteously.
A baraita supports Rabbi's interpretation, explicitly limiting the verse to those who act like Esau.
Antoninus raises a second objection from the verse 'There are Edom, her kings and all her princes' (Ezekiel 32:29), which seems to include all Edomite leaders in Gehinnom.
Rabbi resolves that the verse says 'her kings' but not all kings, and 'all her princes' but not all princes, leaving room for exceptions.
A baraita supports Rabbi's interpretation, explicitly excluding Antoninus ben Asverus and Ketiah bar Shalom from the condemnation.

items.text: The story of Ketiah bar Shalom
items.text_en: The story of Ketiah bar Shalom
items.desc_en: Ketiah bar Shalom defends the Jews before a Roman emperor, is executed, and dedicates his property to Rabbi Akiva. A bat kol declares him destined for the World to Come, and Rabbi comments on acquiring one's world in a single moment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the story of Ketiah bar Shalom, introducing a Roman emperor who posed a parable to his officials about removing a thorn from one's foot.
Ketiah bar Shalom argues that the Jews cannot be destroyed because they are as essential as the four winds, and rebukes the emperor for being called a 'cut' kingdom.

The emperor acknowledges Ketiah's wisdom but orders his execution; Ketiah circumcises himself, dedicates his property to Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Akiva rules that the property is divided between Aaron and his sons.
A bat kol declares Ketiah bar Shalom destined for the World to Come, and Rabbi weeps, commenting that some acquire their world in a single moment while others take many years.

items.text: Conclusion: Antoninus and Adarkhan serve Rabbi and Rav
items.text_en: Conclusion: Antoninus and Adarkhan serve Rabbi and Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Antoninus served Rabbi, and Adarkhan served Rav. Upon Antoninus's death, Rabbi said the bundle was separated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Antoninus served Rabbi and Adarkhan served Rav, and upon Antoninus's death Rabbi said the bundle was separated.

items.text: Continuation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Continuation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a bundle of wood becomes separated, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a bundle of wood becomes separated, it is permitted.

items.text: The Conversion of Onkelos
items.text_en: The Conversion of Onkelos
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates how Onkelos converted, evading three Roman cohorts sent by the emperor through scriptural arguments, ultimately leading to their conversion as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Onkelos converting and the first Roman cohort sent to capture him.
Onkelos convinces the second cohort by arguing that God carries the fire before Israel, unlike earthly kings.
Onkelos converts the third cohort by explaining that God guards His servants from outside, unlike human kings.

items.text: Antoninus and Rabbi: The Verse of Two Nations
items.text_en: Antoninus and Rabbi: The Verse of Two Nations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'two nations' as 'two proselytes' referring to Antoninus and Rabbi, who always had lettuce, cucumbers, and radishes on their table, with a clarification about cucumbers being harmful or beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'two nations are in your womb' from Genesis.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets 'nations' as 'proselytes', referring to Antoninus and Rabbi, who always had lettuce, cucumbers, and radishes on their table, with a statement about their digestive effects.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael objects that cucumbers are called 'קישואין' because they are as harmful to the body as swords.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: large cucumbers are harmful, small ones are beneficial.

items.text: Dispute on Burning as a Statute or Honor
items.text_en: Dispute on Burning as a Statute or Honor
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that Rabbi Meir holds burning is not a gentile statute, while the Rabbis hold it is. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that permits burning for kings, which is resolved by concluding that all agree burning is an honor, and the dispute is about whether a death without burning is significant for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's listing of both birthday and death day that Rabbi Meir holds burning is not a gentile statute (חוקה), since he considers even a death without burning as significant for idolatry.
The Gemara infers that the Rabbis hold burning is a gentile statute (חוקה), since they exclude a death without burning from the Mishnah's list.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that permits burning for kings, arguing that if burning were a gentile statute (חוקה), Jews would be prohibited from doing it by the verse 'וּבְחֻקֹּתֵיהֶם לֹא תֵּלֵכוּ' (and in their statutes you shall not walk).

The Gemara resolves that all agree burning is not a statute (חוקה) but an honor (חשיבותא), and the dispute is about whether a death without burning is significant enough for idolatry: Rabbi Meir holds it is, the Rabbis hold it is not.

items.text: Laws of Burning and Uprooting for Kings
items.text_en: Laws of Burning and Uprooting for Kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses what is burned for kings (their bed and utensils) and cites a case where Onkelos burned seventy maneh of balsam for Rabban Gamliel. It also discusses uprooting for kings, with Rav Pappa specifying a horse that was ridden, and a baraita distinguishing between uprooting that causes a tereifah and that which does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halacha that one burns for kings and for princes, citing a verse as proof that this is not an Amorite practice.
The Gemara asks what items are burned for kings, and cites a case where Onkelos the convert burned seventy maneh of balsam for Rabban Gamliel the Elder.
The Gemara objects that the baraita only lists bed and utensils, not balsam, and resolves that the balsam was worth seventy maneh, not that seventy maneh of balsam were burned.
The Gemara asks whether anything else is uprooted for kings, and Rav Pappa answers that a horse which the king rode is uprooted.

The Gemara asks whether a pure animal is not uprooted, and cites a baraita distinguishing between uprooting that causes a tereifah (forbidden) and that which does not (permitted), ending with a question about the latter.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'menasher'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'menasher'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'menasher parsoteha' refers to a calf pulling a wagon, clarifying the context of the Roman festival.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'menasher parsoteha' refers to a calf pulling a wagon, clarifying the context of the Roman festival.

items.text: Dispute over the wording of 'day of shaving the beard'
items.text_en: Dispute over the wording of 'day of shaving the beard'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah reads 'day of shaving the beard and letting down the lock' or 'day of shaving the beard and removing the lock', and resolves it by citing a baraita that includes both versions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma about the correct wording of the Mishnah: whether it says 'day of shaving his beard and letting down his lock' or 'day of shaving his beard and removing his lock'.
The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing a baraita that includes both versions, indicating that both readings are valid.

items.text: The seventy-year cycle ritual in Rome
items.text_en: The seventy-year cycle ritual in Rome
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel describes a unique Roman festival every seventy years: a perfect man is mounted on a lame man, dressed in Adam's clothes, with Rabbi Yishmael's skull on his head, and a proclamation is made. Rav Ashi comments that the proclamation's wording implies the master himself is a forger.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel introduces a unique Roman festival every seventy years, describing the ritual with a perfect man riding a lame man, dressed in Adam's clothes, with Rabbi Yishmael's skull.

The description continues: they hang gold on his neck, cover markets with onyx, and announce a proclamation about the brother of our master being a forger, concluding with 'Woe to this one when that one arises'.
Rav Ashi comments that the wording of the proclamation implies the master himself is a forger, causing the wicked to stumble.

items.text: Why the Tanna omitted this festival
items.text_en: Why the Tanna omitted this festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah did not list this festival because it occurs only once every seventy years, while the Mishnah only lists annual festivals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna of our Mishnah did not include this festival in the list.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna only counts festivals that occur every year, not those that occur once every seventy years.

items.text: Listing of Roman and Persian festivals
items.text_en: Listing of Roman and Persian festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists additional Roman and Persian festivals, such as Murtardi, Turiyaski, Muharnekai, and Muhrin, and then the Persian and Babylonian festivals, including Muharnekai, Aknita, Bachnunei, and Asara B'Adar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what are the festivals of the Persians.
The Gemara answers that the Persian festivals are Murtardi, Turiyaski, Muharnekai, and Muhrin.
The Gemara asks what are the festivals of the Babylonians.
The Gemara answers that the Babylonian festivals are Muharnekai, Aknita, Bachnunei, and Asara B'Adar.

items.text: Five permanent idolatrous temples
items.text_en: Five permanent idolatrous temples
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda in the name of Rav lists five permanent idolatrous temples: Bel in Babylon, Nevo in Bursif, Tar'ata in Mappag, Tzrifa in Ashkelon, and Nishra in Arabia. Rav Dimi adds Yareid in Ein Baki and Nidbaka in Akko, with a variant. Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Chisda what 'permanent' means, and is told they are worshipped all year round.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda / Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda / Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda reports in Rav's name that there are five permanent idolatrous temples: Bel in Babylon, Nevo in Bursif, Tar'ata in Mappag, Tzrifa in Ashkelon, and Nishra in Arabia.
When Rav Dimi came, he added the marketplace in Ein Bekhi and Nadbekha in Akko, with a variant tradition and an alternate version from Rav Dimi of Neharde'a.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda's question
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Chisda what 'permanent' means in this context.
Rav Chisda explains that 'permanent' means they are fixed forever, worshipped constantly all year round.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on festivals in the diaspora
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on festivals in the diaspora
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that in the diaspora, only the actual day of the festival is forbidden. The Gemara questions this from the fact that Rav Yehuda permitted Rav Brona and Rav Giddel to sell wine and wheat on the festival of the Arabs, and answers that the Arab festival is not fixed.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that in the diaspora, engaging in business with gentiles is prohibited only on the actual day of their festival.
The Gemara questions whether it is even prohibited on the festival day itself.
The Gemara objects from the fact that Rav Yehuda permitted Rav Beruna and Rav Giddel to sell wine and wheat on the festival of the Arab merchants.
The Gemara answers that the Arab festival is different because it does not have a fixed time, so the Sages did not include it in the prohibition.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on a city with idolatry
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on a city with idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a city has an idolatrous shrine, the outskirts are permitted, and vice versa. It also discusses the permissibility of going to such a place. The Gemara clarifies the case of the outskirts, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina regarding the 'itloz' of Gaza, with a variant tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: if a city has idolatry, the outskirts are permitted for business, and vice versa, and discusses the permissibility of traveling to such a place.
The Gemara asks what constitutes 'outside' the city in this context.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina answers that it is like the bazaar of Gaza, which is outside the city walls.
An alternative version reports that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asked Rabbi Chanina about the bazaar of Gaza.
Rabbi Chanina responds by asking if Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish had ever been to Tyre and seen a Jew and a gentile there, implying a practical observation.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'the Sages were not concerned' in the case of two pots on one stove, and seeks to clarify the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'the Sages were not concerned' in the case of two pots on one stove, and seeks to clarify the reasoning.

items.text: Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Sages were not concerned about the possibility of the gentile switching meat for neveilah, just as they were not concerned about the gentile using idolatrous wine.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Sages were not concerned about the possibility of the Jew turning his back and the gentile placing neveila (נבילה) in the pot, just as here they were not concerned about the possibility of the gentile substituting the meat with that of an idolatrous sacrifice.

items.text: Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rava interprets the Mishnah's phrase as referring to bishulei akum (cooking by gentiles), and similarly here the Sages were not concerned about their festival day.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'the Sages were not concerned' refers to the prohibition of בישולי גוים (cooking by gentiles).
Rava concludes that similarly, in the Mishnah's case, the Sages were not concerned about the gentile's festival day.

items.text: Rabbah bar Ulla's answer
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Ulla's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla explains that the Sages were not concerned about the steam (tzinora) from the gentile's pot, and similarly here they were not concerned about the period before their festivals.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla explains that the Sages were not concerned about the steam (צינורא) from the gentile's pot, and similarly here they were not concerned about the period before their festivals.

items.text: Baraita on entering a city with idolatry
items.text_en: Baraita on entering a city with idolatry
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir forbids entering a city with idolatry or passing through it to another city, while the Sages permit if the road is not designated for that place.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir forbids entering a city that contains an idolatrous shrine, while the Sages permit it if the road is not exclusively designated for that place.
The baraita then presents the Sages' position: entering is forbidden only if the road is designated for that place, but permitted otherwise.

items.text: Cases of bending before idolatry
items.text_en: Cases of bending before idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases: a thorn, coins, a spring, and water-spouting faces, where one may not bend down due to the appearance of bowing to idolatry, unless it does not appear so.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a thorn before idolatry, ruling that one may not bend to remove it due to the appearance of bowing, unless it does not appear so.
The Mishnah continues with additional cases: a spring before idolatry, water-spouting faces, and a pipe, each with similar restrictions due to appearance or danger.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'not seen'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'not seen'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'if it is not seen' means if it does not appear as bowing to idolatry, not that it is hidden, citing Rav Yehuda's principle that mar'it ayin applies even in private.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'if it is not visible' in the baraita, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that wherever the Sages prohibited due to מראית העין (appearance of impropriety), it is forbidden even in innermost chambers.
The Gemara resolves: rather, 'if it is not visible' means if it does not appear as if he is bowing to the idol, then it is permitted.
The Gemara resolves that 'not seen' means it does not appear as if one is bowing to idolatry, so the action is permitted.

items.text: Need for all cases
items.text_en: Need for all cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why all three cases (thorn, coins, spring) are necessary: each teaches a unique aspect, such as the possibility of avoiding the thorn, the monetary loss of coins, and the danger of thirst from the spring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all three cases are necessary, and explains that if only the thorn case were taught, one might think the prohibition applies only there because one can avoid it, but not to coins where avoidance is impossible.

The Gemara continues that if only coins were taught, one might think the prohibition applies only there due to monetary loss, but not to the thorn where there is pain; and if both were taught, one might think the prohibition does not apply to the spring where there is danger of death, so all three are necessary.

items.text: Danger of drinking from rivers and pools
items.text_en: Danger of drinking from rivers and pools
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the danger mentioned in the baraita is from leeches (עלוקה). A baraita is cited prohibiting drinking water from rivers or pools with one's mouth or one hand, and the danger is again identified as leeches.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions 'faces' (פרצופות), and answers that it is because the Tanna established a pattern to teach a related baraita.
A baraita is cited that prohibits placing one's mouth directly on a pipe to drink, due to danger.
The Gemara asks what the danger is, and answers that it is from leeches (עלוקה).
A baraita is cited that prohibits drinking from rivers or pools with one's mouth or one hand, and identifies the danger as leeches.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Chanina and remedy for swallowing a leech
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Chanina and remedy for swallowing a leech
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Chanina's ruling that one who swallows a leech may have hot water heated for him on Shabbat. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua suggests drinking vinegar (חלא) as a remedy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina's ruling that one who swallows a leech may have hot water heated for him on Shabbat, and a supporting story about Rabbi Nechemya permitting this.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua suggests that while waiting, the person should drink vinegar (חלא) as a remedy for the leech.

items.text: Remedy for swallowing a wasp
items.text_en: Remedy for swallowing a wasp
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin states that one who swallows a wasp (זיבורא) will not live, but should be given a quarter-log of vinegar (חלא שמגז) to possibly live long enough to arrange his affairs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin states that one who swallows a wasp will not live, but should be given a quarter-log of vinegar (חלא שמגז) to possibly live long enough to arrange his affairs.

items.text: Danger of drinking water at night and remedy for shabrire
items.text_en: Danger of drinking water at night and remedy for shabrire
items.desc_en: A baraita prohibits drinking water at night due to the danger of shabrire (a demon). If thirsty, one should wake another and say 'I am thirsty for water', or tap a cup on a barrel and recite a formula invoking his mother's warning against shabrire.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by prohibiting drinking water at night due to danger.
The gemara asks what the specific danger is.
The gemara answers that the danger is from shabrire (a demon).
The gemara asks what remedy exists if one is thirsty.
The baraita provides two remedies: waking another person and saying 'I am thirsty for water', or tapping a cup on a barrel and reciting a formula invoking his mother's warning against shabrire.

items.text: Mishnah: Shops in a city with idolatry
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shops in a city with idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a city with idolatry, shops adorned with wreaths are forbidden, while unadorned ones are permitted, as was the case in Beit She'an.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that in a city with idolatry, shops adorned with wreaths are forbidden, while unadorned ones are permitted, citing the precedent of Beit She'an.

items.text: Resh Lakish limits the prohibition to fragrant adornments
items.text_en: Resh Lakish limits the prohibition to fragrant adornments
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains that the Mishnah only forbids shops adorned with roses and myrtle, from which one benefits by their scent, but shops adorned with fruits are permitted, based on the verse 'לא ידבק בידך מאומה מן החרם' which prohibits benefit.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish limits the Mishnah's prohibition to shops adorned with roses and myrtle (which give scent), but permits those adorned with fruits.
Resh Lakish cites the verse 'לֹא יִדְבַּק בְּיָדְךָ מְאוּמָה מִן הַחֵרֶם' (nothing from the banned item shall cling to your hand) to prove that only benefit from the adornment is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on benefiting from idolatry
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on benefiting from idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav permits causing benefit to idolatry, while Rabbi Yochanan prohibits even benefiting from idolatry, arguing a fortiori that causing benefit is certainly forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav permits causing benefit to idolatry.
Rabbi Yochanan prohibits even benefiting from idolatry, arguing a fortiori that causing benefit is certainly forbidden.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Nathan on tax exemption for idolatrous wreaths
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Nathan on tax exemption for idolatrous wreaths
items.desc_en: A baraita describes a day when idolatry exempts from tax those who place a wreath on their head or donkey in its honor. A Jew in such a situation faces a dilemma: placing the wreath benefits him (forbidden), not placing it causes benefit to idolatry (forbidden). The baraita then rules that items acquired in an idolatrous market must be destroyed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Nathan describing a day when idolatry exempts from tax those who place a wreath in its honor.
The baraita presents the dilemma of a Jew at such an event: placing the wreath benefits him (forbidden), not placing it benefits idolatry (forbidden).
The baraita rules that items acquired in an idolatrous market must be destroyed: animals by crippling, produce by rotting, and metal by disposal in the Dead Sea.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states the dilemma of benefiting vs. causing benefit, contradicting the earlier position that causing benefit is permitted.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya explains that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Nathan, while Rabbi Yochanan holds they do not disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty from the baraita of Rabbi Nathan, which implies that both benefiting and causing benefit are forbidden, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's leniency.
Rav Mesharshiya resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Nathan, while Rabbi Yochanan holds they do not disagree.

items.text: Baraita on attending gentile fairs and its implications
items.text_en: Baraita on attending gentile fairs and its implications
items.desc_en: A baraita permits attending a gentile fair to buy animals, slaves, and property, and even allows a priest to become impure for such purposes. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei debate whether a priest may become impure to study Torah. Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yosei, implying that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Nathan, contradicting his earlier position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits attending a gentile fair to buy animals, slaves, and property, and to register them in their courts, because it is like rescuing from their hands.
The baraita adds that a priest may become impure in the Diaspora and even in a בית הפרס (rabbinically impure field) to litigate with them.
The baraita states that a priest may become impure to study Torah and marry, but Rabbi Yehuda limits this to when no other teacher is available.
Rabbi Yosei argues that even when a teacher is available, one should become impure because not everyone merits learning from everyone.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei's story and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's story and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei cites a precedent of Yosef the priest who followed his rabbi to Sidon to study, and Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: distinction between wholesaler and retailer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: distinction between wholesaler and retailer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan maintains that the Sages do not disagree with Rabbi Nathan, resolving the contradiction by distinguishing between buying from a retailer (who pays tax) and buying from a wholesaler (who does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan by pointing out that the baraita implies the Sages disagree with Rabbi Nathan.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between buying from a retailer (who pays tax) and buying from a wholesaler (who does not), maintaining that the Sages do not actually disagree with Rabbi Nathan.

items.text: Discussion on animal maiming and the definition of עיקור
items.text_en: Discussion on animal maiming and the definition of עיקור
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an animal is maimed despite causing pain, citing the verse 'You shall maim their horses.' It then defines עיקור as cutting the hooves below the knee, and raises a contradiction with a baraita about consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah mandates maiming an animal, given the prohibition of causing צער בעלי חיים (unnecessary suffering to living creatures).
Abaye answers that the Torah itself commanded maiming horses in the verse 'את סוסיהם תעקר' (You shall maim their horses), overriding the concern for animal suffering.
The Gemara cites the definition of עיקור (maiming) as cutting hooves below the knee, then raises a contradiction with a baraita about consecration.
The baraita states that if one consecrates an animal in the present era, the animal is maimed, implying a different definition of עיקור that may contradict the earlier definition.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Methods of disposal for idolatrous items
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Methods of disposal for idolatrous items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for certain items like vegetables, money, and metal vessels, one must take them to the Dead Sea. It defines 'uprooting' as locking the door in front of it so it dies on its own.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that vegetables, money, and metal vessels must be taken to the Dead Sea, and defines 'uprooting' as locking the door so the item dies on its own.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on why not to slaughter or blemish a consecrated animal
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on why not to slaughter or blemish a consecrated animal
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the reason for not slaughtering a consecrated animal is due to disgrace of sacred items, and not doing so to avoid stumbling. He then cites a verse to prohibit making it into a bench. Rava offers an alternative reason: it appears as blemishing consecrated items, but this is only relevant when the Temple stands; now it is not applicable. The Gemara questions if it would be like blemishing a blemished animal, but concludes it is different because here it is not fit for its value or itself.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes the Mishnah's case from the general rule due to the disgrace of sacred objects, and the Gemara asks why not simply slaughter the animal, answering that it would lead to stumbling.
The Gemara objects that one could make the animal into a gistra (a board), and Abaye cites the verse 'You shall not do so to the Lord your God' to forbid destroying sacred objects.
Rava answers that the concern is appearing to blemish sacred animals, but the Gemara notes this applies only when the Temple stands; now that it does not, there is no issue.
The Gemara objects that blemishing a blemished animal is still forbidden, but the Gemara distinguishes: a blemished animal has value for its meat, whereas this animal has no value at all.
Abaye answers by citing a verse that prohibits treating sacred items in a degrading manner.
Rava offers an alternative reason: it appears as blemishing consecrated animals.
The Gemara objects that this would actually be a genuine blemish, not just an appearance.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's reason applies only when the Temple stands; now that the animal is unfit for sacrifice, the concern does not apply.
The Gemara objects that it should be like blemishing an already blemished animal, which is forbidden even when unfit for sacrifice.
The Gemara answers that a blemished animal is still fit for its monetary value, whereas here it is fit for neither its value nor itself.

items.text: Rabbi Yona's inquiry about a gentile slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Yona's inquiry about a gentile slave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona finds Rabbi Illai at the entrance of Tyre and asks about the status of a gentile slave in the context of the Mishnah's rule about a beast being uprooted. Rabbi Illai responds with a baraita that one does not raise or lower gentiles and shepherds of small cattle.

sub.text: Rabbi Yona's question to Rabbi Illai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona's question to Rabbi Illai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona asks Rabbi Illai whether the rule of 'uprooting' applies to a Canaanite slave, and Rabbi Illai cites a baraita that one neither raises nor lowers gentile shepherds.
Rabbi Illai responds by citing a baraita that one does not raise or lower gentiles and shepherds of small cattle, implying the slave is not uprooted.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about buying a slave from a gentile
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about buying a slave from a gentile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the Mishnah's allowance to buy a beast, slaves, and maidservants from gentiles includes a gentile slave or only an Israelite slave. Rabbi Zeira assumes it is an Israelite slave, but Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says even a gentile slave, because it brings him under the wings of the Shechinah. Rav Ashi questions this reasoning for a beast, and explains that the reason is to minimize their numbers, and here too it is permitted to minimize them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the Mishnah's allowance to buy slaves from gentiles includes a gentile slave or only an Israelite slave.
Rabbi Zeira answers that it is an Israelite slave, reasoning that a gentile slave would be of no use to a Jew.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's statement via Ravin
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's statement via Ravin
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish permits even a gentile slave, because it brings him under the wings of the Shechinah.
Rav Ashi objects that the reasoning of bringing under the Shechinah cannot apply to a beast, which is also permitted in the Mishnah.
Rav Ashi resolves that the Mishnah's allowance for a beast is to minimize gentile ownership, and the same reasoning applies to a gentile slave.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yirmeya buying from a homeowner
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yirmeya buying from a homeowner
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bought a sandal and Rabbi Yirmeya bought bread. Each thought the other bought from a merchant, but they actually bought from a homeowner. Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba rules that the prohibition of buying from a gentile only applies when buying from a merchant who pays tax, but from a homeowner who does not pay tax it is permitted. He adds that if Rabbi Yochanan were in a place where tax is collected even from homeowners, he would prohibit it, but they bought from a non-permanent homeowner.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: A story about Rabbi Yaakov buying a sandal and Rabbi Yirmeya buying bread from a homeowner, where each thought the other bought from a merchant, and Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that buying from a homeowner is permitted because no tax is taken from him.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's resolution
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba adds that if Rabbi Yochanan were in a place where tax is taken, he would forbid even buying from a homeowner, but here they bought from a non-regular homeowner.

items.text: Mishnah: Items forbidden to sell to a gentile
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items forbidden to sell to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items forbidden to sell to a gentile: fir-cones, white figs, frankincense, and a white rooster. Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a white rooster among other roosters, and if alone, one must cut off its toe. All other items are permitted by default but forbidden if specified for idolatry. Rabbi Meir adds that a tall palm tree, a chatzav, and a niklaves are forbidden to sell to gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items forbidden to sell to a gentile: fir-cones, dates, palm-branches, frankincense, and a white rooster; Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a white rooster among others or after cutting its toe.

The Mishnah concludes that other items are permitted by default but forbidden if designated for idolatry, and Rabbi Meir adds that a tall palm tree, a thorn-bush, and a niklaves are forbidden to sell to gentiles.

items.text: Identifying איצטרובלין
items.text_en: Identifying איצטרובלין
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what איצטרובלין is, initially suggesting it is תורניתא, but rejects this because תורניתא has no root and thus is not subject to Sabbatical year laws, yet the Mishnah lists it among items added for the Sabbatical year. Rav Safra and Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar identify it as פירי דארזא (cedar fruit).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what איצטרובלין is and initially suggests it is תורניתא (a type of pine cone).

The Gemara objects that if איצטרובלין were תורניתא, it would lack a root and thus not be subject to Sabbatical year laws, contradicting the Mishnah which lists it among items added for the Sabbatical year.
The Gemara cites a baraita stating the rule that anything without a root is exempt from Sabbatical year laws, supporting the objection.

sub.text: Rav Safra and Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Safra and Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra, and similarly Ravin citing Rabbi Elazar, resolve the question by identifying איצטרובלין as פירי דארזא (cedar fruit), which has a root and is subject to Sabbatical year laws.

items.text: Identifying בנות שוח and פטוטרות
items.text_en: Identifying בנות שוח and פטוטרות
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan explains that בנות שוח are white figs, and regarding פטוטרות, they taught that the law applies to their clusters (בפטוטרותיהן שנו).

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan identifies בנות שוח as white figs.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan explains that the law regarding פטוטרות applies to their clusters.

items.text: Identifying לבונה and the law of חבילה
items.text_en: Identifying לבונה and the law of חבילה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies לבונה as לבונה זכה (pure frankincense). A baraita teaches that one may sell all these items in a bundle (חבילה), and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira defines a bundle as no less than three maneh.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies לבונה (frankincense) in the Mishnah as לבונה זכה (pure frankincense).
A baraita teaches that one may sell all these items in a bundle (חבילה), and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira defines a bundle as no less than three maneh.

items.text: Concern about resale for idolatry
items.text_en: Concern about resale for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the gentile might resell the items to others for idolatrous use. Abaye answers that we are commanded only about the direct prohibition of placing a stumbling block before a blind person (לפני), but not about a secondary cause (לפני דלפני).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the gentile might resell the items to others for idolatrous use.
Abaye answers that we are commanded only about the direct prohibition of placing a stumbling block before a blind person (לפני), but not about a secondary cause (לפני דלפני).

items.text: Sale of a white rooster
items.text_en: Sale of a white rooster
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona citing Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Zevid (or an alternate version) explains the distinction: if the gentile says 'a rooster for whom?' it is permitted to sell him a white rooster, but if he says 'a white rooster for whom?' it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Yona citing Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Zevid
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona citing Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Zevid
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona, citing Rabbi Zeira (or Rav Zevid), resolves the mishnah's rule: if the gentile asks 'a rooster for whom?' it is permitted to sell a white rooster, but if he asks 'a white rooster for whom?' it is forbidden.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a white rooster among other roosters. It considers two scenarios: if the gentile specifies 'a white rooster for whom?', even among roosters it should be forbidden; rather, the case is where he says 'a rooster for whom?', and even then, according to Rabbi Yehuda, among roosters it is permitted but alone it is forbidden, while the first Tanna forbids even among roosters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: if the gentile specifies 'a white rooster for whom?', even among other roosters it should be forbidden.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the gentile says 'a rooster for whom?', and Rabbi Yehuda permits it among roosters but forbids it alone, while the first Tanna forbids even among roosters.

items.text: Resolution: the case of 'this and that'
items.text_en: Resolution: the case of 'this and that'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the case is where the gentile says 'this and that' (זה וזה), meaning he points to two roosters, one white and one not. A baraita supports this: Rabbi Yehuda says the prohibition applies only when he says 'this white rooster', but if he says 'this and that' it is permitted; additionally, if the gentile is having a feast for his son or has a sick person in his house, it is permitted even if he specifies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by stating that the case is where the gentile says 'this and that' (זה וזה), pointing to two roosters.

A baraita supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: Rabbi Yehuda rules that the prohibition applies only when the gentile specifies 'this white rooster', but if he says 'this and that' it is permitted.
The baraita adds that even if the gentile specifies 'this rooster', if he is having a feast for his son or has a sick person in his house, the sale is permitted.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a feast for his son
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a feast for his son
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita states that if a gentile makes a feast for his son, it is forbidden only on that day and for that person. Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya resolves that the case in the previous baraita refers to a banquet (טווזיג), which is a general celebration, not specifically for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that if a gentile makes a feast for his son, it is forbidden only on that day and for that person, implying that it is indeed forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya resolves that the case in the previous baraita refers to a banquet (טווזיג), which is a general celebration, not specifically for idolatry.

items.text: General rule: unspecified vs. specified
items.text_en: General rule: unspecified vs. specified
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other items, unspecified (סתמאן) is permitted and specified (פירושן) is forbidden. The Gemara clarifies: unspecified means the gentile says 'white wheat', and specified means he says 'for idolatry'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: for all other items, unspecified (סתמאן) is permitted and specified (פירושן) is forbidden.
The Gemara asks: what are the cases of unspecified and specified?
The Gemara answers: unspecified means the gentile says 'white wheat', and specified means he says 'for idolatry'.

items.text: Clarifying the distinction between ambiguous and explicit requests
items.text_en: Clarifying the distinction between ambiguous and explicit requests
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier Mishnah's distinction between ambiguous and explicit requests is necessary: ambiguous requests (e.g., 'wheat') are permitted, while explicit ones (e.g., 'white wheat') are forbidden. It then clarifies that for a rooster, even an ambiguous request is forbidden, and explains why the explicit case is taught: to counter the assumption that the buyer is merely infatuated with idolatry, not actually worshipping it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's distinction between ambiguous and explicit requests is necessary: ambiguous requests (e.g., 'wheat') are permitted, explicit ones (e.g., 'white wheat') are forbidden.
The Gemara objects that for a rooster, even an ambiguous request is forbidden, contradicting the pattern.
The Gemara answers that the ambiguous request for a rooster is actually explicit (e.g., 'white wheat' implies idolatry), while the explicit case is when the buyer says 'for idolatry'.
The Gemara explains that the explicit case is taught to counter the assumption that the buyer is merely infatuated with idolatry, not actually worshipping it.

items.text: Rav Ashi's queries about a buyer specifying a defective item
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's queries about a buyer specifying a defective item
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises two unresolved questions (תיקו). First, if a buyer asks for a 'white rooster with a cut foot,' may one sell him a whole white rooster? Second, if a buyer repeatedly asks for a white rooster but accepts black and red ones, may one then sell him a white one? In both cases, the concern is whether the buyer is cunningly trying to obtain a white rooster for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether selling a complete white rooster to someone who requested a 'cut white rooster' is permitted, since the request for a defect may indicate the buyer is not for idolatry, or whether he is being deceptive.
Rav Ashi further asks whether, if the buyer repeatedly asks for a white rooster but accepts black and red ones, selling a white one is permitted, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's additional prohibitions and the difficulty with 'palm tree'
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's additional prohibitions and the difficulty with 'palm tree'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir who forbids selling a 'good palm tree' (דקל טב) and other items. Rav Chisda expresses confusion about the tractate's structure. The Gemara questions why a 'good palm tree' is forbidden but a 'bad palm tree' would be permitted, given the general prohibition on selling attached produce. The answer is that 'good palm tree' refers to its fruits, not the tree itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Avimi that the tractate of Avodah Zarah originally had 400 chapters, but they only know five and do not understand what they are saying.

The Gemara asks what the difficulty is: Rabbi Meir says that a 'good palm tree' is forbidden to sell to gentiles, implying a bad palm tree is permitted, but a Mishnah forbids selling anything attached to the ground.
Rav Chisda answers that 'good palm tree' refers to its fruits, not the tree itself, and Rav Huna agrees.
Abimi answers that 'good palm tree' refers to its fruits, not the tree itself, and Rav Huna confirms this interpretation.

items.text: Identifying the obscure terms 'חצב' and 'נקלבס'
items.text_en: Identifying the obscure terms 'חצב' and 'נקלבס'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'חצב' is 'קשיבא' (a type of wood) and 'נקלבס' is 'קורייטי' (a type of ship). Abaye questions Rav Dimi about the usefulness of this identification, and Rav Dimi responds that knowing the local name helps when traveling to that region.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'חצב' is 'קשיבא' (a type of wood) and 'נקלבס' is 'קורייאטי' (a type of ship) according to Rabbi Chama bar Yosef.
Abaye objects to Rav Dimi that explaining 'נקלבס' as 'קורייאטי' is unhelpful because they still do not know what it means.
Rav Dimi answers that the explanation is helpful because when one goes to that place and says 'קורייאטי', people will understand and show the item.

items.text: Mishnah on selling livestock and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Mishnah on selling livestock and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling small livestock to gentiles depends on local custom, but large livestock is universally forbidden. The Gemara questions whether this is merely a custom or an actual prohibition, and raises a contradiction from a baraita that forbids leaving animals in gentile inns due to suspicion of bestiality. Rav resolves this by distinguishing between selling and secluding animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for selling small livestock to gentiles depends on local custom, while large livestock is universally forbidden, with Rabbi Yehuda and Ben Beteira offering exceptions.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's rule is merely a matter of custom (מנהגא) rather than an actual prohibition (איסורא).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that forbids leaving animals in gentile inns due to suspicion of bestiality, implying a real prohibition.

Rav resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between selling and secluding animals: where selling is permitted, seclusion is also permitted, and where seclusion is forbidden, selling is also forbidden.
