items.text: Rabbi Elazar's leniency and Rav's retraction
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's leniency and Rav's retraction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar permits selling large livestock even where seclusion is forbidden, because a gentile cares about his animal's fertility. Rav retracts his earlier stricter view, agreeing that a gentile will not cause the animal to become barren.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar permits selling large livestock even where seclusion is forbidden, because a gentile cares about his animal's fertility.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa citing Rav Sheila bar Avimi in Rav's name
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa citing Rav Sheila bar Avimi in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: Rav retracts his earlier stricter view, agreeing that a gentile cares about his animal's fertility.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reason
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah forbids selling large livestock everywhere, even where bestiality is not suspected. It answers that the concern is the gentile using the animal for labor on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah forbids selling large livestock everywhere, even where bestiality is not suspected.
The Gemara answers that although bestiality is not a concern, the concern is that the gentile will use the animal for labor on Shabbat.

items.text: Refutation and Rami bar Rav Yeiva's new reason
items.text_en: Refutation and Rami bar Rav Yeiva's new reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that once sold, the animal belongs to the gentile, so why forbid? It suggests a decree due to borrowing or renting, but those also transfer ownership. Rami bar Rav Yeiva instead explains the decree is due to a test: the Jew might sell the animal near Shabbat and call it, causing the animal to walk, which is a prohibited act of leading on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that once sold, the animal belongs to the gentile, so why forbid selling? It suggests a decree due to borrowing or renting.
The Gemara objects that borrowing and renting also transfer ownership, so the decree is unfounded.
Rami bar Rav Yeiva explains the decree is due to a test: the Jew might sell the animal near Shabbat and call it, causing the animal to walk, which is a prohibited act of leading on Shabbat.

items.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi challenges the assumption that renting transfers ownership, citing a mishnah about renting a house to a gentile. The Gemara distinguishes idolatry as more severe, based on the verse 'Do not bring an abomination into your house.'

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi challenges the assumption that renting transfers ownership, citing a mishnah that prohibits renting a house to a gentile because he would bring idolatry into it, implying renting does not transfer ownership.
The Gemara distinguishes idolatry as more severe, citing the verse 'Do not bring an abomination into your house' to explain why renting is prohibited there despite not transferring ownership.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's proof and conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's proof and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya challenges the idea that renting transfers ownership, citing a mishnah about a rented cow and terumah feed. The Gemara concludes that renting does not transfer ownership, so the decree stands due to borrowing, renting, and the test scenario.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya objects to the premise that renting transfers ownership, citing a mishnah where a rented cow's feeding rules show the renter does not own it.

The Gemara concludes from the mishnah that renting does not transfer ownership, so the decree against selling a large animal to a gentile stands due to concerns of borrowing, renting, and the test scenario.

items.text: Rav Adda's leniency for a donkey via a broker
items.text_en: Rav Adda's leniency for a donkey via a broker
items.desc_en: Rav Adda permitted selling a donkey through a broker, reasoning that the test concern does not apply (the donkey does not know the Jew's voice), and borrowing/renting are unlikely since the broker does not own the animal. Additionally, the broker can reveal any defects.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda permits selling a donkey through a broker, reasoning that the test concern does not apply (the donkey does not know the Jew's voice), and borrowing/renting are unlikely since the broker does not own the animal, and the broker can reveal any defects.

items.text: Rav Huna's sale of a cow for slaughter
items.text_en: Rav Huna's sale of a cow for slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Huna sold a cow to a gentile, and when questioned by Rav Chisda, he explained that he sold it for slaughter, implying the animal would not be used for labor.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Huna sold a cow to a gentile.
Rav Chisda asks Rav Huna why he sold the cow, implying a violation of the rabbinic prohibition.
Rav Huna answers that he sold the cow for slaughter, so it would not be used for labor or breeding.

items.text: Derivation attempt from shemittah and refutations
items.text_en: Derivation attempt from shemittah and refutations
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the rule from a mishnah about selling a plowing cow during shemittah, where Beit Hillel permits it because the cow can be slaughtered. Rabbah rejects the parallel because one is not commanded about shemittah rest for animals, unlike Shabbat. Abaye counters with a field, where one is commanded, yet Beit Hillel permits selling it. Rav Ashi further objects with vessels, where one is not commanded, yet selling them is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source for the principle that a sale is permitted if the item can be used for a permitted purpose, citing the mishnah where Beit Hillel permits selling a plowing cow during shemittah because it can be slaughtered.
Rabbah rejects the parallel, arguing that in shemittah one is not commanded about animal rest, whereas on Shabbat one is commanded, so the cases are not analogous.
Abaye counters that even where one is commanded, as with a field in shemittah, Beit Hillel permits selling it because it can be left fallow, undermining Rabbah's distinction.
Rav Ashi objects that even where one is not commanded, as with vessels in shemittah, selling them is prohibited, citing the mishnah listing forbidden vessels.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by stating that the criterion is whether a plausible alternative use exists: if there is a plausible alternative, we attribute the sale to that use and permit it even if the seller is commanded; if not, we do not attribute it and prohibit it even if the seller is not commanded.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that the principle depends on whether a permitted use can be plausibly attributed; if so, the sale is permitted even where commanded, and if not, it is forbidden even where not commanded.

items.text: Rabbah sells a donkey to a suspect Jew
items.text_en: Rabbah sells a donkey to a suspect Jew
items.desc_en: Rabbah sells a donkey to a Jew suspected of selling to idolaters. Abaye questions this, arguing that since the Jew will resell to an idolater, it is as if Rabbah sold directly to an idolater. Rabbah defends himself by saying he sold to a Jew, but Abaye retorts that selling to a Jew who resells to an idolater is no different.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah sells a donkey to a Jew suspected of selling to a gentile, and Abaye challenges him, arguing that selling to such a Jew effectively enables sale to a gentile.

items.text: Proof from Cuthite laws and weapons sale
items.text_en: Proof from Cuthite laws and weapons sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about selling small cattle to Cuthites, which varies by custom. It argues that Cuthites are not suspected of bestiality, as shown by leniencies in other contexts. Another baraita prohibits selling weapons to Cuthites, not because of bloodshed (since they are trusted), but because they might resell to an idolater. This supports the principle that selling to a Jew suspected of reselling to an idolater is akin to selling to an idolater.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the sale of small cattle to Cuthites depends on local custom, implying a leniency.
The Gemara questions whether the restriction is due to suspicion of bestiality, and refutes this by citing a baraita that Cuthites are trusted with animals in mixed-gender settings.
Another baraita prohibits selling weapons to Cuthites, not due to bloodshed suspicion, but because they might resell to an idolater.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rabbah's chase
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rabbah's chase
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that a Cuthite does not repent, but a Jew does. However, Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha states that just as it is forbidden to sell to an idolater, so too it is forbidden to sell to a Jew suspected of selling to an idolater. Rabbah then runs after the buyer for three parasangs (or one) but does not catch him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a Jew might repent, but cites Rav Nachman's ruling that it is equally forbidden to sell to a Jew suspected of selling to gentiles, and Rabbah runs after the buyer but fails to catch him.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha states that just as it is forbidden to sell to an idolater, so too it is forbidden to sell to a Jew suspected of selling to an idolater, rejecting the distinction.
Rabbah runs after the buyer for three parasangs (or one) but does not catch him, concluding the incident.

items.text: Selling to a Jewish bandit
items.text_en: Selling to a Jewish bandit
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Abba states that just as it is forbidden to sell to an idolater, so too it is forbidden to sell to a Jewish bandit. The Gemara clarifies: if the bandit is suspected of murder, it is obvious (like an idolater); if not, why forbid? The case involves a tax collector (משמוטא) who might kill to save himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Abba states that just as it is forbidden to sell to an idolater, so too it is forbidden to sell to a Jewish bandit.
The Gemara asks: what is the case? If the bandit is suspected of murder, it is obvious — that is like an idolater.
The Gemara answers: the case involves a tax collector (משמוטא) who does not ordinarily kill but might kill to save himself, so selling to him is forbidden.

items.text: Selling shields to idolaters
items.text_en: Selling shields to idolaters
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute about selling shields to idolaters: some forbid, others permit. The Gemara questions the rationale: if because shields protect them, then even wheat and barley should be forbidden. The discussion is cut off with 'Rav said'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about selling shields to gentiles, with a dispute, and questions the reason, arguing that if the concern is that shields protect them, then even grain should be forbidden.
The Gemara questions the rationale: if the reason is that shields protect them, then even wheat and barley should be forbidden.
The discussion is cut off with 'Rav said', indicating a new statement or resolution that is not fully recorded here.

items.text: Debate on selling shields to gentiles
items.text_en: Debate on selling shields to gentiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of the dispute about selling shields: one prohibits because when weapons are exhausted they kill with the shields, another permits because they flee. Rav Nachman rules in favor of the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the dispute about selling shields is impossible to resolve as presented, and thus another version is needed.
One version prohibits selling shields because when weapons are exhausted, the gentiles kill with the shields themselves.
Another version permits selling shields because when weapons are exhausted, the gentiles flee rather than fight.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules in accordance with the permissive version.

items.text: Prohibition of selling iron anvils
items.text_en: Prohibition of selling iron anvils
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah prohibits selling iron anvils because they weaken weapons. Rav Zevid specifies this applies to Indian iron. Rav Ashi explains that currently we sell them to Persians who protect us.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah prohibits selling iron anvils to gentiles because they weaken weapons.
The Gemara objects that if the reason is weakening weapons, then even picks and axes should be prohibited.
Rav Zevid specifies that the prohibition applies only to Indian iron, which is used for weapons.
Rav Ashi explains that currently we sell to Persians who protect us, so the prohibition does not apply.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken animal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken animal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken animal because it cannot heal. The Sages object that it can be bred and give birth, leading to delaying its slaughter. Rabbi Yehuda responds that it cannot conceive.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken animal because it cannot heal and live.
The Sages object that the animal can be bred and give birth, leading to delaying its slaughter.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that the animal cannot conceive, so it will not give birth.

items.text: Ben Beteira permits selling a horse; Rabbi Yohanan rules accordingly
items.text_en: Ben Beteira permits selling a horse; Rabbi Yohanan rules accordingly
items.desc_en: Ben Beteira permits selling a horse because it performs labor for which one is not liable for a sin-offering. Rabbi prohibits due to weapon and large animal concerns. Rabbi Yohanan explains the large animal concern and rules in accordance with Ben Beteira.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Ben Beteira permits selling a horse because it performs labor for which one is not liable for a sin-offering, while Rabbi prohibits due to two concerns: weapon and large animal.
The Gemara questions: the weapon concern is understandable (the horse kills by trampling), but what is the large animal concern?
Rabbi Yohanan explains: when the horse grows old, the owner might grind it in a mill on Shabbat (violating the prohibition of using a large animal for labor).
Rabbi Yohanan rules the הלכה (binding law) in accordance with Ben Beteira, permitting the sale of a horse.

items.text: Inquiry about a fattened ox
items.text_en: Inquiry about a fattened ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a fattened ox is permitted for sale. It considers the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, questioning whether the ox's typical purpose for slaughter changes the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about a fattened ox, asking whether it is permitted for sale, and notes that the answer depends on the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
The Gemara considers the possibility that Rabbi Yehuda permits only a broken animal, but a fattened ox, which one might delay for slaughter, would be forbidden.
The Gemara considers the alternative possibility that even the Rabbis would permit a fattened ox, since its typical purpose is for slaughter, unlike a regular animal.

items.text: Resolution from the practice of Rabbi's household
items.text_en: Resolution from the practice of Rabbi's household
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel reports that Rabbi's household would offer a fattened ox on their festival, with various deductions. The Gemara explains that Rabbi sought to uproot the practice gradually, and Rav Ashi notes that delaying makes the ox work harder.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel reports that Rabbi's household would offer a fattened ox on their festival, with progressive deductions until they stopped entirely.
The Gemara asks whether the reason for the deductions was concern that one might delay slaughtering the ox, then immediately challenges its own assumption by asking about the first deduction.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi sought to uproot the practice entirely, doing so gradually step by step.
The Gemara objects that if one delays slaughtering the ox, it will become strong and perform forbidden labor.

sub.text: Rav Ashi citing Zevida bar Tora
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi citing Zevida bar Tora
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi in the name of Zevida bar Tora resolves that delaying the ox actually makes it work harder, so the concern is unfounded.

items.text: Mishnah on dangerous animals and buildings; Gemara on selling a lion
items.text_en: Mishnah on dangerous animals and buildings; Gemara on selling a lion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits selling bears, lions, and anything harmful to the public, and lists prohibited buildings. The Gemara discusses whether a large wild animal is like a small animal for sale, and questions the ruling about a broken lion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of selling dangerous animals and lists prohibited and permitted buildings to construct with gentiles.

sub.text: Rav Chanin bar Rav Chisda / Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanin bar Rav Chisda / Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a large wild animal (חיה גסה) is like a small domestic animal (בהמה דקה) for the purpose of פירכוס (checking for signs of life after slaughter), but not for sale to gentiles.
The Gemara adds that even for sale, in places where it is customary to sell large wild animals, one may sell them, and where not, one may not.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: the reason given is that these animals cause public harm, implying that if they do not cause public harm, selling them is permitted.
Rabbah bar Ulla resolves the objection by limiting the Mishnah's leniency to a broken lion that cannot harm the public.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution for the lion
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution for the lion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that a lion is considered broken for labor, aligning with Rabbi Yehuda's view that only animals capable of labor are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by stating that a lion is generally considered broken for labor, aligning with Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Chanan bar Rava
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Chanan bar Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that prohibits selling large wild animals even where small domesticated animals are permitted, refuting Rav Chanan bar Rava's position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited as an objection: just as large domesticated animals may not be sold to gentiles, so too large undomesticated animals may not be sold, even where small animals are permitted, refuting Rav Chanan bar Rava.
The Gemara declares that the baraita constitutes a decisive refutation of Rav Chanan bar Rava's opinion.

items.text: Ravina's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction between the mishnah and baraita by explaining that the mishnah refers to a broken lion, and the baraita to a whole lion, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Ravina raises a contradiction between the mishnah and the baraita: the mishnah forbids selling only dangerous animals, implying that harmless ones are permitted.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by explaining that the mishnah refers to a broken lion, and the baraita to a whole lion, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Ashi supports the resolution by stating that a typical lion is considered broken for work.

items.text: Rav Nachman's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman questions whether a lion is considered a large animal at all, suggesting it might be a small animal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects: who says a lion is classified as a large undomesticated animal? Perhaps it is a small one.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the mishnah that a lion is considered a large animal, as it is listed with bears and other dangerous animals, and concludes that Rav Chanan bar Rava is refuted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces that Rav Ashi infers from the mishnah and raises a refutation.
The gemara cites the mishnah that one may not sell bears or lions to gentiles, implying that without public danger, one may sell them.
Rav Ashi concludes that the reason a lion is permitted is because a typical lion is broken for work, so Rav Chanan bar Rava's position is refuted.

items.text: What labor does a large animal do?
items.text_en: What labor does a large animal do?
items.desc_en: Abaye reports that Mar Yehuda told him that large animals like the עֲרוֹד (hyena) can grind millstones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what work does a large undomesticated animal actually perform? Abaye answers that Mar Yehuda told him that the hyena (ערוד) grinds millstones.

Abaye answers that Mar Yehuda told him that the household of Mar Yochani (an important family) would grind millstones using the עֲרוֹד (hyena), a large undomesticated animal, thus demonstrating its capacity for labor.

items.text: The status of large animals for פירבוס (breaking in)
items.text_en: The status of large animals for פירבוס (breaking in)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and others transmit a tradition that a large wild animal is like a small domesticated animal for the purpose of breaking in (פירבוס), with multiple attributions to Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Rav Yehuda taught him a tradition from a great authority, but he does not know if it is from Rav or Shmuel.
Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Shmuel and later Rabbah bar Yirmeya citing Rav, confirming the tradition was transmitted in both names.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's encounter with Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's encounter with Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Asi citing Rav Chama bar Gurya in Rav's name, and when questioned about Rabbah bar Yirmeya's authority, Rav Asi dismisses the concern, saying the tradition is established from both sources.

The gemara concludes with a formal chain of transmission: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Asi citing Rabbah bar Yirmeya citing Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav, that a large wild animal is like a small domesticated animal for breaking in (פירבוס).

items.text: The three types of basilicae
items.text_en: The three types of basilicae
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan lists three types of basilicae (public buildings), and Rava distinguishes which are permitted and which are forbidden to build with gentiles.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan lists three types of basilicae (public buildings): those of kings, bathhouses, and treasuries.
Rava rules that two of the basilicae (kings' and treasuries) are permitted to build with gentiles, and one (bathhouses) is forbidden, with a mnemonic from Psalms.
An alternative tradition reports that Rava said all three basilicae are permitted.
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah that forbids building a basilica, a gardom (judgment platform), an amphitheater, and a bema (speaker's platform) with gentiles.
The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the Mishnah's list: the forbidden structures are specifically the gardom, amphitheater, and bema (not the basilicae themselves).

items.text: The arrest of Rabbi Eliezer for heresy
items.text_en: The arrest of Rabbi Eliezer for heresy
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Eliezer was arrested for heresy, brought before a governor, and after being released, his disciples came to comfort him. Rabbi Akiva suggests that perhaps heresy had come upon him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by recounting that Rabbi Eliezer was arrested for heresy and brought before a governor, who rebuked him for engaging in such trivial matters.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that the Judge is trustworthy, which the governor misunderstands as referring to himself, leading to Rabbi Eliezer's release.
After Rabbi Eliezer returns home and refuses comfort, Rabbi Akiva asks permission to speak and suggests that perhaps heresy had come upon him.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's story of entrapment by minut
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's story of entrapment by minut
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer recounts how he was led astray by a teaching from Yeshu the Nazarene regarding the use of a harlot's hire for a toilet, which led him to apostasy. He then cites a verse warning against approaching heresy and authority.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Eliezer how he was led astray, and Rabbi Eliezer recounts meeting a disciple of Yeshu the Nazarene who asked about using a harlot's hire for a toilet.

sub.text: Yeshu the Nazarene's teaching (quoted by the disciple)
sub.text_en: Yeshu the Nazarene's teaching (quoted by the disciple)
sub.desc_en: The disciple cites Yeshu's teaching that since the harlot's hire comes from filth, it may return to filth, permitting a toilet for the High Priest.
Rabbi Eliezer states that this teaching enticed him into apostasy (מינוּת), and he violated the verse warning against approaching heresy and authority.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about harlot's hire
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about harlot's hire
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the Rabbis interpret the verse 'from the hire of a harlot', citing Rav Chisda's teaching that a hired harlot eventually hires others. This view is disputed by Rabbi Pedat, who limits the Torah's prohibition to incestuous relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the verse 'from the hire of a harlot'.
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis interpret it according to Rav Chisda, who taught that any hired harlot eventually hires others, as the verse says.
Rabbi Pedat disputes Rav Chisda, arguing that the Torah only prohibits incestuous relations, citing the verse 'do not approach to uncover nakedness'.

items.text: Ulla's practice and the prohibition of closeness
items.text_en: Ulla's practice and the prohibition of closeness
items.desc_en: Ulla's practice of kissing his sisters on the hand or chest is cited, and he himself states that any closeness is forbidden, based on the principle of keeping far from a vineyard.

sub.desc_en: Ulla's practice of kissing his sisters on the hand or chest when returning from the study hall is described.
The gemara notes that Ulla's own practice contradicts his stated principle.
Ulla states that any closeness (קריבה בעלמא) is forbidden, based on the principle of keeping far from a vineyard (לך לך אמרין נזירא סחור סחור לכרמא לא תקרב).

items.text: The two daughters of the leech and the fate of penitents
items.text_en: The two daughters of the leech and the fate of penitents
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva explains that the 'two daughters' crying 'give, give' are heresy and authority, which cry from Gehinnom. The Gemara then interprets a verse to mean that if sinners repent, they will not attain the paths of life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the leech's two daughters crying 'give, give' and asks what this means.
Mar Ukva explains that the two daughters are heresy (מינות) and authority (הרשות), which cry from Gehinnom, having demanded 'bring, bring' in this world.
An alternative version states that Rav Chisda said in the name of Mar Ukva that Gehinnom itself cries out, demanding the two daughters who cried 'bring, bring' in this world.
The Gemara questions the verse 'all who enter it will not return' — if they do not return, how can they attain the paths of life?
The Gemara resolves that the verse means: even if they repent, they will not attain the paths of life.

items.text: Question about death for those who leave heresy
items.text_en: Question about death for those who leave heresy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one who leaves heresy dies, citing a case where a woman who committed a light sin and heresy did not die. It concludes that she did not repent properly, so she did not die.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one who leaves heresy dies, citing a case where a woman who committed a light sin and heresy did not die despite Rav Chisda's instruction to provide for her.
The Gemara answers that the woman did not repent properly, so she did not die.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Dordya's repentance
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Dordya's repentance
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one who leaves a regular sin dies, citing the story of Rabbi Elazar ben Dordya, who repented after a lifetime of sin and was accepted. It concludes that his sin was like heresy because he was so immersed in it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an alternative version of the earlier claim: that one who leaves heresy dies, but one who leaves a regular sin does not.
The Gemara objects by citing the case of the woman who came before Rav Chisda and died, implying she repented from a regular sin.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the woman's statement 'the lightest of the light' implies she was also involved in heresy.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita about Rabbi Elazar ben Dordya, who was a habitual sinner with prostitutes.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar ben Dordya's sin was considered like heresy because he was so deeply immersed in it, so the principle that one who leaves heresy dies still holds.

items.text: Rabbi's reaction and the story of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan
items.text_en: Rabbi's reaction and the story of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan
items.desc_en: Rabbi weeps and comments that one can acquire the world to come in an hour. He also notes that penitents are called 'Rabbi'. The daf ends with Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan approaching a crossroads with a path to idolatry and a path to a brothel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi weeps and declares that one can acquire the world to come in many years or in a single hour.
Rabbi adds that penitents are not only accepted but also called 'Rabbi'.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan approach a crossroads with a path to idolatry and a path to a brothel, and one suggests taking the path to idolatry.

items.text: The plan to subdue the evil inclination
items.text_en: The plan to subdue the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Two sages discuss going to the entrance of a brothel to subdue their evil inclination and receive reward. When they arrive, they see the prostitutes and are subdued before them. One asks the other the source for this idea, and he quotes Proverbs 2:11: 'Discretion (mezimah) will watch over you, understanding will guard you.'

sub.desc_en: The first sage notes that the inclination to idolatry is subdued; the second proposes going to the brothel entrance to overpower their inclination and earn reward, and when they arrive the prostitutes yield before them.
The first sage asks the second for the source of the idea that the Torah protects against lewdness.
The second sage cites Proverbs 2:11, interpreting 'mezimah' as the Torah that guards against lewdness.

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse
items.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rava: What is 'mezimah'? If it means Torah, which is called 'zimah' (plan) and is translated as 'counsel of sins', then the verse should say 'zimah'. Rava explains: It means that from the matter of zimah (sin) it will guard you, and Torah will protect you.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rava what 'mezimah' means, proposing that if it refers to Torah (called 'zimah'), the verse should have said 'zimah' instead.
Rava explains that the verse means: from the matter of zimah (sin) it will guard you, and Torah will protect you.

items.text: The arrest of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon
items.text_en: The arrest of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon were arrested, Rabbi Elazar said to Rabbi Chanina: Fortunate are you for being arrested on one charge, woe is me for being arrested on five. Rabbi Chanina replied: Fortunate are you for being arrested on five charges and you will be saved, woe is me for being arrested on one charge and I will not be saved, because you engaged in Torah and acts of kindness, while I engaged only in Torah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the arrest of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon, with Rabbi Elazar lamenting his five charges versus Rabbi Chanina's one.

Rabbi Chanina responds that Rabbi Elazar's five charges will lead to salvation due to his engagement in both Torah and acts of kindness, while his own single charge is fatal because he only studied Torah.

items.text: Support from Rav Huna
items.text_en: Support from Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna: Anyone who engages only in Torah is like one who has no God, as it is stated: 'And many days for Israel without a true God' (2 Chronicles 15:3). What does 'without a true God' mean? That anyone who engages only in Torah is like one who has no God.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who engages only in Torah study is like one without a God, citing the verse from II Chronicles 15:3.

items.text: Questioning Rabbi Chanina's lack of acts of kindness
items.text_en: Questioning Rabbi Chanina's lack of acts of kindness
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: Did Rabbi Chanina not engage in acts of kindness? It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: A person should not give money to a charity fund unless a Torah scholar like Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon is appointed over it. The Gemara answers: He was trusted, but he did not actually do the work. Another baraita: He said: Purim money was exchanged for me with charity money, and I distributed it to the poor. The Gemara answers: He did do it, but not as he should have.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon truly did not engage in acts of kindness.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that one should only give charity money to a fund supervised by a Torah scholar like Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina was trusted to oversee the fund, but he himself did not perform the acts of charity.
The Gemara objects with another baraita where Rabbi Chanina himself recounts that he distributed charity money that was mixed with his Purim funds.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina did perform acts of charity, but not to the extent that he should have.

items.text: The trial of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and the miracles
items.text_en: The trial of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and the miracles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta was brought before the Romans. They asked why he taught Torah and why he stole. He answered: If one is a swordsman, he is not a scribe, and if a scribe, not a swordsman; since one is not present, the other is also not present. They asked why he is called 'Rabbi'; he said he is a teacher of tarsiyim (weavers). They brought two bundles and asked which is warp and which is woof; a miracle occurred: a wasp sat on the warp and a bee on the woof. They asked why he did not come to the house of judgment; he said he was old and feared being trampled. A miracle occurred: an old man was trampled that day. They asked why he freed his slave; he said it never happened. One stood to testify against him; Elijah came disguised as a courtier and said: Since miracles happened for him in all matters, a miracle will also happen here, and that man is showing his wickedness. He did not heed; Elijah threw him 400 parasangs away.

sub.desc_en: The Romans bring Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and accuse him of teaching Torah and stealing; he responds that the two charges are mutually exclusive.
They ask why he is called 'Rabbi'; he answers that he is a teacher of weavers.
They bring two coils of wool and ask which is warp and which is woof; a miracle occurs with hornets indicating the correct identification.
They ask why he did not come to the house of judgment; he says he feared being trampled, and a miracle occurs as an old man is trampled that day.
They ask why he freed his slave; he denies it, and Elijah appears disguised as a courtier to warn the potential witness.
The witness ignores the warning, but Elijah throws the letter he was carrying 400 parasangs away, preventing his testimony.

items.text: The trial of Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon
items.text_en: The trial of Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon was brought before the Romans. They asked why he engaged in Torah. He answered: 'As the Lord my God commanded me' (Deuteronomy 4:5). Immediately they decreed burning for him, execution for his wife, and sitting in a brothel for his daughter. The burning was because he...

sub.desc_en: The Romans brought Rabbi Chanina ben Tradyon and asked why he engaged in Torah; he answered with a verse from Deuteronomy.
Immediately the Romans decreed burning for him, execution for his wife, and sitting in a brothel for his daughter, with the reason for burning introduced.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chanina could have pronounced the Divine Name, given the Mishnah that lists such a person as having no share in the World to Come. It answers that he did so for study purposes, as permitted by the verse 'you shall not learn to do' but you may learn to understand and teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chanina could have pronounced the Divine Name, given the Mishnah that lists such a person as having no share in the World to Come.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina did so for study purposes, as permitted by the verse 'you shall not learn to do' but you may learn to understand and teach.

items.text: Reason for punishment: public pronouncement
items.text_en: Reason for punishment: public pronouncement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chanina was punished not for the act itself but because he pronounced the Name in public. His wife was executed for failing to protest his actions, establishing the principle that one who can protest but does not is punished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Chanina was punished, given that his act was permissible for study.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina was punished because he pronounced the Name in public (בפרהסיא).
The Gemara explains that his wife was executed for failing to protest his public act.
The Gemara establishes the principle that one who can protest but does not is punished.

items.text: His daughter's punishment and Rabbi Yochanan's story
items.text_en: His daughter's punishment and Rabbi Yochanan's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that his daughter was sentenced to sit in a brothel. Rabbi Yochanan recounts how her beautiful gait once led Roman nobles to comment, and she immediately became meticulous about her steps, illustrating that sins one tramples in this world surround him on judgment day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that his daughter was sentenced to sit in a brothel.
Rabbi Yochanan recounts how his daughter's beautiful gait once led Roman nobles to comment, and she immediately became meticulous about her steps.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains the verse 'עֲוֹן עֲקֵבַי יְסוּבֵּנִי' (the iniquity of my heels surrounds me) to mean that sins one tramples in this world surround him on judgment day.

items.text: The family's acceptance of divine judgment
items.text_en: The family's acceptance of divine judgment
items.desc_en: When the three were led out, they each recited a verse accepting the judgment: Rabbi Chanina said 'The Rock, His work is perfect', his wife said 'A God of faithfulness and without iniquity', and his daughter said 'Great in counsel and mighty in deed'. Rabbi commented on how great they were to have three verses of justification ready.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces that when the three were led out, they accepted the divine judgment.
Rabbi Chanina recites the verse 'The Rock, His work is perfect' to justify the judgment.
His wife recites the verse 'A God of faithfulness and without iniquity' to justify the judgment.
His daughter recites the verse 'Great in counsel and mighty in deed' to justify the judgment.
Rabbi comments on how great these righteous people were to have three verses of justification ready at the time of judgment.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's warning and Rabbi Chanina's merit
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's warning and Rabbi Chanina's merit
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that when Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma was ill, Rabbi Chanina visited him. Rabbi Yosei warned him that the Roman empire was divinely ordained and that he had heard Rabbi Chanina was publicly teaching Torah. Rabbi Chanina replied 'Heaven will have mercy'. Rabbi Yosei insisted, predicting he would be burned with his Torah scroll. Rabbi Chanina asked about his share in the World to Come, and upon hearing that he had once mistakenly used Purim money for charity, Rabbi Yosei declared his portion and lot to be with him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma visiting the ill Rabbi Chanina and warning him that the Roman empire is divinely ordained and that he has heard Rabbi Chanina is publicly teaching Torah with a Torah scroll in his lap.
Rabbi Chanina replies 'Heaven will have mercy', but Rabbi Yosei insists that he will be burned with his Torah scroll, prompting Rabbi Chanina to ask about his share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yosei asks if any incident occurred, and upon hearing that Rabbi Chanina mistakenly used Purim money for charity, he declares that his portion and lot shall be with Rabbi Chanina.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's execution and his response
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's execution and his response
items.desc_en: Shortly after, Rabbi Yosei died and was eulogized by Roman nobles. On their return, they found Rabbi Chanina teaching Torah publicly and arrested him. They wrapped him in a Torah scroll, surrounded him with vine branches, set them on fire, and placed wet sponges on his heart to prolong his death. His daughter asked if she should see him thus; he replied that being burned alone would be hard, but with the Torah scroll, the One who avenges the Torah will avenge him. His students asked what he saw; he said the parchment burns but the letters fly up. They urged him to open his mouth to let the fire enter, but he refused, saying it is better that the One who gave the soul take it, and not harm himself.

sub.desc_en: The narrative reports that shortly after Rabbi Yosei's death, Roman nobles found Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon publicly teaching Torah with a Torah scroll in his lap.

The Romans wrapped Rabbi Chanina in a Torah scroll, surrounded him with vine branches, set them on fire, and placed wet sponges on his heart to prolong his death; his daughter asked if she should see him thus, and he replied that being burned alone would be hard, but with the Torah scroll, the One who avenges the Torah will avenge him.

His students asked what he saw; he said the parchment burns but the letters fly up. They urged him to open his mouth to let the fire enter, but he refused, saying it is better that the One who gave the soul take it, and not harm himself.

items.text: The executioner's repentance and the Bat Kol
items.text_en: The executioner's repentance and the Bat Kol
items.desc_en: The executioner (Klastoniri) asked Rabbi Chanina if he would bring him to the World to Come if he increased the flame and removed the sponges. Rabbi Chanina agreed and swore to him. The executioner did so, and Rabbi Chanina's soul departed quickly. The executioner then jumped into the fire. A Bat Kol declared that both Rabbi Chanina and the executioner are destined for the World to Come. Rabbi wept, saying some acquire their world in one hour, others over many years.

sub.desc_en: The executioner asks Rabbi Chanina if he will bring him to the World to Come by increasing the flame and removing the sponges.
Rabbi Chanina agrees and swears to the executioner.

sub.text: Narrative: executioner's action and Rabbi Chanina's death
sub.text_en: Narrative: executioner's action and Rabbi Chanina's death
sub.desc_en: The executioner increases the flame and removes the sponges, causing Rabbi Chanina's soul to depart quickly.
The executioner jumps into the fire.
A Bat Kol declares that both Rabbi Chanina and the executioner are destined for the World to Come.
Rabbi weeps and remarks that some acquire their world in one hour, others over many years.

items.text: Rabbi Meir rescues his sister-in-law from the brothel
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir rescues his sister-in-law from the brothel
items.desc_en: Bruriah, Rabbi Meir's wife and Rabbi Chanina's daughter, told him it was disgraceful that her sister sat in a brothel. Rabbi Meir took a tarkab of dinars and went, reasoning that if no transgression had occurred, a miracle would happen; if she had sinned, no miracle would occur. He disguised himself as a horseman and propositioned her, but she repeatedly refused, saying she was menstruating, or that there were many prettier women. He realized she had not sinned. He then went to her guard, bribed him with half the money, and taught him to say 'God of Meir answer me' if in trouble.

sub.desc_en: Bruriah, Rabbi Meir's wife and Rabbi Chanina's daughter, tells him it is disgraceful that her sister sits in a brothel; Rabbi Meir takes a tarkab of dinars and goes, reasoning that if no transgression occurred a miracle will happen, but if she sinned no miracle will occur.
Rabbi Meir disguises himself as a horseman and propositions her; she refuses, claiming she is menstruating and that there are prettier women, so he realizes she has not sinned.
Rabbi Meir goes to the guard, bribes him with half the tarkab of dinars, and teaches him to say 'God of Meir answer me' if in trouble.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's escape and flight to Babylonia
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's escape and flight to Babylonia
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Meir was saved from dogs by invoking 'Elaha d'Meir aneini', then was captured and sentenced to crucifixion but again saved. The Romans placed his image at the gate of Rome, and he escaped by entering a brothel; Elijah disguised as a harlot helped him. He fled to Babylonia, either due to this incident or the Beruriah incident.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir was saved from dogs, and he invokes 'Elaha d'Meir aneini' to drive them away.
The story continues: Rabbi Meir is captured and sentenced to crucifixion, but again saved by the same invocation.
The Romans place Rabbi Meir's image at the gate of Rome, and he escapes by entering a brothel, with Elijah disguised as a harlot helping him.
Rabbi Meir flees to Babylonia, with two versions of the reason: this incident or the Beruriah incident.

items.text: Baraita: Attending amphitheaters and circuses is a 'seat of scoffers'
items.text_en: Baraita: Attending amphitheaters and circuses is a 'seat of scoffers'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who goes to amphitheaters (istadin) and circuses (karkom) and sees various performers is considered to have attended a 'moshav leitzim' (seat of scoffers), and the verse 'Ashrei ha'ish' applies, indicating these things lead to neglect of Torah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that attending amphitheaters and circuses constitutes a 'moshav leitzim' (seat of scoffers), leading to neglect of Torah.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot on amphitheaters and circuses
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot on amphitheaters and circuses
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita permits attending amphitheaters because one can shout and save someone, and circuses are permitted for the settlement of the state, provided one does not engage in business with them. The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding circuses by distinguishing between engaging in business and not, but the contradiction regarding amphitheaters remains. It is resolved by attributing the views to different Tannaim: the first baraita is the anonymous Tanna, while Rabbi Natan permits it for two reasons: shouting to save and testifying about a woman to allow her to remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot regarding amphitheaters and circuses.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding circuses by distinguishing between engaging in business and not, but notes the contradiction regarding amphitheaters remains.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding amphitheaters by attributing the views to different Tannaim: the first baraita is the anonymous Tanna, while Rabbi Natan permits it for two reasons.

items.text: Baraita on theaters and circuses due to idolatry
items.text_en: Baraita on theaters and circuses due to idolatry
items.desc_en: Another baraita prohibits going to theaters (tertaya'ot) and circuses (kirkesi'ot) because they fertilize for idolatry, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: where they fertilize, it is forbidden due to suspicion of idolatry; where they do not, it is forbidden due to 'moshav leitzim'. Rabbi Chanina from Sura explains the difference between them is whether one engages in business (nasa v'natan).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's position: one may not go to theaters (טרטיאות) and circuses (קרקסיאות) because they fertilize for idolatry.
The Sages distinguish: where they fertilize, it is forbidden due to suspicion of idolatry; where they do not, it is forbidden due to 'moshav leitzim' (seat of scoffers).
The gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.
Rabbi Chanina mi'Sura answers: the difference between them is whether one engages in business (nasa v'natan) at the venue.

items.text: Derashot on the progression from walking to scoffing
items.text_en: Derashot on the progression from walking to scoffing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi expounds the verse 'Ashrei ha'ish' to show that walking leads to standing, standing to sitting, sitting to scoffing, and scoffing brings punishment. Rabbi Eliezer says scoffing brings suffering, and Rava asks the rabbis not to scoff to avoid suffering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi asks a rhetorical question about the verse 'Ashrei ha'ish', noting the logical inconsistency of the progression from not walking to standing, sitting, and scoffing.
He explains that the verse teaches a progression: walking leads to standing, standing to sitting, sitting to scoffing, and scoffing brings punishment.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that scoffing brings suffering, citing the verse 'Al tithloshazu pen yechzeku mosreichhem'.
Rava asks the rabbis not to scoff, so that suffering will not come upon them.

items.text: Consequences of scoffing: diminished sustenance, Gehinnom, destruction
items.text_en: Consequences of scoffing: diminished sustenance, Gehinnom, destruction
items.desc_en: Rav Ketina says scoffing diminishes one's sustenance; Reish Lakish says the scoffer falls into Gehinnom; Rabbi Oshaya says the haughty fall into Gehinnom; Rabbi Chanilai bar Chanilai says scoffing causes world destruction. Rabbi Eliezer concludes that scoffing begins with suffering and ends with destruction. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi then interprets 'Ashrei ha'ish' as referring to avoiding theaters, circuses, and stadiums.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ketina states that scoffing diminishes one's sustenance, citing the verse 'משך ידו את לוצצים' (He stretched out His hand against scoffers).
Reish Lakish says the scoffer falls into Gehinnom, interpreting 'עברה' (wrath) as Gehinnom based on the verse 'יום עברה היום ההוא' (that day is a day of wrath).
Rabbi Oshaya teaches that the haughty fall into Gehinnom, using the same verse as Reish Lakish.
Rabbi Chanilai bar Chanilai states that scoffing causes world destruction, citing the verse 'כי כלה ונחרצה שמעתי' (for I have heard of destruction and decree).
Rabbi Eliezer concludes that scoffing begins with suffering and ends with destruction.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi interprets 'Ashrei ha'ish' as referring to avoiding theaters, circuses, and stadiums.

items.text: Warning against complacency and the obligation to study Torah
items.text_en: Warning against complacency and the obligation to study Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara warns that one might think: since I have not attended theaters or circuses, I will indulge in sleep. But the verse teaches 'u'vetorato yehgeh yomam valayla' — one must engage in Torah study day and night. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan begins to expound 'Ashrei ha'ish' as referring to... (the text breaks off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: one might think that since he avoided theaters and circuses, he may indulge in sleep.
The Gemara counters with the verse 'וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה' (and in His Torah he meditates day and night), teaching that one must engage in Torah study instead of sleeping.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan begins to expound the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ' (Happy is the man) as referring to one who avoids these entertainments, but the text breaks off.

items.text: Interpretation of Psalm 1:1 on Abraham
items.text_en: Interpretation of Psalm 1:1 on Abraham
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the first verse of Psalm 1, applying each phrase to Abraham's avoidance of wicked groups: the generation of the Dispersion, the people of Sodom, and the Philistines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the first clause of Psalm 1:1, applying 'walked not in the counsel of the wicked' to Abraham's avoidance of the generation of the Dispersion, and 'stood not in the way of sinners' to his avoidance of Sodom.
The Gemara interprets the third clause of Psalm 1:1, applying 'nor sat in the seat of the scornful' to Abraham's avoidance of the Philistines, citing the episode with Samson.

items.text: Question on 'Happy is the man' and answers
items.text_en: Question on 'Happy is the man' and answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'Happy is the man' (אִישׁ) and not 'woman', and provides two answers: one about repentance in one's prime, and another about overcoming one's evil inclination like a man.

items.text: Interpretation of 'in His commandments he delights greatly' and 'his delight is in the Torah of the Lord'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'in His commandments he delights greatly' and 'his delight is in the Torah of the Lord'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that one should delight in the commandments themselves, not their reward, citing a mishnah. Rabbi then teaches that a person learns Torah only from the place their heart desires.

items.text: Anecdote of Levi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi with Rabbi
items.text_en: Anecdote of Levi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi with Rabbi
items.desc_en: Levi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were studying before Rabbi. When they finished a book, Levi wanted Proverbs, but Rabbi Shimon wanted Psalms. Rabbi overruled Levi, and when they reached the verse about delight, Rabbi expounded it. Levi then said Rabbi gave them permission to leave.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Levi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were studying before Rabbi, and when they finished a book, Levi requested Proverbs while Rabbi Shimon requested Psalms.
The narrator reports that Rabbi compelled Levi to acquiesce and brought Psalms, then Rabbi expounded the verse.
Rabbi expounds the verse, stating that a person can learn Torah only from a place in the Torah that his heart desires.
Levi says that Rabbi has given them permission to leave, implying he wishes to study Proverbs instead.

items.text: Rava's teachings on Torah study
items.text_en: Rava's teachings on Torah study
items.desc_en: Rava delivers several teachings: one should study where their heart desires; initially Torah is called by God's name, ultimately by the student's name; one should learn first then review; and one should always study even if they forget or don't understand.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avdimi bar Chama teaches that one who engages in Torah study has their desires fulfilled by God, citing the verse 'כי אם בתורת ה' חפצו'.
Rava states that a person should always study Torah in a place their heart desires, citing the same verse.
Rava teaches that initially the Torah is called by God's name, but ultimately it is called by the student's name, as the verse shifts from 'תורת ה׳' to 'תורתו'.
Rava teaches that one should first study Torah broadly and only then analyze it deeply, as the verse first says 'בתורת ה׳' and then 'ובתורתו יהגה'.
Rava teaches that one should always study and review even if they forget or do not understand, citing the verse 'גרסה נפשי לתאבה' which uses the word 'גרסה' (breaks) rather than 'טחנה' (grinds).

items.text: Contradictions resolved: initial vs. final status
items.text_en: Contradictions resolved: initial vs. final status
items.desc_en: Rava and Ulla resolve apparent contradictions in verses about God's throne and wisdom, explaining that initially it is lowly (on the roofs, at the head of heights) but ultimately elevated (on a throne, on the way).

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between two verses: one says 'upon the roofs' and another says 'upon a throne'.
Rava resolves the contradiction: initially the Torah is 'upon the roofs', but ultimately it is 'upon a throne'.
The Gemara raises another contradiction: one verse says 'at the head of heights' and another says 'by the path'.
The Gemara resolves: initially the Torah is 'at the head of heights', but ultimately it is 'by the path'.
Ulla raises a contradiction: one verse says 'drink water from your cistern' and another says 'flowing waters from your well'.
Ulla resolves: initially one drinks from one's own cistern, but ultimately one produces flowing waters from one's own well.

items.text: Teachings on Torah study in bundles and the hunter metaphor
items.text_en: Teachings on Torah study in bundles and the hunter metaphor
items.desc_en: Rava explains that studying Torah in bundles (superficially) diminishes it, but gathering it by hand increases it. Rav Sheizvi and Rav Sheshet discuss the fate of a deceitful hunter, and Rav Dimi gives a parable about breaking the wings of the first bird caught.

sub.text: Rava said Rav Sechora said Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava said Rav Sechora said Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Huna's interpretation of Proverbs 13:11: studying Torah in bundles diminishes it, but gathering little by little increases it.
Rava notes that the Sages know this principle but transgress it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak testifies that he practiced this method and his learning endured.

sub.text: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.text_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi interprets Proverbs 12:27: the deceitful hunter will not live long.
Rav Sheshet offers an opposite reading: the cunning hunter will indeed roast his prey.
Rav Dimi gives a parable: breaking the wings of the first bird caught ensures all remain; otherwise they escape.

items.text: Learning from one teacher vs. many
items.text_en: Learning from one teacher vs. many
items.desc_en: The house of Rabbi Yannai and Rav Chisda teach that one who learns Torah from only one teacher never sees a blessing. Rav Chisda feared his students would leave him, and they did go to Rava, who distinguished between reasoning (where multiple teachers are better) and memorization (where one is better).

sub.desc_en: The House of Rabbi Yannai interprets the verse 'like a tree transplanted' (שָׁתוּל) rather than 'planted' (נָטוּעַ) to teach that one who learns Torah from only one teacher never sees a sign of blessing.
Rav Chisda hesitantly tells his students the same principle, fearing they will leave him, and indeed they go to Rava.
Rava resolves the tension by distinguishing: for reasoning (סְבָרָא) multiple teachers are better, but for memorization (גְּמָרָא) one teacher is preferable.

items.text: Opening statement on dividing one's years
items.text_en: Opening statement on dividing one's years
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai teaches that one should divide his years into three parts: one-third for Scripture, one-third for Mishnah, and one-third for Talmud.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai teaches that one should divide his years into three parts: one-third for Scripture, one-third for Mishnah, and one-third for Talmud.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on lifespan
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on lifespan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can divide his years if he does not know how long he will live, and answers that the division refers to days, not years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can divide his years into thirds if he does not know how long he will live.
The Gemara answers that the division refers to each day, not to one's entire lifespan.

items.text: Rava's teaching on the verse 'whose fruit gives in its season'
items.text_en: Rava's teaching on the verse 'whose fruit gives in its season'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that if one studies Torah at the proper time, his leaf will not wither; otherwise, he is like the wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that if one studies Torah at the proper time, his leaf will not wither, but if not, the verse applies to him as a wicked person.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's teaching on the dangers of improper teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's teaching on the dangers of improper teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav teaches that a student who has not reached the level to teach but does so, and one who has reached it but refrains, both cause harm. The Gemara clarifies the age of forty and notes that Rava taught earlier because he was exceptional.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Huna citing Rav interprets the verse 'כי רבים חללים הפילה' (for many slain she has felled) as referring to a student who teaches before reaching the level of authority, and 'ועצומים כל הרוגיה' (and mighty are all her slain) as referring to a student who has reached the level but refrains from teaching.
The Gemara asks up to what age this restriction applies, and answers until forty years.
The Gemara objects that Rava taught before the age of forty, contradicting the rule.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's case was exceptional because his peers were equal to him in knowledge, so he was permitted to teach earlier.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Adda's teaching on the conversation of Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda's teaching on the conversation of Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda in the name of Rav teaches that even the casual conversation of Torah scholars requires study, as derived from the verse 'and its leaf shall not wither'.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Adda citing Rav, or Rav Acha bar Abba citing Rav Hamnuna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda citing Rav, or Rav Acha bar Abba citing Rav Hamnuna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda (or Rav Acha bar Abba) in the name of Rav (or Rav Hamnuna) teaches that even the casual conversation of Torah scholars requires study, as the verse says 'and its leaf shall not wither'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching on success through Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching on success through Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who engages in Torah study will have his possessions succeed, citing verses from Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi demonstrates that the principle that one who engages in Torah study will have his property succeed is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and tripled in the Writings, citing verses from each section.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who engages in Torah study will have his possessions succeed, citing verses from Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

items.text: Rabbi Alexandri's proclamation on life and Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri's proclamation on life and Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri proclaims that whoever wants life should guard his tongue from evil and engage in Torah, which is called 'good'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri proclaims 'Who wants life?' and the crowd gathers, asking him to give them life.
Rabbi Alexandri answers by citing the verse 'Who is the man who desires life... guard your tongue from evil'.
The gemara raises a possible objection: one might think that after guarding one's tongue, one may indulge in sleep.
The gemara resolves that the verse continues 'turn from evil and do good', and 'good' refers only to Torah, as it says 'for I have given you a good teaching, do not forsake My Torah'.

items.text: Discussion on building for idolatry and the final hammer blow
items.text_en: Discussion on building for idolatry and the final hammer blow
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of one who builds a structure for idolatry, with Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Yochanan that the wages are permitted. The Gemara questions this, and Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabba bar Ulla explain that it refers to the final hammer blow, which has no monetary value, implying that rental is considered from beginning to end.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one reaches the dome where the idol is placed, the wages are permitted.
Rabbi Elazar reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if one built the structure, his wages are permitted.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, since the building materials are mere accessories to idolatry and are not forbidden until they are actually worshipped.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the ruling is needed for the case of the idol itself, and then raises a difficulty according to the opinion that a gentile's idol is forbidden immediately.
Rabba bar Ulla resolves the difficulty by explaining that the ruling refers to the final hammer blow, which has no monetary value, so the wages are permitted.
The Gemara concludes that Rabba bar Ulla holds that rental is considered from beginning to end, so the final blow's lack of value does not affect the overall permissibility.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on ornaments for idolatry and selling attached items
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on ornaments for idolatry and selling attached items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not make ornaments for idolatry, but Rabbi Eliezer permits it for wages. It also discusses selling attached items. The Gemara begins to ask for the source of these laws.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of making ornaments for idolatry, lists examples, records Rabbi Eliezer's leniency for wages, and discusses selling attached items with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
The Gemara asks for the biblical source of these Mishnaic laws.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina begins to provide the scriptural derivation for the Mishnah's rules.

items.text: Deriving multiple prohibitions from "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם"
items.text_en: Deriving multiple prohibitions from "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם"
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם" to include three prohibitions: not granting a dwelling place in the land, not showing favor, and not giving a free gift. This is derived through a verbal analysis of the unusual spelling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse 'לֹא תְחׇנֵּם' and interpreting it as a prohibition against granting a dwelling place in the land.
The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for a different meaning: not to show them favor (חן).
The Gemara answers that if the verse meant only 'do not show favor', it would have been spelled 'לֹא תְחוּנֵּם'; the unusual spelling 'לֹא תְחׇנֵּם' teaches two prohibitions.
The Gemara objects further that the verse is still needed for a third meaning: not to give them a free gift.
The Gemara resolves that if the verse meant only 'do not give a free gift', it would be spelled 'לֹא תְחִינֵּם'; the actual spelling 'לֹא תְחׇנֵּם' teaches all three prohibitions.

items.text: Baraita supporting the three interpretations
items.text_en: Baraita supporting the three interpretations
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states the three interpretations of "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם": no dwelling place, no favor, and no free gift.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states the three interpretations of "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם" (no dwelling place, no favor, and no free gift), supporting the earlier gemara's derivation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah on giving neveilah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah on giving neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a tannaitic dispute regarding the verse "לֹא תֹאכְלוּ כׇּל נְבֵלָה..." Rabbi Meir argues that both a ger and a gentile may receive neveilah either as a gift or through sale, while Rabbi Judah insists the verse is literal: a ger receives it as a gift, a gentile only through sale. The Gemara explains their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute about giving neveilah as a gift, citing the verse and presenting Rabbi Meir's position that both a ger and a gentile may receive it either as a gift or through sale.
The baraita records Rabbi Judah's opposing position that the verse is literal: a ger receives neveilah as a gift, a gentile only through sale.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's position seems straightforward, and then presents Rabbi Judah's objection: if the verse intended both options for both recipients, why does it use the word 'אוֹ' (or) to separate gift and sale?

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir interprets the word 'אוֹ' to prioritize giving the neveilah as a gift to a ger over selling it to a gentile, while Rabbi Judah counters that since one is commanded to sustain a ger but not a gentile, no verse is needed to establish that priority.

items.text: Prohibition against praising a gentile woman and a challenge from a story
items.text_en: Prohibition against praising a gentile woman and a challenge from a story
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's ruling that one may not say "how beautiful this gentile woman is," based on the interpretation of "לֹא תְחׇנֵּם" as not showing favor. A challenge is raised from stories of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva who commented on a beautiful gentile woman, but the Gemara resolves that they were merely acknowledging God's creations, not praising the woman herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's ruling that one may not say 'how beautiful this gentile woman is,' based on the interpretation of 'לֹא תְחׇנֵּם' as not showing favor.
A challenge is raised from stories of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva who commented on a beautiful gentile woman, seemingly violating Rav's prohibition.

The Gemara resolves that they were merely acknowledging God's creations, not praising the woman herself, as per the principle that one who sees beautiful creatures says 'ברוך שככה ברא בעולמו' (Blessed is He who created such in His world).

items.text: Prohibition against gazing at any woman
items.text_en: Prohibition against gazing at any woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further challenge: is looking at a woman even permitted? It cites a baraita that prohibits gazing at a beautiful woman, even an unmarried one, and certainly at a married woman, even an ugly one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether gazing at a woman is even permitted.
The Gemara cites a baraita that prohibits gazing at a beautiful woman, even an unmarried one, and certainly at a married woman, even an ugly one.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibited sales and description of the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibited sales and description of the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that may not be sold to gentiles, including colored garments, certain animals, and birds. It then describes the Angel of Death as covered with eyes, holding a drawn sword with a drop of gall, which causes death, putrefaction, and paleness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items prohibited for sale to gentiles: colored garments, donkeys, pigs, and birds when paired, even if the seller is as full of eyes as the Angel of Death.

sub.text: Mishnah's description of the Angel of Death
sub.text_en: Mishnah's description of the Angel of Death
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Angel of Death as covered with eyes, standing at the head of a dying person with a drawn sword and a drop of gall, which causes death, putrefaction, and paleness.

items.text: Gemara's comment: The Angel of Death stands at a corner
items.text_en: Gemara's comment: The Angel of Death stands at a corner
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Angel of Death stands at a corner (keren zavit), clarifying the description from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Angel of Death stands at a corner (קֶרֶן זָוִית) rather than directly in front of the patient.

items.text: Discussion on colored garments: Rav Yehuda, Rav Pappa, Rava, and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Discussion on colored garments: Rav Yehuda, Rav Pappa, Rava, and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the prohibition applies even to garments spread on a wall. Rav Pappa adds that it applies only when the owner is known. Rava supports this from the Mishnah's wording. Rav Chisda distinguishes between old and new garments, but the Gemara resolves the difficulty by saying the craftsman is busy with his work.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the prohibition of colored garments applies even to garments spread on a wall.
Rav Pappa adds that the prohibition applies only when the owner of the garments is known.
Rava supports Rav Pappa's position by noting that the Mishnah says 'colored garments of a woman' and not 'colored garments' in general, implying the owner is known.
Rav Chisda distinguishes between old and new garments, arguing that new garments are always prohibited because the craftsman looks at them, raising an objection to the previous ruling.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by citing a parallel case where the craftsman is busy with his work (בעבדתיה טריד), so he does not look at the garment, and applies the same reasoning here.

items.text: Analysis of the Angel of Death's drop: Death and putrefaction
items.text_en: Analysis of the Angel of Death's drop: Death and putrefaction
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's statement that the drop causes death. It questions whether this contradicts the father of Shmuel, who said the Angel of Death would cut the simanim like an animal. It answers that the drop cuts the simanim. Regarding putrefaction, it supports Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana's teaching that one who does not want his deceased to putrefy should turn him over.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's statement that the drop causes death contradicts the teaching of Avuh deShmuel, who said the Angel of Death cuts the simanim (shechita organs) like an animal.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting that the drop itself cuts the simanim (the trachea and esophagus), so both accounts are consistent.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana's teaching from Bei Rav that one who does not want his deceased to putrefy should turn him over, supporting the Mishnah's statement that the drop causes putrefaction.

items.text: Aggadic passage: The path to holiness and the dispute between Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Aggadic passage: The path to holiness and the dispute between Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita on the verse 'And you shall guard yourself from every evil thing,' leading to Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's chain from Torah to resurrection. It then notes a dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that humility is greatest, citing a verse about 'anavim' rather than 'chasidim.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע' (guard yourself from every evil thing) and interprets it as a warning against daytime thoughts that lead to nocturnal impurity.

Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair derives from this a chain of virtues from Torah leading to resurrection, concluding that חסידות (piety) is the greatest of all, citing the verse 'אָז דִּבַּרְתָּ בְחָזוֹן לַחֲסִידֶיךָ' (Then You spoke in a vision to Your pious ones).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disputes Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, arguing that ענוה (humility) is the greatest virtue, citing the verse 'לְבַשֵּׂר עֲנָוִים' (to bring good news to the humble) rather than 'לַחֲסִידִים' (to the pious).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on selling trees, sheep, and standing grain
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on selling trees, sheep, and standing grain
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a tree, sheep, or standing grain on condition that the buyer cuts, shears, or reaps immediately, while Rabbi Meir requires them to be already cut, shorn, or reaped. The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary to fully delineate their positions.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a tree, sheep, or standing grain on condition of immediate cutting, shearing, or reaping, while Rabbi Meir requires them to be already cut, shorn, or reaped.
The Gemara asks why all three cases are necessary, suggesting that one might think Rabbi Meir would concede to Rabbi Yehuda in the case of sheep, where delay causes loss.
The Gemara further asks that if only the first two cases were taught, one might think Rabbi Yehuda would concede to Rabbi Meir regarding sheep, whose quality is known.
The Gemara concludes that all three cases are necessary to prevent erroneous concessions from either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Inquiry and resolution: Selling an animal on condition to slaughter
items.text_en: Inquiry and resolution: Selling an animal on condition to slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: what is the law regarding selling an animal on condition to slaughter? It considers whether the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's leniency (that the item is not in the gentile's domain) applies to an animal, which is in the gentile's domain. A baraita resolves the question: Rabbi Yehuda permits it, and Rabbi Meir requires it to be already slaughtered.
