sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: what is the law regarding selling an animal to a gentile on condition that he slaughter it?
The Gemara analyzes the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's leniency regarding trees and grain, and considers whether it applies to an animal which is in the gentile's domain.
A baraita is cited to resolve the question: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling an animal on condition to slaughter, while Rabbi Meir requires it to be already slaughtered.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition on renting houses and fields in Israel and Syria
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition on renting houses and fields in Israel and Syria
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not rent houses to gentiles in the Land of Israel, and certainly not fields. In Syria, the law is different.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not rent houses to gentiles in the Land of Israel, and certainly not fields, but in Syria the rule is different.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei regarding renting and selling houses and fields to gentiles in different regions, with an additional restriction on renting a bathhouse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's ruling: in Eretz Yisrael one may rent houses to gentiles but not fields, while outside the land one may sell houses and rent fields.

Rabbi Yosei presents his alternative ruling: in Eretz Yisrael only renting houses is permitted, in Syria selling houses and renting fields, and outside the land both selling houses and fields are permitted.

The Mishnah adds that even where renting is permitted, it is not for a dwelling because the gentile would bring idolatry into the house, and one may never rent a bathhouse to a gentile because it would be called by the Jew's name.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why fields are more restricted than houses, suggesting it is due to two concerns: land acquisition and exemption from tithes. It then raises an objection that houses also have two concerns (land acquisition and exemption from mezuzah), but Rav Mesharshiya resolves that mezuzah is an obligation of the resident, not the house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'no need to mention fields,' suggesting it is because fields involve two concerns: land acquisition (חנייתקרקע) and exemption from tithes (מעשר).
The Gemara objects that houses also have two concerns: land acquisition and exemption from mezuzah (מזוזה).
Rav Mesharshiya resolves that mezuzah is an obligation of the resident (חובת הדר), not of the house itself, so it does not constitute a concern for the house's sale.

items.text: Discussion on Syria: renting vs. selling
items.text_en: Discussion on Syria: renting vs. selling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why selling houses in Syria is prohibited while renting is permitted, and suggests it is a decree due to the land of Israel. It then addresses an objection that renting fields in Syria would be a decree upon a decree, and explains that the ruling is based on the status of conquest by an individual.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why selling houses in Syria is prohibited while renting is permitted, and suggests it is a decree due to the land of Israel.
The Gemara objects that if selling is a decree, then renting should also be forbidden as a decree upon a decree.
The Gemara answers that renting fields in Syria is not a decree upon a decree because the ruling is based on the status of conquest by an individual (כיבוש יחיד).

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Meir's view on Syria and outside the land
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Meir's view on Syria and outside the land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: in Syria, fields with two concerns are prohibited, but houses without two concerns are permitted; outside the land, the same logic applies.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir prohibits fields in Syria because they have two concerns (land acquisition and tithe exemption), while houses lack the second concern and are permitted.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei's view
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: in Israel, fields with two concerns are prohibited, houses without them permitted; in Syria, since conquest by an individual is not considered conquest, fields are prohibited but houses permitted; outside the land, since it is distant, no decree is made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yosei's ruling regarding houses and fields in Israel.
The Gemara explains that fields in Israel have two concerns (land acquisition and tithe exemption) so the Sages decreed against renting them, while houses lack the second concern.
The Gemara explains that in Syria, since conquest by an individual is not considered conquest, fields are prohibited but houses permitted.
The Gemara explains that outside the land, since it is distant, no decree is made at all.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and additional restrictions
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and additional restrictions
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei, but Rav Yosef adds that one may not make a gentile neighborhood. The Gemara defines a neighborhood as at least three people, and addresses a concern about indirect sale to multiple gentiles, which Abaye resolves by saying we are only commanded about direct causes, not indirect ones.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei's lenient position.
Rav Yosef adds a condition: one may not sell houses to gentiles in a way that creates a gentile neighborhood (שכונה).
A baraita defines a neighborhood (שכונה) as no fewer than three people.
The Gemara raises a concern: what if one Jew sells to one gentile and another Jew sells to two others, effectively creating a neighborhood indirectly?
Abaye resolves: we are commanded only about a direct cause (לפני), not about an indirect cause (לפני דלפני).

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'in a place where they said to rent' that there are places where renting is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'even in a place where they said to rent' that there are places where renting is not permitted.

items.text: Gemara's inference about the anonymous Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about the anonymous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, because if it followed Rabbi Yosei, he permits renting in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, because if it followed Rabbi Yosei, he would permit renting in all cases.

items.text: Baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on a bathhouse
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on a bathhouse
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a Jew may not rent out his bathhouse to a gentile, because it is called by the Jew's name and the gentile will work in it on Shabbat and festivals.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that a Jew may not rent out his bathhouse to a gentile, because it is called by the Jew's name and the gentile will work in it on Shabbat and festivals.

items.text: Gemara's question: renting to a Samaritan
items.text_en: Gemara's question: renting to a Samaritan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but what about renting to a Samaritan? It is permitted. The Gemara objects: the Samaritan might work on Chol HaMoed! The Gemara answers: we also work on Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but what about renting to a Samaritan (כותי)? It is permitted.
The Gemara objects: the Samaritan might work on Chol HaMoed (חול המועד), which is forbidden for Jews.
The Gemara answers: we also work on Chol HaMoed, so the Samaritan's work is not a problem.

items.text: Gemara's question: renting a field to a gentile
items.text_en: Gemara's question: renting a field to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but what about renting a field to a gentile? It is permitted. What is the reason? The sharecropper does his own work. The Gemara objects: regarding a bathhouse, one might also say the sharecropper does his own work. The Gemara answers: people do not work as sharecroppers in a bathhouse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but what about renting a field to a gentile? It is permitted, because the sharecropper does his own work.
The Gemara objects: regarding a bathhouse, one might also say the sharecropper does his own work.
The Gemara answers: people do not work as sharecroppers in a bathhouse.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on a field
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on a field
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says a Jew may not rent his field to a Samaritan, because it is called by his name and the Samaritan will work on Chol HaMoed. But a gentile is permitted, because people say the sharecropper does his own work. The Gemara objects: if so, regarding a Samaritan too they would say the sharecropper does his own work!

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling that a Jew may not rent his field to a Samaritan (כותי), because it is called by his name and the Samaritan will work on Chol HaMoed.
The baraita continues that renting to a gentile is permitted, because people will say the sharecropper does his own work.
The Gemara objects: if so, regarding a Samaritan too people would say the sharecropper does his own work, undermining the distinction.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reason for prohibiting a Samaritan sharecropper
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reason for prohibiting a Samaritan sharecropper
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah forbids a Samaritan sharecropper only because the field is called by his name, and not also due to the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind. It answers that the Mishnah includes both reasons: one is the stumbling block, and the other is the field being called by his name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prohibits a Samaritan sharecropper only because the field is called by his name, and not also due to the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind (לפני עור לא תתן מכשול).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah includes both reasons: one is the stumbling block (לפני עור), and the other is the field being called by his name.

items.text: Case of gentile and Jew holding myrtle branches on Shabbat
items.text_en: Case of gentile and Jew holding myrtle branches on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava permitted a case where a gentile held myrtle branches on Shabbat and a Jew on a weekday, based on a prior agreement. Ravina objected with a baraita stating that a Jew and gentile who received a field as partners may not tell the gentile to take his portion on Shabbat and the Jew on a weekday, but if they stipulated from the beginning it is permitted, and if they later calculate it is forbidden. Rava was embarrassed, but it was later revealed that they had stipulated from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a gentile held myrtle branches on Shabbat and a Jew on a weekday, and Rava permitted it.

Ravina objects to Rava by citing a baraita that a Jew and gentile who received a field as partners may not tell the gentile to take his portion on Shabbat and the Jew on a weekday, but if they stipulated from the beginning it is permitted.
The baraita adds that if they later calculate the division it is forbidden, and Rava was embarrassed.
It was later revealed that the parties had stipulated from the start, resolving the objection.

items.text: Case of orlah saplings with gentile and Jew alternating years
items.text_en: Case of orlah saplings with gentile and Jew alternating years
items.desc_en: Rav Geviha from Bei Ktil reported a case where a gentile ate from orlah saplings during the orlah years and a Jew during the permitted years, and Rava permitted it. The Gemara notes that Ravina's earlier objection actually supports Rava, and the embarrassment was unfounded because the stipulation was from the start.

sub.desc_en: Rav Geviha reports a case of orlah saplings where a gentile ate during the orlah years and a Jew during the permitted years, and Rava permitted it.
The Gemara objects that Ravina had previously challenged Rava on a similar case, but then notes that the challenge actually supports Rava.
The Gemara resolves that Ravina's embarrassment was unfounded because the stipulation was made from the start.

items.text: Inquiry about a standard partnership without stipulation
items.text_en: Inquiry about a standard partnership without stipulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is in a standard case without explicit stipulation. It attempts to derive from the baraita: if stipulation permits, then standard is forbidden; but the end of the baraita says if they later calculate it is forbidden, implying standard is permitted. The Gemara concludes that no inference can be drawn from this baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about the law in a standard partnership without explicit stipulation.
The Gemara attempts to derive from the baraita that if stipulation permits, then standard is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that the end of the baraita implies the opposite: if later calculation is forbidden, then standard is permitted.
The Gemara concludes that no inference can be drawn from this baraita.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and the Mishnah on seclusion with gentiles
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and the Mishnah on seclusion with gentiles
items.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the statement 'We have returned to you, before their festivals.' The Mishnah then forbids leaving an animal in gentile inns due to suspicion of bestiality, a woman secluding with them due to suspicion of adultery, and a man secluding with them due to suspicion of murder.

sub.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the formulaic statement 'We have returned to you, before their festivals.'

The Mishnah forbids leaving an animal in gentile inns due to suspicion of bestiality, a woman secluding with them due to suspicion of adultery, and a man secluding with them due to suspicion of murder.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah and resolution regarding females
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah and resolution regarding females
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits buying animals from gentiles for sacrifices without concern for bestiality, yet one might worry about a male animal that was ridden or a female that was mounted. Rav Sheila bar Avina in the name of Rav resolves that a gentile cares about his animal's fertility and would not let it be rendered barren.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits buying animals from gentiles for sacrifices without concern for bestiality, yet one might worry about a male animal that was ridden or a female that was mounted.

sub.text: Rav Sheila bar Avina in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Sheila bar Avina in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheila bar Avina in the name of Rav resolves that a gentile cares about his animal's fertility and would not let it be rendered barren.

items.text: Question about males and answer
items.text_en: Question about males and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about male animals, where the concern is not about fertility but about the animal being weakened. Rav Kahana answers that males are not purchased because they lose flesh (become emaciated) from the act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that the concern about bestiality explains why female animals are not purchased from gentiles, but what about male animals, where the concern is not about fertility?
Rav Kahana answers that male animals are not purchased because they become emaciated (lose flesh) from the act, so the gentile would not risk it.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about a gentile shepherd
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about a gentile shepherd
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction: a baraita permits buying an animal from a gentile shepherd, yet one might fear the shepherd himself mounted it. The answer is that the shepherd fears losing his wages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits buying an animal from a gentile shepherd, yet one should fear the shepherd himself mounted it.
The Gemara answers that the gentile shepherd fears losing his wages, so he refrains from bestiality.

items.text: Contradiction about not entrusting an animal to a gentile shepherd
items.text_en: Contradiction about not entrusting an animal to a gentile shepherd
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita says one should not entrust an animal to a gentile shepherd, implying fear of bestiality, but the previous answer said the shepherd fears losing wages. Rabbah resolves that gentiles fear each other (knowing each other's behavior), but we (Jews) do not know them and thus do not fear, citing a proverb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita forbids entrusting an animal to a gentile shepherd, implying fear of bestiality, but the previous answer claimed the shepherd fears losing wages.
Rabbah resolves that gentiles fear each other (knowing each other's behavior), but Jews do not know them and thus do not fear, citing a proverb.

items.text: Question about buying males from females
items.text_en: Question about buying males from females
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why not buy males from females (since the female might entice the male)? The answer is that since the male is sexually aroused by the female, it fears (the owner might catch it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why not buy males from females, since we fear the female might entice the male to mount her?
The Gemara answers: since the male is sexually aroused by the female, it fears (the owner might catch it).

items.text: Contradiction from Rav Yosef's baraita about a widow and a dog
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rav Yosef's baraita about a widow and a dog
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rav Yosef's baraita: a widow should not raise a dog, yet one might think the dog would fear her. The answer is that since the dog is attached to her (for food), people say it follows her for the food, not for bestiality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rav Yosef's baraita: a widow should not raise a dog, yet one would expect the dog to fear her due to her presence.
The Gemara answers that since the dog is attached to her for food, people say it follows her for the food, not for bestiality.

items.text: Reason for not secluding females with females and the serpent's contamination
items.text_en: Reason for not secluding females with females and the serpent's contamination
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why females are not secluded with females (gentile women with Jewish female animals). Mar Ukva bar Chama answers because gentiles frequent their friends' wives, and if they don't find the wife, they might find the animal. Alternatively, even if they find the wife, they prefer the animal, as Rabbi Yochanan said: when the serpent came upon Eve, it injected זוהמא (moral contamination) into her; gentiles, who did not stand at Sinai, still have this contamination, while Jews lost it at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why females (gentile women) are not secluded with female Jewish animals.
Mar Ukva bar Chama answers that gentiles frequent their friends' wives, and if they do not find the wife, they may find the animal and bestialize it.
An alternative answer is given: even if the gentile finds his friend's wife, he prefers the animal, as Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about the serpent's contamination explains.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that when the serpent came upon Eve, it injected זוהמא (moral contamination) into her; Jews lost this contamination at Sinai, but gentiles who did not stand at Sinai retain it, explaining their greater lust for animals.

items.text: Inquiry about birds and supporting evidence
items.text_en: Inquiry about birds and supporting evidence
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about the status of birds (whether they are also subject to bestiality concerns). It brings evidence from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Chanina, who saw a gentile buy a goose, mount it, strangle it, roast it, and eat it. Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti adds a similar story about an Arab who bought a thigh, hollowed it out, mounted it, roasted it, and ate it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: what is the halachic status of birds regarding bestiality concerns?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Chanina brings evidence: he saw a gentile buy a goose from the market, mount it, strangle it, roast it, and eat it.
Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti adds a similar story: he saw an Arab buy a thigh, hollow it out for mounting, mount it, roast it, and eat it.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: ab initio vs. post facto
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: ab initio vs. post facto
items.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between ab initio (initial purchase) and post facto (after the fact). The Mishnah's prohibition is ab initio, while the baraita permitting purchase is post facto.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Supporting proof from a baraita about seclusion
items.text_en: Supporting proof from a baraita about seclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove Ravina's distinction from a baraita about a woman secluded with gentiles: if for money she is permitted to her husband (post facto), but ab initio she may not seclude. The Gemara deflects this proof, suggesting the baraita's leniency is due to fear of financial loss, not a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for proof of the distinction between לכתחילה (a-priori) and בדיעבד (post-facto), citing a baraita that forbids a woman from secluding with gentiles a-priori but permits her to her husband post-facto if she was imprisoned for money.
The Gemara initially infers the distinction, but then deflects by suggesting the baraita's leniency is due to the gentile's fear of financial loss, not a general principle.
The Gemara supports the deflection by noting that the baraita's continuation, regarding imprisonment for capital crimes, does not add any further leniency, implying the financial case is exceptional.

items.text: Rabbi Pedat's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Pedat's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pedat resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah's prohibition to Rabbi Eliezer, who fears bestiality, and the baraita's permission to the Sages, who do not. He cites a dispute about purchasing a red heifer from gentiles.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pedat resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah's prohibition to Rabbi Eliezer, who fears bestiality, and the baraita's permission to the Sages, who do not, citing their dispute about purchasing a red heifer from gentiles.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Eliezer's reason is like Rav Yehuda's
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Eliezer's reason is like Rav Yehuda's
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Eliezer's position might not be due to fear of bestiality but rather because of a different concern, as per Rav Yehuda citing Rav: if a sack was placed on the cow, it becomes unfit, implying a concern for misuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's reason is necessarily fear of bestiality, suggesting it might be a different concern.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Eliezer's reason is like Rav Yehuda's ruling: placing a sack on a cow disqualifies it, implying a concern for misuse rather than bestiality.

items.text: Rejection: the concern for bestiality is real
items.text_en: Rejection: the concern for bestiality is real
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the alternative, arguing that one would not forfeit a valuable animal for minor pleasure, but in the case of a woman, the yetzer (urge) overpowers, so the concern for bestiality stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages cannot be about whether we fear bestiality, because one would not forfeit a valuable animal for minor pleasure.
The Gemara resolves that in the case of a woman, the yetzer (urge) overpowers, so the concern for bestiality stands, unlike the case of an animal.

items.text: Another alternative: scriptural derivation from Sheilah
items.text_en: Another alternative: scriptural derivation from Sheilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Eliezer's reason is scriptural: the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel, and they shall take' excludes gentiles. This is rejected because the same reasoning would apply to all offerings, but the Mishnah only mentions the red heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Eliezer's reason might be the scriptural derivation taught by Sheilah: the verse 'דבר אל בני ישראל ויקחו אלי' (Speak to the children of Israel and they shall take for Me) excludes gentiles from bringing the red heifer.

The Gemara rejects this because the Mishnah explicitly states that Rabbi Eliezer invalidates all offerings from gentiles, not just the red heifer, while the 'קיחה' (taking) derivation would only apply where the word 'קיחה' appears in the verse.

items.text: Distinction between red heifer and other offerings
items.text_en: Distinction between red heifer and other offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages is only regarding the red heifer, whose blood is expensive, but regarding other offerings they concede to Rabbi Eliezer that they may be purchased from non-Jews.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by distinguishing the red heifer, whose high price deters gentiles from risking it, from other offerings where the Sages concede to Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and proof from Scripture
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and proof from Scripture
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the dispute is only about the red heifer, then who authored the baraita that states one may purchase animals for offerings from non-Jews? It cannot be Rabbi Eliezer or the Sages. Moreover, a baraita explicitly states that Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues cited the verse 'All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you... they shall come up with acceptance on My altar' to argue that animals from non-Jews are acceptable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the dispute is only about the red heifer, then who authored the baraita that states one may purchase animals for offerings from non-Jews? It cannot be Rabbi Eliezer or the Sages.

Moreover, a baraita explicitly states that Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues cited the verse 'All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you... they shall come up with acceptance on My altar' to argue that animals from non-Jews are acceptable.

items.text: Proof that the red heifer is a sacrifice of the altar
items.text_en: Proof that the red heifer is a sacrifice of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the dispute that the red heifer is a sacrifice of the altar, because if it were a sacrifice for Temple maintenance, bestiality would not disqualify it. The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because the Torah calls it a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the dispute that the red heifer is a sacrifice of the altar, because if it were for Temple maintenance, bestiality would not disqualify it.
The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because the Torah calls it a sin-offering, so it is treated as an altar sacrifice.

items.text: Challenge from a case of a breached birth
items.text_en: Challenge from a case of a breached birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the red heifer is a sin-offering, then it should be disqualified if it was born by caesarean section, but a baraita states that Rabbi Shimon validates it. The Gemara initially suggests that Rabbi Shimon's position is consistent with his view that a breached birth is a valid offspring, but Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Shimon conceded that regarding sacrifices it is not sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the red heifer is a sin-offering, then it should be disqualified if born by caesarean section, yet a baraita states that Rabbi Shimon validates it.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion that Rabbi Shimon's position is consistent with his view that a breached birth is a valid offspring, citing Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Shimon conceded regarding sacrifices it is not sacred.

items.text: Alternative answer: the red heifer is unique due to blemishes
items.text_en: Alternative answer: the red heifer is unique due to blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a different answer: the red heifer is different because since a blemish disqualifies it, matters of immorality and idolatry also disqualify it, as derived from the verse 'for their corruption is in them, a blemish in them' and the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that wherever corruption is mentioned it refers to immorality or idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a different answer: the red heifer is different because since a blemish disqualifies it, matters of immorality and idolatry also disqualify it, as derived from the verse 'for their corruption is in them, a blemish in them' and the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

The Gemara supports this with scriptural proof: corruption refers to immorality (from the generation of the flood) and idolatry (from the warning against making graven images), and therefore since a blemish disqualifies the red heifer, these matters also disqualify it.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's scriptural basis and a challenge from terumah
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's scriptural basis and a challenge from terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the main topic: Sheilah taught that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is from the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel and let them take' – the children of Israel take, not non-Jews. The Gemara challenges: If so, regarding terumah the same would apply, but Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that people asked Rabbi Eliezer about honoring parents and he cited a non-Jew as an example, implying non-Jews can also take terumah.

sub.desc_en: Sheilah teaches that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is from the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel and let them take' – the children of Israel take, not non-Jews.
The Gemara challenges: If so, regarding תרומה (priestly portion) the same would apply – only Israelites take, not non-Jews.

The Gemara objects: If you say that indeed non-Jews cannot take תרומה, but Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that Rabbi Eliezer cited a non-Jew (Dama ben Netina) as an example of honoring parents, implying non-Jews can take תרומה for the ephod.

items.text: Opening narrative about the red heifer
items.text_en: Opening narrative about the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story about a non-Jew who had a red heifer born in his herd, and the Sages came to purchase it. The non-Jew refused payment beyond the loss he incurred for his father's sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Dama ben Netina, who refused to wake his father for a key, losing a huge profit, and later a red heifer was born in his herd.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the narrative
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the narrative
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the narrative's relevance, noting that the verse mentions אבני שוהם interrupting the context. It then explains that the purchase was through Jewish merchants, addressing the concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the narrative's relevance, noting that the verse mentions אבני שוהם (onyx stones) interrupting the context, and then rejoins with 'and stones to be set'.
The Gemara adds further evidence from the latter clause of the narrative, where the Sages purchased a red heifer from a gentile, contradicting Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the purchase was through Jewish merchants, not directly from the gentile.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's concern about bestiality
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's concern about bestiality
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer is not concerned about bestiality (רביעה). It cites a case where a red heifer was bought from a non-Jew named Dama or Remetz, and Rabbi Eliezer responded that Israelites guarded it from birth, showing he has two concerns: the purchase and bestiality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer is not concerned about the possibility of bestiality (רביעה) with the animal.
A baraita is cited: the Rabbis told Rabbi Eliezer about an incident where a red heifer was purchased from a gentile named Dama or Remetz.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that this is no proof, because Israelites were guarding the heifer from the time it was born.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Eliezer has two requirements: the purchase must be from a Jew, and he is also concerned about bestiality.

items.text: Refining the guarding requirement
items.text_en: Refining the guarding requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the guarding from birth, suggesting the mother might have been violated during pregnancy. It cites Rava's ruling that a fetus is affected. The Gemara then adjusts to guarding from conception, and further questions about the mother's mother, concluding that such extensive concern is not applied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the guarding from birth, raising the concern that the mother might have been violated during pregnancy.
Rava's ruling is cited: the offspring of an animal that was gored or violated is considered as if it participated in the act, and is therefore forbidden.
The Gemara adjusts the guarding requirement to begin from the time of conception, not birth.
The Gemara raises a further concern: perhaps the mother was violated before conception, citing a mishna where Rabbi Eliezer forbids offspring of disqualified animals.
Rava's opinion is presented: the dispute applies only when the violation occurred while the animals were consecrated; if non-sacred, all agree the offspring are permitted.

Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana's alternative opinion is raised: the dispute applies when the violation occurred while non-sacred, but if consecrated, all agree the offspring are forbidden, challenging the previous resolution.
The Gemara concludes that the guarding extends to the mother from conception, and that concern for the mother's mother is not applied.

items.text: How guarding is known and the heifer's value
items.text_en: How guarding is known and the heifer's value
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that a red cup is passed before the cow when a male mounts, indicating conception. The Gemara asks why its blood is expensive, and answers because two hairs disqualify it, and Rav Kahana says it is a מוחזקת (established) case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how it is known that the mother was guarded from the time of conception.
Rav Kahana answers that a red cup is passed before the cow when the male mounts, ensuring the offspring will be red.
The Gemara asks why the heifer's blood is expensive if its conception can be induced so easily.
The Gemara answers that two hairs of a different color can disqualify the heifer, making the method unreliable.
The Gemara asks why the Sages specifically sought Dama's cow rather than using their own.
Rav Kahana answers that Dama's herd was מוחזקת (established) for producing red heifers.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on all offerings and future gentiles
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on all offerings and future gentiles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha discuss that Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies all offerings from non-Jews. His colleagues cite the verse 'All the flock of Kedar will be gathered to you' to argue that future gentiles will bring offerings, but Rabbi Eliezer says they will be converts. Rav Yosef and Abaye debate the proof text.

sub.desc_en: One of the sages opens by stating that Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies all offerings from gentiles.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues (via the second sage)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues (via the second sage)
sub.desc_en: The second sage asks what objection Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues raised, citing the verse 'All flocks of Kedar shall be gathered unto you' (Isaiah 60:7) as proof that offerings come from gentiles.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that in the future all gentiles will be calculating converts, so the offerings come from converts, not gentiles.
Rav Yosef asks for the scriptural source for Rabbi Eliezer's claim, citing Zephaniah 3:9 about God turning a pure language to the peoples.
Abaye objects that the verse might only mean they abandon idol worship, not that they accept all commandments.
Rav Yosef rejects the objection, pointing to the end of the verse 'to serve Him with one consent,' which implies full acceptance of all mitzvot.

items.text: Challenges from biblical precedents
items.text_en: Challenges from biblical precedents
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections from Moses and Jethro offering sacrifices before the Torah was given, suggesting non-Jews could offer. It distinguishes that this was before the Torah, but notes a dispute about Jethro's timing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid each transmit the same tradition: Rabbi Eliezer disqualified all offerings from gentiles, and his colleagues challenged him with the verse 'All flocks of Kedar...', to which he replied that all gentiles will become calculating converts in the future.
Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse 'For then will I turn to the peoples a pure language...' (Zephaniah 3:9) as the scriptural basis for the future conversion of the gentiles.
Rav Yosef objects that the verse might only mean the gentiles will abandon idol worship, not that they will fully convert and cease forbidden sexual practices like bestiality.
Abaye counters that the verse concludes 'to serve Him with one consent,' indicating full acceptance of all mitzvot, not just rejection of idolatry.
The Gemara raises an objection from the verse where Moses demanded offerings from Pharaoh, a gentile, before the Exodus.
The Gemara answers that the halakha before the giving of the Torah was different, so this precedent does not apply.
The Gemara raises another objection from the verse where Jethro, a gentile, brought offerings after the Exodus.
The Gemara answers that Jethro's incident also occurred before the giving of the Torah, according to one opinion.
The Gemara notes that this answer works for the opinion that Jethro came before the Torah, but leaves the issue unresolved for the opinion that he came after the Torah.

items.text: Question about Jethro and the sale of animals
items.text_en: Question about Jethro and the sale of animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Jethro's animals were acquired before or after the giving of the Torah, and concludes that he bought them from Israelites. It then cites a verse about Saul bringing the best of the flock from Amalek, explaining that 'best' refers to their monetary value, to encourage buyers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Jethro could offer animals after the Torah was given, given the prohibition on gentile offerings.
The Gemara resolves that Jethro bought the animals from Israelites, so they were not originally gentile-owned.
The Gemara cites a verse where Saul says the people brought the best of the flock from Amalek to sacrifice, implying animals from gentiles were used.
The Gemara explains that 'the best' refers to the monetary value of the best animals, not the animals themselves, so they were sold and the proceeds used for offerings.
The Gemara asks why they specifically sold the best animals rather than inferior ones.
The Gemara explains that selling superior-quality animals attracts buyers, making the sale easier.

items.text: Araunah the Jebusite and the threshing sledges
items.text_en: Araunah the Jebusite and the threshing sledges
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse where Araunah offers David oxen for an offering, and Rav Nachman explains that Araunah was a resident alien. It then defines 'moriggim' as a threshing sledge, with Ulla and Rav Yosef providing explanations and a supporting verse.

items.text: Objection from the cows offered by the Philistines
items.text_en: Objection from the cows offered by the Philistines
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Philistines offering female cows as a burnt offering, which is normally invalid. It answers that this was a temporary ruling. The Gemara then questions whether a female burnt offering is ever valid, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies a verse to show it was a female.

items.text: The age limit for a female animal to be rendered unfit
items.text_en: The age limit for a female animal to be rendered unfit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a female animal under three years old can be rendered unfit (by a non-Jew), but at three years it cannot. The Gemara challenges this with the Philistine cows, and Rav Huna bar Rav Natan questions whether a cow under three can give birth. The Gemara resolves that the cows were 'mechavverta' (white) as originally explained.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a female animal under three years old can be rendered unfit (by a non-Jew), but at three years it cannot.
The Gemara answers all previous objections by explaining that the animals in question were less than three years old, citing the Philistine cows as an example.
Rav Huna bar Rav Natan objects that if the cows were under three, they could not have given birth, contradicting the verse that mentions their calves.
The Gemara rejects the age-based explanation, citing a baraita that a cow under three does not give birth, and resolves that the cows were 'mechavverta' (white) as originally explained.

items.text: The song of the cows and related interpretations
items.text_en: The song of the cows and related interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse about the cows going straight to Beit Shemesh, explaining that they sang a song. Various rabbis propose different songs: Rabbi Meir says they sang the Song of the Sea, Rabbi Yochanan says they sang a thanksgiving psalm, and others suggest various psalms and hymns. Rav and Rav Ashi then comment on Persian words derived from biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'וַיִּשַּׁרְנָה' (and they went straight) means in the verse about the cows.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir explains that the cows recited a song.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah in the name of Rav explains that the cows straightened their faces toward the Ark and recited a song.
The Gemara asks what song the cows recited.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir says the cows recited the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1).
Rabbi Yochanan himself says the cows recited the thanksgiving psalm from Isaiah 12:4.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says the cows recited an orphaned psalm, Psalm 98:1.
Rabbi Elazar says the cows recited Psalm 99:1.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says the cows recited Psalm 93:1.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says the cows recited a non-biblical song praising the Ark of the Covenant.
Rav Ashi teaches Rabbi Yitzchak's statement in the context of Numbers 10:35, when the Ark set forward.
Rav explains that the Persians call a book 'דְּבִיר' (devir) based on Judges 1:11.
Rav Ashi explains that the Persians call a menstruating woman 'דַּשְׁתָּנָא' (dashtana) based on Genesis 31:35.

items.text: Identifying the Book of the Upright and its allusion to Joshua
items.text_en: Identifying the Book of the Upright and its allusion to Joshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan identifies 'Sefer HaYashar' as the Book of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who are called 'upright'. The Gemara asks where in that book the sun standing for Joshua is hinted, and answers that it is in the blessing 'and his seed shall be the fullness of nations' (Genesis 48:19), which was fulfilled when the sun stood for Joshua.

items.text: Dispute over the duration of the sun's standing for Joshua
items.text_en: Dispute over the duration of the sun's standing for Joshua
items.desc_en: Three amoraim debate how long the sun stood still: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says 24 hours, Rabbi Elazar says 36 hours, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says 48 hours. A second version of the dispute is presented, with slightly different calculations based on the verse 'and did not hasten to set for a whole day'.

items.text: The sun stood for Moses and Nakdimon ben Gurion as well
items.text_en: The sun stood for Moses and Nakdimon ben Gurion as well
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the sun stood for Joshua, Moses, and Nakdimon ben Gurion. For Joshua it is from Scripture, for Nakdimon from tradition. For Moses, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derive it from a verbal analogy or from the verse itself, indicating that the sun stood for Moses when the nations trembled.

items.text: Objection from the verse 'there was no day like it' and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the verse 'there was no day like it' and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse 'there was no day like it before or after' (Joshua 10:14), which seems to contradict the idea that the sun stood for Moses. Two answers are given: either the hours were not as many, or the hailstones were not present for Moses.

items.text: Identifying the Book of the Upright in Samuel and its allusion to Judah
items.text_en: Identifying the Book of the Upright in Samuel and its allusion to Judah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse in Samuel about teaching the sons of Judah the bow, and again identifies 'Sefer HaYashar' as the Book of the Patriarchs. Three amoraim offer different identifications: Rabbi Elazar says it is the Book of Deuteronomy, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it is the Book of Judges, and the Gemara explains how each is hinted in the verse about the bow.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the thigh and what is upon it' in Samuel
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the thigh and what is upon it' in Samuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'the thigh and what is upon it' (וְהֶעָלֶיהָ) in the story of Saul. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to the thigh and the tail, Rabbi Elazar says thigh and breast, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says thigh and the spinal cord (שופי). Each explains the word 'וְהֶעָלֶיהָ' accordingly.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: seclusion with non-Jews
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: seclusion with non-Jews
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about the prohibition of a woman being alone with non-Jews, questioning whether the same rule applies to a Jewish man alone with two women, citing a mishnah that prohibits it.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's allowance for a Jewish woman to be alone with two men applies even to פרוצים (immoral men), citing a baraita that even ten such men are not permitted, as illustrated by a story where ten men carried a woman out on a bier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's allowance for a Jewish woman to be alone with two men applies even to פרוצים (immoral men), citing a baraita that even ten such men are not permitted, as illustrated by a story where ten men carried a woman out on a bier.

items.text: Distinction between a gentile and a Jew regarding his wife
items.text_en: Distinction between a gentile and a Jew regarding his wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the woman's husband is with her; a gentile's wife does not guard him from sin, but a Jewish wife does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the woman's husband is with her; a gentile's wife does not guard him from sin, but a Jewish wife does.

items.text: Concern for murder and two resolutions
items.text_en: Concern for murder and two resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern about murder (שפיכות דמים) when a woman is alone with a gentile. Rabbi Yirmeya answers that we are dealing with a woman of importance (אשה חשובה) who is feared, while Rav Idi says a woman's weapons are upon her (כלי זיינה עליה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern about murder (שפיכות דמים) when a woman is alone with a gentile.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that we are dealing with a woman of importance (אשה חשובה) who is feared, so murder is not a concern.
Rav Idi bar Avin says a woman's weapons are upon her (כלי זיינה עליה), so murder is not a concern.

items.text: Difference between the two opinions
items.text_en: Difference between the two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the practical difference between Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Idi: a woman who is important among men but not among women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions of Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Idi bar Avin.
The Gemara answers that the difference is a woman who is important among men but not important among women.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Idi
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Idi
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav Idi bar Avin, stating that a woman, even if peace is with her, should not be alone with gentiles because they are suspected of sexual immorality.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav Idi bar Avin, stating that a woman, even if peace is with her, should not be alone with gentiles because they are suspected of sexual immorality.

items.text: Guidelines for a Jew encountering a gentile on the road
items.text_en: Guidelines for a Jew encountering a gentile on the road
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita with rules: a Jew should walk to the right of a gentile; Rabbi Yishmael distinguishes between a sword and a stick. When ascending or descending, the Jew should be above. If asked where he is going, he should exaggerate the distance, as Jacob did with Esau.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule that a Jew should not be alone with gentiles, and then states that if a Jew encounters a gentile on the road, he should position the gentile to his right.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael distinguishes: if the gentile carries a sword, position him to the right; if a stick, to the left.
The baraita adds rules for ascending or descending: the Jew should be above the gentile, and should not bend down, lest the gentile break his skull.
The baraita instructs that if asked where he is going, the Jew should exaggerate the distance, citing Jacob's example with Esau.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva's students and bandits
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva's students and bandits
items.desc_en: A story is told of Rabbi Akiva's students who, when encountering bandits, said they were going to Akko but stopped at Keziv, and the bandits praised Rabbi Akiva and his students for never being harmed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of Rabbi Akiva's students who, when encountering bandits, said they were going to Akko but stopped at Keziv, and the bandits praised Rabbi Akiva and his students for never being harmed.

items.text: Beginning of a story about Rav Menashe
items.text_en: Beginning of a story about Rav Menashe
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Menashe who was going somewhere, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Menashe who was traveling, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yehuda and the bandits
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehuda and the bandits
items.desc_en: A story is told about bandits who encountered Rabbi Yehuda and asked where he was going; he misled them, and when they discovered his deception, they cursed him. The bandits then failed in their robberies for 22 years, and all but one sought to annul the curse; the one who did not was eaten by a lion.

sub.desc_en: The story opens with bandits encountering Rav Menashe, who misleads them about his destination; when they discover the deception, they accuse him of being a student of Yehuda the swindler, and Rav Menashe curses them with excommunication.

The curse takes effect: the bandits fail in their robberies for twenty-two years; all but one weaver seek to annul the curse, and the weaver who does not is eaten by a lion, illustrating the adage about a weaver who is not shy.

items.text: Transitional comment
items.text_en: Transitional comment
items.desc_en: A brief comment contrasts the bandits of Babylonia with the robbers of the Land of Israel, serving as a pivot to the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the behavior of Babylonian thieves with that of bandits in the Land of Israel, transitioning to the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Jewish woman may not deliver or nurse a gentile's child
items.text_en: Mishnah: Jewish woman may not deliver or nurse a gentile's child
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Jewish woman may not deliver the child of a gentile woman because she would be raising a child for idolatry, but a gentile woman may deliver a Jewish woman's child. Similarly, a Jewish woman may not nurse a gentile's child, but a gentile woman may nurse a Jewish child in the Jewish woman's home.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a Jewish woman may not deliver or nurse a gentile's child, but a gentile woman may deliver or nurse a Jewish child under certain conditions.

items.text: Baraita on midwifery and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraita on midwifery and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir forbids a Jewish woman from delivering a gentile's child and also forbids a gentile woman from delivering a Jewish woman's child due to suspicion of bloodshed. The Sages permit a gentile woman to deliver a Jewish woman's child when others are present, but Rabbi Meir forbids even then, as she might secretly kill the infant. A story is brought illustrating such a danger, and the Gemara explains that the Sages dismiss the story as an isolated incident.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the statement of Rabbi Meir: a Jewish woman may not deliver a gentile's child, and a gentile woman may not deliver a Jewish woman's child due to suspicion of bloodshed.
The Sages permit a gentile woman to deliver a Jewish woman's child when others are present, but Rabbi Meir forbids even then, as she might secretly kill the infant by pressing on his temple.
A story is brought illustrating the danger: a gentile midwife boasted of killing many Jewish infants, extracting blood like river foam.
The Gemara explains that the Sages dismiss the story as mere bragging, not a real incident.

items.text: Baraita on nursing and the need for both rulings
items.text_en: Baraita on nursing and the need for both rulings
items.desc_en: A baraita parallels the earlier one regarding nursing: Rabbi Meir forbids a Jewish woman from nursing a gentile's child and a gentile woman from nursing a Jewish child; the Sages permit the latter when others are present. The Gemara explains that both cases (midwifery and nursing) are necessary to teach, as each has a unique leniency or stringency that would not be inferred from the other.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a Jewish woman may not nurse a gentile child, and a gentile woman may not nurse a Jewish child; Rabbi Meir forbids even with supervision, while the Sages permit with others present.
The Gemara explains that if only the case of midwifery were taught, one might think the Sages concede to Rabbi Meir regarding nursing due to the possibility of poison.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary to teach, as each has a unique stringency or leniency that would not be inferred from the other.

items.text: Rav Yosef's attempts to permit for fee due to enmity, rebutted by Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attempts to permit for fee due to enmity, rebutted by Abaye
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: a baraita permits a Jewish woman to deliver a gentile's child for a fee. Rav Yosef explains that fee is permitted to avoid enmity. He then tries to extend this to Shabbat delivery, nursing, and even to the rule of not raising gentiles from a pit, but Abaye refutes each attempt, showing that the gentile cannot claim enmity because the Jew can offer a plausible excuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that permits a Jewish woman to deliver a gentile's child for a fee, unlike the mishna's blanket prohibition.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by explaining that the fee is permitted to avoid enmity (איבה).
Rav Yosef thought to extend the leniency to delivering a gentile's child on Shabbat for a fee, due to enmity.
Abaye refutes Rav Yosef's extension: the Jew can excuse herself by saying that Shabbat is desecrated only for those who keep it, not for gentiles who do not.
Rav Yosef thought to extend the leniency to nursing a gentile's child for a fee, due to enmity.
Abaye refutes this extension: the woman can excuse herself by saying she wishes to marry (if unmarried) or not to become repulsive to her husband (if married).
Rav Yosef thought to extend the leniency to raising a gentile from a pit for a fee, due to enmity, citing the baraita that one may not raise or lower gentiles.
Abaye refutes this extension: the Jew can excuse himself by saying his son is on the roof or he has an appointment at court, so no enmity arises.

items.text: Baraita cited by Rabbi Avahu before Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita cited by Rabbi Avahu before Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches before Rabbi Yochanan a baraita: gentiles and shepherds of small cattle may not be raised from a pit nor lowered into it. The daf ends mid-sentence, likely continuing the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches before Rabbi Yochanan a baraita stating that gentiles and shepherds of small cattle may not be raised from a pit.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lowering heretics and apostates
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lowering heretics and apostates
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that while one does not lower a gentile into a pit, for heretics, informers, and apostates, one lowers them and does not raise them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not lower a gentile into a pit, but for heretics, informers, and apostates, one lowers them and does not raise them.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the apostate
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the apostate
items.desc_en: A student challenges the Mishnah by citing a verse that includes an apostate in the obligation to return lost property, implying one must raise them. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to an apostate who eats non-kosher meat to defy God, which is considered a heretic.

sub.desc_en: A student challenges the Mishnah by citing a verse that includes an apostate in the obligation to return lost property, implying one must raise them.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to an apostate who eats non-kosher meat to defy God, which is considered a heretic.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina on the definition of an apostate
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina on the definition of an apostate
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina argue whether one who eats non-kosher meat to defy God is an apostate or a heretic. One says it makes him a heretic, the other says even that is an apostate, and only an idolater is a heretic. A challenge is raised from a baraita that calls one who eats a single insect an apostate, even though it is defiant, and the Gemara answers that he does so to taste the forbidden flavor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about the definition of an apostate versus a heretic.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that calls one who eats a single insect an apostate, even though it is defiant.
The Gemara resolves that the person ate the insect to taste the forbidden flavor, not purely to defy God.

items.text: Clarification of 'lower but do not raise'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'lower but do not raise'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can lower someone already in a pit. Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet explains it refers to a case where there is a ledge, and one pushes it away. Rabba and Rav Yosef say it refers to covering a stone on the well's mouth, and Ravina says it refers to removing a ladder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that one lowers heretics, informers, and apostates into a pit but does not raise them, and questions why the phrase 'but does not raise' is needed since they are already being lowered.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama in the name of Rav Sheshet explains that the phrase teaches that if there is a ledge in the pit, one scrapes it off, using a pretext that he is preventing animals from descending upon the trapped person.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both explain that the phrase teaches that if there is a stone covering the well's mouth, one covers it, using the pretext of passing his animals over it.
Ravina explains that the phrase teaches that if there is a ladder in the pit, one removes it, using the pretext that he needs it to lower his son from the roof.

items.text: Baraita on circumcision by a gentile
items.text_en: Baraita on circumcision by a gentile
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a Jew may circumcise a gentile for the purpose of conversion, but not for a medical procedure. A gentile may not circumcise a Jew because they are suspected of bloodshed, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages permit it if others are present, but Rabbi Meir forbids even then due to the risk of the knife slipping.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that a Jew may circumcise a gentile for conversion but not for a medical procedure, and a gentile may not circumcise a Jew because they are suspected of bloodshed.
The Sages permit a gentile to circumcise a Jew when others are present, but not when they are alone.
Rabbi Meir forbids even when others are present, due to the risk that the gentile might tilt the knife and cause injury.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on gentile circumcision
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on gentile circumcision
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Meir seems to allow a Samaritan (Kuti) to circumcise over a Roman (Armai), but another source shows he prefers a Roman. The Gemara suggests reversing the opinions, but then objects that Rabbi Yehuda holds a Roman is acceptable, yet another source says he deems gentile circumcision invalid. The Gemara concludes that the contradiction remains unresolved, leaving the matter open.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's position by citing a baraita where he prefers an Aramean (gentile) over a Samaritan for circumcision, contradicting his earlier ruling.
The baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's opposing view that a Samaritan is preferable over an Aramean for circumcision.
The Gemara suggests reversing the opinions in the baraita to resolve the contradiction: Rabbi Meir would then prefer the Samaritan, and Rabbi Yehuda the Aramean.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda cannot prefer an Aramean, citing a baraita where he deems gentile circumcision invalid based on the verse 'וְאַתָּה אֶת בְּרִיתִי תִשְׁמֹר' (and you shall keep My covenant).
The Gemara concludes not to reverse the opinions, leaving the contradiction unresolved and the matter open.

items.text: Opening statement: Expert gentile physician
items.text_en: Opening statement: Expert gentile physician
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: if a gentile physician is an expert for the public, it is permitted for a Jew to be treated by him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if a gentile physician is an expert for the public, it is permitted for a Jew to be treated by him.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on circumcision by a Cuthean
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on circumcision by a Cuthean
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda considers a Cuthean (Samaritan) valid, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a Cuthean may not circumcise a Jew because he does it for the sake of Mount Gerizim. Rabbi Yosei objects, arguing that circumcision is not explicitly required to be for its own sake from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda considers a Cuthean valid for circumcision, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda forbids a Cuthean from circumcising a Jew because he does it for the sake of Mount Gerizim.
Rabbi Yosei objects, arguing that the Torah does not require circumcision to be performed for its own sake, and therefore a Cuthean may circumcise a Jew indefinitely.

items.text: Resolution: The baraita is from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.text_en: Resolution: The baraita is from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the initial assumption and attributing the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who derives the disqualification of a gentile's circumcision from the verse 'And you shall keep My covenant.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the initial assumption and attributing the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives the disqualification of a gentile's circumcision from the verse 'And you shall keep My covenant.'

items.text: Scriptural sources for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the scriptural basis: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'to God circumcise' that circumcision must be for God's sake, while Rabbi Yosei derives from 'circumcised he shall be circumcised' that any circumcision is valid. The Gemara addresses the apparent redundancy of the verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Yehuda's position, and answers that it derives from the verse 'לַה׳ הִמּוֹל' (to God circumcise).
Rav Chisda states that Rabbi Yosei derives his position from the verse 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' (circumcised he shall be circumcised).
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Yosei, isn't it written 'לַה׳ הִמּוֹל' (to God circumcise)?
The Gemara answers: that verse is written with regard to Passover, not circumcision.
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Yehuda, isn't it also written 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' (circumcised he shall be circumcised)?
The Gemara answers: the Torah spoke in the language of people, so the doubled verb does not teach a novel halakha.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on the source
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on the source
items.desc_en: It is stated: Daru bar Pappa in the name of Rav says the source is 'And you shall keep My covenant,' while Rabbi Yochanan says it is 'circumcised he shall be circumcised.' The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between them, initially suggesting a circumcised Arab or Gabnuni.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a dispute was reported: Daru bar Pappa in the name of Rav derives the invalidity of a gentile's circumcision from 'ואתה את בריתי תשמר' (and you shall keep My covenant), while Rabbi Yochanan derives it from 'המול ימול' (he must be circumcised).

The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions, and initially suggests a circumcised Arab or Gabnuni: according to the one who says 'המול ימול' (he must be circumcised) it is permitted, but according to the one who says 'את בריתי תשמר' (you shall keep My covenant) it is not.

items.text: Rejection of the first difference and new proposal
items.text_en: Rejection of the first difference and new proposal
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the circumcised Arab/Gabnuni difference based on a mishnah about vows, showing that circumcised gentiles are still considered uncircumcised. It then proposes a difference regarding a Jew whose brothers died from circumcision and who was not circumcised, but this too is rejected based on another mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous difference (circumcised Arab/Gabnuni) by citing a mishnah (Nedarim 31b) that one who vows not to benefit from ערלים (uncircumcised) is permitted with uncircumcised Jews but forbidden with circumcised gentiles, proving that circumcised gentiles are still considered uncircumcised.

The Gemara proposes a new practical difference: a Jew whose brothers died from circumcision and who was not circumcised — according to the opinion that derives from 'וְאַתָּה אֶת בְּרִיתִי תִשְׁמֹר' (you shall keep My covenant) such a Jew may perform circumcision, but according to the opinion that derives from 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' (he must be circumcised) he may not.

The Gemara objects to this new difference by citing another mishnah (Nedarim 31b) that one who vows not to benefit from מולים (circumcised) is forbidden with uncircumcised Jews and permitted with circumcised gentiles, proving that uncircumcised Jews are still considered circumcised.

items.text: Final difference: a woman
items.text_en: Final difference: a woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the practical difference is a woman: according to Rav (who requires 'And you shall keep My covenant'), a woman is not subject to circumcision and thus not included, while according to Rabbi Yochanan (who uses 'circumcised he shall be circumcised'), a woman is considered as if circumcised. The Gemara addresses a challenge from the story of Zipporah.

items.text: Mishnah: Healing and haircuts from gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: Healing and haircuts from gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One may receive healing from them for monetary loss but not for life-threatening situations. One may not get a haircut from them anywhere, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: in a public domain it is permitted, but not in private.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may receive healing from gentiles for monetary loss but not for life-threatening situations.
Rabbi Meir states that one may not get a haircut from a gentile anywhere.
The Sages say that in a public domain it is permitted to get a haircut from a gentile, but not in private.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's terms
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara first considers whether 'monetary healing' means for pay and 'life-threatening healing' means for free, but rejects this. It then explains that 'monetary healing' refers to one's animal and 'life-threatening healing' to one's own body, citing Rav Yehuda's statement that even a thorn in the side should not be treated by them. Finally, Mar Ukva permits asking a gentile about the efficacy of a specific remedy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'monetary healing' and 'life-threatening healing'.
The Gemara suggests that 'monetary healing' means for pay and 'life-threatening healing' means for free, but rejects this because the Mishnah should have simply said 'for pay but not for free'.
The Gemara suggests that 'monetary healing' refers to a non-life-threatening matter and 'life-threatening healing' to a life-threatening matter.
Rav Yehuda objects that even a non-life-threatening wound like a bloodletting incision may not be treated by gentiles.
The Gemara resolves that 'monetary healing' refers to one's animal and 'life-threatening healing' to one's own body.
Rav Yehuda's statement that even a bloodletting wound may not be treated by gentiles supports the resolution that 'life-threatening healing' refers to one's own body.
Mar Ukva permits asking a gentile about the efficacy of a specific remedy, even though one may not be treated by them.

items.text: Initial assumption about borrowing from idolaters
items.text_en: Initial assumption about borrowing from idolaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one might think an idolater would lend an item to a Jew, just as he would lend to anyone else, and then the Jew might come to harm through that item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the rationale that a gentile, thinking the Jew will ask others as well, will give good advice to avoid harming his own reputation.

items.text: Rava's ruling on uncertain vs. certain death
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on uncertain vs. certain death
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Chisda) quotes Rabbi Yochanan: if the patient's life is in doubt (ספק חי ספק מת), one may not be healed by idolaters; if death is certain (ודאי מת), one may. The Gemara questions why certain death is allowed despite momentary life (חיי שעה), and proves from a biblical verse that we do not worry about momentary life.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Chisda) quotes Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if the patient's life is in doubt (ספק חי ספק מת), one may not be healed by idolaters; if death is certain (ודאי מת), one may.
The Gemara questions why certain death is allowed despite momentary life (חיי שעה), and answers that we do not worry about momentary life.

items.text: Objection from the story of Ben Dama
items.text_en: Objection from the story of Ben Dama
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that prohibits any medical treatment from heretics, even for momentary life. It recounts the story of Ben Dama, who was bitten by a snake and died because Rabbi Yishmael prevented him from being healed by a heretic, citing the verse 'one who breaches a fence will be bitten by a snake'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source that we are not concerned with temporal life.
The Gemara cites the lepers' reasoning in II Kings 7:4 as proof that temporal life is not a concern.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that prohibits any dealings with heretics and forbids being treated by them even for temporal life.
The baraita recounts the incident of Ben Dama, who was bitten by a snake and died because Rabbi Yishmael prevented him from being healed by a heretic.
Rabbi Yishmael declares Ben Dama fortunate for not transgressing the Sages' ordinance, citing the verse 'one who breaches a fence will be bitten by a snake'.

items.text: Distinction for heresy due to enticement
items.text_en: Distinction for heresy due to enticement
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the case of heretics (מינות) from ordinary idolaters, because heresy is more alluring and may lead one to follow them. It then clarifies that the snake that bit Ben Dama was the 'snake of the Sages' (חיויא דרבנן), which has no cure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes heresy (מינות) from ordinary idolatry because it is enticing and may lead one to follow them.
Mar clarifies that the snake that bit Ben Dama was the 'snake of the Sages' (חיויא דרבנן), which has no cure.

items.text: Ben Dama's intended proof and Rabbi Yishmael's public/private distinction
items.text_en: Ben Dama's intended proof and Rabbi Yishmael's public/private distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what Ben Dama intended to cite: the verse 'וחי בהם' (live by them), implying not die by them. Rabbi Yishmael counters that this applies only in private, but in public (פרהסיא) one must give up life rather than violate God's name, as derived from 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verse Ben Dama intended to cite, and answers that he would have cited 'וחי בהם' (live by them), implying not die by them.
Rabbi Yishmael counters that the leniency of 'וחי בהם' applies only in private, but in public (פרהסיא) one must give up life rather than profane God's name, as derived from 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on wounds that violate Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on wounds that violate Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan: for any wound that would permit desecrating Shabbat, one may not be healed by idolaters. An alternative version of the statement is also cited.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan: for any wound that would permit desecrating Shabbat, one may not be healed by idolaters.
An alternative version of the same statement is cited, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Defining a mortal wound and related conditions
items.text_en: Defining a mortal wound and related conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the difference between a 'mortal wound' and other wounds, citing Rav Adda bar Matna who states that the back of the hand and foot are like a mortal wound. Rav Zutra bar Toviya and Rav Shemen bar Abba add that any wound requiring estimation and a certain fever are also treated as mortal wounds for Shabbat desecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the rule that one may not be treated by gentiles for a mortal wound, then asks what the difference is between two versions of Rabbi Yochanan's statement, and answers by citing Rav Adda bar Matna who says that the back of the hand and foot are like a mortal wound.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya says in the name of Rav that any wound requiring estimation (whether it is fatal) permits desecrating Shabbat for its treatment.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a burning fever is like a mortal wound and permits desecrating Shabbat for its treatment.

items.text: Defining the boundary of a mortal wound and a question about teeth
items.text_en: Defining the boundary of a mortal wound and a question about teeth
