items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami defines a mortal wound as from the lip inward. Rabbi Eliezer raises a question about the gums and teeth: are they considered external like a wound on the body, or internal like a mortal wound?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from what point a wound is considered an internal injury, and Rabbi Ami answers: from the lips inward.
Rabbi Eliezer raises a dilemma: are afflictions of the gums and teeth considered external injuries because they are firm, or internal injuries because they are inside the mouth?

items.text: Abaye's attempted proof from a baraita about tooth pain
items.text_en: Abaye's attempted proof from a baraita about tooth pain
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a baraita stating that one who has a toothache may not sip vinegar through the teeth, implying that only mild pain is prohibited, but severe pain is permitted. The Gemara deflects this proof, suggesting the tanna might call even severe pain 'חושש'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about one who has a toothache not sipping vinegar, inferring that only mild concern is prohibited but severe pain is permitted.
The Gemara deflects the proof by suggesting the tanna might call even severe pain 'חושש' (concern).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's treatment for צפדינא and its implication
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's treatment for צפדינא and its implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yochanan suffered from צפדינא (a throat ailment) and was treated by a matron. He later revealed the remedy publicly, circumventing his oath. The Gemara concludes that this shows צפדינא is like a mortal wound, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak distinguishes it because it starts in the mouth and ends in the intestines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story about Rabbi Yochanan suffering from צפדינא and being treated by a matron, who prepared medicine on Thursday and Friday; he later revealed the remedy publicly.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan violated his oath and caused a desecration of God's name, but resolves that he informed her from the outset that he would reveal it.
The Gemara infers that צפדינא is like a mortal wound, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak distinguishes it because it starts in the mouth and ends in the intestines.

items.text: Symptoms and remedies for צפדינא
items.text_en: Symptoms and remedies for צפדינא
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the symptoms of צפדינא (blood from the gums when biting) and its causes (cold wheat, hot barley, or leftover drink). Various remedies are suggested, including a mixture of leaven water, olive oil, and salt, or goose fat on a goose wing. Abaye recounts being cured by an Arab's advice using olive pits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the symptoms of צפדינא and describes the test of placing something between the teeth to see if blood comes from the gums.
The Gemara lists the causes of צפדינא: very cold wheat foods, very hot barley foods, and remnants of fried fish drink.
The Gemara asks what remedy the matron performed for Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Acha brei d'Rava says the remedy was leaven water, olive oil, and salt.
Mar bar Rav Ashi says the remedy was goose fat applied with a goose wing.
Abaye reports that he tried all these remedies but was not cured.
Abaye recounts that an Arab told him to burn olive pits on a new hoe and apply them to the gums, and he was cured.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's treatment and the rule against healing from idolaters
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's treatment and the rule against healing from idolaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan could receive treatment from a non-Jewish matron, given the rule that one may not seek healing from idolaters for a wound that desecrates Shabbat. It answers that an important person is different. Further, it distinguishes Rabbi Yochanan as a licensed physician, unlike Rabbi Avahu who was also a physician but was endangered by a heretic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan could receive treatment from a non-Jewish matron, given the rule that one may not seek healing from idolaters for a wound that desecrates Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that an important person is different, implying that Rabbi Yochanan's stature allowed him to receive treatment.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Avahu was also an important person, yet Yaakov the heretic placed poison on his leg, endangering him.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was a licensed physician, unlike Rabbi Avahu who was also a physician but was endangered by heretics who were willing to die with their victims.

items.text: Other dangerous conditions and their remedies
items.text_en: Other dangerous conditions and their remedies
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that פדעתא (a wound) is dangerous and permits Shabbat desecration, listing remedies. Rav Safra describes עינבתא (a throat ailment) as the angel of death's feather, with remedies including beets in honey. Rava discusses סימטא (a fever) and its treatment. The daf ends with Rabbi Yaakov falling ill.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that a wound (פדעתא) is dangerous and permits Shabbat desecration.
The Gemara asks for the remedy and provides two: cress in vinegar to stop blood, and scrapings of yavla and thornbush or worms from trash to promote healing.
Rav Safra describes a throat ailment (עינבתא) as the forerunner of the Angel of Death.
The Gemara asks for the remedy and provides: tigna in honey or parsley in wine, and in the meantime rubbing a matching grape on the boil.
Rava states that an abscess (סימטא) is the forerunner of fever.
The Gemara asks for the remedy and provides: snapping the abscess sixty times and tearing it crosswise, but only if the head has not whitened.
The daf begins a new narrative about Rabbi Yaakov falling ill, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Remedies for a boil (פיקעא) on the neck
items.text_en: Remedies for a boil (פיקעא) on the neck
items.desc_en: Rav Ami (or Rav Asi) instructs a series of remedies for a boil on the neck, including using a leek, tying it with a cord, applying white clay, and burning it. If the boil is on the lower neck, different remedies are prescribed, such as fat from an unopened goat, dried gourd leaves, almond shells, or oil and flax in summer and grape wool in winter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a remedy for a boil (פיקעא) on the neck, citing Rav Ami or Rav Asi who instructs using seven seeds of ice plant, binding them, dipping in white naphtha, burning, and spreading the ashes, while also placing a bramble kernel against the anus.
The Gemara asks what remedy applies for a boil on the lower crevice (deeper in the rectum) as opposed to the upper one.
The Gemara answers that for a lower boil, one should bring the fat of a goat that has not yet given birth, melt it, and apply it.
The Gemara provides alternative remedies: if the fat is unavailable, use dried pumpkin leaves, snail shells, or oil mixed with wax on worn flax or cotton clothing depending on the season.

items.text: Remedies for ear pain
items.text_en: Remedies for ear pain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu had an earache, and Rabbi Yochanan (or the study hall) instructed him. Abaye and Rava cite their mothers and a doctor respectively, stating that the kidney is only for the ear. Various remedies are given, including kidney of a bald goat, fat of a camel locust, oil with wicks, and a reed from a hundred-year-old cane. The section ends with a mnemonic about wet and dry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Avahu had an earache and Rabbi Yochanan (or the study hall) instructed him, then asks what they instructed.
Abaye reports that his mother said the kidney was created only for the ear.
Rava adds that Minyomei the doctor said all liquids harm the ear except kidney fluid.
The Gemara prescribes the first remedy: take the kidney of a bald goat, tear it vertically and horizontally, place it on coals, and apply the tepid fluid to the ear.
The Gemara offers an alternative remedy: melt the fat of a large beetle and apply it to the ear.

The Gemara prescribes a third remedy: fill the ear with oil, prepare seven wicks of alfalfa with garlic ends, light them, and place the other end in the ear, replacing each wick, while avoiding drafts.
The Gemara presents another version: use seven wax tapers smeared with alfalfa oil, placing one end in the flame and one in the ear, replacing each, while avoiding drafts.
The Gemara prescribes a fifth remedy: take dried but uncombed fiber, place it in the ear, and bring the ear opposite a flame, while avoiding drafts.
The Gemara prescribes a sixth remedy: take the tube of a hundred-year-old reed, salt it with rock salt, burn it, and stick it in the ear.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic: moist cures for dry afflictions and dry cures for moist afflictions.

items.text: Raising ears on Shabbat
items.text_en: Raising ears on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Zutra quotes Rabbi Chanina that one may raise ears on Shabbat. Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah teaches that this is permitted by hand but not with a remedy, while others say the opposite. The reason given is that a remedy might cause bleeding (מזריף זריף).

sub.text: Rabbah bar Zutra quoting Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Zutra quoting Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Zutra quotes Rabbi Chanina that one may raise ears (set a dislocated jaw) on Shabbat.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah teaches that raising ears is permitted by hand but not with a remedy.
An alternative tradition states the opposite: raising ears is permitted with a remedy but not by hand.
The Gemara explains the reason: manual manipulation might cause bleeding (מזריף זריף), which is a Torah violation, whereas applying a remedy is only a rabbinic violation.

items.text: Eye ailments and Shabbat: the case of a rebellious eye
items.text_en: Eye ailments and Shabbat: the case of a rebellious eye
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav that an eye that has 'rebelled' (מרדה) may be painted on Shabbat. Initially, it was thought that this only applies if the ingredients were ground before Shabbat, but Rabbi Yaakov clarifies from Rav Yehudah that even grinding on Shabbat and bringing through a public domain is permitted. The story of Mar Shmuel's maidservant who lost an eye because no one treated her on Shabbat is cited as a precedent, with the reason that the eye's health depends on the heart.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav that an eye that has 'rebelled' (מרדה) may be painted on Shabbat.
The Gemara initially assumes that this leniency only applies if the ingredients were ground before Shabbat, but not if one grinds them on Shabbat or brings them through a public domain.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov clarifying from Rav Yehudah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov clarifying from Rav Yehudah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov clarifies from Rav Yehudah that even grinding the ingredients on Shabbat and bringing them through a public domain is permitted.

Rav Yehudah permitted painting the eye on Shabbat; Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah initially criticized him, but later when he himself suffered eye pain, Rav Yehudah told him it is permitted for everyone but prohibited for him due to his earlier disrespect.

Rav Yehudah explains that the ruling is from Mar Shmuel, citing the story of Mar Shmuel's maidservant whose eye popped out because no one treated her on Shabbat, and Mar Shmuel subsequently taught that a rebellious eye may be painted on Shabbat because the eye's tendons depend on the heart's valves.

items.text: Examples of eye ailments that permit treatment on Shabbat
items.text_en: Examples of eye ailments that permit treatment on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah lists specific eye conditions that permit treatment on Shabbat: ריר (saliva), דיצא (a type of discharge), דמא (blood), דמעתא (tears), קידחא (inflammation), and תחילת אוכלה (beginning of an infection). He excludes סוף אוכלה (end of an infection) and פצוחי עינא (opening the eye).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for examples of eye ailments that are life-threatening and permit treatment on Shabbat.

Rav Yehudah lists specific eye conditions that permit treatment on Shabbat: ריר (saliva), דיצא (a type of discharge), דמא (blood), דמעתא (tears), קידחא (inflammation), and תחילת אוכלה (beginning of an infection).
Rav Yehudah excludes סוף אוכלה (end of an infection) and פצוחי עינא (opening the eye) from the list of conditions that permit treatment on Shabbat.

items.text: Dangerous conditions and their remedies
items.text_en: Dangerous conditions and their remedies
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah lists dangerous conditions: a wasp sting, a lizard bite, a thorn, and eye pain accompanied by fever. He then gives rules for treatment: hot for hot, cold for cold, and their opposites are dangerous. Specific remedies are given for scorpion stings (hot water) and wasp stings (cold water), and their opposites are dangerous.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah lists dangerous conditions: a wasp sting, a lizard bite, a thorn, and eye pain accompanied by fever.
Rav Yehudah gives the rule: hot foods for hot conditions and cold foods for cold conditions, and their opposites are dangerous.
Rav Yehudah gives specific remedies: hot water for scorpion stings and cold water for wasp stings, and their opposites are dangerous.
Rav Yehudah gives the remedy for a thorn: hot water, and cold water is dangerous.

items.text: Dangers of certain foods after bloodletting
items.text_en: Dangers of certain foods after bloodletting
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists several dangerous combinations: after bloodletting, certain foods like milk, cheese, onions, and eggs are harmful; conversely, eating them before bloodletting is beneficial. It also notes that eating fish after bloodletting is dangerous, and that eating fish before blood is beneficial, but a third time is dangerous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general warning about the danger of reversing the order of certain foods and bloodletting.
The Gemara specifies that vinegar after bloodletting and small fish after a fast are beneficial, but the reverse is dangerous.
The Gemara lists additional dangerous combinations: cress before bloodletting, fever with bloodletting, and eye pain with bloodletting.
The Gemara states that on the second day after eating fish one may let blood, and vice versa, but on the third day it is dangerous.

items.text: Remedy for eating forbidden foods after bloodletting
items.text_en: Remedy for eating forbidden foods after bloodletting
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one who lets blood should not eat milk, cheese, onions, or eggs. If he did, Abaye prescribes a remedy: take a quarter-log of wine and a quarter-log of vinegar, mix them, and drink it. The mixture should be taken to the east of the city because of the strong smell.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that one who lets blood must not eat milk, cheese, onions, or cress.
Abaye prescribes a remedy of mixing a quarter-log of vinegar and a quarter-log of wine and drinking it.
Abaye adds that one should defecate only to the east of the city due to the offensive odor.

items.text: Remedies for heart, spirit, and kidney ailments
items.text_en: Remedies for heart, spirit, and kidney ailments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that one may apply a poultice (unkli) on Shabbat. Rabbi Abba explains that this is a compress for the heart. The remedy involves taking cumin, leek, and other herbs. For heart ailments, the remedy is taken with wine; for spirit (wind) ailments, with water; for kidney ailments, with beer, each with a biblical verse as a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one may lift the unkali (a compress for the heart) on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks what the unkali is.
Rabbi Abba explains that the unkali is the edge of the ribs near the heart.
The Gemara asks what the cure is for this condition.

The Gemara prescribes a remedy of cumin, caraway, mint, wormwood, satureja, and hyssop, and specifies that for heart ailments it is taken with wine, for wind ailments with water, and for kidney ailments with beer, each with a biblical verse as a mnemonic.

items.text: Practical applications and a personal story
items.text_en: Practical applications and a personal story
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava grinds all the ingredients together and takes a handful of five fingers. Rav Ashi grinds each separately and takes a thumbful and a pinkyful. Rav Pappa says he tried all these but was not cured until an Arab told him to take a new jug, fill it with water, add a ladle of honey that had been hung in the stars, and drink it the next day; he did so and was cured.

items.text: Six things that heal and ten that harm the sick
items.text_en: Six things that heal and ten that harm the sick
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that six things heal the sick: cabbage, beets, water of sisin, dried and a stomach, the spleen, and the diaphragm of the liver. Some add small fish. Ten things cause a relapse: beef, fat, roasted meat, poultry, roasted egg, eggs, shaving, bath, cheese, and liver. Some add nuts, others add cucumbers, which are called 'kishuin' because they are as hard on the body as swords.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists six items that heal the sick, with some adding small fish.
The baraita lists ten items that cause a relapse, with additional opinions about nuts and cucumbers, and a folk etymology for cucumbers.

items.text: Shaving by a non-Jew: concern for idolatry
items.text_en: Shaving by a non-Jew: concern for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not have a haircut from them (non-Jews) anywhere. The Gemara explains: A Jew being shaved by a non-Jew should look in a mirror; a non-Jew being shaved by a Jew, when he reaches his forelock, the Jew should withdraw his hand. The Gemara questions: If in public, why a mirror? If in private, what does seeing help? It answers: Even in private, the mirror makes it appear as if he is an important person.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not have a haircut from non-Jews anywhere, and the baraita elaborates: a Jew being shaved by a non-Jew should look in a mirror; a non-Jew being shaved by a Jew, when he reaches his forelock, the Jew should withdraw his hand.
The Gemara questions the baraita: if the haircut is in a public domain, why need a mirror? If in a private domain, what does seeing help?
The Gemara answers: even in a private domain, the mirror makes the Jew appear as an important person, deterring the non-Jew from harming him.

items.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna's practice and justification
items.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna's practice and justification
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna was being shaved by a non-Jew in the alleys of Nehardea. The non-Jew said: 'Chana, Chana, your curls are beautiful for a pair!' He replied: 'May it come to me that I have transgressed the words of Rabbi Meir.' The Gemara asks: Did he not transgress the Rabbis? It answers: The Rabbis only forbade in public, but in private they did not. He thought the alleys of Nehardea, since many people pass, are like public domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna was being shaved by a non-Jew in the alleys of Nehardea; the barber commented on his curls, and Rav Chana bar Bizna admitted he had transgressed Rabbi Meir's ruling.
The Gemara asks: Did he not also transgress the Rabbis' ruling, since the alleys are a private domain?
The Gemara explains that Rav Chana bar Bizna considered the alleys of Nehardea, since many people pass, to be like a public domain, so he thought the Rabbis permitted it.

items.text: The measure of the forelock and a mnemonic for Rav Malkiya vs. Rav Malkiyo
items.text_en: The measure of the forelock and a mnemonic for Rav Malkiya vs. Rav Malkiyo
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how much of the forelock the Jew should leave when shaving a non-Jew: three fingerbreadths on each side. Rav Malkiya and Rav Malkiyo are distinguished by their rulings: Rav Malkiyo is associated with 'shapud, shfachot, and gumot', while Rav Malkiya is associated with 'blorit, efer mikleh, and gevinah'. Rav Pappa gives a mnemonic: 'Mishnah and matnita are Rav Malkiya, shema'tata are Rav Malkiyo.' The difference between them is the case of shfachot.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that when a Jew cuts a non-Jew's hair, upon reaching the forelock he must remove his hand.
The Gemara asks how much space must be left around the forelock.

sub.text: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Ada bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Ada bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rav Malkiya in the name of Rav Ada bar Ahava answers: three fingerbreadths in each direction.
Rav Chanina bar Rav Ika distinguishes between two sages: Rav Malkiyo is associated with rulings on skewer, maidservants, and follicles; Rav Malkiya with forelock, burnt ashes, and cheese.

Rav Pappa gives a mnemonic: rulings from Mishnah and baraita are from Rav Malkiya, while unattributed halakhic statements (שמעתתא) are from Rav Malkiyo, with the mnemonic that Mishnah is a queen (מלכתא).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions (Rav Chanina bar Rav Ika and Rav Pappa).
The Gemara answers: the difference between them is the case of maidservants (שפחות).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: List of forbidden items
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of forbidden items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates items of gentiles that are forbidden for benefit: wine, vinegar that was originally wine, earthenware from Hadrian, and perforated hides. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between round and elongated tears. Additional items include meat entering or leaving an idolatrous temple, wineskins, and cheese, with disputes between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items of gentiles that are forbidden for benefit: wine, vinegar that was originally wine, Hadrianic earthenware, and perforated hides.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a circular tear (forbidden) and an elongated tear (permitted) on hides.
Rabbi Akiva rules that meat entering an idolatrous temple is permitted, but meat exiting is forbidden as offerings to the dead.
The Mishnah adds that it is forbidden to do business with those going to an idolatrous festival, but permitted with those returning.
Rabbi Meir rules that wineskins and jugs of gentiles containing Jew's wine are forbidden for benefit.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir and say that such vessels are not forbidden for benefit.
Rabbi Meir rules that grape seeds and skins of gentiles are forbidden for benefit.
The Sages distinguish: moist grape residues are forbidden, but dry ones are permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's account: Rabbi Yishmael questions Rabbi Yehoshua about gentile cheese
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's account: Rabbi Yishmael questions Rabbi Yehoshua about gentile cheese
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda relates that Rabbi Yishmael asked Rabbi Yehoshua why gentile cheese was forbidden. Rabbi Yehoshua first answered that it is because they curdle it with the stomach of a neveilah. Rabbi Yishmael countered that the stomach of an olah is more stringent, yet the Sages said it is not subject to me'ilah. Rabbi Yehoshua then gave a second reason: because they curdle it with the stomach of calves used for idolatry. Rabbi Yishmael asked why it is not forbidden for benefit, and Rabbi Yehoshua diverted the conversation to a biblical reading of Song of Songs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishna states that fish stew and cheese of Beit Unyaki belonging to gentiles are prohibited, and according to Rabbi Meir their prohibition includes benefit, while the Sages say benefit is not prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda relates that Rabbi Yishmael asked Rabbi Yehoshua why the Sages prohibited gentile cheese.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that the cheese is prohibited because it is curdled with the stomach contents of a neveilah (unslaughtered animal carcass).

Rabbi Yishmael objects that the stomach of an olah (burnt-offering) is more stringent than that of a neveilah, yet the Sages said one may not derive benefit from it but is not liable for me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property), so the neveilah reason is insufficient.
Rabbi Yehoshua gives a second reason: the cheese is prohibited because it is curdled with the stomach contents of calves used for idol worship.
Rabbi Yishmael asks why, if the reason is idolatry, the Sages did not prohibit deriving benefit from the cheese.
Rabbi Yehoshua diverts the conversation to a different matter, asking Rabbi Yishmael how he reads the verse in Song of Songs.
Rabbi Yishmael answers that he reads the verse in the feminine form: 'For your love (dodayikh) is better than wine.'
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects Rabbi Yishmael's reading, arguing that the next verse 'Your ointments have a goodly fragrance' teaches that the verse is in the masculine form.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the prohibition of gentile wine from the Torah
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the prohibition of gentile wine from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the prohibition of gentile wine. Rabbah bar Avuah cites a verse linking wine to sacrifices, which are forbidden for benefit. The Gemara then derives the prohibition of sacrifices from the verse about eating sacrifices of the dead, and the prohibition of a corpse from a gezeirah shavah with the eglah arufah. The derivation concludes with the principle that the eglah arufah is like consecrated items because the word 'kaparah' is written regarding it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the prohibition of gentile wine.
Rabbah bar Avuah cites the verse 'אֲשֶׁר חֵלֶב זְבָחֵימוֹ יֹאכֵלוּ יִשְׁתּוּ יֵין נְסִיכָם' to derive that just as a sacrifice is forbidden for benefit, so too gentile wine is forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition of benefit from a sacrifice itself.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of benefit from a sacrifice from the verse 'וַיִּצָּמְדוּ לְבַעַל פְּעוֹר וַיֹּאכְלוּ זִבְחֵי מֵתִים', comparing it to a corpse which is forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition of benefit from a corpse.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of benefit from a corpse via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'שָׁם' from the עגלה ערופה (heifer whose neck is broken).
The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition of benefit from the עגלה ערופה (heifer whose neck is broken).
The school of Rabbi Yannai states that the word 'כַּפָּרָה' (atonement) is written regarding the עגלה ערופה, equating it to consecrated items which are forbidden for benefit.

items.text: Gemara: Vinegar of gentiles and the need for a double seal
items.text_en: Gemara: Vinegar of gentiles and the need for a double seal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions vinegar that was originally wine, as it seems obvious that vinegar is not wine. Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah teaches that our vinegar in the hand of a gentile does not require a double seal, because gentiles do not libate vinegar and they would not bother to forge a seal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions vinegar that was originally wine, as it seems obvious that vinegar is not wine and its prohibition should lapse.
Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah teaches that our vinegar in the hand of a gentile does not require a double seal, because gentiles do not libate vinegar and they would not bother to forge a seal.

items.text: Gemara: Cooked wine of gentiles and the need for a double seal
items.text_en: Gemara: Cooked wine of gentiles and the need for a double seal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a teaches that cooked wine of gentiles that was originally wine is forbidden. The Gemara questions this, as cooking should remove the prohibition. Rav Ashi explains that the teaching is about our cooked wine in the hand of a gentile: it does not require a double seal, because gentiles do not libate cooked wine and would not bother to forge a seal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a teaches that cooked wine of gentiles that was originally wine is forbidden.
The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, since cooking should remove the prohibition.
Rav Ashi explains that the teaching is about our cooked wine in the hand of a gentile: it does not require a double seal.
Rav Ashi provides the reasoning: gentiles do not libate cooked wine and would not bother to forge a seal.

items.text: Transition from previous daf: explanation of seal forgery
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf: explanation of seal forgery
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a single seal suffices: since there is one seal, the gentile would not bother to forge it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a single seal suffices because a gentile will not bother to forge it.

items.text: Baraita on cooked wine and aluntit
items.text_en: Baraita on cooked wine and aluntit
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that cooked wine and aluntit of gentiles are forbidden, but aluntit in its natural state is permitted. It defines aluntit as a mixture of old wine, clear water, and balsam, used for a bathhouse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that cooked wine and aluntit of gentiles are forbidden, but aluntit in its natural state is permitted.
The Gemara asks for the definition of aluntit.
The Gemara answers by citing a baraita about Shabbat that distinguishes between anomlin and aluntit.
The Gemara asks for the definitions of anomlin and aluntit.
The baraita defines anomlin as wine, honey, and pepper, and aluntit as aged wine, clear water, and balsam, used for a bathhouse.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef: diluted wine and cooked wine
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef: diluted wine and cooked wine
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that diluted wine is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids, and cooked wine is not subject to libation. A question is raised whether cooked wine is subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids, and a testimony by Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi resolves that it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that diluted wine is not subject to the halakha of exposure, and cooked wine is not subject to the halakha of libation.
A dilemma is raised: Is cooked wine subject to the halakha of exposure or not?
The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's testimony that cooked wine is not subject to the halakha of exposure.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael's illness and the ruling on cooked wine
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael's illness and the ruling on cooked wine
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael fell ill, Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud and the Sages visited him. They discussed whether cooked wine is subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids. Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud reported in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, citing Rabbi Chiyya, that cooked wine is not subject to this prohibition. Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael signaled his agreement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael fell ill, and Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud and the Sages visited him.
While seated, the Sages raised the dilemma: Is cooked wine subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids (גילוי) or not?

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud reported that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said in the name of the great man Rabbi Chiyya that cooked wine is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids.
The Sages asked Rabbi Yishmael ben Zeirud: May we rely on this ruling?
Rabbi Yannai bar Yishmael motioned to them: Upon me and upon my neck, i.e., you can certainly rely on this claim.

items.text: Anecdotes about cooked and diluted wine
items.text_en: Anecdotes about cooked and diluted wine
items.desc_en: Shmuel and Avlet were served cooked wine; Shmuel gestured that it is not subject to libation. Rabbi Chiyya's maidservant left cooked wine uncovered, and Rabbi Chiyya told her it is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids. Similarly, Rav Adda bar Ahavah's servant left diluted wine uncovered, and he was told it is not subject to that prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel and Avlet were sitting together; cooked wine was brought before them, and Avlet withdrew his hand.
Shmuel told Avlet that cooked wine is not subject to the prohibition of libation.
Rabbi Chiyya's maidservant left cooked wine uncovered; Rabbi Chiyya told her it is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah's servant left diluted wine uncovered; Rav Adda bar Ahavah told him it is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids.

items.text: Rav Pappa's qualification and the story of the snake
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's qualification and the story of the snake
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies that diluted wine is only safe if it is very diluted, but if it is only slightly diluted, a snake will drink it. The Gemara questions this with a story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna who saw a snake coming toward his wine and threw water into it, causing the snake to retreat. The Gemara explains that the snake risked its life for the wine but not for the dilution. Another story about Rabbi Yannai in a tavern shows that a snake diluted wine itself to drink it. The Gemara concludes that a snake drinks wine that it dilutes itself, but not wine diluted by others.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies that only well-diluted wine is safe from snakes, but partially diluted wine is drunk by snakes.
The Gemara questions whether a snake actually drinks partially diluted wine.
The Gemara objects with a story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who saw a snake approach his wine and threw water into it, causing the snake to retreat, implying snakes avoid diluted wine.
The Gemara explains that a snake risks its life for undiluted wine but not for diluted wine.
The Gemara objects with a story of Rabbi Yannai, where a snake diluted wine itself to drink it, showing snakes do risk their lives for diluted wine.
The Gemara resolves that a snake drinks wine it dilutes itself, but not wine diluted by others.

items.text: Rava's halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Rava's halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi or Rav Mesharshiya questions whether the story provides a practical solution to danger. Rava then rules definitively: diluted wine is subject to both the prohibitions of uncovered liquids and libation; cooked wine is subject to neither.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi (or Rav Mesharshiya) questions whether the earlier story provides a practical solution for a situation involving danger.
Rava rules definitively: diluted wine is subject to both the prohibitions of uncovered liquids and libation; cooked wine is subject to neither.

items.text: The servant of Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi and the rule of 'fear of them'
items.text_en: The servant of Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi and the rule of 'fear of them'
items.desc_en: The servant of Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi left a jug of water uncovered and slept near it. Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi told him that the rule 'fear of them' applies only by day, but not by night. The Gemara then rejects this distinction, stating that the rule of 'fear of them' is never applied.

sub.desc_en: The servant of Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi noticed that a jug of water had been left uncovered, and he had been sleeping near it.
Rav Chilkiyah bar Tovi told his servant that the rule 'fear of a sleeping person is upon them' applies only by day, but not by night.
The Gemara rejects the distinction between day and night, stating that the rule of 'fear of them' is never applied.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's practices regarding water from gentile and widow homes
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's practices regarding water from gentile and widow homes
items.desc_en: Rav would not drink water from a gentile's home due to lack of care about uncovered liquids, but would drink from a widow's home because she maintains her husband's habits. Shmuel would not drink from a widow's home because she lacks fear of a man and does not cover the water, but would drink from a gentile's home because although they are not careful about uncovered liquids, they are careful about snakes. An alternative version states that Rav would not drink from a gentile's home but would from a widow's, while Shmuel would not drink from either.

sub.desc_en: Rav states he would not drink water from a gentile's home due to lack of care about uncovered liquids, but would drink from a widow's home because she maintains her husband's habits.

Shmuel states he would not drink water from a widow's home because she lacks fear of a man and does not cover the water, but would drink from a gentile's home because they are careful about cleanliness.
An alternative version states that Rav would not drink from a gentile's home but would from a widow's, while Shmuel would not drink from either.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's three wines without uncovered liquid concern
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's three wines without uncovered liquid concern
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists three types of wine that are not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids: sharp, bitter, and sweet. He explains each: sharp wine is a strong wine that bursts skins, bitter is wormwood wine, sweet is sweet wine. Rav Chama teaches a different version: sharp is wine with pepper, bitter is absinthe, sweet is well water.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that three types of wine—sharp, bitter, and sweet—are not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids, and defines each.
Rav Chama teaches an alternative version: sharp is wine with pepper, bitter is absinthe, sweet is well water.

items.text: Rav Shimon ben Lakish on 'kerina' and Rava's qualification
items.text_en: Rav Shimon ben Lakish on 'kerina' and Rava's qualification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states that 'kerina' is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids. Rabbi Abahu explains it is sweet wine from Asia. Rava qualifies that in its place it is subject to the prohibition because it is a local wine. Rava also rules that wine that has formed a film is subject to the prohibitions of uncovered liquids and libation for up to three days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states that 'kerina' is not subject to the prohibition of uncovered liquids.
The Gemara asks what 'kerina' refers to.
Rabbi Abahu explains that 'kerina' is sweet wine that comes from Asia.
Rava qualifies that in its place of origin, 'kerina' is subject to the prohibition because it is a local wine.
Rava rules that wine that has formed a film is subject to the prohibitions of uncovered liquids and libation for up to three days.

items.text: Dispute about giluy after three days
items.text_en: Dispute about giluy after three days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after three days, wine is no longer subject to giluy or yeyn nesekh. The Nehardeans disagree, holding that even after three days we still worry about giluy because a snake may occasionally drink.

items.text: Baraita on toses and shachalayim
items.text_en: Baraita on toses and shachalayim
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that fermenting wine (toses) is not subject to giluy, and its fermentation period is three days. Shachalayim (a type of drink) are also not subject to giluy, but the diaspora Jews treat them as prohibited. This applies only if they have no chalala (a certain substance); if they do, it attracts snakes.

items.text: Kutach haBavli and mei tif tif
items.text_en: Kutach haBavli and mei tif tif
items.desc_en: Kutach haBavli (Babylonian buttermilk) is not subject to giluy, but diaspora Jews treat it as prohibited. Rav Menashei says if it has bubbles (nikurei), we worry. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Shmuel says that mei tif tif (dripping water) is not subject to giluy. Rav Ashi adds that this applies only when the drips fall one after another.

items.text: Pi te'ena and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.text_en: Pi te'ena and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Shmuel says that the mouth of a fig (pi te'ena) is not subject to giluy. The Gemara suggests this aligns with the tanna Rabbi Eliezer, who says one may eat grapes and figs at night without concern, based on the verse 'The Lord protects the simple.'

items.text: Three types of venom
items.text_en: Three types of venom
items.desc_en: Rav Safra in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua Daroma teaches that there are three types of venom: that of a young snake sinks, that of a middle-aged snake bubbles, and that of an old snake floats. The Gemara questions whether an old snake's venom is weaker, citing a baraita that says three things increase in strength with age: fish, snake, and pig. It resolves that their physical strength increases but their venom's potency decreases.

items.text: Practical halakha of sinking venom
items.text_en: Practical halakha of sinking venom
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical implication of a young snake's venom sinking: if a barrel of liquid was uncovered, even if nine people drank and did not die, the tenth may not drink, as a case occurred where nine drank and survived but the tenth died. Rabbi Yirmeya identifies this as the sinking type. The same applies to a melon that was uncovered.

items.text: Laws of uncovered water and dispute with Acheirim
items.text_en: Laws of uncovered water and dispute with Acheirim
items.desc_en: A baraita lists prohibitions for uncovered water: not to pour it in public, sprinkle the house, knead clay, or give it to one's own or another's animal, nor wash face, hands, or feet. Acheirim say that if there is a wound (sirta), it is prohibited; if not, it is permitted. The Gemara notes that Acheirim and the first tanna differ regarding the back of the hand, back of the foot, and the pomegranates of the face (i.e., cheeks).

items.text: Contradiction about feeding uncovered water to animals
items.text_en: Contradiction about feeding uncovered water to animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita says one may not give uncovered water to one's own animal, but another baraita says one may give it to one's own animal. It resolves that the latter refers to a cat, which is not harmed by snake venom. The Gemara then questions why one may not give it to another's cat, and explains that one's own cat will recover if it becomes weak, but another's cat might be sold, causing a loss.

items.text: Three types of wine
items.text_en: Three types of wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira teaches that there are three types of wine: yeyn nesekh is forbidden for benefit and imparts severe impurity in the size of an olive-bulk.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that סתם יינם (wine of gentiles) is forbidden for benefit and imparts impurity, but wine deposited with a gentile is forbidden only for drinking, not for benefit.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's leniency for benefit by citing a baraita that deposited produce is considered the gentile's for shemittah and tithes. It answers that the case is where the Jew designated a corner, but then questions why drinking is not permitted, citing Rabbi Yochanan's encounter with a baraita that permits drinking. The Gemara dismisses this baraita with a proverb.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah's leniency to Rabbi Eliezer and the baraita's stringency to the Sages, citing a Tosefta where Rabbi Eliezer permits wine in a gentile's courtyard with a seal, while the Sages forbid it.

items.text: Halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: A chain of Amoraim reports that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, permitting wine deposited with a gentile when there is a seal.

items.text: Debate on seals
items.text_en: Debate on seals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether wine is guarded by a single seal or only by a double seal. The Gemara reconciles their views by linking them to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, and presents an alternative version where both agree that wine requires a double seal, differing only on the Sages' position.

items.text: Definition of double seal
items.text_en: Definition of double seal
items.desc_en: Rava defines what constitutes a double seal: a lid tied and sealed over the mouth of a barrel, a tightly woven basket, or a wineskin with its opening tied inward and sealed.

items.text: Historical ruling on Samaritan wine
items.text_en: Historical ruling on Samaritan wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that initially certain Samaritan wines were forbidden due to suspected gentile contact, but later the Sages ruled that sealed barrels are permitted, explaining the reasoning: gentiles are not particular about open barrels but are about sealed ones. A contradiction is raised from a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sends a barrel of wine via a Cuthean, or brine or fish-sauce via a gentile, it is permitted if the sender recognizes the seal and stopper, otherwise it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira initially resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between the city and the road, but Rabbi Yirmeya objects that city dwellers also travel. Rabbi Yirmeya instead explains the Mishnah refers to between the vats, where the Cuthean fears being caught.

items.text: Reasons for forbidding gentile beer
items.text_en: Reasons for forbidding gentile beer
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama citing Rabbi Yitzchak says gentile beer is forbidden due to intermarriage, while Rav Nachman says due to exposure (giluy). The Gemara questions what exposure is relevant, concluding it refers to a place where water is scarce and thus susceptible to snake venom.

items.text: Distinction between old and new beer
items.text_en: Distinction between old and new beer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises that old beer should be permitted since it is not left to age, but the reason is a decree of old beer due to new beer, as Rabbi says old beer is permitted because one does not leave it to age.

items.text: Practices of Rav Pappa and Rav Achai
items.text_en: Practices of Rav Pappa and Rav Achai
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa had beer brought to the door of his shop and drank, while Rav Achai had it brought home; both acted due to intermarriage concerns, but Rav Achai was more stringent.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's stringency
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's stringency
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna visited Margvan and refused both wine and beer; wine due to the danger of the place (shimtza), and beer due to a secondary danger.

items.text: Rav's ruling on Aramaean beer
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on Aramaean beer
items.desc_en: Rav permits Aramaean beer but forbids it to his son Chiyya due to health concerns; the Gemara explains Rav holds the prohibition is due to exposure, and the wormwood in the beer neutralizes the venom, but for Chiyya who is sick, it is dangerous.

items.text: Shmuel's teaching on venom and Aramaeans
items.text_en: Shmuel's teaching on venom and Aramaeans
items.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that all creeping things have venom, but snake venom kills while that of creeping things does not. He then tells Chiyya bar Rav that his father said Aramaeans drink exposed liquids and survive because they eat vermin, which toughens their bodies.

items.text: Rav Yosef's statement
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef begins a statement, but the text is cut off; likely introducing another point or concluding the discussion.

items.text: Opening ruling on gentile beer lees
items.text_en: Opening ruling on gentile beer lees
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that gentile beer lees are forbidden because they are mixed with wine of libation. Rav Ashi adds that if the lees come from a storehouse, they are permitted because the mixture has spoiled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that gentile beer lees are forbidden because they are mixed with wine of libation (יין נסך).
Rav Ashi adds that if the lees come from a storehouse, they are permitted because the mixture has spoiled (מסרא סרי).

items.text: Explanation of Hadrianic earthenware
items.text_en: Explanation of Hadrianic earthenware
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what 'Hadrianic earthenware' is: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says it is earthenware of Hadrian the emperor. Rav Dimi adds that it was virgin soil, worked and planted, and used for wine vessels that were broken and mixed with the wine. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says our first (vessel) is like their third.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Hadrianic earthenware' (חרס הדריינ) refers to.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that it is earthenware of the emperor Hadrian.
Rav Dimi elaborates that it was virgin soil, worked and planted, used for white wine vessels that were broken and mixed with the wine.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that our first (vessel) is like their third (in terms of absorption).

items.text: Inquiry about using vessels for bed legs
items.text_en: Inquiry about using vessels for bed legs
items.desc_en: A question is raised: may one use these vessels to support bed legs? This is a case of wanting the object's existence through another object. The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan: one forbids, one permits, and the halakha follows the one who forbids.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: may one use these vessels to support bed legs, which is a case of wanting the object's existence through another object (רוצה בקיומו על ידי דבר אחר), and asks whether it is permitted or forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the question by citing a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan: one forbids and one permits, and the halakha follows the one who forbids.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on gentile vessels
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on gentile vessels
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: wine stored in gentile vessels is forbidden for drinking but permitted for benefit. Shimon ben Gudda testified before Rabban Gamliel's son that Rabban Gamliel drank from it in Akko, and they did not agree with him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: wine stored in gentile vessels (דרדורין and רוקבאות) is forbidden for drinking but permitted for benefit, challenging the previous discussion.
The baraita reports that Shimon ben Gudda testified before Rabban Gamliel's son that Rabban Gamliel drank from such wine in Akko, but the Sages did not agree with him.

items.text: Second objection from gentile wine skins
items.text_en: Second objection from gentile wine skins
items.desc_en: Another objection: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai says that gentile wine skins are forbidden to be used as mats for a donkey. Here, one desires the object's existence through another object, and it is taught that it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai rules that gentile wine skins are forbidden to be used as mats for a donkey, yet here one desires the object's existence through another object, and it is taught that it is forbidden.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between skins and flasks
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between skins and flasks
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, gentile flasks should also be forbidden for purchase. Rava explains the decree: lest the skin burst and one sew it onto his own skin. For the one who says 'desiring existence through another object is forbidden', the distinction is that with flasks the prohibition is not in its own form, but with skins the prohibition is in its own form.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the prohibition of gentile skins applies to purchase, why are gentile flasks (קנקנים) not also forbidden for purchase?
Rava explains the decree: the concern is that a skin (נוד) might burst, and one might sew it onto his own skin, which is not a concern with flasks.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution for the alternative view
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution for the alternative view
sub.desc_en: For the one who holds that 'desiring existence through another object is forbidden', the distinction is that with flasks the prohibition is not in its own form, but with skins the prohibition is in its own form.

items.text: Reconciliation of contradictory testimonies
items.text_en: Reconciliation of contradictory testimonies
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: in one place it says 'they did not agree with him', and in another it says 'they agreed with him'. The resolution: 'they did not agree' refers to his entire faction, but his son agreed with him. Alternatively, the names Gudda and Guda are different people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one baraita says 'they did not agree with him' regarding wine in gentile flasks, while another baraita says 'they agreed with him'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: 'they did not agree' refers to his entire faction, but his son agreed with him; alternatively, the names Gudda and Guda are different people.

items.text: Definition of a 'lubuv' hide
items.text_en: Definition of a 'lubuv' hide
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'lubuv hides'. The rabbis taught: what is a lubuv hide? Any that is cut opposite the heart and pierced like an archway; if it has a clot of blood, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'lubuv hides' (עורות לבובין), introducing the topic.
The rabbis taught the definition of a lubuv hide: any that is cut opposite the heart and pierced like an archway; if it has a clot of blood, it is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on salted fish
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on salted fish
items.desc_en: Rav Huna qualifies the Mishnah's leniency regarding fish without blood vessels: it is permitted only if unsalted, but if salted, it is forbidden because salt draws out the blood.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and Abaye's question
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and Abaye's question
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a round tear (forbidden) and an elongated tear (permitted) in the hide. Rav Yehudah cites Shmuel that the halakhah follows him. Abaye questions whether this implies disagreement, and is told to accept the ruling without further inquiry.

items.text: Meat entering idolatry is permitted
items.text_en: Meat entering idolatry is permitted
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that meat brought into an idolatrous temple is permitted. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan identifies this as disagreeing with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a gentile's unspecified intent is for idolatry.

items.text: Meat exiting idolatry is forbidden as זִבְחֵי מֵתִים
items.text_en: Meat exiting idolatry is forbidden as זִבְחֵי מֵתִים
items.desc_en: Meat taken out of idolatry is forbidden because it is like זִבְחֵי מֵתִים (sacrifices to the dead). The Gemara identifies this as the view of Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, who derives from the verse about Baal Peor that such offerings convey impurity in a tent, like a corpse.

items.text: Commerce with those going to or returning from idolatrous festivals
items.text_en: Commerce with those going to or returning from idolatrous festivals
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules: for a gentile going to a festival, commerce is forbidden on the way (since he goes to worship), but permitted on return (the past is past). For a Jew going, commerce is permitted on the way (he might change his mind), but forbidden on return (since he has already sinned).

items.text: Gemara's question about a Jew going to a fair
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a Jew going to a fair
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a previous ruling about a Jew going to a fair, citing a baraita that prohibits both going and returning. Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by limiting the baraita to an apostate Jew.

items.text: Baraita on gentile and Jew going to a fair
items.text_en: Baraita on gentile and Jew going to a fair
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a gentile going to a fair is permitted both ways, while a Jew is permitted only on the way there but prohibited on return. The Gemara questions why a Jew is suspected of having idolatry money on return but a gentile is not, and answers that a gentile might have sold other items, while a Jew would have sold his own goods locally.

items.text: Reish Lakish on tied wineskins
items.text_en: Reish Lakish on tied wineskins
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish comments on the Mishnah's ruling that 'those that come' are permitted, limiting it to when the wineskins are not tied together; if tied, they are prohibited because the gentile intends to return.

items.text: Baraita on gentile wineskins and Rav Papa's clarification
items.text_en: Baraita on gentile wineskins and Rav Papa's clarification
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the status of gentile wineskins: new and scraped are permitted, old and pitched are prohibited. It then describes a case where a gentile prepared them and a Jew poured wine, with another Jew supervising. Rav Papa clarifies that the Jew pours the wine and another Jew supervises to prevent inadvertent libation.

items.text: Rav Zevid's alternative explanation and Rav Ashi's objection
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's alternative explanation and Rav Ashi's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains the baraita as originally stated, that the gentile pours the wine, and it is permitted because the wine is thrown into dirt. Rav Papi infers that a gentile pouring wine into a Jew's salt-pit is permitted. Rav Ashi objects, distinguishing between wine going to waste and not.

items.text: Case of Bar Adi the Arab and ruling on wineskins
items.text_en: Case of Bar Adi the Arab and ruling on wineskins
items.desc_en: Bar Adi the Arab forced Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's wineskins, poured wine into them, and returned them. The academy ruled to fill them with water for three days and pour out. Rava required a full day's interval. A dispute arises whether this applies only to Jewish wineskins or also to gentile ones, and whether it applies to flasks as well.

items.text: Baraita on gentile flasks
items.text_en: Baraita on gentile flasks
items.desc_en: A baraita states that new scraped flasks of gentiles are permitted, old pitched ones are prohibited. If a gentile pours wine into them, a Jew pours water; if a gentile pours wine, a Jew pours brine or fish-sauce, and there is no concern.

items.text: Unresolved inquiry
items.text_en: Unresolved inquiry
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an unresolved inquiry (איבעיא להו) that is not answered in this section.

items.text: Opening question and baraita
items.text_en: Opening question and baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: is the ruling about using vessels from gentiles for wine a leniency for initial use or only after the fact? A baraita from Rav Zevid bar Oshaya is cited: new vessels may be used for wine initially, old ones only for brine and fish sauce initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ruling about using vessels from gentiles for wine applies לכתחילה (as an ideal standard) or only בדיעבד (after the fact).

sub.text: Baraita of Rav Zevid bar Oshaya
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rav Zevid bar Oshaya
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: new vessels may be used for wine initially, old ones only for brine and fish sauce initially, implying a leniency for initial use.

items.text: Inquiry about returning vessels to the furnace
items.text_en: Inquiry about returning vessels to the furnace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks Rabbi Ami about vessels that were returned to the furnace and whitened. Rabbi Ami responds that if brine burns, fire certainly does. Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Asi) states that once the pitch falls off, they are permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks Rabbi Ami about vessels that were returned to the furnace and whitened.
Rabbi Ami responds that if brine burns, fire certainly does.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement (or Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement (or Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan) states that once the pitch falls off, the vessels are permitted.

items.text: Refinement and dispute about kinnsa
items.text_en: Refinement and dispute about kinnsa
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi clarifies that even if the pitch is only loosened, not fallen, the vessels are permitted. A dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about kinnsa (a type of vessel) is recorded: one prohibits, one permits, and the halakha follows the one who prohibits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi clarifies that even if the pitch is only loosened (רְפַאי מִירְפָא) and not fallen, the vessels are permitted.

sub.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
sub.desc_en: A dispute about kinnsa (a type of vessel) is recorded: one prohibits, one permits, and the halakha follows the one who prohibits.

items.text: Inquiry about beer in vessels
items.text_en: Inquiry about beer in vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether beer may be placed in such vessels. Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda prohibit, while Rava permits. Ravina permitted Rav Chiya bar Rav Yitzchak to put beer in them, but he put wine instead, and Ravina did not consider it a problem, attributing it to chance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether beer may be placed in such vessels.

sub.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda prohibit placing beer in such vessels.
Rava permits placing beer in such vessels.
Ravina permitted Rav Chiya bar Rav Yitzchak to put beer in such vessels.
Rav Chiya bar Rav Yitzchak put wine instead of beer, but Ravina did not consider it a problem, attributing it to chance.

items.text: Case of vessels from Pakusna
items.text_en: Case of vessels from Pakusna
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna had vessels from Pakusna; he filled them with water and placed them in the sun, causing them to crack. Rabbi Abba declared them permanently forbidden, arguing that the rabbis only permitted filling with water, not placing in the sun.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna had vessels from Pakusna; he filled them with water and placed them in the sun, causing them to crack.
Rabbi Abba declared the vessels permanently forbidden, arguing that the rabbis only permitted filling with water, not placing in the sun.
Rabbi Abba explains that the rabbis only permitted filling with water, not placing in the sun, so the vessels remain forbidden.

items.text: Vessels of natron
items.text_en: Vessels of natron
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosna quoting Rabbi Ami states that vessels of natron have no permanent purification. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin explains these are vessels from a mine of natron.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosna in the name of Rabbi Ami states that vessels of natron have no permanent purification.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin clarifies that these are vessels from a mine of natron (צריף).

items.text: Case of forced wine in barrels
items.text_en: Case of forced wine in barrels
items.desc_en: The house of Parzak Rufila forced barrels from Pumbedita and put wine in them; they returned them. When asked, Rav Yehuda ruled that since it is not something kept for storage, shaking them in water suffices to permit them.

sub.desc_en: The house of Parzak Rufila forced barrels from Pumbedita, put wine in them, and then returned them.
They came and asked Rav Yehuda about the status of the barrels.
Rav Yehuda ruled that since the barrels are not kept for long-term storage, shaking them in water suffices to permit them.

items.text: Rulings on earthenware and tax vessels
items.text_en: Rulings on earthenware and tax vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Avira rules that Aramaean earthenware jars, since they do not absorb much, may be shaken with water and permitted. Rav Papi similarly rules for tax collectors' vessels.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avira rules that Aramaean earthenware jars, since they do not absorb much, may be shaken with water and permitted.
Rav Papi similarly rules for tax collectors' vessels, which also do not absorb much, that shaking with water suffices.

items.text: Dispute about cups used by gentiles
items.text_en: Dispute about cups used by gentiles
items.desc_en: Rav Asi prohibits cups used by gentiles, while Rav Ashi permits. The dispute is about the second use; some say it is about the third use. The halakha is that the first and second uses are forbidden, the third is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Asi forbids cups used by gentiles, while Rav Ashi permits them.
The gemara clarifies the dispute: all agree the first use is forbidden; the dispute is about the second use.
An alternative version states that all agree the first and second uses are forbidden; the dispute is about the third use.
The gemara rules: the first and second uses are forbidden, the third is permitted.

items.text: Ruling on kuniya vessels
items.text_en: Ruling on kuniya vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that white and black kuniya vessels are permitted, green ones are forbidden because they are glazed. If they have cracks, all are forbidden. Marimar teaches that all kuniya vessels are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that white and black kuniya vessels are permitted, but green ones are forbidden because they are glazed.
Rav Zevid adds that if the vessels have cracks, all are forbidden.
Marimar teaches that all kuniya vessels, regardless of color, are permitted.

items.text: Inquiry about kuniya vessels for Passover
items.text_en: Inquiry about kuniya vessels for Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about using kuniya vessels for Passover, comparing to chametz. Marimar is asked: green ones are certainly forbidden, but what about white and black? If they have cracks, they are forbidden; if smooth, what is the ruling? The text breaks off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why kuniya vessels for Passover differ from chametz, and inquires about using them for Passover.
Marimar responds that green kuniya vessels are certainly forbidden due to absorption, but white and black ones require further inquiry.
The Gemara asks further: if the vessels have cracks they are certainly forbidden, but if smooth, what is the ruling?
The text breaks off with 'amar' (he said), indicating the response is incomplete.

items.text: Gemara's question on earthenware vessels and the distinction from wine libation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on earthenware vessels and the distinction from wine libation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why earthenware vessels used by gentiles for wine are considered to have absorbed and are forbidden, while Marimar permitted all earthenware vessels. It suggests that the difference is that wine libation is rabbinic, but the Gemara objects that rabbinic enactments follow Torah law. The resolution is that one vessel is used with hot liquid and the other with cold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that earthenware vessels used by gentiles for chametz (leaven) absorb and are forbidden, citing the Torah principle that earthenware never expels absorbed matter.
The Gemara asks why earthenware vessels for chametz are forbidden while Marimar permitted all earthenware vessels for wine libation (יין נסך).
The Gemara objects that if one claims chametz is Torah law while wine libation is rabbinic, rabbinic enactments follow Torah law, so the distinction fails.
The Gemara resolves that the chametz vessel is used with hot liquid (absorbing more) while the wine vessel is used with cold liquid (absorbing less).

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's questions and the answers from the study hall
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's questions and the answers from the study hall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva was asked three questions: whether one may fast by hours, whether gentile wine jugs are forbidden, and what Moses wore during the seven days of consecration. He did not know. He went to the study hall and received answers: one may fast by hours and if one completes the fast, one recites the fast prayer; gentile jugs are permitted after twelve months; Moses wore a white linen garment without a seam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Akiva visited Ginzak and was asked three questions, none of which he could answer.
The Beit Midrash answers all three questions: one may fast by hours, gentile wine jugs are permitted after twelve months, and Moses served in a white linen garment without a woolen lining.

items.text: Tannaic source on grape pits and skins of gentiles
items.text_en: Tannaic source on grape pits and skins of gentiles
items.desc_en: The Tannaic source states that moist grape pits and skins of gentiles are forbidden, while dry ones are permitted. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines moist as within twelve months and dry as after twelve months.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that grape pits and skins of gentiles are forbidden when moist (within twelve months) and permitted when dry (after twelve months), as clarified by Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel.
The gemara asks for the definition of moist and dry in this context.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines moist as within twelve months and dry as after twelve months.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the scope of prohibition and permission
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the scope of prohibition and permission
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that when these items are forbidden, they are forbidden even for benefit; when permitted, they are permitted even for eating.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that when grape pits and skins are forbidden, they are forbidden even for benefit; when permitted, they are permitted even for eating.

items.text: Rav Zevid and Rav Chaviva on wine lees and seals
items.text_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Chaviva on wine lees and seals
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that gentile wine lees are permitted after twelve months. Rav Chaviva bar Rava rules that gentile wine seals are permitted after twelve months. Rav Chaviva adds another statement about seals.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that gentile wine sediment (דורדיא) is permitted after twelve months.
Rav Chaviva rules that gentile wine jug stoppers (גולפי) are permitted after twelve months.
Rav Chaviva begins an additional statement about seals, but the text is cut off at the end of the section.

items.text: Opening statements on permitted items after twelve months
items.text_en: Opening statements on permitted items after twelve months
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika and Rav Acha bar Rava rule that certain gentile products (abatta, purtzanei, and gulfei shechimei) are permitted after twelve months of the year.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika rules that the gentile product abatta (אבטא) is permitted after twelve months of the year.
Rav Acha bar Rava rules that the gentile products gulfei shechimei and ukamei (גולפי שחימי ואוכמי) are permitted after twelve months.

items.text: The law of murias (fish brine) from a craftsman
items.text_en: The law of murias (fish brine) from a craftsman
items.desc_en: A beraita states that murias from a craftsman is permitted, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel adds that chilak from a craftsman is also permitted. Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu teaches that the first two batches are permitted, but the third is forbidden because wine is added to extract oil.

sub.desc_en: The beraita opens by stating that murias (fish brine) from a craftsman is permitted, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel adds that chilak (another brine) from a craftsman is also permitted.
Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu teaches that the first two batches of murias from a craftsman are permitted, but the third is forbidden because wine is added to extract oil.

items.text: The case of the murias ship and the concern for wine admixture
items.text_en: The case of the murias ship and the concern for wine admixture
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba from Acco guards a ship of murias, and Rava questions why it wasn't guarded before. Rabbi Abba explains that the ratio of murias to wine is 1:4, so there was no concern. Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira if the wine might have come from Tyre, but Rabbi Zeira dismisses this due to the presence of sediment and froth.

sub.desc_en: A ship of murias arrived at the port of Acco, and Rabbi Abba from Acco set guards over it.
Rava asks Rabbi Abba who guarded the ship until now, implying earlier concern was needed.
Rabbi Abba explains that until now there was no concern because the ratio of murias to wine is one kista to four, so wine admixture was not profitable.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the wine might have come from Tyre, where wine is cheap, making admixture plausible.
Rabbi Zeira dismisses the concern, noting that Tyrian wine has sediment and froth, making it unsuitable for murias production.

items.text: The reason for forbidding cheese from the house of Unyaki
items.text_en: The reason for forbidding cheese from the house of Unyaki
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains that cheese from Unyaki is forbidden because most calves in that city are slaughtered for idolatry. The Gemara questions why the majority matters, since Rabbi Meir is concerned even for a minority. The answer is that since there is a majority of calves not slaughtered for idolatry and other animals not slaughtered for idolatry, the minority of calves slaughtered becomes a minority of a minority, which Rabbi Meir does not consider.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish opens by asking why cheese from Unyaki is forbidden and answers that it is because most calves in that city are slaughtered for idolatry.
The Gemara questions why the majority matters, since Rabbi Meir is concerned even for a minority.
The Gemara begins its answer by noting that if one says 'majority,' there is still a minority.

The Gemara resolves that since there is a majority of calves not slaughtered for idolatry and other animals not slaughtered for idolatry, the minority of calves slaughtered becomes a minority of a minority, which Rabbi Meir does not consider.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on slaughter for idolatry
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on slaughter for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim questions Reish Lakish, noting that he himself permits an animal slaughtered for idolatry if only the blood or fat is offered. The Gemara cites the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan forbids it, considering intent from one act to another, while Reish Lakish permits it. Reish Lakish responds that the case is where one worships the animal through the act of slaughter itself.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim's question to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim's question to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim questions Reish Lakish: if the calves are slaughtered for idolatry, what is the law? You yourself permit it!

The Gemara cites the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan forbids an animal slaughtered for idolatry even if only the blood or fat is offered, because he considers intent from one act to another, learning from the law of outside the Temple.
Reish Lakish permits the animal, holding that intent from one act to another is not considered.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's response to the question
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's response to the question
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish resolves the contradiction: the case is where one worships the animal through the act of slaughter itself (גמר זביחה), not through a separate offering.

items.text: The status of manure from a stoned ox and from idolatrous calves
items.text_en: The status of manure from a stoned ox and from idolatrous calves
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi quoting Rav rules that one who betroths a woman with manure from a stoned ox is betrothed, but with manure from idolatrous calves she is not betrothed. Two explanations are given: a logical one (the owner desires the manure of idolatrous calves but not of the stoned ox) and a scriptural one (from verses about the stoned ox and idolatry).

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi citing Rav rules that betrothal with manure from a stoned ox is valid, but with manure from idolatrous calves it is invalid.
The gemara offers a logical explanation: the owner desires the manure of idolatrous calves (since they are valuable), but not of the stoned ox (which is worthless).
The gemara offers a scriptural explanation: verses about idolatry (forbidding any benefit) and the stoned ox (only its flesh is forbidden, implying its manure is permitted) support the distinction.

items.text: Rava's conclusion linking the two topics
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion linking the two topics
items.desc_en: Rava states that both issues (the cheese and the manure) are taught in a Mishnah, citing the argument about rennet from a neveilah versus rennet from an olah, implying a connection between the prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rava says that both positions (on cheese and on dung) are taught in a Mishnah, as the Mishnah states that cheese is forbidden because they curdle it with rennet of a neveila, and the interlocutor replied that the rennet of an olah is more stringent than that of a neveila.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reasoning about milk and its byproducts
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reasoning about milk and its byproducts
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's language that the Sages permitted the byproducts of forbidden items, but then questions why they did not simply say that the prohibition is not in its original form. It resolves that since the rennet curdles the milk, it is considered as if the forbidden item is still present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's language that the Sages permitted the byproducts of forbidden items, and then notes that the Mishnah's response implies that idolatry's byproducts are forbidden.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not simply answer that the prohibition is not in its original form, citing the case of מורייס (fish brine) where the Rabbis permitted it for that reason.
The Gemara answers that since the rennet curdles the milk, it is considered as if the forbidden item is still present in its original form.

items.text: Homiletical interpretation of the verse 'For your love is better than wine'
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretation of the verse 'For your love is better than wine'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching by Rav Dimi that the congregation of Israel says before God that His words are more beloved to them than the wine of Torah.
