sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of the verse 'For your love is better than wine' in the context of the Mishnah's homiletical interpretation.
Rav Dimi explains that the congregation of Israel says before God that His words are more beloved to them than the wine of Torah.

items.text: Why this particular verse was cited
items.text_en: Why this particular verse was cited
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi explains that the verse was chosen because it begins with 'Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth', and the response advises not to rush to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this particular verse (Song of Songs 1:2) was cited in the previous discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or Rabbi Shimon bar Ami)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or Rabbi Shimon bar Ami)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or Rabbi Shimon bar Ami) explains that the verse was chosen because it begins with 'Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth', and the response advises not to rush to answer.

items.text: Reason for not revealing the decree's rationale immediately
items.text_en: Reason for not revealing the decree's rationale immediately
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that it is a new decree and one should not be hasty in questioning it. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reveals the reason is due to 'nikur' (piercing), but Ulla notes that in the West they would not reveal the reason for a decree for twelve months to prevent disrespect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not immediately reveal the reason for the decree.
Ulla explains that the decree is new and one should not be hasty in questioning it.
The Gemara asks what the decree actually was.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reveals that the decree is due to 'ניקור' (piercing of the cheese).
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not simply state the reason of 'ניקור' (piercing) immediately.
Ulla explains that in the West (Eretz Yisrael), when a new decree is issued, the reason is not revealed for twelve months to prevent people from disrespecting it.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge and Rabbi Chanina's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge and Rabbi Chanina's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya challenges that if the reason is nikur, then dry or aged cheese should be permitted. Rabbi Chanina responds that it is impossible without milk residue, implying the prohibition remains.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya challenges that if the reason for the prohibition is ניקור (the concern of removing fat), then dry or aged cheese should be permitted, citing Rabbi Chanina's statement that dry cheese is permitted but one does not leave it to dry, and aged cheese is permitted but one does not leave it to age.

Rabbi Chanina responds that the prohibition remains because cheese cannot be made without צחצוחי חלב (milk residue), and Shmuel adds that it is because they curdle it with the skin of a neveila's rennet stomach.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Shmuel regarding the reason for the decree
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Shmuel regarding the reason for the decree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says the decree is because cheese cannot be made without milk residue, while Shmuel says it is because they use the skin of a neveilah's rennet. The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency with a Mishnah that forbids a gentile's rennet, and resolves the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states the decree is because cheese cannot be made without milk residue, while Shmuel says it is because they use the skin of a neveilah's rennet.
The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, citing a Mishnah that forbids a gentile's rennet (קיבה), implying it is permitted in principle.
The Gemara asks whether a gentile's rennet is not considered neveilah, challenging the Mishnah's categorization.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah teaches one case: the rennet of a gentile's slaughter is neveilah and forbidden.
The Gemara concludes that there is no contradiction in Shmuel's position.

items.text: Distinguishing between earlier and later versions of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Distinguishing between earlier and later versions of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about gentile cheese by distinguishing between the Mishnah before and after the retraction of the decree, asserting that the Mishnah itself remained unchanged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about gentile cheese by distinguishing between the Mishnah before and after the retraction of the decree, asserting that the Mishnah itself remained unchanged.

items.text: Three reasons for the prohibition of gentile cheese
items.text_en: Three reasons for the prohibition of gentile cheese
items.desc_en: Rav Malkiya, Rav Chisda, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each propose a reason for the prohibition: because they smooth its surface with pig fat, because they curdle it with vinegar, or because they curdle it with sap of orlah. The Gemara then identifies the tannaitic source for the last opinion and clarifies that Rabbi Yehoshua agrees with Rabbi Eliezer regarding sap of fruit.

sub.text: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.text_en: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.desc_en: Rav Malkiya in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahavah states that gentile cheese is prohibited because they smooth its surface with pig fat.
Rav Chisda offers a second reason: they curdle the cheese with vinegar.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gives a third reason: they curdle it with sap of orlah (fruit of a tree in its first three years).

sub.text: Gemara's identification of the tannaitic source
sub.text_en: Gemara's identification of the tannaitic source
sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the tannaitic source for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's opinion: Rabbi Eliezer rules that curdling with sap of orlah is forbidden because it is a fruit.
The Gemara clarifies that even Rabbi Yehoshua, who disputes Rabbi Eliezer regarding sap of the tree trunk, agrees regarding sap of the fruit, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Objection: why is gentile cheese not forbidden for benefit?
items.text_en: Objection: why is gentile cheese not forbidden for benefit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, the cheese should be forbidden for benefit as well, yet the Mishnah only forbids eating it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to both Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, the cheese should be forbidden for benefit, which is a difficulty.
The Gemara asks why gentile cheese is not forbidden for benefit (הנאה), given that according to both Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak it involves a forbidden substance.
The Gemara declares the difficulty unresolved (קשיא).

items.text: Aggadic homily on the Torah scholar
items.text_en: Aggadic homily on the Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda expounds a verse from Song of Songs, comparing a Torah scholar to an open flask of perfume, and deriving that hidden matters are revealed to him, the angel of death loves him, and he inherits both worlds.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's homily
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's homily
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda delivers a homiletic interpretation of the verse 'לְרֵיחַ שְׁמָנֶיךָ טוֹבִים' (Song of Songs 1:3), comparing a Torah scholar to an open flask of perfume, and deriving multiple benefits from the word 'עֲלָמוֹת'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's homily (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's homily (continued)
sub.desc_en: The homily continues, deriving from the same verse that hidden matters are revealed to the scholar, the angel of death loves him, and he inherits both this world and the world to come.

items.text: Mishnah: items forbidden only for consumption
items.text_en: Mishnah: items forbidden only for consumption
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items of gentiles that are forbidden but not for benefit: milk milked without Jewish supervision, their bread and oil (though Rabbi and his court permitted oil), boiled vegetables, pickled foods, minced fish, brine without a fish, hilka, asafoetida, and salt of salacondite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items of gentiles that are forbidden but not forbidden for benefit: milk milked by a gentile without Jewish supervision, their bread and oil (with Rabbi and his court permitting the oil).
The Mishnah lists specific forbidden items: milk milked without Jewish supervision, their bread and oil (though Rabbi and his court permitted oil).
The Mishnah continues listing additional forbidden items: boiled vegetables, pickled foods, minced fish, brine without a fish, hilka, asafoetida, and salt of salacondite.

items.text: Gemara on gentile milk: why is it forbidden?
items.text_en: Gemara on gentile milk: why is it forbidden?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why gentile milk is forbidden, considering that kosher milk is white and non-kosher milk is green, and that kosher milk curdles while non-kosher does not. It concludes that the concern is when one needs the milk for cooking, where the tests are inconclusive, and even for cheese, some non-kosher milk may curdle between the curds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why gentile milk is forbidden, given that kosher milk is white and non-kosher milk is green, and kosher milk curdles while non-kosher does not.
The Gemara answers that the concern applies when one needs the milk for cooking (לכמכא), where the tests are inconclusive.
The Gemara objects that one could take a sample and test if it curdles, but the answer is that even kosher milk has whey that does not curdle, so the test is inconclusive.
Alternatively, even if one needs the milk for cheese, some non-kosher milk may curdle between the curds, so the test is unreliable.

items.text: Gemara on gentile bread: was it ever permitted?
items.text_en: Gemara on gentile bread: was it ever permitted?
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether Rabbi permitted gentile bread. Rav Kahana reports that Rabbi Yochanan said bread was not permitted in court, implying someone permitted it. A story is told about Rabbi in the field, but it is clarified that he did not permit bread. Various Amora'im debate the circumstances, and a story about Aivu eating bread from a gentile baker is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens the discussion on gentile bread by citing Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, who states that bread was not permitted in the court, implying that someone else permitted it.
Rav Dimi recounts a story where Rabbi went to the field, a gentile brought him fine bread, and Rabbi questioned why the sages forbade it.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi only questioned the prohibition in the field due to the concern of חתנות (intermarriage), and he did not actually permit bread.
Rav Yosef (or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda) objects with a different version of the story: Rabbi saw bread pressed on students and asked for a baker, but he meant a Jewish baker, not a gentile one.

sub.text: Rabbi Chelbo and Rabbi Yochanan's positions
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo and Rabbi Yochanan's positions
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo and Rabbi Yochanan each qualify the leniency: Rabbi Chelbo limits it to places without a Jewish baker, and Rabbi Yochanan limits it to the field, not the city, due to the concern of חתנות (intermarriage).
A story is told about Aivu who ate bread from a gentile baker, and Rava (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) rebuked those who spoke with him, because he ate gentile bread.

items.text: Gemara on gentile oil: who decreed it?
items.text_en: Gemara on gentile oil: who decreed it?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing the prohibition of gentile oil, with Rav attributing the decree to Daniel and Shmuel offering a different view, but the text cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing the oil of gentiles, citing Rav who said Daniel decreed upon it, and Shmuel who said something else (the text is cut off).

items.text: Gemara's correction of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's correction of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the absorption of impure vessels' and clarifies that it should read 'the absorption of forbidden vessels', since not everyone eats pure food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the absorption of impure vessels', asking whether everyone eats pure food.
The Gemara corrects the Mishnah to read 'the absorption of forbidden vessels' instead of 'impure vessels'.

items.text: Samuel's challenge to Rav on the origin of the oil prohibition
items.text_en: Samuel's challenge to Rav on the origin of the oil prohibition
items.desc_en: Samuel argues that his view (that the prohibition on gentile oil was enacted by the court of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) is supported by Rabbi Simlai's teaching that Rabbi Yehuda and his court permitted oil. He challenges Rav's view that Daniel decreed it, citing the rule that a later court cannot annul an earlier court's decree unless greater. Simlai of Lud responds that the people of Lud are disrespectful, and Rav is embarrassed.

sub.desc_en: Samuel opens by contrasting his own view with Rav's: his view aligns with Rabbi Simlai's teaching that Rabbi Yehuda and his court permitted gentile oil.
The Gemara explains Samuel's reasoning: the oil prohibition was based on the principle of נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a spoiled flavor), which is permitted, so the court could permit it.
Samuel objects to Rav's view that Daniel decreed the oil prohibition, citing the rule that a later court cannot annul an earlier court's decree unless greater in wisdom and number.
Simlai of Lud responds that the people of Lud are disrespectful, and when Rav asks to send a message, he is embarrassed.

items.text: Rav's scriptural proof and the dispute with Samuel
items.text_en: Rav's scriptural proof and the dispute with Samuel
items.desc_en: Rav cites Daniel 1:8 to prove that Daniel decreed against gentile oil, interpreting 'the king's wine and his feasts' as two feasts: wine and oil. The Gemara explains that Rav holds Daniel taught this to all Israel, while Samuel holds Daniel only kept it for himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav cites Daniel 1:8 to prove that Daniel decreed against gentile oil, interpreting the verse as referring to two feasts: wine and oil.
The Gemara explains that Rav holds Daniel taught his decree to all Israel, while Samuel holds Daniel only kept it for himself.

items.text: Questioning whether Daniel decreed oil at all
items.text_en: Questioning whether Daniel decreed oil at all
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav's own tradition (via Bali Avimi) lists oil among the eighteen decrees of Hillel and Shammai, not Daniel. It resolves that Daniel decreed only in the city, while the students of Hillel and Shammai extended it to the field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Daniel decreed about oil at all, given Rav's tradition listing oil among the eighteen decrees of Hillel and Shammai.
The Gemara resolves that Daniel decreed only in the city, while the students of Hillel and Shammai extended the decree to the field.

items.text: How Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could permit oil despite the eighteen decrees
items.text_en: How Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could permit oil despite the eighteen decrees
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could permit oil if it was part of the eighteen decrees, which even Elijah cannot annul. Rav Mesharshiya answers that the eighteen decrees spread among the majority of Israel, but oil did not, so the court relied on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, who said a decree is only imposed if the majority can bear it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could permit oil if it was part of the eighteen decrees, which even Elijah cannot annul.

Rav Mesharshiya answers that the eighteen decrees spread among the majority of Israel, but oil did not, so the court relied on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, who said a decree is only imposed if the majority can bear it.

items.text: Opening verse and its implication
items.text_en: Opening verse and its implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Malachi 3:9, 'With a curse you are cursed, and you rob Me, the whole nation,' interpreting that the curse applies only when the entire nation is involved, not partially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Malachi 3:9 to show that the curse applies only when the entire nation is involved, not partially.

items.text: Bali's statement: the Eighteen Matters include bread, oil, wine, and their daughters
items.text_en: Bali's statement: the Eighteen Matters include bread, oil, wine, and their daughters
items.desc_en: Bali quotes Rav via Avimi of Nehardea that bread, oil, wine, and their daughters are among the Eighteen Matters. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'their daughters' refers to a decree that gentile daughters are considered niddot from their cradle.

sub.text: Bali citing Avimi of Nehardea in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Bali citing Avimi of Nehardea in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Bali states that bread, oil, wine, and their daughters are all among the Eighteen Matters decreed by the Sages.
The Gemara asks what 'their daughters' means in this context.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the decree on their daughters means that gentile daughters are considered נידות (menstruants) from their cradle.

items.text: Geniva's alternative: all decrees are due to idolatry, with a chain of reasoning
items.text_en: Geniva's alternative: all decrees are due to idolatry, with a chain of reasoning
items.desc_en: Geniva says in Rav's name that all these decrees were made because of idolatry. Rav Acha bar Adda quotes Rabbi Yitzchak explaining the chain: bread and oil because of wine, wine because of their daughters, daughters because of another matter, and that other matter because of yet another.

sub.desc_en: Geniva states in Rav's name that all these decrees were made because of idolatry.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Adda quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda quotes Rabbi Yitzchak explaining the chain: bread was decreed because of oil.
The gemara questions why oil would be more stringent than bread.
The gemara corrects: bread and oil were decreed because of wine, wine because of their daughters, daughters because of another matter, and that other matter because of yet another.

items.text: Biblical basis for daughters and the extension to other nations
items.text_en: Biblical basis for daughters and the extension to other nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the prohibition of intermarriage with the seven Canaanite nations is biblical, but the Sages extended it to all nations. According to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who includes all who cause estrangement, the biblical prohibition applies to marriage, and the Sages extended it even to casual relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the decree on daughters can be rabbinic, given the biblical prohibition of intermarriage with the seven Canaanite nations, and notes that for other nations it is not biblical.

The Gemara answers that according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who includes all who cause estrangement, the biblical prohibition applies to marriage, and the Sages extended it even to casual relations.

items.text: Objection: casual relations were already decreed by the court of Shem and by halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai
items.text_en: Objection: casual relations were already decreed by the court of Shem and by halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that casual relations were already forbidden by the court of Shem (citing the story of Tamar) and by a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai that zealots may strike one who cohabits with an Aramean woman. The Gemara refines: the biblical prohibition applies only to a gentile man with a Jewish woman, but the Sages extended it to a Jewish man with a gentile woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that casual relations (זְנוּת) were already decreed by the court of Shem, citing the verse where Judah ordered Tamar to be burned.
The Gemara refines that the biblical prohibition applies only to a gentile man with a Jewish woman, but the Sages extended it to a Jewish man with a gentile woman.
The Gemara objects that a Jewish man cohabiting with a gentile woman is already forbidden by a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, as Mar said that zealots may strike such a man.

items.text: Further refinement: public vs. private, and the Hasmonean court's decree
items.text_en: Further refinement: public vs. private, and the Hasmonean court's decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the biblical prohibition applies only to public acts, but the Sages extended it to private ones. However, the Hasmonean court already decreed that a Jewish man cohabiting with a gentile woman is liable for נשג״א or נשג״ז (acronyms for specific sins).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the biblical prohibition applies only to public acts (בפרהסיא), but the Sages extended it to private ones (בצינעא).
The Gemara objects that even private acts were already decreed by the Hasmonean court.
Rav Dimi reports that the Hasmonean court decreed liability for a Jewish man cohabiting with a gentile woman under the acronym נשג״א, and Ravin reports under the acronym נשג״ז.

items.text: The decree on yichud (seclusion) and its layers
items.text_en: The decree on yichud (seclusion) and its layers
items.desc_en: The Hasmonean court decreed only on intercourse, not yichud; the Sages extended it to yichud with a gentile woman. But the court of David already decreed on yichud with a Jewish woman, which is biblical for a married woman. The students of Shammai and Hillel then extended it to yichud with a gentile woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Hasmonean court decreed only on intercourse (ביאה) with a gentile woman, but not on yichud (seclusion).
The Gemara objects that the court of David had already decreed on yichud (with a Jewish woman), implying the Hasmonean decree was redundant.
Rav Yehuda explains that David's court decreed on yichud with a married Jewish woman (אשת איש), not on yichud with an unmarried Jewish woman.
The Gemara resolves that David's decree was only on yichud with a Jewish woman, not with a gentile woman, so the later sages decreed on yichud with a gentile woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a biblical source for yichud with a married woman, showing that David's decree was an extension to an unmarried Jewish woman, and the students of Shammai and Hillel extended it to a gentile woman.
The Gemara summarizes the layers: biblical yichud is for a married woman, David decreed on an unmarried Jewish woman, and the students of Shammai and Hillel decreed on yichud with a gentile woman.

items.text: The decree on a gentile child's zavah impurity
items.text_en: The decree on a gentile child's zavah impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'another matter because of another matter' refers to a decree that a gentile child imparts zavah impurity, to prevent a Jewish child from becoming accustomed to homosexual acts. The Gemara recounts a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya about the age at which a gentile child becomes susceptible to zavah impurity: Rabbi says from birth, Rabbi Chiya says from nine years and one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by the phrase 'another matter because of another matter' in the list of decrees.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the decree was that a gentile child imparts zavah impurity, to prevent a Jewish child from becoming accustomed to homosexual acts.

Rabbi Zeira recounts a chain of tradition about the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya regarding the age at which a gentile child becomes susceptible to zavah impurity: Rabbi says from birth, Rabbi Chiya says from nine years and one day.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion about a gentile minor girl and zavah impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion about a gentile minor girl and zavah impurity
items.desc_en: Ravina concludes that a gentile girl three years and one day old, since she is fit for intercourse, also transmits zavah impurity. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but suggests it might have been necessary to teach that she does not know how to entice, unlike a male minor.

sub.desc_en: Ravina rules that a gentile minor girl three years and one day old, since she is fit for intercourse, also transmits zavah impurity.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is not obvious, and suggests one might have thought a female minor does not know how to entice, unlike a male minor.
The Gemara answers that Ravina's statement teaches us that this distinction does not apply.

items.text: Story: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah permits oil, and is asked to permit bread
items.text_en: Story: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah permits oil, and is asked to permit bread
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah, leaning on Rabbi Simlai, mentions that they permitted oil the previous night. Rabbi Simlai asks him to also permit bread, but Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah fears being called a 'permissive court', citing the precedent of Yosef ben Yoezer who permitted three things and was called 'Yosef the Permitter'.

sub.text: Narrative: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah and Rabbi Simlai
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah and Rabbi Simlai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah, leaning on Rabbi Simlai, mentions that they permitted oil the previous night, and Rabbi Simlai asks him to also permit bread.

Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah objects that permitting bread would cause them to be called a 'permissive court', citing the precedent of Yosef ben Yoezer who permitted three things and was called 'Yosef the Permitter'.

items.text: Rabbi Simlai's response and the identification of the 'permissive court'
items.text_en: Rabbi Simlai's response and the identification of the 'permissive court'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai argues that Yosef ben Yoezer permitted three things, while Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah permitted only one, so permitting one more would still be only two. Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah reveals he already permitted another thing: a case of a conditional divorce where the husband died within twelve months, and the Sages permitted the woman to remarry. The Gemara identifies these Sages as the same court that permitted oil.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai argues that Yosef ben Yoezer permitted three things, while Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah permitted only one, so permitting one more would still be only two.
Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah reveals that he already permitted another thing, prompting the Gemara to ask what it is.

The Gemara cites a baraita about a conditional divorce where the husband died within twelve months, and identifies the 'our Sages' who permitted the woman to remarry as the same court that permitted oil.

items.text: Explanation: The court followed Rabbi Yosi's principle
items.text_en: Explanation: The court followed Rabbi Yosi's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the court held like Rabbi Yosi, who says that the time of the document proves its intent. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi ruled similarly but was not universally accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the court held like Rabbi Yosi, who says that the time of the document proves its intent.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's report
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's report
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi ruled similarly but was not universally accepted.

items.text: Question about the timing of the divorce in the permitted case
items.text_en: Question about the timing of the divorce in the permitted case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks a sage whether the court permitted the woman to remarry immediately upon the husband's death or only after twelve months. The Gemara raises a similar question from a Mishnah where the husband says 'from now if I do not come', and the woman is divorced immediately upon death. The Gemara concludes that the question applies to both cases, but the court's ruling was specific to that case.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks the sage whether the Beit Din who permitted the woman to remarry did so immediately or only after twelve months, since the condition was fulfilled.
The Gemara objects that the same question applies to the Mishnah where the husband writes 'from now if I do not come', and the woman is divorced immediately upon death.
The Gemara concedes that the question applies to both cases, but notes that Rabbi Elazar was present at the court that issued the ruling, so he asked specifically about that case.

items.text: Abaye's clarification of the dispute regarding conditional divorce
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification of the dispute regarding conditional divorce
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that all agree that if the condition is 'when the sun goes out of its sheath' (impossible), the divorce takes effect only at that future time, and if the husband dies at night it is a posthumous divorce. If the condition is 'on condition that the sun goes out', it is effective immediately, following Rav Huna's principle that 'al menat' is like 'me'achshav'. The dispute is only over 'if the sun goes out': Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi holds like Rabbi Yosi that the time of the document proves it is like 'from today if I die', while the Rabbis disagree and treat it as a simple 'if I die'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that everyone agrees that when a husband says 'when the sun leaves its sheath' (i.e., at a future time), he speaks of the event occurring, and if he dies at night the get is after death (a conditional get that takes effect only upon death).

Abaye explains that when the husband says 'on condition that the sun leaves its sheath', he speaks from now, following Rav Huna's rule that 'על מנת' is equivalent to 'from now', making the get effective immediately from the living husband.

Abaye concludes that the dispute is only over the phrase 'if the sun goes out', where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows Rabbi Yosi's principle that the document's date proves the time, treating it like 'from today if I die', while the Rabbis reject that and treat it like 'this is your get if I die' alone.

items.text: Discussion of the testimony of Yosef ben Yoezer
items.text_en: Discussion of the testimony of Yosef ben Yoezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the baraita about Yosef ben Yoezer's testimony, explaining what 'ayal kamtza' is. Rav Papa says it is a type of locust (shoshiva), and Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla says it is susbil. They disagree about whether a long head renders it forbidden or permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita (תוספתא) about Yosei ben Yoezer's testimony regarding the 'deer of the pit' (אייל קמצא), the liquids of the 'house of slaughter' (משקה בית מטבחיא), and the purity of one who touches a corpse, for which he was called 'Yosef the Permitter'.
The Gemara cites the baraita about Yosef ben Yoezer's testimony regarding the ayal kamtza, liquids of the slaughterhouse, and proximity to a corpse.

The Gemara asks what 'אייל קמצא' means, and provides two identifications: Rav Pappa says it is a 'שושיבא' (type of deer), and Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla says it is a 'סוסביל' (an antelope).
The Gemara asks what 'ayal kamtza' refers to.
Rav Papa identifies ayal kamtza as a type of locust called shoshiva.

Rav Pappa explains that the dispute is about whether a 'שושיבא' with a long head is forbidden or permitted, while Rav Chiyya bar Ami in Ulla's name says it is a 'סוסביל', and the rabbis explain the practical difference between them.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla identifies ayal kamtza as a different type of locust called susbil.

items.text: Dispute about the fish susbil
items.text_en: Dispute about the fish susbil
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all agree a fish with a long head is forbidden, but they dispute when its fins cover most of its body only with difficulty: one opinion requires a majority that is visible, the other a majority that is recognizable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute over the fish susbil: both agree a long-headed one is forbidden, but they debate whether the required majority of fin coverage must be merely a majority (Mar X) or a recognizable majority (Mar Y).

items.text: Dispute about liquids of the slaughterhouse
items.text_en: Dispute about liquids of the slaughterhouse
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue over the meaning of 'd'chan' regarding liquids of the Temple slaughterhouse. Rav says they are completely pure, as rabbinic impurity was not decreed for them; Shmuel says they are pure from imparting impurity to others but have self-impurity, since biblical impurity of liquids is only rabbinic for imparting impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'דְּכַן' (pure) means regarding the liquids of the Temple slaughterhouse.
Rav says they are completely pure (דְּכַן מַמָּשׁ), because the rabbinic impurity of liquids was not decreed for the Temple slaughterhouse liquids.

Shmuel says they are pure from imparting impurity to others but have self-impurity, because biblical impurity of liquids is only rabbinic for imparting impurity, and the rabbis did not decree that for the slaughterhouse liquids.

items.text: Question about Yosef Sharya's ruling on corpse impurity
items.text_en: Question about Yosef Sharya's ruling on corpse impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling of Yosef Sharya, who permitted one who touches a corpse to be pure. It notes that the Torah explicitly states that one who touches a corpse is impure, and suggests that the rabbis decreed impurity even for one who touches one who touched a corpse, but Yosef restored the biblical law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Yosef Sharya's ruling that one who touches a corpse is pure, noting that the Torah explicitly states such a person is impure.

The Gemara answers that the Torah only declares impure one who directly touches a corpse, but one who touches a person who touched a corpse is pure; the rabbis decreed impurity for the latter, and Yosef restored the biblical law.

items.text: Objection: touching one who touched a corpse is also biblical
items.text_en: Objection: touching one who touched a corpse is also biblical
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even touching one who touched a corpse is biblical, as the verse says 'and whoever touches the impure shall be impure'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that secondary contact (דְיִקְרַב בִּדְיִקְרַב) also seems to be from the Torah, citing the verse 'וכל אשר יגע בו הטמא יטמא'.

items.text: Resolution via Mar Zutra's distinction
items.text_en: Resolution via Mar Zutra's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman: biblically, touching one who touched a corpse in a connection imparts seven-day impurity, but without connection only evening impurity. The rabbis decreed seven-day impurity even without connection, and Yosef restored the biblical law.

sub.text: Rabbis before Rava citing Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabbis before Rava citing Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The rabbis present before Rava a tradition from Mar Zutra citing Rav Nachman: biblically, touching one who touched a corpse in a connection (חיבורין) imparts seven-day impurity, without connection only evening impurity; the rabbis decreed seven-day impurity even without connection, and Yosef restored the biblical law.

The Gemara explains the biblical source: the verse 'הנוגע במת... וטמא שבעת ימים' (one who touches a corpse is impure seven days) and 'והנפש הנוגעת תטמא עד הערב' (the touching soul is impure until evening) are reconciled by distinguishing between touching with connection (חיבורין) and without connection.

items.text: Rava's correction: the ruling was about doubt in the public domain
items.text_en: Rava's correction: the ruling was about doubt in the public domain
items.desc_en: Rava rebukes the rabbis for attributing a false ruling to Rav Nachman, clarifying that Rav Nachman actually permitted doubtful impurity in the public domain. The Gemara notes this is learned from the Sotah, but Rabbi Yochanan said the law is so but not to be taught, yet Yosef taught it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rebukes the rabbis for attributing a false ruling to Rav Nachman, clarifying that Rav Nachman actually permitted doubtful impurity in the public domain.
The Gemara objects that the law of doubtful impurity is derived from the Sotah, which applies only in a private domain, not a public one.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution citing Rabbi Yochanan and Yosef Sharya
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution citing Rabbi Yochanan and Yosef Sharya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan said the law is so but not to be taught publicly, yet Yosef Sharya taught it publicly.

items.text: Supporting baraita about Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the ruling: Rabbi Yehuda set boundaries for the public domain, and when people came before Rabbi Yannai, he told them to immerse in the river's backwater, indicating that doubtful impurity in the public domain is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the leniency: Rabbi Yehuda describes marking poles for the public domain, and Rabbi Yannai instructs people to immerse in river water — implying practical leniency regarding doubt in public domain.

items.text: Derivation of the prohibition of cooked foods from a non-Jew
items.text_en: Derivation of the prohibition of cooked foods from a non-Jew
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from a verse that just as water is unchanged, so only unchanged food is permitted from a non-Jew. The Gemara refines this: the food must not be changed by fire, and rejects objections about roasted wheat and flour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural source for the prohibition of cooked foods (שלוקות) from a non-Jew?
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'אוכל בכסף תשברני... ומים בכסף תתן לי' that just as water is unchanged, so only unchanged food from a non-Jew is permitted.
The Gemara objects: if so, roasted wheat (קליות) would be forbidden, but a baraita permits them.
The Gemara refines the analogy: just as water is unchanged from its natural state, so only food unchanged from its natural state is forbidden.
The Gemara objects again: if so, ground wheat (flour) would be forbidden, but a baraita permits flour and fine flour from roasted wheat.
The Gemara further refines: just as water is unchanged by fire, so only food unchanged by fire is forbidden, and the Gemara questions whether the verse mentions fire at all.

items.text: Clarification of the prohibition's basis
items.text_en: Clarification of the prohibition's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition of בישולי גוים is rabbinic, with the verse serving merely as a support (אסמכתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the prohibition of בישולי גוים is rabbinic, with the verse serving only as a support (אסמכתא).

items.text: Two versions of Rav's ruling on exempt foods
items.text_en: Two versions of Rav's ruling on exempt foods
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak cites Rav with two formulations: one exempts food eaten raw as-is, the other exempts food not served on a king's table to accompany bread. The Gemara notes the practical difference between them: small fish, ardi, and dayisa.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav (Sura version)
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav (Sura version)
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak cites Rav's first formulation: anything eaten raw as-is is exempt from the prohibition of בישולי גוים (food cooked by a gentile).

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav (Pumbedita version)
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav (Pumbedita version)
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak cites Rav's second formulation: anything not served on a king's table to accompany bread is exempt from the prohibition.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two formulations.
The Gemara answers: the difference lies in small fish, ardi (a type of small fish), and dayisa (a dish of flour and honey).

items.text: Rav Asi's ruling on salted small fish and the case of כָּסָא דְּהַרְסָנָא
items.text_en: Rav Asi's ruling on salted small fish and the case of כָּסָא דְּהַרְסָנָא
items.desc_en: Rav Asi says salted small fish are exempt from בישולי גוים. Rav Yosef adds that if a non-Jew roasts them, a Jew may rely on them for an eruv, but if the non-Jew makes a כָּסָא דְּהַרְסָנָא (a dish of flour and fish brine), it is forbidden. The Gemara clarifies that the flour is primary, not the fish brine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states in Rav's name that salted small fish are not subject to the prohibition of בישולי גוים (food cooked by a non-Jew).
Rav Yosef adds that if a non-Jew roasts these fish, a Jew may rely on them for an עירוב תבשילין (eruv of cooked foods).
Rav Yosef rules that if a non-Jew makes a כָּסָא דְּהַרְסָנָא (a dish of flour and fish brine), it is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that the ruling is obvious, but then considers a possible mistaken assumption.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling teaches that the flour is the primary ingredient, not the fish brine.

items.text: Rav Berona's case: non-Jew igniting a marsh
items.text_en: Rav Berona's case: non-Jew igniting a marsh
items.desc_en: Rav Berona says if a non-Jew sets fire to a marsh, all locusts in it are forbidden. The Gemara questions whether this is due to בישולי גוים, and cites a contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a non-Jew roasting a head is permitted. The resolution: the case involved a non-Jew who did not know which locusts were kosher, and the incident actually occurred with a non-Jew.

sub.desc_en: Rav Berona states in Rav's name that if a non-Jew ignites a marsh, all locusts in it are forbidden.
The Gemara questions the case: if the non-Jew didn't know which locusts are kosher, the same would apply to a Jew; therefore the prohibition must be due to בישולי גוים (non-Jewish cooking).

The Gemara objects: if it's about בישולי גוים, how can it be forbidden? Rabbi Yochanan permits a non-Jew roasting a head, since the intent is to remove hair; here too the intent is to clear the marsh, not to cook the locusts.

The Gemara resolves: in fact the non-Jew did not know which locusts were kosher, and the incident actually occurred with a non-Jew, so the prohibition is not due to בישולי גוים but due to the non-Jew's lack of knowledge.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling and Ravina's application
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling and Ravina's application
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan that a non-Jew roasting a head is permitted even from the ear. Ravina applies this: if a non-Jew throws a palm branch into a furnace and an Israelite places a gourd there first, it is permitted, as the non-Jew intends to strengthen the furnace, not cook the gourd.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan that a non-Jew who roasts a head is permitted to eat from it, even from the ear.
Ravina applies the principle: if a non-Jew throws a palm branch into a furnace and an Israelite first places a gourd there, it is permitted.
The gemara objects that Ravina's ruling is obvious.
The gemara explains that the ruling is necessary lest one think the non-Jew intends to cook the gourd, but in fact he intends only to strengthen the furnace.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's case: non-Jew turning meat on coals
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's case: non-Jew turning meat on coals
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: if an Israelite placed meat on coals and a non-Jew turned it, it is permitted. The Gemara questions this, suggesting it might be forbidden if the meat would not have cooked without the turning. The resolution: the meat would have cooked in two hours, but the non-Jew cooked it in one hour; accelerating cooking is not considered a significant act. A contradiction from Rabbi Asi's ruling about food not yet at the Ben Derosai stage is resolved by distinguishing a case where the Israelite had already placed the meat in embers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel's ruling: if an Israelite placed meat on coals and a non-Jew turned it, the meat is permitted.

The Gemara questions the case: if the meat would have cooked without the non-Jew's turning, the ruling is obvious; if it would not have cooked without the turning, why is it permitted — it is cooking by a non-Jew.
The Gemara resolves: the meat would have cooked in two hours, but the non-Jew cooked it in one hour; accelerating cooking is not considered a significant act, so the meat is permitted.
The Gemara objects from Rabbi Asi's ruling: food not yet at the Ben Derosai stage is subject to the prohibition of non-Jewish cooking, contradicting the leniency.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rabbi Asi's case is different because the Israelite had placed the meat in embers (סילתא), and the non-Jew removed it and placed it in an oven, which is a more significant cooking act.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's ruling: an Israelite may leave meat on coals, and a non-Jew may turn it until the Israelite returns from synagogue or study hall, without concern. Similarly, a woman may place a pot on a stove and a non-Jewish woman may tend it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's ruling: an Israelite may leave meat on coals, and a non-Jew may turn it until the Israelite returns from synagogue or study hall, without concern; similarly, a woman may place a pot on a stove and a non-Jewish woman may tend it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman may stir a pot (of a gentile) without concern, even if she comes from the bathhouse or synagogue.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman may stir a pot without concern, even after coming from the bathhouse or synagogue.

items.text: Gemara's question: gentile placed, Jew stirred
items.text_en: Gemara's question: gentile placed, Jew stirred
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where a gentile placed the pot and a Jew stirred it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak permits it via a kal vachomer argument. Rabbi Yochanan permits both scenarios (gentile placed/Jew stirred or Jew placed/gentile stirred) and only prohibits when both beginning and end are by a gentile. Ravina rules that bread baked by a gentile but stirred by a Jew is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where a gentile placed the pot and a Jew stirred it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak permits it via a kal vachomer argument: if the end is by a gentile it is permitted, then if the end is by a Jew it is certainly permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan permits both scenarios (gentile placed/Jew stirred or Jew placed/gentile stirred) and only prohibits when both beginning and end are by a gentile.
Ravina rules that bread baked by a gentile but stirred by a Jew is permitted.

items.text: Dispute over salted fish and roasted egg
items.text_en: Dispute over salted fish and roasted egg
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah permits salted fish and Bar Kapara permits roasted egg, while Rabbi Yochanan prohibits both. Rav Dimi reports that Chizkiyah and Bar Kapara permit both, but Rabbi Yochanan prohibits. Rabbi Chiya Parva'ah rules in favor of the two (Chizkiyah and Bar Kapara) against Rabbi Yochanan, but Rav Zevid cites Abaye that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan, leading to Rabbi Chiya's death.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah permits salted fish and Bar Kapara permits roasted egg, while Rabbi Yochanan prohibits both.
Rav Dimi reports that Chizkiyah and Bar Kapara permit both salted fish and roasted egg, while Rabbi Yochanan prohibits both.
Rabbi Chiya Parva'ah rules in favor of Chizkiyah and Bar Kapara against Rabbi Yochanan, citing the principle that the opinion of one does not stand against two.
Rav Zevid objects, citing Abaye that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan.
They gave Rabbi Chiya Parva'ah a drink of vinegar and he died.

items.text: Baraita on permitted and prohibited items
items.text_en: Baraita on permitted and prohibited items
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items like capers, caperberries, milk, hot water, and roasted grains as permitted, but roasted egg as prohibited. Oil was permitted by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court.

sub.text: Baraita on permitted and forbidden items
sub.text_en: Baraita on permitted and forbidden items
sub.desc_en: A baraita lists permitted items (capers, etc.) and states that roasted egg is forbidden, while oil was permitted by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court.

items.text: Explanation of terms and a tradition
items.text_en: Explanation of terms and a tradition
items.desc_en: The baraita identifies 'mitlaya' as 'pasilya' and 'shi'ata'. Rabba bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan about a practice that emerged from Egypt 40 years ago, while Rabba bar bar Chanah himself says 60 years, and they do not disagree.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies that מִטַלְיָא, פַּשִׂלְיָא, and שִׁיעֲתָא are the same item.
The Gemara asks what שִׁיעֲתָא means.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana / Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana / Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan said the practice came from Egypt forty years ago, while Rabba bar bar Chana himself said sixty years ago, and they do not disagree.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah's own statement
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah's own statement
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah himself says the practice emerged 60 years ago.
The gemara resolves that the two statements do not disagree; each refers to a different event.

items.text: Preparation of a medicinal mixture
items.text_en: Preparation of a medicinal mixture
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes a process of mixing seeds of celery, flax, and shablilta, soaking them, placing them in new pots with water, adding gurgishta, and applying them to the head for healing. Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Chanina about the use of 'millin' or 'be-millin'.

sub.desc_en: A detailed description of a remedy involving seeds and a process for healing from head to toe.
Rav Ashi reports that Rabbi Chanina said the remedy involves מִילִּין (a type of preparation) or perhaps בְּמִילִּין.

items.text: Gentile's pot of hot water
items.text_en: Gentile's pot of hot water
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a gentile's kuspan (pot) heated in a large cauldron is prohibited, but in a small one it is permitted. Rabbi Yannai defines a small cauldron as one a sparrow cannot enter. The Gemara refines this to a sparrow's head. Another baraita permits both, resolved by the dispute over whether pagum (tainted) flavor is prohibited or permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a gentile's pot heated in a large cauldron is forbidden, but in a small cauldron it is permitted.
Rabbi Yannai defines a small cauldron as one into which a sparrow cannot enter.
The Gemara objects that perhaps they could have heated the pot and then inserted it into the cauldron, making the size irrelevant.
The Gemara refines the definition: a small cauldron is one into which only a sparrow's head, not its whole body, can enter.
The Gemara objects with another baraita that permits both large and small cauldrons, contradicting the first baraita.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita follows the view that נותן טעם לפגם (tainted flavor) is forbidden, while the second follows the view that it is permitted.

items.text: Gentile's cooked oil
items.text_en: Gentile's cooked oil
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet prohibits a gentile's cooked oil. Rav Safra questions this, arguing it is not prohibited due to mixture (it spoils), bishul akum (it is edible raw), or gi'ulei akum (it is pagum and permitted).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that cooked oil of Aramaeans is forbidden.

Rav Safra objects: why be concerned? It is not subject to mixing (it spoils), it is edible raw (so not subject to gentile cooking), and any absorbed taste is נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a spoiled taste) and thus permitted.
Rav Safra argues that the oil is not forbidden due to mixture (it spoils), bishul akum (it is edible raw), or gi'ulei akum (it is pagum and permitted).

items.text: Gentile's cooked dates
items.text_en: Gentile's cooked dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about gentile-cooked dates (ahinei). Sweet ones are certainly permitted, bitter ones certainly prohibited; the question is about intermediate ones. Rabbi Asi responds that Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) prohibited them, and that is Levi.

sub.desc_en: They asked Rabbi Asi about the law of cooked beets (or similar vegetables) of Aramaeans.
Rabbi Asi answers: sweet ones are certainly permitted, bitter ones certainly forbidden; for intermediate ones, Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) forbids, and that is Levi.

items.text: Dispute over shatita (porridge)
items.text_en: Dispute over shatita (porridge)
items.desc_en: Rav permits shatita, while Shmuel's father and Levi prohibit. All agree that wheat and barley shatita is permitted, and challah (cheese) shatita is prohibited. They dispute over water shatita: one says we decree it because of challah, the other does not. An alternative version reverses the dispute. Rav cites a proof from Barzillai the Gileadite sending shatita to David, and notes that today no one is concerned about the opinion of Shmuel's father and Levi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the dispute over shatita (porridge): Rav permits it, while Shmuel's father and Levi prohibit it, and clarifies the points of agreement and disagreement regarding different types of shatita.
An alternative version reverses the dispute, stating that all agree water shatita is prohibited, and they disagree over wheat and barley shatita.
Rav cites a proof from Barzillai the Gileadite sending shatita to David, and notes that today no one is concerned about the opinion of Shmuel's father and Levi.

items.text: Pickled vegetables with wine
items.text_en: Pickled vegetables with wine
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah says that pickled vegetables (kavshin) that usually have wine added are only prohibited if it is known wine was added, but then even benefit is prohibited. He distinguishes from murias (fish brine) which is permitted for benefit because it removes phlegm, while wine adds flavor. Rabbi Yochanan permits even when known, and questions the distinction from murias according to Rabbi Meir who prohibits benefit from it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case of pickled vegetables (kavshin) that usually have wine added.

Chizkiyah rules that if it is known wine was added, the vegetables are prohibited even for benefit, distinguishing from murias (fish brine) which is permitted for benefit because it removes phlegm, while wine adds flavor.
Rabbi Yochanan permits even when known, and questions the distinction from murias according to Rabbi Meir who prohibits benefit from it.

items.text: Distinction between known and unknown origin
items.text_en: Distinction between known and unknown origin
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains a distinction: in one case the origin is known, in another it is not, leading to different rulings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the origin is known and one where it is not.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's list: brine without fish
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's list: brine without fish
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba quoting Rav identifies the 'brine without fish' as סוּלְתָּנִית and explains it is forbidden because its mixture rises with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the brine listed in the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba in the name of Rav identifies the brine as סוּלְתָּנִית (a type of brine) and explains it is forbidden because its mixture rises with it.

items.text: Baraita on fish that shed or grow scales
items.text_en: Baraita on fish that shed or grow scales
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that fish which currently have no scales but will grow them later are permitted, while fish that have scales now but shed them when taken from the sea are also permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that fish which currently lack scales but will grow them later are permitted, and fish that have scales now but shed them when taken from the sea are also permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's announcement about fish innards and roe
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's announcement about fish innards and roe
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu announces in Caesarea that fish innards and roe may be purchased from anyone, as they are assumed to come only from kosher fish sources.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu announces in Caesarea that fish innards and roe may be purchased from anyone.
The Gemara explains the presumption that these items only come from kosher fish sources (Pilosa and Aspamya).
Abaye provides a supporting example that a certain fish (צחנתא) from the Bab Nahara river is permitted.

items.text: Reasoning about the permissibility of צַחַנְתָּא
items.text_en: Reasoning about the permissibility of צַחַנְתָּא
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores why the fish from Bab Nahara is permitted, rejecting reasons of swift water and saltiness, and concluding it is because the river lacks mud where non-kosher fish dwell. Ravina adds that now other rivers flow into it, making it forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the fish from Bab Nahara is permitted, and proposes that it might be because the waters are swift, but then rejects this by noting that non-kosher fish are observed standing there.
The Gemara proposes that the waters are salty, which non-kosher fish cannot tolerate, but rejects this as well because such fish are observed there.
The Gemara concludes that the fish is permitted because the river lacks mud where non-kosher fish dwell.
Ravina adds that now other rivers flow into it, making the fish forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's rule: sea donkey and sea ox
items.text_en: Abaye's rule: sea donkey and sea ox
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that a sea donkey (a type of fish) is permitted, but a sea ox is forbidden, with a mnemonic based on purity laws.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the sea donkey (a type of fish) is permitted, while the sea ox is forbidden, providing a mnemonic based on purity laws.

items.text: Rav Ashi's rule: שְׁפַר נוּנָא and קְדַשׁ נוּנָא
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's rule: שְׁפַר נוּנָא and קְדַשׁ נוּנָא
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that שְׁפַר נוּנָא is permitted and קְדַשׁ נוּנָא is forbidden, with a mnemonic from the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳'. An alternative version says קְבַר נוּנָא is forbidden, with a mnemonic of gentile graves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that שְׁפַר נוּנָא (a type of fish) is permitted and קְדַשׁ נוּנָא is forbidden, with a mnemonic from the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳'.
An alternative version states that קְבַר נוּנָא is forbidden, with a mnemonic of gentile graves.

items.text: Stories of rabbis identifying kosher fish
items.text_en: Stories of rabbis identifying kosher fish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva, Rav Ashi, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah each encounter unfamiliar fish and use signs like scales or local names to determine permissibility.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva arrived at Ginzak, was brought a fish resembling a beetle, wrapped it in a palm branch, saw scales, and permitted it.
Rav Ashi arrived at Tamdorya, was brought a fish resembling a צלופחא (eel-like fish), examined it toward the sun, saw scales, and permitted it.
Rav Ashi arrived at another place, was brought a fish resembling a שפרנונא (a kosher fish), wrapped it in white nets, saw scales, and permitted it.

sub.text: Story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah arrived at Akra de-Agma, was brought a צחנתא (a fish), and heard a man calling it 'באטי' (a name suggesting impurity).

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's deduction from the name 'Bati'
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's deduction from the name 'Bati'
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah hears a fish called 'Bati', deduces it contains something impure, and refrains from eating it; the next day he finds a non-kosher creature inside, applying the verse 'No harm befalls the righteous'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah hears the fish called 'Bati' and deduces that it contains something impure.
He refrains from eating the fish based on his deduction.
The next morning he examines the fish and finds a non-kosher creature inside.
He applies the verse 'No harm befalls the righteous' to himself.

items.text: Reason for the prohibition of חִילְתִּית (asafetida) from a non-Jew
items.text_en: Reason for the prohibition of חִילְתִּית (asafetida) from a non-Jew
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that חִילְתִּית is forbidden because it is cut with a knife, and despite the rule that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, the sharpness of the asafetida sweetens the fat, making it a נותן טעם לשבח and thus forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the חִילְתִּית (asafetida) from a non-Jew is forbidden.

The Gemara answers that it is forbidden because it is cut with a knife, and although נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a detrimental flavor) is permitted, the sharpness of the asafetida sweetens the fat, making it a נותן טעם לשבח (imparting a beneficial flavor) and thus forbidden.

items.text: Ruling on buying asafetida from a haber's slave
items.text_en: Ruling on buying asafetida from a haber's slave
items.desc_en: After Rabbi Levi's death, his slave sells asafetida; Rabbi Yochanan rules that a haber's slave is considered like a haber, so one may buy from him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that after Rabbi Levi's death, his slave was selling asafetida, and people came to Rabbi Yochanan to ask whether they may buy from him.
The inquirers ask Rabbi Yochanan whether it is permitted to buy asafetida from the slave.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that a haber's slave is considered like a haber, so one may buy from him.

items.text: Story of Rav Huna bar Minyomi buying techelet
items.text_en: Story of Rav Huna bar Minyomi buying techelet
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Minyomi buys techelet from the household of Rav Amram Chasida; Rav Yosef has no tradition on the matter. Chanan the tailor recounts a similar case where Rav Yehuda from Hagronya ruled that a haber's wife is like a haber, citing Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Minyomi buys techelet from the household of Rav Amram Chasida and brings the case to Rav Yosef, who has no tradition on the matter.
Chanan the tailor recounts a similar case where Rav Yehuda from Hagronya ruled that the wife of a haber is like a haber, citing Shmuel's principle.

items.text: Baraita on the status of a haber's household after his death
items.text_en: Baraita on the status of a haber's household after his death
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that a haber's wife, children, and household retain their presumed reliability until they become suspect, and similarly a courtyard where techelet is sold retains its presumption until invalidated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a haber's wife, children, and household retain their presumed reliability until they become suspect, and similarly a courtyard where techelet is sold retains its presumption until invalidated.

items.text: Dispute about accepting חברות when a spouse or slave changes status
items.text_en: Dispute about accepting חברות when a spouse or slave changes status
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir rules that an am ha'aretz's wife, daughter, or slave who marries or is sold to a haber must accept חברות, but a haber's wife, daughter, or slave who marries or is sold to an am ha'aretz do not need to accept חברות initially. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar require acceptance in both cases, with a story illustrating the change in behavior.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's ruling that when an am ha'aretz's wife, daughter, or slave enters a haber's household, they must accept חברות (the standards of fellowship), but when a haber's wife, daughter, or slave enters an am ha'aretz's household, they do not need to accept חברות לכתחילה (as an initial requirement).

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagree, requiring acceptance of חברות in both directions, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar supports his position with a story of a woman who, when married to a haber, tied תפילין (phylacteries) for him, but when married to a tax collector (מוכס), tied the tax collector's knots for him, showing that one adopts the practices of one's spouse.

items.text: Rav's rule: חבי״ת requires two seals, חמפ״ג requires one
items.text_en: Rav's rule: חבי״ת requires two seals, חמפ״ג requires one
items.desc_en: Rav states that items in the acronym חבי״ת (milk, meat, wine, techelet) are forbidden if only sealed with one seal, while חמפ״ג items are permitted with one seal.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that items in the acronym חבי״ת (milk, meat, wine, techelet) require two seals, while חמפ״ג items are permitted with one seal.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: items permitted with one seal
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: items permitted with one seal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are forbidden unless sealed with one seal, and others (חִילְתִּית, מוּרְיָיס, פַּת, גְּבִינָה) that are permitted with one seal.

items.text: Gemara's question on bread and Rav's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on bread and Rav's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bread is permitted with one seal, explaining that substitution is obvious. Rav Kahana then explains Rav's view that milk is excluded from the list, and a fish piece without a distinguishing mark is included instead, which is like meat but with two types of meat.

items.text: Shmuel's alternative list
items.text_en: Shmuel's alternative list
items.desc_en: Shmuel presents a different list: meat, wine, and תכלת are forbidden with one seal; מוּרְיָיס, חִילְתִּית, and גְּבִינָה are permitted. He rejects the concept of two types of meat for a fish piece without a sign.

items.text: Baraita on purchasing in Syria and support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Baraita on purchasing in Syria and support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items not to be bought in Syria unless from an expert, but if one lodges with a host, they are permitted. This supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that if the host sends items to one's home, they are permitted because the host does not eat forbidden food.

items.text: Discussion of מלח סלקונדרית and its impurities
items.text_en: Discussion of מלח סלקונדרית and its impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what מלח סלקונדרית is, and records a dispute among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel about whether black or white salt is forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan explains the reasons involving fish intestines, and Rabbi Avahu adds a story about a elder who smoothed its surface with pig fat.

items.text: Exclusion from the list: Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Exclusion from the list: Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'these are forbidden' excludes. Chizkiya says it excludes a known item, while Rabbi Yochanan says it excludes מוּרְיָיס and גבינת בית אוניקי, and the anonymous view follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Second Mishnah: items permitted for consumption
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: items permitted for consumption
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items permitted for consumption, including milk milked by a gentile with an Israelite watching, honey, dubdevaniyot, pickles without wine/vinegar, untrefied טרית, brine with fish, חילתית leaves, and rolled olives. Rabbi Yose adds restrictions on שלחין and locusts.

items.text: Gemara on milk: the case of an Israelite sitting by the flock
items.text_en: Gemara on milk: the case of an Israelite sitting by the flock
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about an Israelite sitting by a gentile's flock while the gentile milks. It explains that even if there is an unclean animal in the flock, the Israelite's presence (when standing) deters the gentile from mixing milk, and the baraita teaches that fear of being seen prevents substitution.

items.text: Gemara on honey: no concerns
items.text_en: Gemara on honey: no concerns
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why honey is permitted: it is not subject to substitution (it spoils), it is eaten raw so not subject to gentile cooking, and if cooked by gentiles, the taste is imparted to a detriment and thus permitted.

items.text: Gemara on dubdevaniyot and the dispute of Shammai and Hillel
items.text_en: Gemara on dubdevaniyot and the dispute of Shammai and Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that dubdevaniyot, even if dripping, are not susceptible to impurity. It raises a contradiction with a mishnah where Shammai says grapes for the vat are susceptible, and Hillel agrees. The resolution is that there the liquid is wanted, here it is not.

items.text: Definitions of טרית and ציר
items.text_en: Definitions of טרית and ציר
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining a טרית that is not טרופה as one whose head and spine are recognizable, and brine that contains fish as one with at least one or two כילביות.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction about kilbit
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction about kilbit
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction about the kilbit (a type of fish) by distinguishing between open and closed barrels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about kilbit by distinguishing between open barrels (where the fish swims freely, so one kilbit suffices) and closed barrels (where two are needed).

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on fish signs
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on fish signs
items.desc_en: Rav Huna requires both head and spine to be recognizable, while Rav Nachman requires only one. Rav Ukva bar Chama raises an objection from the Mishnah about fish signs, and Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to specific fish (ara and palmuda) whose heads resemble impure fish.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: Rav Huna requires both head and spine to be recognizable, while Rav Nachman requires only one of them.
Rav Ukva bar Chama raises an objection from the Mishnah that fish are permitted by the signs of fins and scales, not by head and spine.
Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to specific fish (ara and palmuda) whose heads resemble impure fish, so head and spine are needed for them.

items.text: Ulla's distinction: brine vs. fish itself
items.text_en: Ulla's distinction: brine vs. fish itself
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla states that the dispute is only for pickling in brine, but for the fish itself, all agree that head and spine must be recognizable. Rabbi Zeira reports that he used to rely on this leniency for brine but stopped after hearing Ulla's ruling.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Ulla's ruling that the dispute about fish identification applies only to pickling in brine, but for the fish itself all agree it is forbidden unless head and spine are recognizable.
Rabbi Zeira reports that he used to rely on the leniency for brine but stopped after hearing Ulla's ruling.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling and the baraita about pieces
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling and the baraita about pieces
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that head and spine must be recognizable for each individual fish. A baraita is cited about pieces with a sign, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitted an entire barrel based on one piece. Rav Pappa explains the baraita applies when pieces are identical, teaching that we do not suspect chance occurrence.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that for each individual fish, the head and spine must be recognizable.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about pieces with a sign, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitted an entire barrel based on one piece.
Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita applies when the pieces are identical, teaching that we do not suspect chance occurrence.

items.text: Incident with the boat of fish and conflicting reports
items.text_en: Incident with the boat of fish and conflicting reports
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana permitted a boat of fish based on scales, but Rava objected because scales are common there. Rav Yirmiya from Difti reports that Rav Pappi said the permission was only for brine, while Rav Ashi reports that Rav Pappa said it was even for the fish itself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts an incident: a boat of fish (צחנתא) arrived at Sikra, and Rav Huna bar Chinana saw scales on it and permitted it.
Rava objects: how could one permit such fish in a place where scales are common (so scales are not a reliable sign)?
The gemara reports that Rava's shofar (public announcement) declared the fish forbidden, while Rav Huna bar Chinana's shofar declared it permitted, indicating a dispute.

sub.text: Rav Yirmiya from Difti citing Rav Pappi
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmiya from Difti citing Rav Pappi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmiya from Difti reports that Rav Pappi said Rav Huna bar Chinana's permission was only for brine (ציר), not for the fish itself.
Rav Ashi reports that Rav Pappa said Rav Huna bar Chinana's permission was even for the fish itself (גופן).

items.text: Rav Yirmiya's conclusion: neither forbids nor permits
items.text_en: Rav Yirmiya's conclusion: neither forbids nor permits
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmiya concludes that he neither forbids nor permits, because Rav Pappa said one thing and Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla said another, requiring head and spine for each fish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmiya concludes that he neither forbids nor permits, because Rav Pappa said one thing and Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla said another, requiring head and spine for each fish.

items.text: Rav Chinana bar Idi's ruling on open vs. closed barrels
items.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi's ruling on open vs. closed barrels
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi states before Rav Adda bar Ahava that if a non-Jew brings a barrel of jars and a kilbit is found in one, open jars are all permitted, but closed ones: only that jar is permitted and the rest are forbidden. He heard this from three authorities: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi states before Rav Adda bar Ahava the ruling that if a non-Jew brings a barrel of jars and a kilbit is found in one, open jars are all permitted, but closed ones: only that jar is permitted and the rest are forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Idi's response to Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi's response to Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks for the source, and Rav Chinana bar Idi replies that he heard this ruling from three authorities: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Rav's ruling on fish innards and the contradiction about fish eggs
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on fish innards and the contradiction about fish eggs
items.desc_en: Rav says fish innards and their 'embryos' may only be bought from an expert. Ulla raises a contradiction: impure fish spawn, pure fish lay eggs, so how can they have embryos? Rabbi Zeira resolves that both lay eggs, but one spawns externally and the other internally.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that fish innards and their embryos may only be purchased from an expert.
Ulla raises a contradiction: if Rav speaks of embryos, but impure fish spawn externally and pure fish lay eggs, how can there be embryos?
Rabbi Zeira resolves that both types lay eggs, but the impure fish spawns externally and the pure fish spawns internally, so embryos exist.

items.text: Signs for fish embryos and eggs
items.text_en: Signs for fish embryos and eggs
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that an expert is needed to check signs, as a baraita lists signs for eggs and fish embryos: shape, pointed ends, and yolk/white arrangement. Rava adds that this applies when they are not mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why an expert is needed, and answers that it is to check the signs.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the signs for eggs are the same as the signs for fish embryos, clarifying that the signs for fish themselves are already given in the Torah.
The baraita lists the signs for eggs: shape, pointed ends, and arrangement of yolk and white, distinguishing kosher from non-kosher.
Rava adds that these signs apply only when the eggs have become liquefied (i.e., their contents are mixed).

items.text: Return to Rabbi Dostai's reading
items.text_en: Return to Rabbi Dostai's reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Dostai's reading of 'their embryos' as a proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Dostai of Beirei, who cited the word 'עוּבָּרָן' (their embryos) as proof that non-kosher fish have embryos.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about fish innards
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about fish innards
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between a baraita that says signs of eggs are like signs of fish fetuses and the earlier ruling about fish innards. It explains that the baraita actually refers to signs of fish innards, and one can find a single innard in the case of a certain fish called שילפוחא.

items.text: The case of no expert: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: The case of no expert: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what to do if there is no expert present. Rav Yehuda says that if the seller says 'I salted them,' the fish innards are permitted. Rav Nachman requires the seller to say 'These are fish and these are their innards.' Rav Yehuda then instructs a certain Adda Dayala according to his own view.

items.text: The leaf of חילתית and its chips
items.text_en: The leaf of חילתית and its chips
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about the leaf of חילתית is necessary only for the chips within it. One might have thought we should worry that the idolater mixed in wine, but the Gemara teaches that the chips are merely dried sap that came with the leaf.

items.text: The case of גלוסקאות olives
items.text_en: The case of גלוסקאות olives
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling about גלוסקאות olives is necessary even when they are very soft. One might have thought that wine was poured on them, but the Gemara teaches that the softness is due to oil.

items.text: Definition of שלחין according to Rabbi Yose
items.text_en: Definition of שלחין according to Rabbi Yose
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what שלחין are, and Rabbi Yose bar Chanina defines them as any fruit whose pit slips out when held in the hand.
