items.text: Baraita on locusts, capers, and apple wine
items.text_en: Baraita on locusts, capers, and apple wine
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that locusts, capers, and caperberries from a storehouse or ship are permitted, but those sold in a shop are forbidden because the shopkeeper sprinkles wine on them. Similarly, gentile apple wine from a storehouse is permitted, but sold in a shop is forbidden because they mix in wine.

items.text: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael about apple wine
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael about apple wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi once had a stomach ache and asked if anyone knew whether gentile apple wine is forbidden or permitted. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yose told him that his father once had a stomach ache, drank seventy-year-old gentile apple wine, and was healed. Rabbi was upset that he had not been told earlier. They found a gentile with three hundred barrels of such wine, Rabbi drank and was healed, and he blessed God for entrusting the world to guardians.

items.text: Explanation of 'and likewise for terumah'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'and likewise for terumah'
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'and likewise for terumah' refers to a priest suspected of selling terumah as non-sacred produce. In his presence it is forbidden, but produce from a storehouse is permitted because the priest fears the rabbis will discover and penalize him.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the conclusion of the chapter: 'We have returned to you, Ein Ma'amidin.'

items.text: Mishnah: All idols are forbidden
items.text_en: Mishnah: All idols are forbidden
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all idols are forbidden because they are worshipped once a year, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say only those holding a staff, bird, or ball are forbidden. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says any idol holding something is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Explaining the dispute about idols
items.text_en: Gemara: Explaining the dispute about idols
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages disagree if idols are worshipped once a year. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef says in Rabbi Yochanan's name that in Rabbi Meir's place they worshipped idols once a year, and Rabbi Meir was concerned for the minority and decreed other places like that place, while the Sages were not concerned and did not decree. Rav Yehuda says in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah refers to the statue of kings. Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in Rabbi Yochanan's name that it refers to statues standing at the entrance of a province.

items.text: Rabbah's initial statement and objection
items.text_en: Rabbah's initial statement and objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah initially distinguishes between village and city idols, claiming that city idols are permitted because they are made for adornment. The Gemara objects that village idols are certainly made for worship, so the distinction is flawed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that the dispute about idolatry only applies to village idols, but city idols are universally permitted because they are made for adornment (לנוי).
The Gemara objects that village idols are certainly made for worship, so Rabbah's distinction is flawed.

items.text: Rabbah's corrected statement
items.text_en: Rabbah's corrected statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rabbah's statement: the dispute applies to city idols, but village idols are universally forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah revises his statement: the dispute is about city idols, but village idols are universally forbidden.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's terms: מקל, צפור, כדור
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's terms: מקל, צפור, כדור
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms in the Mishnah: a 'staff' (מקל) represents one who subdues himself under the entire world like a staff, a 'bird' (צפור) represents one who grasps himself under the entire world like a bird, and a 'ball' (כדור) represents one who grasps himself under the entire world like a ball.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains the Mishnah's terms 'מקל' (staff), 'ציפור' (bird), and 'כדור' (ball) as symbols of self-subjugation under the entire world.

items.text: Addition of sword, crown, and ring
items.text_en: Addition of sword, crown, and ring
items.desc_en: A Tanna adds a sword, crown, and ring to the list of forbidden objects. The Gemara explains the initial and final perceptions of each: the sword initially seems like a mere robber's tool but ultimately symbolizes one who kills himself under the entire world; the crown initially seems like a mere wreath but ultimately like a crown on a dog; the ring initially seems like a mere signet but ultimately like one who signs himself under the entire world for death.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna adds a sword, crown, and ring to the list of forbidden objects.
The Gemara explains that the sword initially seems like a mere robber's tool but ultimately symbolizes one who kills himself under the entire world.
The Gemara explains that the crown initially seems like a mere wreath but ultimately like a crown on a dog.
The Gemara explains that the ring initially seems like a mere signet but ultimately like one who signs himself under the entire world for death.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's addition of a pebble and a splinter
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's addition of a pebble and a splinter
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds even a pebble and a splinter to the list of forbidden objects.

sub.text: Baraita on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's addition
sub.text_en: Baraita on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's addition
sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that even a pebble (צרור) or a splinter (קיסם) are included in the list of forbidden items.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inquiry about excrement
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inquiry about excrement
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if one holds excrement in his hand, is it considered that everyone despises him like excrement, or that he despises himself before everyone like excrement? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether holding excrement in one's hand is considered a degrading act that shows submission.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו), debating whether the excrement degrades everyone before him or degrades him before everyone.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on broken idol fragments
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on broken idol fragments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who finds broken fragments of idols is permitted to use them, but finding a hand or foot form is forbidden because such forms are worshipped. Shmuel says this applies even to broken fragments of actual idolatry. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah mentions 'broken idols' specifically because of the latter clause about hand and foot forms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that broken idols are permitted, but a hand or foot form is forbidden because such forms are worshipped.
Shmuel says the permission applies even to broken fragments of actual idolatry; the Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'broken idols' rather than 'broken idolatry'.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's wording is due to the latter clause about hand and foot forms, but the same rule applies to broken idolatry.
The Gemara asks why a hand or foot form is forbidden, given that broken fragments are permitted.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's ruling about hand and foot forms
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's ruling about hand and foot forms
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a hand or foot form is forbidden, implying that the reason is because such forms are worshipped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a hand or foot form is forbidden, given that it might be merely decorative.
The Gemara questions why a hand or foot form is forbidden, implying that the reason is because such forms are worshipped.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that broken pieces of an idol are permitted, noting that the pieces themselves are the idol. Shmuel resolves this by explaining the Mishnah refers to pieces still attached to their base.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that broken pieces of an idol are permitted, arguing that the pieces themselves are the idol.
Shmuel resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah refers to pieces still attached to their base.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that an idol that broke on its own is forbidden because it was never nullified, while Reish Lakish permits it, arguing that the owner implicitly nullifies it, reasoning that if the idol could not save itself, it cannot save him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding an idol that broke on its own.
Rabbi Yochanan forbids because the idol was never nullified; Reish Lakish permits, arguing the owner implicitly nullifies it, reasoning that if the idol could not save itself, it cannot save him.

items.text: First objection from the story of Dagon
items.text_en: First objection from the story of Dagon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse about Dagon's head and hands being cut off, implying the idol remained forbidden. Reish Lakish deflects, explaining that the Philistines abandoned Dagon and worshipped the threshold instead, so the case is different.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish by citing the verse about Dagon's head and hands being cut off, implying the idol remained forbidden.
Reish Lakish rejects the proof, explaining that the Philistines abandoned Dagon and worshipped the threshold instead, so the case is different.

items.text: Second objection from the Mishnah of broken images
items.text_en: Second objection from the Mishnah of broken images
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a Mishnah: one who finds broken images may use them, implying broken idol fragments are forbidden. The Gemara reinterprets: the Mishnah means the images themselves are forbidden (like Rabbi Meir), not their fragments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish by citing a Mishnah: one who finds broken images may use them, implying that broken idol fragments are forbidden.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: it does not forbid broken idol fragments but rather the images themselves are forbidden, aligning with Rabbi Meir's view.

items.text: Attempted proof from Rabbi Meir to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Rabbi Meir to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that if Rabbi Meir forbids images but permits their fragments, then the Rabbis should likewise forbid an idol but permit its fragments. The Gemara rejects this: with images, it is uncertain if they were worshipped or nullified, but with an idol, it was certainly worshipped and uncertainly nullified, so uncertainty cannot override certainty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that if Rabbi Meir forbids images but permits their fragments, then the Rabbis should likewise forbid an idol but permit its fragments.

The Gemara rejects the analogy: with images, it is uncertain whether they were worshipped or nullified, but with an idol, it was certainly worshipped and only uncertainly nullified, so uncertainty cannot override certainty.

items.text: Challenge to the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty
items.text_en: Challenge to the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a case where a chaver died and left produce presumed tithed, even though it was certainly immersed but uncertainly tithed. The Gemara resolves that it is a case of certainty and certainty (since a chaver is assumed to tithe), or alternatively, the produce was never immersed, making it a case of uncertainty and uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty by citing a baraita about a chaver who died and left a granary full of produce, which is presumed tithed even though it was certainly immersed but uncertainly tithed.
The Gemara objects that in this case, there is certainty of immersion but uncertainty of tithing, yet the uncertainty overrides the certainty.
The Gemara answers that it is a case of certainty and certainty, because a chaver is presumed (חזקה) not to release untithed produce from his hand, as per Rabbi Chanina the Seer.

The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the produce was never immersed, making it a case of uncertainty and uncertainty, as it is possible the owner acted like Rabbi Oshaya, who said one may bring produce in its chaff to exempt it from tithes.

items.text: Second challenge to the principle
items.text_en: Second challenge to the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins another challenge to the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty, citing a story of a maidservant, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that uncertainty cannot override certainty by citing a baraita introduced by Rabbi Yehuda about a maidservant, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: case of a priest checking a stillborn
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: case of a priest checking a stillborn
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a priest looked into a pit to determine the sex of a stillborn, and the Sages declared it pure because weasels and badgers are commonly found there, implying they might have dragged it away.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a priest looked into a pit to determine the sex of a stillborn, and the Sages declared it pure because weasels and badgers are commonly found there, implying they might have dragged it away.

items.text: Gemara's question: doubt vs. certainty
items.text_en: Gemara's question: doubt vs. certainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a doubt (whether the animals dragged it) can override the certainty that a stillborn was deposited, since the priest's looking assumes the stillborn is there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a doubt (whether the animals dragged the stillborn) can override the certainty that a stillborn was deposited, since the priest's looking assumes the stillborn is there.

items.text: First answer: reinterpreting the Mishnah
items.text_en: First answer: reinterpreting the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara first suggests that the Mishnah meant she deposited something like a stillborn, not a definite one. It then addresses the phrase 'to know if male or female' by explaining it means to determine if it was a miscarriage or a stillborn, and if a stillborn, its sex.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: she deposited something like a stillborn (כְּמִין נֵפֶל), not a definite stillborn, to avoid the problem of doubt overriding certainty.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly says 'to know if male or female,' implying a definite stillborn, not just something like one.
The Gemara resolves: the phrase means to determine first if it was a miscarriage (רוּחַ) or a stillborn (נֵפֶל), and if a stillborn, then its sex.

items.text: Alternative answer: certainty of dragging
items.text_en: Alternative answer: certainty of dragging
items.desc_en: An alternative answer states that since weasels and badgers are commonly found there, they certainly dragged it, so the doubt is resolved.

sub.desc_en: The gemara offers an alternative answer: since weasels and badgers are commonly found there, they certainly dragged the fetus, resolving the doubt.

items.text: Objection from a found hand or foot
items.text_en: Objection from a found hand or foot
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if one finds a form of a hand or foot, they are forbidden because they were worshipped. But why? They are broken pieces! Shmuel explains that the ruling applies when they are still on their base.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a found hand or foot form is forbidden, but it is broken pieces, so why should it be forbidden?
Shmuel explains that the ruling applies when the hand or foot is still standing on its base, not when it is a mere broken piece.

items.text: Objection: gentile nullifies idol, Jew does not
items.text_en: Objection: gentile nullifies idol, Jew does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a gentile can nullify his own or another's idol, but a Jew cannot nullify a gentile's idol. Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! Abaye says the case is where the Jew damaged it, but the Gemara notes that damaging nullifies. Abaye distinguishes: a gentile's damage nullifies, a Jew's does not. Rava says even a Jew's damage nullifies, but there is a decree lest the Jew lift it and then nullify it, making it an idol in a Jew's hand, which is never nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita: a gentile nullifies his own or another's idol, but a Jew does not nullify a gentile's idol — why should this not be like an idol that broke on its own (which is permitted)?
Abaye answers that the case is where the Jew damaged (פחסה) the idol, but the Gemara objects that damaging should nullify it according to a mishnah.
Abaye distinguishes: a gentile's damage nullifies the idol, but a Jew's damage does not.
Rava says even a Jew's damage nullifies, but there is a decree lest the Jew lift it and then nullify it, making it an idol in a Jew's hand, which is never nullified.

items.text: Objection: stones from a merkulis
items.text_en: Objection: stones from a merkulis
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a gentile who brings stones from a merkulis and paves roads with them is permitted, but a Jew who does so is forbidden. Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a gentile who brings stones from a merkulis and paves roads with them is permitted, but a Jew who does so is forbidden. Why should this not be like an idol that broke on its own?
The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle, meaning the Jew's action is considered a direct act of worship, not a passive benefit from broken idolatry.

items.text: Objection: gentile planes an idol
items.text_en: Objection: gentile planes an idol
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a gentile who planes an idol for his own use renders it and the shavings permitted, but for the idol's use the idol is forbidden and shavings permitted; a Jew who planes an idol, whether for his own use or the idol's, both are forbidden. Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita: a gentile who planes an idol for his own use renders both the idol and shavings permitted, but for the idol's use the idol is forbidden and shavings permitted; a Jew who planes an idol, whether for his own use or the idol's, both are forbidden — why should this not be like an idol that broke on its own?
The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle (that an idol broken by human action is not considered as if it broke on its own).

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yosi's method of grinding and scattering
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yosi's method of grinding and scattering
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yosi says one may grind an idol and scatter it to the wind or throw it into the sea. The Sages said it becomes fertilizer, and it is written 'nothing of the banned thing shall cling to your hand.' Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yosi's ruling that one may grind an idol and scatter it, and the Sages' objection that it becomes fertilizer, violating the verse 'nothing of the banned thing shall cling to your hand.'
The Gemara asks why this case should not be like an idol that broke on its own, which is permitted.
The Gemara answers that here too, the case is like Rava's principle (that an idol broken by a Jew is forbidden due to a decree).

items.text: Objection: found a dragon with its head cut off
items.text_en: Objection: found a dragon with its head cut off
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yosi ben Yasyan says if one finds a form of a dragon with its head cut off, if it is uncertain whether a gentile or Jew cut it, it is permitted; if a Jew definitely cut it, it is forbidden. Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! The Gemara answers: here too, it is like Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yosi ben Yasyan's ruling: finding a dragon form with its head cut off is permitted if uncertain who cut it, but forbidden if a Jew definitely cut it, questioning why it is not treated like an idol that broke on its own.
The Gemara answers that here too, the ruling follows Rava's principle, which distinguishes between an idol broken by a Jew (forbidden) and one broken by a gentile (permitted).

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yosi on vegetables in the rainy season
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yosi on vegetables in the rainy season
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yosi says one should not buy vegetables in the rainy season because the idolatrous libation falls on them. Why? It should be like an idol that broke on its own! The Gemara distinguishes: there, the essence of the idolatry remains intact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Rabbi Yosi's ruling that one should not buy vegetables in the rainy season because idolatrous libation falls on them, asking why this should not be permitted like an idol that broke on its own.
The Gemara distinguishes: there, the essence of the idolatry remains intact, so the case is different from a broken idol.

items.text: Challenge from the case of shards of an asherah
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of shards of an asherah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier ruling that an asherah and its shards are prohibited if used for its benefit, but the shards are permitted. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that idolatry is not nullified through its natural growth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier ruling by citing a baraita where shards of an asherah are permitted even though the tree itself remains an idol.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that idolatry is not nullified through its natural growth, so the shards are permitted because they grew from the tree after it became an asherah.

items.text: Resolving the bird's nest on an asherah
items.text_en: Resolving the bird's nest on an asherah
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan with a baraita about a bird's nest on an asherah tree, where one may knock it down with a reed. The Gemara initially assumes the nest was made from the tree's wood, but concludes it was made from outside wood, and discusses the laws of me'ilah regarding consecrated items.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan with a baraita about a bird's nest on an asherah tree, where one may knock it down with a reed.
The Gemara initially assumes the nest was made from the tree's own wood, which would make it forbidden, yet the baraita permits knocking it down.
The Gemara concludes the nest was made from outside wood brought from elsewhere, not from the asherah tree itself.

sub.text: Gemara's proof from the consecrated case
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof from the consecrated case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves the resolution from the consecrated case: if the wood were from the tree, it would be consecrated and subject to me'ilah, but the baraita says no me'ilah applies.
The Gemara resolves the consecrated case by explaining the nest is from growths that came after the tree's consecration, and there is no me'ilah in such growths.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of 'knock it down'
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of 'knock it down'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that 'knock it down' refers to the chicks. Rabbi Yaakov explains to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tahlifa that chicks are permitted in both cases, eggs are forbidden, and Rav Ashi adds that chicks needing their mother are like eggs.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'knock it down' as referring to knocking down the chicks.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tahlifa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tahlifa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov explains to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tahlifa that chicks are permitted in both cases (sacred tree and asherah), while eggs are forbidden in both cases.
Rav Ashi adds that chicks that still need their mother are like eggs and therefore forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Vessels with celestial images
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vessels with celestial images
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who finds vessels with images of the sun, moon, or dragon must take them to the Dead Sea. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between honored and despised vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who finds vessels with images of the sun, moon, or dragon must take them to the Dead Sea, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between honored and despised vessels.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why only these images are forbidden, citing a baraita that slaughtering for the sun, moon, etc., is considered idolatry. Abaye explains that people worship anything they find, but they specifically fashion and worship these three significant ones; other images are merely decorative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether only these celestial bodies are worshipped, citing a baraita that lists many entities for which slaughter is considered idolatry.
Abaye answers that people worship everything they find, but they only depict and worship these three significant ones; other images are mere decoration.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: people worship anything they find, but they specifically fashion and worship only these three significant images; other images are merely decorative.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's baraita and its analysis
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's baraita and its analysis
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet teaches a baraita: all constellations are permitted except the sun and moon, all faces except the human face, and all forms except the dragon. The Gemara analyzes whether this refers to a finder or a maker, concluding it refers to a maker, and resolves contradictions with the Mishnah and verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet recites a baraita listing three categories: constellations (except sun and moon), faces (except human face), and forms (except dragon form) are permitted.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the first clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the first clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the baraita refers to a maker, citing the verse prohibiting making images of heavenly servants.
The Gemara answers that the baraita clearly refers to a finder, as in the Mishnah.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the middle clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the middle clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if it refers to a finder, the human face should not be forbidden, as the Mishnah only mentions the dragon.
The Gemara revises its answer, saying the baraita refers to a maker, following Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's principle.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the last clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the last clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if it refers to a maker, the dragon form should also be forbidden by the verse prohibiting making idols of silver and gold.

items.text: Opening statement on the dragon image
items.text_en: Opening statement on the dragon image
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that certain images are permitted, but the image of a dragon is forbidden. This sets up the discussion about the specific case of finding such an image.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's structure: finder vs. maker
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's structure: finder vs. maker
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's cases all refer to a finder or include a maker. Abaye resolves that the first and last clauses refer to a finder, while the middle clause refers to a maker.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: all cases are finders, middle clause follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: all cases are finders, middle clause follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the entire Mishnah deals with a finder, and the middle clause reflects Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, who adds additional forbidden images like a nursing woman and Sar Afis, which are associated with Eve and Joseph.

items.text: Definition of a dragon image
items.text_en: Definition of a dragon image
items.desc_en: The Sages define what constitutes a dragon image: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says it has scales between its joints, and Rabbi Asi demonstrates that these are between the neck joints. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina rules in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar and the ring with a dragon image
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar and the ring with a dragon image
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana relates that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar found a ring with a dragon image, and a gentile nullified it. The Gemara derives three halakhot: a gentile can nullify his own or another's idol, only an expert can nullify, and nullification can be done under coercion.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah of finding lost items and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah of finding lost items and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina objects based on a Mishnah that says items found in public places belong to the finder due to owner's despair. Abaye resolves that while the owner despairs of the item, they do not despair of the idolatrous prohibition, as they assume a gentile might worship it or a Jew might sell it to a gentile.

items.text: Discussion on images of heavenly servants: Rabban Gamliel's case
items.text_en: Discussion on images of heavenly servants: Rabban Gamliel's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabban Gamliel could have images of the moon on his wall, given the prohibition of making likenesses of God's servants. Abaye limits the prohibition to servants that can be replicated, citing a baraita about not making a house like the Temple or a menorah like the original. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda adds a restriction for wood, but the Sages refute this with the Hasmonean example.

items.text: Question on servants that cannot be replicated and Abaye's incomplete answer
items.text_en: Question on servants that cannot be replicated and Abaye's incomplete answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether images of heavenly servants that cannot be replicated are permitted, citing a baraita that prohibits making likenesses of God's servants in heaven. Abaye begins to answer, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Challenge to the Mishnah's prohibition of human faces
items.text_en: Challenge to the Mishnah's prohibition of human faces
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prohibits all human faces, given that the Torah only forbids the four faces together (of the Chariot). It cites a baraita that permits all faces except the human face, raising a contradiction.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's answer: 'Do not make Me' excludes other servants
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer: 'Do not make Me' excludes other servants
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Yehoshua reports from Rabbi Yehoshua that the verse 'Do not make with Me' permits making images of other celestial servants, but not of God.

items.text: Objection: Baraita forbids all celestial servants
items.text_en: Objection: Baraita forbids all celestial servants
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that interprets 'Do not make with Me' to prohibit making images of all celestial servants, including Ofanim, Seraphim, and holy Chayot.

items.text: Abaye's distinction and further clarification
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction and further clarification
items.desc_en: Abaye limits the prohibition to servants in the upper firmament. The Gemara questions whether lower servants are permitted, citing a baraita that includes sun, moon, stars, and constellations. It resolves that the baraita refers to worshipping them, and even a small worm is included from the verse's end.

items.text: Question about mere making and Rabban Gamliel's case
items.text_en: Question about mere making and Rabban Gamliel's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether mere making (without worshipping) is permitted, citing a baraita that forbids making images of sun, moon, etc. It answers that Rabban Gamliel's case is different because others made it for him.

items.text: Discussion of suspicion and the case of Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
items.text_en: Discussion of suspicion and the case of Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Yehuda was told to destroy a ring with a protruding seal due to suspicion, while in the synagogue of Shaf veYativ they did not suspect. It distinguishes between a private individual and a public figure like Rabban Gamliel, and offers alternative answers.

items.text: Alternative answer: Learning is different
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Learning is different
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another answer: learning to understand and teach is permitted, as derived from the verse 'Do not learn to do,' but you may learn to understand and instruct.

items.text: Definition of honored and despised images
items.text_en: Definition of honored and despised images
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses which images are honored and which are despised. Rav and Shmuel debate: Rav says honored are above water, despised below; Shmuel says both are despised, but honored are those on necklaces, earrings, and rings. A baraita supports Shmuel.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Sages on disposal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Sages on disposal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records Rabbi Yosei's opinion to grind and scatter idolatrous objects, while the Sages argue it becomes fertilizer, citing 'Do not let anything from the banned item cling to your hand.' The Gemara begins a baraita where Rabbi Yosei responds.

items.text: First objection: the golden calf was burned but not nullified
items.text_en: First objection: the golden calf was burned but not nullified
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Moses burning the golden calf. The Sages object that the calf was burned only to test the Israelites like sotah, not to nullify it.

items.text: Second objection: Maacah's idol was burned and ground, but Kidron Valley does not grow plants
items.text_en: Second objection: Maacah's idol was burned and ground, but Kidron Valley does not grow plants
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei cites the verse about Asa burning Maacah's idol in Kidron Valley. The Sages object that Kidron Valley does not grow plants, so the ashes were not used for fertilizer. A baraisa clarifies that some parts of Kidron Valley do grow plants.

items.text: Explanation of מפלצתה
items.text_en: Explanation of מפלצתה
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Yosef explain that מפלצתה refers to an obscene object made for daily sexual use.

items.text: Third objection: the copper serpent was ground, but it was not his to nullify
items.text_en: Third objection: the copper serpent was ground, but it was not his to nullify
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei cites the verse about Hezekiah grinding the copper serpent. The Sages object that the serpent was not Moses' property, so he could not nullify it; it was ground only because Israel erred after it.

items.text: Fourth objection: David carried the Philistine idols, but the verse says they were burned
items.text_en: Fourth objection: David carried the Philistine idols, but the verse says they were burned
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei cites the verse that David carried away the Philistine idols. The Sages object that another verse says they were burned, implying 'carried' means literally carried, not nullified.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction via Ittai the Gittite
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction via Ittai the Gittite
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the verses contradict each other. Rav Huna raises the contradiction: one verse says burned, another says carried. The resolution is that before Ittai the Gittite came, the idols were burned; after he came and nullified them, they were carried. The crown of the king of Ammon was also nullified by Ittai.

items.text: Discussion of the crown's weight and placement
items.text_en: Discussion of the crown's weight and placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how the crown weighing a kikar of gold could be placed on David's head. Rav Yehuda says it was fitting for David's head; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says it had a drawing stone; Rabbi Elazar says it had a precious stone worth a kikar.

items.text: The crown as testimony and related aggadic interpretations
items.text_en: The crown as testimony and related aggadic interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'This was mine because I kept Your precepts' as referring to the crown that testified for David. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it was placed where tefillin go and struck him. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says there is room for two tefillin. The crown and testimony are interpreted as a sign of kingship for David's house, and Adonijah's attempt to be king failed because the crown did not strike him. The fifty runners are described as having their spleens removed and feet hollowed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Proclus's question and Rabban Gamliel's initial responses
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Proclus's question and Rabban Gamliel's initial responses
items.desc_en: Proclus asks Rabban Gamliel why he bathes in a bathhouse with a statue of Aphrodite, citing the prohibition on deriving benefit from idolatry. Rabban Gamliel first refuses to answer in the bathhouse, then gives two arguments: the statue is there for the bathhouse's decoration, not vice versa, and since people treat it disrespectfully (urinating before it), it is not treated as a deity and thus permitted.

sub.desc_en: Proclus asks Rabban Gamliel why he bathes in a bathhouse containing a statue of Aphrodite, citing the prohibition on deriving benefit from idolatry.
Rabban Gamliel first refuses to answer in the bathhouse, then argues that the statue is subordinate to the bathhouse, not vice versa.
Rabban Gamliel argues that since people treat the statue disrespectfully (urinating before it), it is not treated as a deity and is therefore permitted.

items.text: Gemara's first question: How could Rabban Gamliel respond in the bathhouse?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: How could Rabban Gamliel respond in the bathhouse?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabban Gamliel could even think about Torah matters in the bathhouse, citing Rabbi Yochanan's rule that one may not think about Torah in a bathhouse or latrine. It then notes that if he used secular language, that too is problematic per Abaye's rule. The Gemara resolves that the response was given only after he left, as a baraita states.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabban Gamliel could discuss Torah in the bathhouse, citing the rule that one may not even think Torah there.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabban Gamliel spoke in a secular language, citing Abaye's rule that sacred matters may not be spoken in a secular language.
A baraita clarifies that Rabban Gamliel only answered after leaving the bathhouse, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's claim: Rabban Gamliel's answer was 'stolen' (first version)
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's claim: Rabban Gamliel's answer was 'stolen' (first version)
items.desc_en: Rav Ham bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya states that Rabban Gamliel's answer was 'stolen' (unconvincing), but he himself says it is not stolen. The 'stolen' aspect is the argument about people urinating before the statue, since Rava notes that Peor, which is worshipped by urinating, is not nullified by such acts. Rabbi Oshaya counters that Peor's worship is precisely that act, whereas Aphrodite's is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya declares that Rabban Gamliel's answer was stolen (weak), but he himself says it is not stolen.
The Gemara asks what the weakness is: Rabban Gamliel's argument about urination is countered by Rava's proof from Peor, which is worshipped despite similar treatment.
Rabbi Oshaya defends the answer: Peor's worship includes that act, but Aphrodite's does not, so the disrespect shows it is not treated as a deity.
Rabbi Oshaya resolves that the answer is not stolen because Peor's worship is precisely that act, whereas Aphrodite's is not, so the urination is a valid sign of contempt.

items.text: Abaye's alternative: The 'stolen' aspect is the boundary argument
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative: The 'stolen' aspect is the boundary argument
items.desc_en: Abaye argues the 'stolen' part is Rabban Gamliel's claim that he did not enter the statue's domain but it entered his, citing a mishnah that one may benefit from an idol's bathhouse or garden only in a non-beneficial manner. Rabbi Oshaya counters that Rabban Gamliel's benefit was not beneficial relative to others, so it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that the first argument (the statue came into his domain) is weak, citing a mishnah that one may not benefit from an idol's bathhouse even if it is not the main purpose.
The Gemara defends the answer: Rabban Gamliel's benefit was not in a favorable manner, comparable to others' benefit, so it is permitted.
Rabbi Oshaya counters that the answer is not stolen because Rabban Gamliel's benefit was not beneficial relative to others (שלא בטובת רבן גמליאל כבטובת אחרים דמי), so it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya: The 'stolen' aspect is the urination argument (second version)
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya: The 'stolen' aspect is the urination argument (second version)
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya claims the 'stolen' part is the urination argument, citing a mishnah that spitting or urinating before an idol does not nullify it. Rabbi Oshaya counters that there the act is momentary anger followed by appeasement, whereas here the statue is constantly degraded.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya argues that the urination argument is weak, citing a mishnah that spitting or urinating before an idol does not nullify it.
The Gemara defends the answer: there the act is temporary anger followed by appeasement, but here the statue is constantly degraded, showing it is not treated as a deity.

items.text: Rabba bar Ulla: The 'stolen' aspect is the decoration argument
items.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla: The 'stolen' aspect is the decoration argument
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla argues the 'stolen' part is Rabban Gamliel's claim that the statue is merely decoration for the bathhouse, since a statement dedicating a house or cup to idolatry has no effect (no consecration for idolatry). Rabbi Oshaya counters that while it is not forbidden, it still constitutes a decoration.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla argues that the second argument (the statue is mere decoration) is weak, citing a baraita that dedicating a house to idolatry has no effect, so the decoration argument is irrelevant.
The Gemara defends the answer: although the dedication is ineffective, the statue still serves as decoration, and the bathhouse is not subordinate to it.
A baraita is cited stating that declaring a house or cup dedicated to idolatry has no effect, because there is no consecration for idolatry.
Rabbi Oshaya counters that while the statue is not forbidden, it still constitutes a decoration (נוי), which is the point of Rabban Gamliel's argument.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mountains and hills worshipped by gentiles are permitted, but what is on them (e.g., plating) is forbidden, citing a verse. Rabbi Yosei HaGlili interprets the verse to exclude the mountains themselves from being forbidden. Rabbi Akiva adds that wherever one finds a high mountain, lofty hill, or lush tree, idolatry is present.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that mountains and hills worshipped by gentiles are permitted, but what is on them (e.g., plating) is forbidden, citing the verse 'לֹא תַחְמֹד כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב עֲלֵיהֶם' (Do not covet the silver and gold upon them).
Rabbi Yosei HaGlili interprets the verse 'אֱלֹהֵיהֶם עַל הֶהָרִים' (their gods upon the mountains) to exclude the mountains themselves from being forbidden.
The Mishnah explains why an asherah (idolatrous tree) is forbidden: because it involves human handiwork (תְּפִיסַת יְדֵי אָדָם), and anything with human handiwork is forbidden.
Rabbi Akiva adds that wherever one finds a high mountain, lofty hill, or lush tree, one should know that idolatry is present there.

items.text: Gemara's question and first answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's view seems identical to the Tanna Kamma's. Rami bar Chama in the name of Resh Lakish answers that the difference between them concerns the plating on a mountain: the Tanna Kamma holds that the plating is not like the mountain and is forbidden, while Rabbi Yosei HaGlili holds that the plating is like the mountain and is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's position differs from the Tanna Kamma's, since both seem to permit mountains and forbid their adornments.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama in the name of Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama in the name of Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama citing Resh Lakish answers that the dispute concerns the plating on a mountain: the Tanna Kamma holds that the plating is not like the mountain and is forbidden, while Rabbi Yosei HaGlili holds that the plating is like the mountain and is permitted.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's alternative answer
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's alternative answer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet offers a different resolution: everyone agrees that the plating on a mountain is not like the mountain, so the dispute must be about something else (implied: the interpretation of the verse).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet asserts that all parties agree that the plating on a mountain is not like the mountain itself, thereby rejecting the earlier dispute's premise and implying a different basis for the disagreement.

items.text: The dispute over a tree planted and later worshipped
items.text_en: The dispute over a tree planted and later worshipped
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the core dispute: Tanna Kamma permits a tree planted and later worshipped, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili forbids it. It then asks for the source of this distinction, citing the Mishnah's statement that an asherah is forbidden because of human involvement, implying that a tree planted and later worshipped is included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the core dispute: Tanna Kamma permits a tree planted and later worshipped, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili forbids it.

The Gemara asks for the source of this distinction, citing the Mishnah's statement that an asherah is forbidden because of human involvement, implying that a tree planted and later worshipped is included.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position and scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position and scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda also forbids a tree planted and later worshipped, deriving it from the verse 'and you shall burn their asherim with fire.' He argues that the phrase 'under every leafy tree' is not needed for the prohibition, but rather for Rabbi Akiva's teaching that such locations indicate idolatry.

sub.text: Stam's introduction of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Stam's introduction of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position that a tree planted and later worshipped is forbidden, and cites his initial scriptural inference from the verse 'under every leafy tree' that might suggest the tree itself is not an object of worship.

sub.text: Baraita citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's resolution
sub.text_en: Baraita citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda resolves the inference by citing the verse 'and you shall burn their asherim with fire,' which teaches that the tree itself is forbidden.

sub.text: Stam's explanation of the remaining verse
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of the remaining verse
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the phrase 'under every leafy tree' is not superfluous but rather serves Rabbi Akiva's teaching that such locations indicate the presence of idolatry.

items.text: The Rabbis' alternative derivation and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's response
items.text_en: The Rabbis' alternative derivation and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Rabbis use the verse 'and you shall burn their asherim with fire' for a tree initially planted for idolatry. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda agrees but derives the case of a tree planted and later worshipped from the verse 'and you shall cut down their asherim,' which implies a tree whose cutting is forbidden but whose root is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'and you shall burn their asherim with fire,' and answers that they use it for a tree initially planted for idolatry.

Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda agrees that the verse is needed for a tree initially planted for idolatry, but derives the case of a tree planted and later worshipped from the verse 'and you shall cut down their asherim,' which implies a tree whose cutting is forbidden but whose root is permitted.

items.text: Clarifying the derivation: 'if not written' logic
items.text_en: Clarifying the derivation: 'if not written' logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Talmud cites 'burn with fire' if the derivation is from 'cut down.' It explains that 'if not written' logic applies: without 'burn with fire,' 'cut down' would apply to a tree initially planted for idolatry; now that 'burn' is written, 'cut down' is available for the tree planted and later worshipped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Talmud explicitly cites the verse 'וַאֲשֵׁרֵיהֶם תִּשְׂרְפוּן בָּאֵשׁ' (burn their asherah with fire), not the verse about cutting down.

The Gemara resolves that the citation is an 'if not written' argument: without 'burn with fire,' the verse 'cut down' would apply to a tree initially planted for idolatry; now that 'burn' is written, 'cut down' is available for a tree planted and later worshipped.

items.text: The Rabbis' use of 'cut down' for the order of destruction
items.text_en: The Rabbis' use of 'cut down' for the order of destruction
items.desc_en: The Rabbis use the verse 'and you shall cut down their asherim' for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching that cutting down idolatry precedes conquest, and conquest precedes eradication. Rav Yosef's baraita and Rav Huna clarify that one must first cut down and then burn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'and you shall cut down their asherim'.
The Gemara answers that the verse is used for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching that cutting down idolatry precedes conquest, and conquest precedes eradication.
Rav Yosef's baraita supports the order by citing verses that imply one should break and leave aside, not immediately burn.
The Gemara objects that leaving aside cannot be the final step, since burning is required.
Rav Huna resolves that one must first cut down (רדוף) and then burn (שרוף), establishing the proper order of destruction.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's source for the order and the Rabbis' alternative
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's source for the order and the Rabbis' alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives the order of destruction from 'you shall surely destroy' (אַבֵּד תְּאַבְּדוּן). The Rabbis use that verse for uprooting idolatry completely. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives uprooting from 'and you shall destroy their name from that place,' while the Rabbis use that for giving it a derogatory name, citing Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derive the principle that destruction of idolatry must be done in stages (first destroy, then eliminate)?

The Gemara answers: He derives it from the verse 'אַבֵּד תְּאַבְּדוּן' (you shall surely destroy), interpreting the double language as 'destroy' first, then 'you shall destroy' — indicating a sequence.
The Gemara objects: But what do the Rabbis do with this verse? They use it to require uprooting idolatry completely (שרש אחריה).

The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derive the requirement to uproot idolatry? It answers: He derives it from the verse 'וְאִבַּדְתֶּם אֶת שְׁמָם מִן הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא' (and you shall destroy their name from that place).
The Gemara objects: But what do the Rabbis do with that verse? They use it to require giving the idolatry a derogatory name, as taught in a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that the verse 'And you shall destroy their name from that place' teaches that one must give the place a derogatory nickname. The Gemara clarifies that this is not for praise but for disgrace, and derives from another verse that one must treat it as an abomination.

items.text: Tanna's statement before Rav Sheishet about mountains and plants
items.text_en: Tanna's statement before Rav Sheishet about mountains and plants
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Sheishet that mountains and valleys worshipped by gentiles are permitted, but their worshippers are killed by the sword, while plants and vegetables are forbidden and their worshippers are killed. Rav Sheishet identifies this as the opinion of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a tree planted and later worshipped is forbidden. The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to a tree planted for worship from the start, since the Tanna compares it to a mountain, which was not planted for worship.

items.text: Dispute about stones of a mountain that became detached
items.text_en: Dispute about stones of a mountain that became detached
items.desc_en: The children of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether stones that became detached from a mountain are forbidden or permitted. One permits them by analogy to a mountain, which has no human involvement. The other objects that a mountain is attached, and a counter-analogy is made to an animal. The Gemara attempts to find a common principle but is refuted, and instead derives the law from a blemished animal and a mountain, or from a perfect animal and a dry tree.

items.text: Reason of the one who forbids
items.text_en: Reason of the one who forbids
items.desc_en: The one who forbids the stones cites the verse 'You shall utterly detest it' to argue that even if a logical derivation would permit it, one should not permit it.

items.text: Chizkiya's question about an egg erected for worship
items.text_en: Chizkiya's question about an egg erected for worship
items.desc_en: Chizkiya asks whether an egg that one erected to bow to it is forbidden. The Gemara initially assumes that the question is about the act of erecting being a significant action, implying that without erecting it is not forbidden, which supports the view that the children of Rabbi Chiya permit. However, the Gemara reinterprets the case as one where the egg was erected but not bowed to, and a gentile later bowed to it. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if an Israelite erected a brick for worship and a gentile bowed to it, it is forbidden. The question is whether an egg is different because its erection is not noticeable, and the matter remains unresolved.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about bowing to a mountain
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about bowing to a mountain
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if one bows to a mountain, what is the status of its stones for use on the altar?

items.text: Opening questions about מחובר and the status of accessories
items.text_en: Opening questions about מחובר and the status of accessories
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises two sequential questions: first, whether there is a concept of worshipping something attached to the ground for the Most High; second, if so, whether accessories of a sacrifice are considered like the sacrifice itself.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer for stringency
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer for stringency
items.desc_en: Rava proposes a kal vachomer: if a harlot's hire (אתנן) is forbidden for the altar even when detached for a common person, then surely a worshipped object, which is forbidden when detached for a common person, should be forbidden when attached for the Most High.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection with a lenient kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection with a lenient kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects by reversing the kal vachomer: if a worshipped object is permitted when attached for the Most High (based on the verse 'their gods upon the mountains'), then a harlot's hire, which is permitted when detached for a common person, should be permitted when attached for the Most High.

items.text: Alternative use of the verse 'בית ה' אלהיך'
items.text_en: Alternative use of the verse 'בית ה' אלהיך'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'בית ה' אלהיך' is needed for a different teaching: to exclude the red heifer (which does not enter the Temple), according to Rabbi Eliezer, or to include metal sheets, according to the Sages.

items.text: Rava's response: only stringent kal vachomer is refuted
items.text_en: Rava's response: only stringent kal vachomer is refuted
items.desc_en: Rava explains that he was arguing for stringency, while Rav Huna argued for leniency; the standard rule is that we refute a kal vachomer that leads to stringency, not leniency.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge from the dispute about Pesach sprinkling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge from the dispute about Pesach sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava's rule by citing a case where Rabbi Akiva refutes Rabbi Eliezer's stringent position with a lenient kal vachomer regarding Pesach sprinkling. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer had forgotten his own tradition, and Rabbi Akiva was merely reminding him.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about prostration to a wheat stack
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about prostration to a wheat stack
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if one prostrates to a stack of wheat, what is the status of the wheat for meal-offerings? Is there a concept of change (שינוי) in a worshipped object?

items.text: Mar Zutra's attempted proof from offspring of forbidden animals
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's attempted proof from offspring of forbidden animals
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman cites a Mishnah that offspring of animals forbidden to the altar are permitted, except Rabbi Eliezer forbids. Rav Nachman clarifies that the dispute is only when the animals were first violated and then became pregnant.

items.text: Two versions of the dispute about bestiality and pregnancy
items.text_en: Two versions of the dispute about bestiality and pregnancy
items.desc_en: Two versions of a dispute are presented: one where the dispute is when the animal was first mounted and then became pregnant, and another where the dispute is when it became pregnant and then was mounted. In both versions, if the animal was pregnant first and then mounted, all agree it is forbidden, and the case here (wheat ground into flour after worship) is compared to that scenario.

items.text: Objection to the comparison
items.text_en: Objection to the comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the comparison: in the case of an animal, it remains an animal throughout, only its face is changed, but here the wheat has become flour, a fundamental change.

items.text: Resh Lakish's question about a palm tree and the lulav
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's question about a palm tree and the lulav
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks: if one bows to a palm tree, is its branch (lulav) permitted for the mitzvah of lulav? The Gemara clarifies that if the tree was initially planted for idolatry, it is forbidden even for mundane use. The question is only for a tree that was planted and later worshipped. According to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, it is forbidden even for mundane use, so the question is only according to the Rabbis: is it considered repulsive for a mitzvah or not?

items.text: Rav Dimi's version: the principle of דיחוי (disqualification) regarding mitzvot
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's version: the principle of דיחוי (disqualification) regarding mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Resh Lakish's question was about an asherah that was nullified: is there a principle of דיחוי (disqualification) regarding mitzvot or not? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a mishnah about covering blood, where Rav Pappa concludes that there is no דיחוי regarding mitzvot. However, the Gemara questions whether Rav Pappa was certain of this principle or only applied it stringently, and the matter remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about bowing to an animal
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about bowing to an animal
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks: if one bows to an animal, is its wool permitted for the tekhelet (blue dye) of tzitzit? The Gemara notes that this question overlaps with earlier ones, but Rav Pappa extends it to other parts: horns for trumpets, legs for flutes, intestines for harps. The question is only according to the opinion that the main aspect of song is vocal (not instrumental), as otherwise it is certainly forbidden. The matter remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbah's question about bowing to a spring
items.text_en: Rabbah's question about bowing to a spring
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks: if one bows to a spring, are its waters permitted for libations? The Gemara clarifies that the question is whether he bows to the water itself (which flows away) or to the guardian spirit of the water. The Gemara objects that public waters cannot be forbidden, but the case is where the water wells up from the ground (private).

items.text: Mishnah: house adjacent to idolatry
items.text_en: Mishnah: house adjacent to idolatry
items.desc_en: The mishnah states: if one's house was adjacent to an idolatrous shrine and it collapsed, he is forbidden to rebuild it. Instead, he must retreat four cubits into his own property and build. The mishnah begins the discussion of the house and the shrine.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The status of an idolatrous house
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The status of an idolatrous house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a house built initially for idolatry is forbidden; if one plastered or whitewashed it for idolatry and added something, one may remove the addition; if one brought an idol in and then removed it, the house is permitted. Rabbi Akiva compares an idol to a menstruant in terms of impurity by carrying.

items.text: Gemara's question and answers about the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers about the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a house built for idolatry can be permitted if the idol is removed, since it would still benefit the owner. Rav Chanina from Sura answers that it was made into a latrine. Further objections about privacy are resolved by saying it was a night-latrine or for children, or that it was fenced with thorns.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Three types of houses
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Three types of houses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three cases: a house built initially for idolatry is forbidden; one that was plastered or whitewashed for idolatry and added something—one removes the addition; one that had an idol brought in and then removed—it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's statement on prostration to a house
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's statement on prostration to a house
items.desc_en: Rav says that one who prostrates to a house renders it forbidden, implying that detached-and-then-attached is like detached. The Gemara questions this against the Mishnah which only mentions building. It resolves that building and prostration are considered one category for nullification, so the Mishnah's three cases are actually four but counted as three.

items.text: Third Mishnah: Three types of stones
items.text_en: Third Mishnah: Three types of stones
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three cases for stones: one hewn initially for a pedestal is forbidden; one plastered or whitewashed for idolatry—one removes the addition and it is permitted; one that had an idol placed on it and then removed—it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Ammi's qualification about plastering the stone itself
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Ammi's qualification about plastering the stone itself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi says that the Mishnah's case of plastering applies only when done to the stone itself. The Gemara questions this by comparing to a house, where plastering is on the house itself and yet it is forbidden. It resolves that Rabbi Ammi's statement was about nullification: even if one plastered the stone itself, removing the addition suffices, and we might have thought the entire stone is forbidden like one hewn initially.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Three categories of asheirah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Three categories of asheirah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three types of asheirah: a tree initially planted for idolatry (forbidden), a tree that was cut and carved for idolatry and then sprouted (one takes the sprout), and a tree under which an idol was placed and later removed (permitted).

items.text: Gemara's discussion on grafting and the statement of Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on grafting and the statement of Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement from the school of Rabbi Yannai that the Mishnah's ruling about taking the sprout applies only when the branch was grafted into the tree's trunk. The Gemara initially questions this from the Mishnah's wording, then reinterprets the statement as referring to nullification, teaching that even if grafted, the sprout is permitted.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and Rabbi Elazar's objection
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and Rabbi Elazar's objection
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one bows to a tree, its offshoots are forbidden. Rabbi Elazar objects from the Mishnah, which implies that only if the tree was cut and carved for idolatry are the offshoots forbidden, but not otherwise. Shmuel deflects by identifying the Mishnah as the opinion of the Rabbis, while he follows Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda, who holds that a tree planted for secular use and later worshipped is forbidden entirely.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree about offshoots; perhaps they agree offshoots are forbidden and disagree about the tree's trunk. He explains that Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda holds the trunk is forbidden based on the verse 'and their asheirah you shall burn with fire,' while the Rabbis permit the trunk based on 'and their asheirah you shall cut down.' The Gemara then questions who authored the Mishnah's ruling about cutting and carving, concluding it cannot be either opinion as stated.

items.text: Two alternative resolutions for the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Two alternative resolutions for the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two resolutions: either the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda, who in the case of cutting and carving reveals he only wants the offshoot, not the trunk; or it follows the Rabbis, who need the case to teach that even though he performed an act on the tree itself, the trunk is not forbidden.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Defining asheirah and the story of Tzidon
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Defining asheirah and the story of Tzidon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines asheirah: according to the first Tanna, any tree under which idolatry is practiced; according to Rabbi Shimon, any tree that is actually worshipped. A story from Tzidon illustrates Rabbi Shimon's approach: a tree was worshipped, and under it was a pile of stones containing an image; Rabbi Shimon permitted the tree since the worship was directed at the image.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the second Mishnah and Rav's and Shmuel's definitions
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the second Mishnah and Rav's and Shmuel's definitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah asks 'which is asheirah' when it already listed three types, and explains that it refers to the disputed case between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. Rav defines a standard asheirah as a tree under which priests sit and do not taste its fruits; Shmuel adds that even if they say the dates are for the tax collector, it is forbidden because they use the proceeds for idolatry. Amemar reports that the elders of Pumbedita rule like Shmuel.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not sit in the shade of an asherah tree, but if one did, he remains pure; one may not pass under it, but if one did, he becomes impure. If the tree overhangs a public domain, passing under it does not impart impurity.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of sitting in the shade
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of sitting in the shade
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about sitting in the shade, noting that it is obvious. Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan explaining that the Mishnah refers to the shade of the tree's shade, not the tree itself. There are two versions of this teaching: one applied to the first clause and one to the second clause.

items.text: Reason for impurity when passing under the tree
items.text_en: Reason for impurity when passing under the tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why passing under the tree imparts impurity: it is impossible that there is no 'tikroves' (offering) of idolatry. It identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, who derives from a verse that an offering to idolatry imparts impurity in a tent, like a corpse.

items.text: Dispute about the case of a tree overhanging a public domain
items.text_en: Dispute about the case of a tree overhanging a public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in the name of Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the Mishnah's phrase: whether it means 'if he passed' (avar) or 'one who passes' (over). They are not in disagreement; it depends on whether there is an alternate path. Rav Sheishet instructs his attendant to run when passing such a tree, but the Gemara questions this, concluding that a distinguished person is different.

items.text: Second Mishnah: planting under an asherah
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: planting under an asherah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may plant vegetables under an asherah during the rainy season but not during the dry season; lettuce may not be planted at any time. Rabbi Yosei says that even vegetables may not be planted during the rainy season because the fallen leaves become fertilizer for them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute is about the principle of 'zeh vazeh gorem' (this and that cause), but notes a contradiction from another Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei permits scattering forbidden items to waste, while the Rabbis forbid it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yosei by distinguishing between cases where the item goes to waste and where it does not. For the Rabbis, it resolves by citing Rav Mari's principle that what improves the hide damages the meat; similarly, what improves the leaves damages the shade. The Gemara then questions whether Rabbi Yosei holds that 'zeh vazeh gorem' is forbidden, citing a baraita where he permits planting a sapling of orlah but not a nut, and Rav Yehudah says he agrees that if planted, it is permitted.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the ruling that if one planted, bent, or grafted a tree from a mixture of permitted and forbidden sources, it is permitted, reflecting Rabbi Yosei's view that a mixture of permitted and forbidden factors (zeh vazeh gorem) is allowed.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yosei distinguish between idolatry and other prohibitions?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yosei distinguish between idolatry and other prohibitions?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between other prohibitions and idolatry. It cites a baraita about a field fertilized with idolatrous dung and a cow fed with idolatrous beans, where one version says the field may be sown and the cow slaughtered, and another says the field must lie fallow and the cow waste away. The Gemara initially suggests that the first version is Rabbi Yosei and the second is the Rabbis, but then rejects this, attributing the dispute to Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis.

items.text: Attempt to identify the dispute with Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis of Se'or
items.text_en: Attempt to identify the dispute with Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis of Se'or
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to identify the dispute as that of Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis regarding leaven (se'or) that fell into dough. It cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer says the status follows the last ingredient, and the Rabbis say it is forbidden only if there is enough to leaven. Abaye explains that the dispute applies only if the forbidden ingredient was removed first. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is as Abaye says, or whether it is based on the principle of 'after the last I come,' which would apply regardless of removal.

items.text: Alternative identification: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis of wood
items.text_en: Alternative identification: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis of wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is that of Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis regarding wood from an asherah. It cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer says one may dispose of the benefit in the Dead Sea, and the Rabbis say there is no redemption for idolatry. This shows that Rabbi Eliezer is lenient regarding mixtures of idolatry, while the Rabbis are stringent.

items.text: Rejection of both identifications
items.text_en: Rejection of both identifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects both identifications. The Rabbis of wood are more stringent, not lenient, so they cannot be the lenient position. The Rabbis of leaven are lenient regarding leaven, but would they be lenient regarding idolatry? No, they would be stringent. Thus, neither fits.

items.text: Resolution: The dispute is between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Resolution: The dispute is between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the original attribution is correct: the lenient version is Rabbi Yosei and the stringent version is the Rabbis. Rabbi Yosei argues to the Rabbis that even according to their own view that zeh vazeh gorem is forbidden, they should concede regarding vegetables in the rainy season. The Rabbis respond as Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana said (elsewhere).

items.text: Halakhic ruling and practical application
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and practical application
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. The Gemara recounts a case where a garden was fertilized with idolatrous dung, and Rav Amram sent to Rav Yosef, who ruled in accordance with this halakha.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Wood and Shuttle from an Asherah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Wood and Shuttle from an Asherah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one takes wood from an asherah, it is forbidden for benefit; if one heats an oven with it, a new oven must be demolished, an old one cooled; bread baked in it is forbidden. If the bread gets mixed with others, all are forbidden. Rabbi Eliezer says one should cast the benefit to the Dead Sea; the Sages respond that there is no redemption for idolatry. The same applies to a shuttle used to weave a garment.

items.text: Gemara's Need for Both Cases
items.text_en: Gemara's Need for Both Cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to state both the case of wood (for bread) and the case of a shuttle: to show that Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies even where the prohibition is more direct, and that the Sages' stringency applies even where the prohibited object is absorbed. Both cases are necessary.

items.text: Ruling in Favor of Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Ruling in Favor of Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rabba bar Nachmani quotes Ze'iri that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, with an alternative version from Rav Chisda citing Abba bar Rav Chisda that Ze'iri said the same.

items.text: Dispute about a Cask of Yayin Nesech and a Case
items.text_en: Dispute about a Cask of Yayin Nesech and a Case
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah limits Rabbi Eliezer's leniency to bread, not a cask; Rav Chisda permits even a cask. The Gemara relates an incident where Rav Chisda instructed a man to throw four zuz into a river to permit his cask of Yayin Nesech mixed with his wine.

items.text: Mishnah: How to Nullify Idolatry
items.text_en: Mishnah: How to Nullify Idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the method for nullifying an idol: by cutting, carving, taking a stick or twig from it, it is nullified. If one smooths it for its own sake it remains forbidden, but for one's own sake it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Status of Shavings
items.text_en: Gemara: Status of Shavings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about shavings from smoothing an idol. Rav Huna and Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav dispute whether they are permitted. A baraisa supports the one who permits, stating that for a gentile smoothing for his own need, both the idol and shavings are permitted, but for an Israelite they are forbidden.

items.text: Dispute: Do Broken Fragments Require Nullification?
items.text_en: Dispute: Do Broken Fragments Require Nullification?
