items.desc_en: Rav says each splinter of a broken idol must be nullified; Shmuel says nullification is only through its normal form. The Gemara clarifies Shmuel's statement: an idol is only nullified through its normal growth, not when broken.

items.text: Analysis of the Dispute about Broken Idols
items.text_en: Analysis of the Dispute about Broken Idols
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to explain the dispute: whether one worships broken fragments. Two alternatives are offered: either the dispute is about secondary fragments (all agree primary fragments are forbidden), or the idol is one of links that can be reassembled, and one holds it is not nullified because it can be restored, while the other holds that nullification is only through its normal form.

items.text: Conclusion of the Perek and New Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the Perek and New Mishnah
items.desc_en: The perek concludes and a new Mishnah begins: Rabbi Yishmael says three stones next to a Merculis are forbidden, two permitted; the Sages say any stones seen with it are forbidden, those not seen are permitted.

items.text: Gemara's Analysis of Stones by a Merculis
items.text_en: Gemara's Analysis of Stones by a Merculis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' view: they hold that one worships broken fragments, so stones seen with the Merculis are forbidden (presumably fallen from it). It then challenges Rabbi Yishmael: if one worships fragments, even two should be forbidden; if one does not worship fragments, even three should be permitted.

items.text: Resolution by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Resolution by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that if it is known the stones fell from the Merculis, all agree they are forbidden; the dispute is only when it is uncertain, where one opinion holds they are not worshiped as fragments, but here the way of the idol is to break, so they are forbidden.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute: nearby stones
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute: nearby stones
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis applies only to distant stones, but for nearby stones (where one could say they fell from the merkulis), all agree they are forbidden.

items.text: Interpretation of 'alongside' and the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'alongside' and the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'alongside' means within four cubits of the merkulis. Rabbi Yishmael holds that a small merkulis is made alongside a large one, so three stones that resemble a merkulis are forbidden, but two are permitted. The Rabbis hold that no small merkulis is made, so stones that are visible with the large one are forbidden, while those not visible are permitted.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about fallen stones
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about fallen stones
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that stones that fell from a merkulis are forbidden only if visible with it, and Rabbi Yishmael says three are forbidden, two permitted. Rava resolves that the baraita refers to stones that were found, not that fell.

items.text: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Yishmael's view on two stones
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Yishmael's view on two stones
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: another baraita has Rabbi Yishmael saying two stones in his domain are forbidden, and three even distant are forbidden. Rava resolves that one case is a single domain, the other two domains separated by a height.

items.text: Clarification of the structure of a merkulis
items.text_en: Clarification of the structure of a merkulis
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a merkulis can have such a configuration, citing a baraita that describes a standard merkulis as having one stone on each side and one on top. Rava explains that baraita refers to the main merkulis.

items.text: Story of stones from a destroyed merkulis used for paving
items.text_en: Story of stones from a destroyed merkulis used for paving
items.desc_en: A story is told about the palace of King Yannai that was destroyed, and gentiles set up a merkulis there. Other gentiles who did not worship it took the stones and paved roads. Some rabbis avoided walking on them, others did not. Rabbi Yochanan criticized those who avoided, citing the precedent of Rabbi Menachem ben Rabbi Simai, who was so pious he would not even look at a coin. The reason for avoiding is a derivation from the verse about Baal Peor that offerings to idolatry have no nullification. The reason for not avoiding is that the stones are not used for idolatry in their current form.

items.text: Introduction of a baraita brought by Rabbah bar Yirmeyah
items.text_en: Introduction of a baraita brought by Rabbah bar Yirmeyah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Abba reports that Rabbah bar Yirmeyah came to their place and brought a baraita: a gentile who brought stones from a merkulis and paved roads with them... (the baraita is cut off, but it likely continues the discussion).

items.text: Gemara's question on the requirement of a breaking throw
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the requirement of a breaking throw
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how an act of throwing excrement can be considered a 'breaking throw' (זריקה משתברת) for liability, and resolves that it refers to moist excrement.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on the principle of 'similar to slaughter'
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on the principle of 'similar to slaughter'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding slaughtering a locust for idolatry hinges on whether we require 'similar to slaughter' (כעין זביחה) or 'similar to the inside' (כעין פנים). It concludes that all agree we require 'similar to the inside', but a locust is different because its neck resembles that of an animal.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on breaking vs. throwing a staff
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on breaking vs. throwing a staff
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Rav that if one breaks a staff before an idol that is worshipped with a staff, he is liable and the staff is forbidden; if he throws it, he is liable but it is not forbidden. Rava objects that throwing should also be considered 'similar to throwing', but Rav Nachman explains that we require a 'breaking throw' (זריקה משתברת), which is absent.

items.text: Discussion on the stones of Mercury and the principle of 'becoming an idol'
items.text_en: Discussion on the stones of Mercury and the principle of 'becoming an idol'
items.desc_en: Rava asks how the stones of Mercury become forbidden. Rav Nachman reports a tradition that they are considered as if one 'grows' the idol. The Gemara then questions this for those who hold that an idol is only forbidden after worship, and Rav Nachman and Rav Ashi offer explanations involving each stone becoming an offering for another.

items.text: Mishnah analysis: items found on an idol's head
items.text_en: Mishnah analysis: items found on an idol's head
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah which states that certain items found on an idol's head are forbidden because they are similar to offerings. It questions how items like grape clusters and wreaths of ears of grain can be forbidden, and Rava answers in the name of Ulla that they were initially designated for that purpose.

items.text: Derivation of exemption for blemished animals and Noahide laws
items.text_en: Derivation of exemption for blemished animals and Noahide laws
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who slaughters a blemished animal for idolatry is exempt, as only 'similar to the inside' is prohibited. Rava questions whether this applies to internal blemishes or missing limbs, leading to a discussion of Rabbi Elazar's derivation that a missing limb is forbidden for Noahides, with further analysis of verses about Noah's ark.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's derivation for slaughtering to Mercury
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's derivation for slaughtering to Mercury
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives that one who slaughters an animal to Mercury is liable from the verse 'and they shall no longer slaughter their sacrifices to the goat-demons', applying it to an atypical manner of worship. The Gemara questions the necessity of this verse, suggesting it is needed for another teaching.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verses about sacrifices at high places
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verses about sacrifices at high places
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier verses discuss sacrifices consecrated and offered during the prohibition of high places, deriving the negative commandment from 'pen'. Then it turns to sacrifices consecrated during the permitted period but offered during the prohibition, deriving both a positive and negative commandment, and concluding that there is no karet penalty.

items.text: Mishnah: Objects found on an idol's head
items.text_en: Mishnah: Objects found on an idol's head
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that money, clothing, or vessels found on an idol's head are permitted, but items like grape clusters, wreaths, wine, oil, and flour that are suitable for the altar are forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's rule from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's rule from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the distinction between ornamental and non-ornamental items from two verses: 'with them' and 'upon them'. It then addresses why money, clothing, and vessels are considered non-ornamental in specific contexts, citing explanations from the school of Rabbi Yannai and Rav Pappa.

items.text: Rav Asi bar Chiyya's rule about the 'kilklin' and its application to Peor and Merkulis
items.text_en: Rav Asi bar Chiyya's rule about the 'kilklin' and its application to Peor and Merkulis
items.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Chiyya distinguishes between items inside the temple precinct (even water and salt are forbidden) and outside (only ornamental items are forbidden). Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina notes that there is no 'kilklin' for Peor or Merkulis, and the Gemara clarifies that this means even the outside area is treated as inside and forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Benefit from an idol's garden or bathhouse
items.text_en: Mishnah: Benefit from an idol's garden or bathhouse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may benefit from an idol's garden or bathhouse without payment, but not with payment. If the property is shared with others, benefit is permitted either way. An idol of a gentile is forbidden immediately, but of a Jew only after it is worshipped.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of 'beTovah' and 'shelo beTovah'
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of 'beTovah' and 'shelo beTovah'
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that 'beTovah' refers to the benefit of the priests, and 'shelo beTovah' to non-priest benefit, excluding the benefit of worshippers which is permitted. A variant teaching applies this to the case of shared property, where 'beTovah' means benefit of others, and the Gemara explains the logic behind each version.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about when an idol is forbidden
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about when an idol is forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's ruling that a gentile's idol is forbidden immediately as following Rabbi Akiva, who reverses the positions: a gentile's idol is forbidden immediately, a Jew's only after worship. Rabbi Yishmael holds the opposite. The Gemara then questions the derivation from the verse about 'places' and explains that it refers to vessels used for idolatry.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gentile's idol is forbidden only after it has been worshipped, while an Israelite's idol is forbidden immediately upon being made.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gentile's idol is forbidden only after it has been worshipped, while an Israelite's idol is forbidden immediately upon being made.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's rule is derived from the verse, and explains that Rabbi Yishmael likens idols to vessels, both requiring worship to become forbidden. Rabbi Akiva disagrees because the word 'et' interrupts the comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's rule is derived from the verse, and explains that Rabbi Yishmael likens idols to vessels, both requiring worship to become forbidden. Rabbi Akiva disagrees because the word 'et' interrupts the comparison.

items.text: Deriving Israelite idol's immediate prohibition
items.text_en: Deriving Israelite idol's immediate prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yishmael knows that an Israelite's idol is forbidden immediately. It suggests a logical inference from the gentile's case, but then raises objections that perhaps it is not forbidden at all. The Gemara cites verses: the golden calf shows sin from the moment of making, 'cursed is the man who makes a graven image' shows a curse from making, and 'it is an abomination to the Lord' shows it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since Rabbi Yishmael has a source that a gentile's idol is not forbidden until worshipped, from where does he derive that an Israelite's idol is forbidden immediately?
The Gemara objects: Why not say that an Israelite's idol is not forbidden at all? The Gemara answers that since it requires interment, it must be forbidden.

The Gemara objects: Perhaps an Israelite's idol is forbidden only when worshipped, like a gentile's. The Gemara answers by citing the verse about the golden calf, showing sin from the moment of making.

The Gemara objects: That verse only makes the person liable for sin, but does not forbid the object. The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'cursed is the man who makes a graven image', showing a curse from the moment of making.

The Gemara objects: That verse only makes the person liable to be cursed, but does not forbid the object. The Gemara answers by citing 'it is an abomination to the Lord', showing the object itself is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of 'abomination'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of 'abomination'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets 'abomination' as something that leads to abomination, not the idol itself being an abomination immediately.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets the term 'abomination' in the verse as referring to an object that leads to abomination, not the idol itself being an abomination immediately upon creation.

items.text: Deriving gentile idol's immediate prohibition for Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Deriving gentile idol's immediate prohibition for Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva knows that a gentile's idol is forbidden immediately. Ulla cites the verse 'the graven images of their gods you shall burn with fire' — from the moment it is graven it becomes a god. The other opinion (Rabbi Yishmael) uses that verse to teach that a gentile who carves an idol makes it forbidden, and another derivation from Shmuel distinguishes between carving for a god (forbidden) and carving from a god (permitted).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Akiva derive that a gentile's object of idol worship is prohibited immediately?

Ulla cites the verse 'פְּסִילֵי אֱלֹהֵיהֶם תִּשְׂרְפוּן בָּאֵשׁ' (the graven images of their gods you shall burn with fire) to show that from the moment it is graven it becomes a god and is forbidden.
The other opinion (Rabbi Yishmael) requires that verse for the teaching of Rabbi Yosef: from where is it derived that a gentile may revoke the status of his god? From the same verse.

The other opinion (Rabbi Akiva) derives from Shmuel's resolution of the contradiction in the verse: if the gentile carved it for a god, 'you shall not covet' applies; if he revoked its status as a god, 'and take it for yourself' applies.

items.text: Deriving Israelite idol's delayed prohibition for Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Deriving Israelite idol's delayed prohibition for Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva knows that an Israelite's idol is forbidden only after worship. Rav Yehuda cites the verse 'and puts it in secret' — until he does secret things (worship). The other opinion uses that verse to teach that an Israelite's idol requires burial. Another derivation from Rav Chisda citing Rav compares it to an asherah near the altar, requiring burial. Resh Lakish uses the same verse to teach that appointing an unfit judge is like planting an asherah, and Rav Ashi adds that in a place of Torah scholars it is like planting near the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva derives that an Israelite's idol is forbidden only after worship.
Rav Yehuda cites the verse 'וְשָׂם בַּסָּתֶר' (and puts it in secret) to show that the idol is forbidden only after secret rites are performed.
Rabbi Yitzchak uses the same verse to derive that an Israelite's idol requires burial (גניזה).
Rav Chisda citing Rav derives the requirement of burial for an Israelite's idol from a comparison of an asherah to an altar, both requiring burial.
Resh Lakish uses the verse about planting an asherah to teach that appointing an unfit judge is like planting an asherah among Israel.
Rav Ashi adds that in a place of Torah scholars, appointing an unfit judge is like planting an asherah next to the altar.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's question about repairing a vessel for an idol
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's question about repairing a vessel for an idol
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks about the status of a vessel that was repaired for an idol. The Gemara clarifies that the question is about an Israelite's idol according to Rabbi Yishmael (who says the idol itself is forbidden immediately). The question is whether the accessories follow the idol (forbidden immediately) or follow the general rule for accessories (forbidden only after worship). The Gemara then explains that Rav Hamnuna's question is actually about whether a repaired vessel returns to its previous impurity status (טומאה ישנה) for rabbinic impurity, and whether the impurity of idolatry is treated as biblical or rabbinic. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks about the status of a vessel welded for idol worship; the Gemara clarifies the question concerns an Israelite's idol.
The Gemara asks which opinion Rav Hamnuna follows, and determines it must be Rabbi Yishmael, who says a Jew's idol is forbidden immediately.
The Gemara asks whether accessories of a Jew's idol follow the rule of gentile accessories (forbidden only after worship) or the rule of the idol itself (forbidden immediately).
The Gemara objects that if the question is about accessories, why specify welding a broken vessel rather than making a new one.
The Gemara explains that Rav Hamnuna's question is about whether a repaired vessel reassumes its previous impurity (טומאה ישנה), citing a mishna about metal vessels.
The Gemara asks whether the reassumption of impurity applies only to Torah impurity or also to rabbinic impurity, and why the question is specific to idolatry.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Hamnuna raises two nested dilemmas: whether rabbinic impurity is reassumed, and if not, whether the Sages treated idolatry impurity as Torah-level; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question about nullifying impurity of idolatrous food
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question about nullifying impurity of idolatrous food
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether the nullification of an idol also purifies the food offerings from their impurity. The Gemara clarifies that the question is specifically about food, not vessels (which can be purified in a mikveh) or the idol itself (which is not subject to impurity nullification).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether nullifying an idol also purifies the food offerings from their impurity.
The Gemara explains that the question is specifically about food, not vessels, because vessels can be purified in a mikveh.
The Gemara adds that the question does not apply to the idol itself, as it is not subject to impurity nullification.

items.text: Unresolved question about nullification of impurity for idolatrous offerings
items.text_en: Unresolved question about nullification of impurity for idolatrous offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether the impurity of idolatrous offerings is nullified along with their prohibition, given that the prohibition is not nullified (as per Rav Giddel). The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Question about utensils from the Temple of Onias
items.text_en: Question about utensils from the Temple of Onias
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks Rabbi whether utensils used in the Temple of Onias may be used in the Jerusalem Temple. The question assumes the view that the Temple of Onias is not considered idolatry. Rabbi responds that they are forbidden, and that they once knew a verse but forgot it.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding King Ahaz's utensils
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding King Ahaz's utensils
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse about King Ahaz's utensils, which were 'prepared' and 'sanctified.' Rabbi explains that 'prepared' means they were stored away, and 'sanctified' means they sanctified other utensils in their place.

items.text: Support from the Hasmonean storage of altar stones and Rav Pappa's distinction
items.text_en: Support from the Hasmonean storage of altar stones and Rav Pappa's distinction
items.desc_en: A support is brought from the Hasmoneans who stored the stones of the altar defiled by the Greeks. Rav Pappa explains that they found a verse permitting this. The Gemara discusses why they did not break the stones, and Abaye explains a similar case with coins. The section concludes with a distinction: utensils used for the Most High should not be used for common purposes.

items.text: Mishnah: Nullification of idolatry by a gentile
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nullification of idolatry by a gentile
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a gentile can nullify his own idol and that of his fellow, but a Jew cannot nullify a gentile's idol. Nullifying an idol nullifies its accessories, but nullifying accessories leaves the idol itself forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi about a gentile nullifying a Jew's idol
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi about a gentile nullifying a Jew's idol
items.desc_en: Rabbi taught Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi that a gentile nullifies his own idol and that of his fellow. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi objects, citing the verse 'and placed in secret' to argue that a Jew's idol cannot be nullified. Rabbi Hillel bar Voles explains that the case involves partnership. The Gemara then analyzes Rabbi's change of view between youth and old age, and presents an alternative version of the dispute.

items.text: Two versions of Rabbi Hillel b. Rabbi Vallas' statement
items.text_en: Two versions of Rabbi Hillel b. Rabbi Vallas' statement
items.desc_en: Two alternative formulations of Rabbi Hillel b. Rabbi Vallas' explanation of the baraita: one attached to the Mishnah and one to the baraita itself. Both clarify that the baraita refers to a case where a gentile has a share in the idol, teaching that a Jew cannot nullify the gentile's share, but a gentile can nullify his own share.

items.text: Mishnah: How to nullify an idol
items.text_en: Mishnah: How to nullify an idol
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions that nullify an idol (cutting its ear, nose, finger, or damaging it even without removing a piece) and actions that do not (spitting, urinating, dragging, throwing excrement). It also records a dispute: Rabbi says selling or mortgaging an idol nullifies it, while the Sages say it does not.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'damaged it without removing a piece'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'damaged it without removing a piece'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the idol was not physically diminished, how was it nullified? Rav Zeira answers: by damaging it in its presence (i.e., striking it before the idol itself).

items.text: Source for spitting and urinating not nullifying
items.text_en: Source for spitting and urinating not nullifying
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that spitting and urinating do not nullify an idol. Chizkiyah cites a verse from Isaiah: even one who curses his king and god and looks upward (to heaven) still looks to the earth, implying that such contemptuous acts do not constitute nullification.

items.text: Dispute over the scope of the Mishnah's debate
items.text_en: Dispute over the scope of the Mishnah's debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between two Amoraim (one citing Rabbi Yochanan, the other citing Rav) about the scope of the Mishnah's debate: one says the dispute is only when selling to a gentile craftsman, but when selling to a Jewish craftsman all agree it is nullified; the other says even when selling to a Jewish craftsman there is a dispute.

items.text: Clarifying the two opinions
items.text_en: Clarifying the two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma: does the second opinion mean that the dispute is only when selling to a Jewish craftsman (but all agree it is not nullified when sold to a gentile craftsman), or does it mean that the dispute applies in both cases?

items.text: Resolution from Rabbi's statement about selling for destruction vs. worship
items.text_en: Resolution from Rabbi's statement about selling for destruction vs. worship
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from Rabbi's statement that his words apply when selling for destruction (to a Jewish craftsman) and the Sages' words apply when selling for worship (to a gentile craftsman). After initial confusion, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi meant his colleagues agree with him when selling for destruction, implying the dispute is only when selling for worship, thus the second opinion is that the dispute applies in both cases.

items.text: Challenge from the law of purchasing metal scraps
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of purchasing metal scraps
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution with a baraita about one who buys metal scraps from gentiles and finds an idol: if he pulled before paying, he returns it; if after paying, he must discard it. This implies that selling to a Jewish craftsman does not nullify the idol, contradicting the view that all agree it is nullified. The Gemara deflects by saying the case is different because the buyer intended to buy scraps, not the idol.

items.text: Baraita: Other cases of nullification
items.text_en: Baraita: Other cases of nullification
items.desc_en: A baraita lists additional cases: if one borrowed money on the idol, or a pile fell on it, or bandits stole it, or the owners abandoned it and went overseas—these do not nullify the idol.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases of abandonment
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases of abandonment
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needs to list three separate cases (borrowed money, collapse, theft) to teach that in each case the idol is not nullified, because each case might otherwise have been thought to imply nullification. It concludes that only when the owners leave for a distant land without taking the idol is it nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the owners are expected to return, as in the war of Joshua, the idol is not nullified.
The Gemara explains that the case of borrowing money on the idol is necessary, because otherwise one might think that not selling it implies nullification.
The Gemara explains that the case of a collapse is necessary, because otherwise one might think that not clearing the debris implies nullification.
The Gemara explains that the case of theft is necessary, because otherwise one might think that not searching for the idol implies nullification.

items.text: Clarification of the comparison to the war of Joshua
items.text_en: Clarification of the comparison to the war of Joshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the comparison to the war of Joshua, noting that the Israelites did return after that war. It explains that the Mishnah means: if the owners are expected to return, it is like the war of Joshua and the idol has no nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the comparison to the war of Joshua, noting that the Israelites did return after that war.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means: if the owners are expected to return, it is like the war of Joshua and the idol has no nullification.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching about an Israelite who erects a brick for idolatry
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching about an Israelite who erects a brick for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah incidentally teaches a principle: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that if an Israelite erects a brick intending to bow to it, and a gentile comes and bows to it, the brick becomes forbidden as an idol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to compare the case to the war of Joshua, and answers that it incidentally teaches a principle.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that if an Israelite erects a brick intending to bow to it, and a gentile comes and bows to it, the brick becomes forbidden as an idol.

items.text: Proof and discussion of the principle from the sin of the Golden Calf
items.text_en: Proof and discussion of the principle from the sin of the Golden Calf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives the principle from the conquest of the Land of Israel, where the Canaanite idols were forbidden even though they were not owned by the Israelites. The Gemara explains that the Israelites' worship of the Golden Calf revealed their desire for idolatry, so the gentiles acted as their agents. It then addresses objections about whether this applies only to the Calf and whether later idols should be permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the idol is forbidden in the case of an Israelite who set up a brick for worship and a gentile bowed to it?

Rabbi Elazar answers by analogy to the initial conquest of the Land of Israel, where the Torah commanded to burn the Canaanite asherahs even though they were not yet owned by the Israelites, showing that a gentile can forbid an object not owned by the Israelite.
The Gemara objects: regarding those original Canaanite idols, mere nullification (ביטול) would have sufficed for the Israelites to permit them, so why was burning necessary?

The Gemara answers: because the Israelites worshipped the Golden Calf, they revealed their desire for idolatry, so the gentiles who later bowed to the Canaanite idols acted as their agents, making the idols forbidden.

The Gemara objects: perhaps the Israelites desired only the Calf itself, not other forms of idolatry; the Gemara answers with the verse 'אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל' (These are your gods, O Israel), which teaches that they desired many gods.

The Gemara objects: perhaps only idols that existed at the time of the Calf were forbidden, but later idols should be permitted; the Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'מַאן מוֹכַח?' (who can prove?).

items.text: Mishnah: Idols abandoned in peace vs. war, and royal bimos
items.text_en: Mishnah: Idols abandoned in peace vs. war, and royal bimos
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an idol abandoned by its worshippers is permitted in peacetime but forbidden in wartime. Royal platforms (bimos) are permitted because they are set up for kings to pass by.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that an idol abandoned by its worshippers is permitted in peacetime but forbidden in wartime, and that royal platforms (bimos) are permitted because they are set up for kings to pass by.

items.text: Rav's ruling on the house of Nimrod
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on the house of Nimrod
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the house of Nimrod is like an idol abandoned in peacetime and is permitted, because although the Canaanites could have returned, they did not, indicating abandonment.

sub.text: Rav via Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav via Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the house of Nimrod is like an idol abandoned in peacetime and is permitted, because although the Canaanites could have returned, they did not, indicating abandonment.

items.text: Explanation of why royal bimos are permitted
items.text_en: Explanation of why royal bimos are permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why royal bimos are permitted just because they are set up for kings. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah means they are set up for kings, but the kings take a different route, so the platforms are effectively abandoned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits royal bimos merely because they are set up when kings pass by.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah means the platforms are set up for kings, but the kings take a different route, so the platforms are effectively abandoned and permitted.

items.text: Dispute about a damaged bimos and a baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute about a damaged bimos and a baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Ulla sits on a damaged bimos, and Rav Yehuda objects citing Rav and Shmuel that a damaged bimos is forbidden. Ulla responds citing Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish that it is permitted. A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, distinguishing between a bimos (single stone) and a mizbeach (many stones).

sub.desc_en: Ulla arrives and sits on a damaged bimos (platform).
Rav Yehuda objects to Ulla, citing Rav and Shmuel that a damaged bimos is forbidden, even for those who hold that broken pieces are not worshipped, because this platform is not degraded.

Ulla dismisses Rav and Shmuel's authority and cites Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish that a damaged bimos is permitted, even for those who hold that broken pieces are worshipped, because the worshippers would replace it with another bimos.

A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, distinguishing between a bimos (single stone) which is permitted when damaged, and a mizbeach (many stones) which is forbidden until most of it is demolished, as explained by Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Hezekiah's biblical prooftext
items.text_en: Hezekiah's biblical prooftext
items.desc_en: Hezekiah cites a verse (Isaiah 36:19) to argue that if an altar's stones are crushed like lime, then the asherah and incense altars will not be rebuilt; otherwise they will. This establishes the principle that only deliberate destruction prevents revival of idolatrous objects.

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah cites a verse (Isaiah 36:19) to argue that only deliberate destruction of an idolatrous altar prevents its revival, establishing the principle for idolatrous objects.

items.text: Tanna on one's own vs. another's idolatrous animal
items.text_en: Tanna on one's own vs. another's idolatrous animal
items.desc_en: A tanna teaches: an animal that is one's own and was worshiped is forbidden, whereas another's animal that was worshiped is permitted. A contradiction is raised from a beraita that defines a worshiped animal as one that is served either unwittingly or intentionally, under duress or willingly — prompting the question of what constitutes duress.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states the rule: an animal that is one's own and was worshiped is forbidden, but another's animal that was worshiped is permitted.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a beraita that defines a worshiped animal broadly, including cases of duress, which seems to conflict with the Tanna's distinction.
The Gemara asks what constitutes duress in this context, suggesting it might be when one forces another's animal and bows to it.

items.text: Rami bar Hama and Rabbi Zeira's objection
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama and Rabbi Zeira's objection
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama answers that duress refers to gentiles forcing him to bow to his own animal. Rabbi Zeira objects: the Torah exempts a victim of coercion, as per the verse about the betrothed maiden (Deuteronomy 22:26), so why would the animal be forbidden?

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama answers that the case of duress in the baraita refers to gentiles forcing him to bow to his own animal.
Rabbi Zeira objects that the Torah exempts a victim of coercion, citing the verse about the betrothed maiden (Deuteronomy 22:26), so why would the animal be forbidden?

items.text: Rava's resolution: private vs. public
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: private vs. public
items.desc_en: Rava explains: all forms of worship were included in the prohibition 'you shall not serve them,' but the verse 'and live by them' (Leviticus 18:5) excludes coercion (you may violate to save your life). The verse 'you shall not profane My holy name' (Leviticus 22:32) reinstates the prohibition for public contexts. Thus, in private, an act under duress does not forbid the animal; in public, it does forbid.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that all forms of worship were included in the prohibition 'you shall not serve them,' but the verse 'and live by them' (Leviticus 18:5) excludes coercion (you may violate to save your life).

Rava adds that the verse 'you shall not profane My holy name' (Leviticus 22:32) reinstates the prohibition for public contexts, so in private an act under duress does not forbid the animal, but in public it does forbid.

items.text: Supporting beraita about imperial statues and Rav Ashi's retort
items.text_en: Supporting beraita about imperial statues and Rav Ashi's retort
items.desc_en: The rabbis cite a beraita about gentile imperial statues during a religious persecution: even after the persecution ends, those statues remain forbidden. Initially offered in support of Rava, Rav Ashi clarifies that it is no support because the Israelite worshiper was a willing apostate.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis cite a beraita about gentile imperial statues during a religious persecution that remain forbidden even after the persecution ends, offering it as support for Rava's position.
Rava rejects the support, arguing that the case involves a Jewish apostate who worshipped willingly, not an unwilling worshiper.
Rav Ashi strengthens Rava's rejection, asserting definitively that the worshiper was indeed a Jewish apostate who acted willingly, not merely a possibility.

items.text: Hezekiah's alternative: libation on the horns
items.text_en: Hezekiah's alternative: libation on the horns
items.desc_en: Hezekiah explains the tanna's case as one who poured wine for idolatry onto the animal's horns. Rabbi Adda bar Ahava objects that this is merely a temporary pedestal (bimos), not an actual act of worship rendering the animal forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah proposes that the tanna's case involves one who poured wine for idolatry onto the animal's horns.
Rabbi Adda bar Ahava objects that this is merely a temporary pedestal (בימוס), not an actual act of worship rendering the animal forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Adda bar Ahava and Rabbi Yochanan: performing an act on the animal
items.text_en: Rabbi Adda bar Ahava and Rabbi Yochanan: performing an act on the animal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Adda bar Ahava explains the case as one who poured wine between the animal's horns, performing a physical act (ma'aseh) on it. He cites Rabbi Yochanan: bowing to another's animal does not forbid it, but performing an act upon it does forbid it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Adda bar Ahava redefines the case as one who poured wine between the animal's horns, thereby performing a physical act (מעשה) on it.
Rabbi Adda bar Ahava cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: bowing to another's animal does not forbid it, but performing an act upon it does forbid it.

items.text: Rav Nachman's message and the quest for the source
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's message and the quest for the source
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman tells them to inform Ulla that Rav Huna in Babylonia interpreted his statement: if another's animal was lying before an idol, slaughtering even one siman (sign of kosher slaughter) forbids it. The Gemara then questions the source of this ruling, considering whether it is derived from priests or from altar stones, but each suggestion is problematic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs them to tell Ulla that Rav Huna in Babylonia interpreted his statement: if another's animal was lying before an idol, slaughtering even one siman (sign of kosher slaughter) forbids it.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that slaughtering one siman forbids the animal?
The Gemara objects: perhaps the case of priests is different because they are intelligent and act with intent.
The Gemara alternatively suggests deriving the ruling from the altar stones, but then objects that it might be like Rav Pappa's case.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding King Ahaz's vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding King Ahaz's vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of King Ahaz's vessels cannot prove that an act of worship prohibits an object, since the vessels were not his to forbid. It resolves that once he performed an act (worship) with them, they became forbidden; similarly, once one performs an act with an animal, it becomes forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of King Ahaz's vessels cannot prove that an act of worship prohibits an object, since the vessels were not his to forbid.
The Gemara resolves that once he performed an act of worship with the vessels, they became forbidden; similarly, once one performs an act with an animal, it becomes forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's rulings on bowing and exchanging
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's rulings on bowing and exchanging
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that bowing to the ground does not forbid it, but digging pits in it does; bowing to animals does not forbid them, but exchanging them for an idol does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that bowing to the ground does not forbid it, but digging pits in it does.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan further rules that bowing to animals does not forbid them, but exchanging them for an idol does.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis on exchanges
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis on exchanges
items.desc_en: There is a dispute: one says that an exchange for an idol is forbidden but an exchange of that exchange is permitted; the other says even the exchange of the exchange is forbidden. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for the stricter opinion, citing the verse 'and you shall be a cherem like it'.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis: one permits the exchange of an exchange, the other forbids even that.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the stricter opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the stricter opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the stricter opinion's scriptural basis: the verse 'וְהָיִיתָ חֵרֶם כָּמֹהוּ' (and you shall be a cherem like it) teaches that anything derived from it is like it.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the lenient opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the lenient opinion
sub.desc_en: The lenient opinion derives from the word 'הוּא' (it) in the verse, limiting the prohibition to the idol itself and not its exchanges.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the lenient opinion and the status of orlah and kilayim
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the lenient opinion and the status of orlah and kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the lenient opinion uses the word 'hu' to exclude orlah and kilayim from the law of exchanges. The stricter opinion counters that orlah and kilayim do not need a special exclusion because they are derived from two verses that come as one (avodah zarah and shevi'it), and such verses do not teach by analogy. The Gemara then analyzes the derivation for shevi'it and concludes that the stricter opinion holds that two verses that come as one do teach, so 'hu' is needed to exclude orlah and kilayim.

sub.text: Stam (anonymous explanation of the lenient opinion)
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous explanation of the lenient opinion)
sub.desc_en: The lenient opinion explains that the word 'הוּא' (it) in the verse is needed to exclude orlah and kilayim of the vineyard from the law of exchanges, so that if one sells them and uses the proceeds for betrothal, the betrothal is valid.

sub.text: Stam (anonymous objection of the stricter opinion)
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous objection of the stricter opinion)
sub.desc_en: The stricter opinion objects that orlah and kilayim do not need a special exclusion, because they are derived from two verses that come as one (avodah zarah and shevi'it), and such verses do not teach by analogy.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the derivation for shevi'it
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the derivation for shevi'it
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the derivation for shevi'it: just as קֹדֶשׁ (sacred property) takes effect on its redemption money and is forbidden, so too shevi'it takes effect on its money and is forbidden; the verse 'תִּהְיֶה' (it shall be) teaches that it remains in its original state and does not become חוּלִּין (non-sacred).

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the shevi'it exchange rule
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the shevi'it exchange rule
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates the practical rule of shevi'it exchanges: the last item purchased is consecrated with shevi'it sanctity, and the original fruit itself remains forbidden.
The stricter opinion holds that two verses that come as one do teach by analogy, so the word 'הוּא' is indeed needed to exclude orlah and kilayim.

items.text: Mishnah: Dialogue with the elders in Rome
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dialogue with the elders in Rome
items.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that the elders in Rome were asked: if God does not desire idolatry, why does He not destroy it? They answered: if people worshipped something unnecessary, He would destroy it, but they worship the sun, moon, stars, and constellations—should He destroy the world because of fools? The questioners countered: then let Him destroy what is unnecessary and leave what is necessary. The elders replied: that would strengthen the idolaters' claim that their gods are real, since they were not destroyed.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask the elders in Rome: if God does not desire idolatry, why does He not destroy it?

The elders answer that if people worshipped something unnecessary, God would destroy it, but since they worship the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, He would not destroy the world because of fools.
The questioners counter: then let God destroy what is unnecessary and leave what is necessary.
The elders answer that destroying only the unnecessary would strengthen the idolaters' claim that their gods are real, since they were not destroyed.

items.text: Gemara: Expanded version of the dialogue and Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Gemara: Expanded version of the dialogue and Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a fuller version of the dialogue, adding that the world continues its course and fools will be punished. It gives two additional analogies: a stolen wheat that grows, and adultery that results in pregnancy. Resh Lakish concludes that God says: not only do the wicked make My coin into a public latrine, but they trouble Me and force Me to seal it against My will.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the philosophers' question to the elders in Rome: if God does not want idolatry, why does He not destroy it?
The elders answer that the world continues its course, and fools who corrupted will be punished.
The baraita gives a second analogy: a stolen se'ah of wheat that is sown and grows, yet the world continues normally.
The baraita gives a third analogy: one who commits adultery with another's wife, yet she becomes pregnant, and the world continues.
Resh Lakish concludes that God says: not only do the wicked make My coin into a public latrine, but they trouble Me and force Me to seal it against My will.

items.text: Dialogue between a philosopher and Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Dialogue between a philosopher and Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: A philosopher asks Rabban Gamliel why God is jealous of idolaters but not of the idol itself. Rabban Gamliel gives a parable of a king whose son named a dog after his father; the king is angry at the son, not the dog. The philosopher objects that the idol has substance, citing a fire that spared an idolatrous temple. Rabban Gamliel gives another parable: a king at war fights the living, not the dead. The philosopher then asks why God does not destroy the idol; Rabban Gamliel answers that if people worshipped something unnecessary, He would, but they worship the sun, moon, etc.—should He destroy the world because of fools?

sub.desc_en: A philosopher asks Rabban Gamliel why God is jealous of idolaters but not of the idol itself, citing the verse 'כִּי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה הוּא אֵל קַנָּא'.
Rabban Gamliel gives a parable of a king whose son named a dog after his father; the king is angry at the son, not the dog, to show God's jealousy is directed at the worshippers, not the idol.
The philosopher objects that the idol has substance (ממש), citing a fire that spared an idolatrous temple while burning the rest of the city.
Rabban Gamliel gives another parable: a king at war fights the living, not the dead, to explain that God does not destroy the idol because it is lifeless.
The philosopher asks why God does not destroy the idol if it is worthless like a dog or dead.
Rabban Gamliel answers that if people worshipped something unnecessary, God would destroy it, but they worship the sun, moon, stars, and streams—should He destroy the world because of fools?

items.text: Opening question on God's destruction of idolatry
items.text_en: Opening question on God's destruction of idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why God would destroy idols if they are merely objects of worship for the wicked, citing verses from Zephaniah and Genesis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why God would destroy idols if they are merely objects of worship for the wicked, citing verses from Zephaniah and Genesis.

items.text: Agrippas questions Rabban Gamliel about God's jealousy
items.text_en: Agrippas questions Rabban Gamliel about God's jealousy
items.desc_en: Agrippas asks why God would be jealous of idols, since jealousy is only between equals. Rabban Gamliel responds with a parable of a man who marries a second wife, showing that jealousy is toward a lesser rival.

sub.desc_en: Agrippas asks Rabban Gamliel why God is described as a jealous God, since jealousy only occurs between equals.
Rabban Gamliel answers with a parable: a man who marries a second wife is only jealous of a lesser wife, not a greater one, explaining God's jealousy toward idols as inferior rivals.

items.text: Zunin questions Rabbi Akiva about idolatry's apparent power
items.text_en: Zunin questions Rabbi Akiva about idolatry's apparent power
items.desc_en: Zunin observes that people who go to idolatry return healthy, implying it has power. Rabbi Akiva explains with a parable of a faithful trustee and oaths: afflictions are sworn to leave at a specific time, and even if the person goes to idolatry, the afflictions do not break their oath.

sub.desc_en: Zunin asks Rabbi Akiva: since we both know idolatry has no substance, why do we see people who go to it broken return healthy?

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's parable of the faithful trustee
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's parable of the faithful trustee
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva answers with a parable: a faithful trustee does not break his oath even when a foolish depositor acts improperly.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's application of the parable to afflictions
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's application of the parable to afflictions
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva applies the parable: afflictions are sworn to leave at a fixed time and do not break their oath even if the person goes to idolatry.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of faithful afflictions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of faithful afflictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'evil and faithful afflictions' as afflictions that are evil in their mission but faithful to their oath.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'חֳלָיִם רָעִים וְנֶאֱמָנִים' (evil and faithful diseases) to mean they are evil in their mission but faithful to their oath.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak questions Rav Yehuda about idolatry bringing rain
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak questions Rav Yehuda about idolatry bringing rain
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak notes that in his place, idolatry appears in dreams and commands human sacrifice, which brings rain. Rav Yehuda responds that God 'smooths over' idolaters with words to drive them from the world, citing Rav's teaching.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak asks Rav Yehuda about an idolatrous practice in his place where a dream commands human sacrifice to bring rain, and it actually works.
Rav Yehuda responds that God 'smooths over' idolaters with words to drive them from the world, citing Rav's teaching on the verse 'which the Lord your God has allotted to all the peoples'.

items.text: Resh Lakish's principle of divine assistance
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's principle of divine assistance
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains the verse 'If to scoffers He scoffs, but to the humble He gives grace' as meaning that one who comes to defile is given an opening, but one who comes to purify is assisted.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains the verse 'אִם לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ' to mean that one who comes to defile themselves is given an opening, but one who comes to purify is assisted.

items.text: Mishnah: Purchasing a winepress from a non-Jew
items.text_en: Mishnah: Purchasing a winepress from a non-Jew
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may buy a trodden winepress from a non-Jew, even if the non-Jew handles the grapes, because wine becomes forbidden only once it flows into the pit. If it has entered the pit, only the wine in the pit is forbidden, and the rest is permitted. One may also tread grapes with a non-Jew in the press.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may buy a trodden winepress from a non-Jew, and wine becomes forbidden only once it flows into the pit; if it entered the pit, only that wine is forbidden.
The Mishnah adds that one may tread grapes together with a non-Jew in the press.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not press grapes or tread with a non-Jew, nor with a Jew who works in impurity, but one may transport barrels to the vat and bring bread to the bakery.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not press grapes or tread with a non-Jew, nor with a Jew who works in impurity, but one may transport barrels to the vat and bring bread from the vat.
The Mishnah adds that with a baker who works in impurity, one may not knead or arrange dough, but may transport bread to the bakery.

items.text: Rav Huna's principle and first challenge
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle and first challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that wine becomes yayin nesekh as soon as it begins to flow. The Gemara challenges this from the Mishnah which permits buying a pressed vat from a non-Jew even if he placed grapes into the heap, implying the wine is not yet forbidden. Rav Huna answers that the case is a sealed and full vat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that wine becomes יין נסך (wine used for libation) as soon as it begins to flow from the grapes.
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah which permits buying a pressed vat from a non-Jew even if he placed grapes into the heap, implying the wine is not yet forbidden.
Rav Huna answers that the Mishnah's case is a sealed and full vat, where the wine does not flow out.

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that wine does not become yayin nesekh until it reaches the pit, contradicting Rav Huna. Again, Rav Huna answers that the case is a sealed and full vat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that wine does not become יין נסך until it descends into the pit, contradicting Rav Huna's principle.
The Gemara resolves that this baraita also refers to a sealed and full vat, where the wine does not flow.

items.text: Third challenge and resolution with earlier and later Mishnah
items.text_en: Third challenge and resolution with earlier and later Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that if wine descended to the pit, only the wine in the pit is forbidden, but the rest is permitted. Rav Huna resolves this by distinguishing between an earlier Mishnah (which did not accept his view) and a later Mishnah (which did).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between wine that descended into the pit (forbidden) and the rest (permitted), implying that flowing wine is not yet forbidden.
Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an earlier version of the Mishnah (which did not forbid flowing wine) and a later version (which did).

items.text: Baraita explaining the earlier and later rulings
items.text_en: Baraita explaining the earlier and later rulings
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: initially, the Sages said one may not press grapes with a non-Jew (due to causing impurity to chullin) and not tread with a Jew who works in impurity (due to assisting transgressors), but they permitted treading with a non-Jew, not concerned for Rav Huna's principle. Later, they ruled that one may not tread with a non-Jew because of Rav Huna's principle.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the earlier ruling: one may not press grapes with a non-Jew (due to causing טומאה (impurity) to חולין (non-sacred produce)) and not tread with a Jew who works in impurity (due to assisting transgressors), but they permitted treading with a non-Jew, not concerned for Rav Huna's principle.
The baraita concludes with the later ruling: one may not tread with a non-Jew in the vat, because of Rav Huna's principle that wine becomes יין נסך (libation wine) once it begins to flow.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not harvest grapes with a Jew who makes his produce impure, but may harvest with a non-Jew in the winepress, as it is permitted to cause impurity to חולין in the Land of Israel. It also states that wine does not become yayin nesekh until it descends into the pit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not harvest grapes with a Jew who makes his produce impure, but may harvest with a non-Jew in the winepress, as it is permitted to cause impurity to חולין (non-sacred produce) in the Land of Israel, and wine does not become יין נסך (wine used for idolatrous libation) until it descends into the pit.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that wine becomes yayin nesekh when it forms a crust (יקַפֶּה), not when it descends into the pit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah by citing a baraita that says wine becomes יין נסך (libation wine) from the time it forms a scum (קיפוי), not from when it descends into the pit.

items.text: Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to the Rabbis and the baraita to Rabbi Akiva, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva says wine becomes yayin nesekh when it forms a crust, while the Rabbis say when it descends into the pit.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah's view to the Sages (רבנן) and the baraita's view to Rabbi Akiva, citing a Tosefta where Rabbi Akiva says wine becomes יין נסך from the time it forms a scum (קיפוי).

items.text: Clarifying the crust
items.text_en: Clarifying the crust
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the crust refers to that of the pit or of the barrel. It brings a baraita to prove that it is the crust of the pit, as the baraita allows drinking from the upper vat and pipe even after the crust has formed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the term קיפוי (crust) in the Mishnah refers to the crust of the pit or the crust of the barrel.
The Gemara brings a baraita that states wine becomes forbidden for libation only when it forms a crust, yet one may still drink from the upper vat and pipe, implying the crust is that of the pit.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that the crust in question is indeed that of the pit.

items.text: Another baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Another baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rav Zevid's academy states that wine becomes yayin nesekh when it descends into the pit and forms a crust, while Rabbi Akiva says when one draws it into barrels. The Gemara resolves the earlier baraita similarly, harmonizing the sources.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Oshaya that states wine becomes יין נסך from when it descends into the pit and forms a scum (קיפוי), while Rabbi Akiva says from when one draws it into barrels (משישלה בחביות), contradicting the earlier resolution.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the earlier baraita (from the first inquiry) to also read: wine becomes יין נסך from when it descends into the pit and forms a scum (קיפוי), with Rabbi Akiva saying from when one draws it into barrels (משישלה בחביות).

items.text: Final analysis
items.text_en: Final analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah represents a third Tannaic opinion, but concludes that the Rabbis were more stringent regarding yayin nesekh, so the Mishnah's ruling (when it descends to the pit) is consistent with the Rabbis' lenient position in other contexts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah says wine does not become יין נסך until it descends into the pit, does this imply that there are three Tannaic opinions (the Sages, Rabbi Akiva, and the Mishnah's view)?

The Gemara answers that it is not three opinions; rather, the case of יין נסך (libation wine) is different because the Sages were more stringent with it, so the Mishnah's ruling is a stringency, not a separate opinion.

items.text: Rava's position aligned with three Tannaim
items.text_en: Rava's position aligned with three Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rava, who does not distinguish between the cases, establishes that the dispute about wine in a pit with a gentile is among three Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rava, who does not distinguish between the cases, aligns the dispute about wine in a pit with a gentile among three Tannaim.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction and the principle of ניצוק
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction and the principle of ניצוק
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the wine in the pit is forbidden only if the gentile returned the cluster to the vat, because the connecting stream (ניצוק) makes it a single unit. The Gemara supports this with a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about a flask that was tapped.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that wine in the pit is forbidden but the rest is permitted.
Rav Huna distinguishes: the Mishnah's leniency applies only if the gentile did not return the cluster to the vat; if he did, the wine in the pit is forbidden.
The Gemara asks: by what principle is the cluster itself forbidden?
The Gemara answers: it is forbidden because of ניצוק (the connecting stream), and this proves that ניצוק is considered a halachic connection.
The Gemara supports this with a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about a flask that was tapped, and applies the same logic here: the pit was tapped.

items.text: Question about treading with a gentile
items.text_en: Question about treading with a gentile
items.desc_en: A child who studied Avodah Zarah for six years is asked whether one may tread with a gentile in the vat. He permits it if the gentile's hands are tied, and rules that libation by foot is not considered libation.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask the child scholar whether one may tread with a gentile in the wine vat.
The child scholar permits treading with the gentile in the vat.
The questioners object that the gentile might perform a libation with his hands.
The child scholar answers that the gentile's hands are tied, preventing libation by hand.
The questioners object that the gentile might perform a libation with his foot.
The child scholar rules that libation by foot is not considered a valid libation, so it is permitted.

items.text: Incident in Nehardea and Shmuel's delay
items.text_en: Incident in Nehardea and Shmuel's delay
items.desc_en: An incident occurred in Nehardea where an Israelite and a gentile trod wine together, and Shmuel waited three festivals before permitting it. The Gemara begins to inquire about his reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident in Nehardea where an Israelite and a gentile trod wine together, and Shmuel waited three festivals before permitting it.
The Gemara asks what Shmuel's reasoning was for delaying the permission, suggesting it might be due to a particular consideration.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Nathan's and Rabbi Shimon's positions
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Nathan's and Rabbi Shimon's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that if a Tanna forbids like Rabbi Nathan, the wine would be forbidden even for benefit; but then corrects that Rabbi Nathan only forbids when the contact is by hand, not by foot. It then suggests that if a Tanna permits like Rabbi Shimon, the wine would be permitted even for drinking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that if we find a Tanna who forbids like Rabbi Nathan, we would forbid the wine even for benefit; but then corrects that Rabbi Nathan only forbids when the contact is by hand, not by foot, and if a Tanna permits like Rabbi Shimon, we would permit even for drinking.

items.text: Incident in Beiram and Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Incident in Beiram and Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: A story is told of a non-Jew who unintentionally touched wine with a palm branch; Rav permitted selling the wine to non-Jews. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rav, citing his own statement that a day-old infant makes wine into yayin nesekh. Rav distinguished between drinking (forbidden) and benefit (permitted).

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts an incident in Beiram where a non-Jew unintentionally touched wine with a palm branch, and Rav permitted selling the wine to non-Jews.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Assi's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Assi's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rav, citing his own statement that even a day-old infant makes wine into יין נסך (wine used for libation to idolatry).
Rav distinguished between drinking (שתייה) which he forbade, and deriving benefit (הנאה) which he permitted, thereby justifying his ruling.

items.text: Rav's statement about a day-old infant
items.text_en: Rav's statement about a day-old infant
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's statement that a day-old infant makes wine into yayin nesekh.

sub.desc_en: Rav's own statement: A one-day-old infant makes yeyn nesekh.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya objects to Rav from a baraita about slaves and children of maidservants who were circumcised but not immersed: their spittle and pressure are impure, and their wine—adults make yayin nesekh, minors do not. The Gemara explains that the baraita refers to children of maidservants, and the word 'and likewise' applies only to spittle and pressure, not to wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya objects to Rav from a baraita about slaves and children of maidservants who were circumcised but not immersed: their spittle and pressure are impure, and their wine—adults make יין נסך (wine used for libation), minors do not.
The Gemara explains that the baraita refers specifically to children of maidservants, not to adult slaves.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'and likewise' (וְכֵן), implying the same rule applies to wine as to spittle and pressure.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'and likewise' applies only to spittle and pressure, not to wine.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the baraita
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the opinion that the spittle is pure, and explains that the baraita teaches that only slaves who were circumcised but not immersed make yayin nesekh, but if they were circumcised and immersed they do not. This excludes the view of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who says that even after circumcision and immersion they make yayin nesekh until idolatry is uprooted from their mouths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works out well for the one who says the spittle is טמא (impure), but for the one who says it is טהור (pure), what can be said?

The Gemara answers: the baraita teaches that slaves are analogous to the children of maidservants — just as the latter make יין נסך (wine used for idolatry) only if circumcised but not immersed, so too slaves only make יין נסך if circumcised but not immersed.

The Gemara concludes: this excludes the view of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who says that even after circumcision and immersion slaves make יין נסך until idolatry is uprooted from their mouths — the baraita teaches that this is not the case.

items.text: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel and Rabba's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel and Rabba's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's statement in the name of Shmuel that slaves who were circumcised and immersed still make yayin nesekh for up to twelve months, as per Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabba objects from the same baraita about slaves and children of maidservants.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that slaves who were circumcised and immersed still make יין נסך (libation wine) for up to twelve months, as per Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

Rabba objects to Rav Nachman by citing the baraita about slaves and children of maidservants who were circumcised but not immersed, implying that once immersed they no longer make יין נסך (libation wine).

items.text: Definition of adult and minor gentiles regarding yayin nesekh
items.text_en: Definition of adult and minor gentiles regarding yayin nesekh
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines that adult gentiles who are familiar with idolatry and its practices make wine into yayin nesekh, while minors who are not familiar do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines that adult gentiles familiar with idolatry make wine into יין נסך (wine used for libation), while minors unfamiliar do not.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution regarding the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution regarding the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that circumcised but not immersed gentiles are permitted, but circumcised and immersed are not, and resolves it by applying the case to sons of maidservants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that circumcised but not immersed gentiles are permitted, while circumcised and immersed are not.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by applying the Mishnah's case to sons of maidservants (בני שפחות), who are circumcised but not fully converted.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's wording 'and similarly'
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's wording 'and similarly'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'and similarly', which implies a parallel case, and resolves that it refers to a gentile's spittle and midras impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah uses the word 'וכן' (and similarly), which implies a parallel case, contradicting the proposed distinction.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'וכן' refers to a gentile's spittle (רוק) and midras impurity (מדרס), not to the case of wine.

items.text: Question for the opinion that the market is pure
items.text_en: Question for the opinion that the market is pure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said according to the opinion that the market is pure, since the Mishnah's case would then be problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that the market is pure (טָהוֹר), what can be said to explain the Mishnah's ruling?

items.text: Answer: The Mishnah teaches a parallel between slaves and sons of maidservants
items.text_en: Answer: The Mishnah teaches a parallel between slaves and sons of maidservants
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that slaves are like sons of maidservants: only adult gentiles make yayin nesekh, not minors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that slaves are analogous to sons of maidservants: only adult gentiles make יין נסך (wine used for libation), not minors.

items.text: Rejection of Rav's opinion that a day-old infant makes yayin nesekh
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav's opinion that a day-old infant makes yayin nesekh
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that this teaching excludes the opinion of Rav, who said that even a day-old infant makes yayin nesekh, and it teaches that this is not the case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rav's opinion that a day-old infant makes yayin nesekh, teaching that this is not the case.

items.text: Story in Mahoza: Rava permits, Rav Huna bar Chinana and Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman prohibit
items.text_en: Story in Mahoza: Rava permits, Rav Huna bar Chinana and Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman prohibit
items.desc_en: A gentile entered a Jewish wine shop, stirred wine with his hand, and took it away. Rava permitted selling the wine to gentiles, but Rav Huna bar Chinana and Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman disagreed and prohibited it, leading to conflicting rulings.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a story in Mahoza where a gentile entered a Jewish wine shop, stirred wine with his hand, and took it away.
Rava permitted selling the wine to gentiles, but Rav Huna bar Chinana and Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman disagreed and prohibited it, leading to conflicting rulings.

items.text: Rav Huna's question to Rava about a gentile stirring wine
items.text_en: Rav Huna's question to Rava about a gentile stirring wine
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman visits Mehoza and asks Rava about a case where a gentile stirred wine. Rava initially rules it is forbidden for benefit, but Rav Huna objects citing Rava's own principle that stirring does not create יין נסך. Rava clarifies he only meant the wine itself is permitted, not its monetary value.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman visits Mehoza, and Rava instructs his attendant Rav Elyakim to close the doors to avoid disturbance.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna enters and asks Rava about a case where a gentile stirred wine.
Rava rules that the wine is forbidden even for benefit (הנאה).
Rav Huna objects, citing Rava's own principle that stirring (שיכרך) does not create יין נסך (wine used for idolatry).
Rava clarifies that his principle only permits the wine itself, not its monetary value (דמיו), so the wine's value is forbidden for benefit.

items.text: Rava's report of Nachmani's proofs from traditions
items.text_en: Rava's report of Nachmani's proofs from traditions
items.desc_en: Rava recounts that when he came to Pumbedita, Nachmani surrounded him with traditions and mishnayot that forbid the wine. The tradition refers to incidents in Nehardea and Tiberias where Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan forbade the wine, with the reason that the locals are not Torah scholars. Rava questions whether Mehoza's residents are Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that when he came to Pumbedita, Nachmani surrounded him with traditions and mishnayot that forbid the wine.
Rava cites traditions from Nehardea and Tiberias where Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan forbade the wine because the locals are not Torah scholars.
Rava questions whether Mehoza's residents are Torah scholars, implying they are not, thus the wine should be forbidden.

items.text: The mishnah about a gentile who heated a pipe or tasted wine
items.text_en: The mishnah about a gentile who heated a pipe or tasted wine
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a gentile heated a pipe and brought up wine, or tasted from a cup and returned it to the barrel, the wine was forbidden. The Gemara initially assumes this means forbidden for benefit, but then clarifies it is only for drinking. The objection is raised that if so, the mishnah should have said 'it may be sold', as in the latter clause. This is a conclusive refutation of Rava's position.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: a gentile who heated a pipe and brought up wine, or tasted from a cup and returned it to the barrel, was forbidden.
The Gemara asks: does the mishnah mean the wine is forbidden even for benefit (הנאה)?
The Gemara answers: no, it is forbidden only for drinking (שתייה), not for benefit.
An objection is raised: if so, the mishnah should have said 'it may be sold' (יימכר), as in the latter clause; this is a conclusive refutation of Rava's position.

items.text: The story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were drinking wine when a man came and they asked him to serve them. After he poured into the cup, it was revealed he was a gentile. One forbade the wine even for benefit, the other permitted it even for drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that both are correct in their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rabbi Yochanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were sitting and drinking wine when a certain man came.
They asked the man to serve them, and after he poured into the cup it was revealed that he was a gentile.
One rabbi forbade the wine even for benefit, and the other permitted it even for drinking.
