items.text: Abaye's counter: Distinguish between direct and indirect heating
items.text_en: Abaye's counter: Distinguish between direct and indirect heating
items.desc_en: Abaye argues the Mishnah's case is different because the cumin is directly heated (מיקלא איסוריה), so its smell dissipates; but here the wine fumes are indirect, so they may linger and transfer substance.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes the Mishnah's case of direct heating (מיקלא איסוריה) from the indirect wine fumes, arguing that direct heat dissipates the forbidden substance's smell, so the baraita's leniency does not apply here.

items.text: Rav Mari's Tannaic dispute: Hot bread on wine barrel
items.text_en: Rav Mari's Tannaic dispute: Hot bread on wine barrel
items.desc_en: Rav Mari cites a Tannaic debate: placing hot bread on a wine barrel of terumah — Rabbi Meir forbids (smell transfers substance), Rabbi Yehuda permits (smell is nothing). Rabbi Yosei permits for wheat but forbids for barley (barley absorbs more). This maps to Abaye vs. Rava.

sub.desc_en: Abaye deflects by citing Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Reish Lakish, who limits the Tannaitic dispute to hot bread and an open barrel, thus distinguishing it from Abaye's case.
Rav Mari adds Rabbi Yosei's position: he permits for wheat bread but forbids for barley bread, because barley absorbs more.
The Gemara infers that the Tannaic dispute is about whether רֵיחָא (smell) is a significant substance (מִילְּתָא) or nothing (לָא כְּלוּם).

items.text: Rava's conclusion: The dispute is Tannaic, not Amoraic
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion: The dispute is Tannaic, not Amoraic
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that the disagreement between Abaye and himself mirrors the Tannaic dispute, confirming that smell's status is a settled Tannaic issue, not an Amoraic innovation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye deflects by citing Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Reish Lakish, who limits the Tannaitic dispute to hot bread and an open barrel, thus distinguishing it from Abaye's case.
Rav Mari adds Rabbi Yosei's position: he permits for wheat bread but forbids for barley bread, because barley absorbs more.
The Gemara infers that the Tannaic dispute is about whether רֵיחָא (smell) is a significant substance (מִילְּתָא) or nothing (לָא כְּלוּם).

items.text: Abaye's retort: Rav Mari's citation is not decisive
items.text_en: Abaye's retort: Rav Mari's citation is not decisive
items.desc_en: Abaye counters that Rav Mari's Tannaic example is inconclusive because it involves hot bread on an open barrel (פת חמה וחבית פתוחה), where smell clearly transfers; but his own case involves indirect fumes, so the parallel fails.

sub.desc_en: Abaye deflects by citing Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Reish Lakish, who limits the Tannaitic dispute to hot bread and an open barrel, thus distinguishing it from Abaye's case.
Rav Mari adds Rabbi Yosei's position: he permits for wheat bread but forbids for barley bread, because barley absorbs more.
The Gemara infers that the Tannaic dispute is about whether רֵיחָא (smell) is a significant substance (מִילְּתָא) or nothing (לָא כְּלוּם).

items.text: Opening statement of the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Opening statement of the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Mishnah's distinctions regarding cases where all agree or disagree about the status of bread and a sealed barrel, and notes that the case at hand resembles hot bread and an open barrel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that all agree bread is forbidden in the case of cold bread and a sealed barrel, all agree it is permitted in the case of hot bread and an open barrel, and the dispute is only about the intermediate cases; the Gemara notes that the present case resembles hot bread and an open barrel.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules the halakha
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows the principle that anything whose benefit is determined by taste (i.e., נותן טעם) is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halacha (הלכה) follows the Mishnah's general principle that any forbidden substance whose benefit is determined by taste is prohibited.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction: hot vs. cold grits
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction: hot vs. cold grits
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda further cites Shmuel that the rule only applies when the forbidden substance fell into hot grits; if it fell into cold grits and then they were heated, it is considered as if it improved and then spoiled, and is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda further reports in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the forbidden substance fell into hot grits, but if it fell into cold grits and was then boiled, it is considered as if it improved and then spoiled, and is forbidden.
Shmuel adds that if the forbidden substance fell into cold grits and then they were heated, it is considered as if it improved and then spoiled, and is prohibited.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's parallel ruling and the practice in Tzippori
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's parallel ruling and the practice in Tzippori
items.desc_en: Ravin and Rabbah bar bar Chanah report that Rabbi Yochanan similarly distinguishes between hot and cold grits. The Gemara adds that this was the practice on Friday afternoons in Tzippori, and they called these dishes 'shachlayim'.

sub.text: Ravin citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan the same ruling as Shmuel, and adds that this was the practice in Tzippori on Shabbat eves, where they called these dishes 'shachlayim'.
The Gemara adds that the same practice was followed on Friday afternoons in Tzippori, where they called these dishes 'שחלייים' (a type of grits).

items.text: First version of Reish Lakish's definition of נותן טעם לפגם
items.text_en: First version of Reish Lakish's definition of נותן טעם לפגם
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish defines that 'imparting a spoiled taste' does not mean the pot lacks salt or spices, but rather that the dish is not lacking anything and is inedible because of the forbidden substance.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish defines the principle of נותן טעם לפגם (a substance that imparts a detrimental taste): it does not mean that the pot lacks salt or has too much spice, but rather that the pot lacks nothing and yet the food is inedible because of the forbidden substance.

items.text: Alternative version of Reish Lakish's definition
items.text_en: Alternative version of Reish Lakish's definition
items.desc_en: Some say Reish Lakish's statement is that one does not say the pot lacks salt or spices, but rather that at present it has spoiled.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Reish Lakish's statement: the principle of נותן טעם לפגם does not require that the pot lack salt or spice, but rather that at present the forbidden substance has spoiled the food.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan on liability
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan on liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that anything whose taste and substance are forbidden incurs lashes, and this is the measure of an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that any forbidden substance whose taste and substance are present is prohibited, and one is liable to lashes for eating an olive's bulk within the time it takes to eat half a loaf.

items.text: Opening statement and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Opening statement and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a forbidden substance imparts flavor but not substance, it is forbidden but lashes are not given; if the flavor is detrimental, it is permitted. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah didn't simply say 'if it imparts detrimental flavor, it is permitted,' and explains that it teaches that even if other things also spoil it, it is still permitted, and the halakha follows the later statement of Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a forbidden substance imparts flavor but not substance, it is forbidden but lashes are not given; if the flavor is detrimental, it is permitted.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not simply say 'if it imparts detrimental flavor, it is permitted.'
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even if other things also spoil it, it is still permitted, and the halakha follows the later statement of Reish Lakish.

items.text: Rav Kahana's inference and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's inference and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana claims that from the words of all the sages (in the Mishnah) we learn that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted. Abaye objects: from all the others it is fine, but Reish Lakish only said 'they said' (the halakha follows the later statement), and he himself does not hold that view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana infers from the words of all the sages that נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a spoiled flavor) is permitted.
Abaye objects: the inference works for all other sages, but Reish Lakish merely reported what 'they said' and does not personally hold that view.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is there anyone who says it is forbidden?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is there anyone who says it is forbidden?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is there indeed someone who says that נותן טעם לפגם is forbidden?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether anyone actually holds that נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a detrimental flavor) is forbidden.

items.text: Answer: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Answer: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers yes, citing a baraita: Rabbi Meir says both detrimental and beneficial flavor are forbidden; Rabbi Shimon says beneficial is forbidden but detrimental is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir forbids both beneficial and detrimental flavor, while Rabbi Shimon permits detrimental flavor.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and the refutation
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: he derives from the libations of gentiles (גיעולי גוים) which are detrimental flavor yet forbidden, so here too it should be no different. The Gemara then refutes this using Rav Huna bar Rav Chiyya's principle that the Torah only forbade a pot used within the day (בת יומא) which is not detrimental, and even that pot has a slight detrimental effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Meir's reasoning for forbidding נותן טעם לפגם (detrimental flavor).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives from גיעולי גוים (libations of gentiles) which are detrimental yet forbidden, so here too it should be no different.
The Gemara raises an objection: what about the other side (the sages who permit)?

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Chiyya's principle
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Chiyya's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara invokes Rav Huna bar Rav Chiyya's principle that the Torah only forbade a pot used within the day (בת יומא) which is not detrimental.
The Gemara further objects that even a בת יומא (day-old pot) has a slight detrimental effect, undermining the distinction.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, citing a verse: 'You shall not eat any neveilah; to the stranger who is in your gates...' — anything fit for a stranger is called neveilah (implying that if it is not fit, it is not forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for permitting נותן טעם לפגם (a forbidden taste that spoils the mixture).

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'לֹא תֹאכְלוּ כָּל נְבֵלָה' that only what is fit for a stranger (a non-Jew) is called neveilah (neveilah), implying that unfit neveilah is permitted.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'for it is carrion' excludes an animal that is not fit for a convert, and Rabbi Meir uses this to exclude a tereifah from the start, while Rabbi Shimon holds that such a tereifah is merely dust and needs no exclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'for it is carrion' excludes an animal that is not fit for a convert, meaning it is not called a neveila.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Meir uses the verse to exclude a tereifah from the start, while Rabbi Shimon holds that such a tereifah is merely dust and needs no exclusion.

items.text: Ulla's distinction: improved then spoiled vs. spoiled from the start
items.text_en: Ulla's distinction: improved then spoiled vs. spoiled from the start
items.desc_en: Ulla states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon applies only when the forbidden substance initially improves the mixture and later spoils it, but if it spoils from the outset, all agree it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Ulla distinguishes the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon: it applies only when the forbidden substance initially improves the mixture and later spoils it, but if it spoils from the outset, all agree it is permitted.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about wine and lentils
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about wine and lentils
items.desc_en: Rav Chagga objects to Ulla from a baraita where wine fell into lentils or vinegar into grits, which spoils from the start, yet Rabbi Shimon permits while the Sages prohibit, showing a dispute even in a case of initial spoilage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chagga objects to Ulla from a baraita about wine falling into lentils and vinegar into grits, where the forbidden substance spoils from the outset yet Rabbi Shimon permits it, showing disagreement even in that case.

items.text: Ulla's resolution: the case involved heating cold grits
items.text_en: Ulla's resolution: the case involved heating cold grits
items.desc_en: Ulla responds that the baraita deals with cold grits that were then heated, making it a case of initial improvement followed by spoilage, hence the dispute applies.

sub.desc_en: Ulla dismisses Rav Chagga's objection, explaining that the baraita deals with cold grits that were heated, making the forbidden substance initially improve and later spoil, so it is prohibited.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's position: dispute even in initial spoilage
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's position: dispute even in initial spoilage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon applies even when the substance spoils from the outset.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon applies specifically when the forbidden substance spoils from the outset.

items.text: Unresolved inquiry about the scope of the dispute
items.text_en: Unresolved inquiry about the scope of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: does Rabbi Yochanan hold that the dispute is only in initial spoilage, but all agree that improvement-then-spoilage is prohibited, or is there a dispute in both cases? The matter stands unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Yochanan's statement: does he mean that only in the case of spoiling from the outset there is a dispute, but when it improves and later spoils all agree it is forbidden, or is there a dispute in both cases?
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Searching for a Tannaitic source for Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: Searching for a Tannaitic source for Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: Rav Amram wonders if there is a Tannaitic source supporting Rabbi Yochanan. He finds a baraita about leaven of terumah or kil'ayim falling into dough, which seems to show a dispute in a case of initial spoilage. Rabbi Zeira distinguishes because dough can leaven other doughs, and the Gemara continues to analyze further baraitot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram wonders whether there is a Tannaitic source that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view.
Rav Amram finds a baraita about leaven of חולין (non-sacred) falling into dough, then leaven of תרומה (priestly portion) or כלאי הכרם (diverse vineyard) falling in, where Rabbi Shimon permits it.
The Gemara notes that this baraita involves initial spoilage (פגם מעיקרא), yet Rabbi Shimon and the Sages dispute it, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's view.
Rabbi Zeira distinguishes dough because it is capable of leavening many other doughs, so the leaven is not considered fully spoiled initially.
The Gemara brings another baraita where leaven of תרומה and חולין fall into dough together, and Rabbi Shimon permits when the non-sacred leaven falls first.
The Gemara again notes that this case involves initial spoilage, yet there is a dispute, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's position.
The Gemara anticipates a possible distinction similar to Rabbi Zeira's, but the text is cut off, leaving the objection unresolved.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's seifa that the dispute is about initial impairment
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's seifa that the dispute is about initial impairment
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the seifa of the Mishnah (wine into lentils, vinegar into grits) that the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon is about a case where the forbidden substance impairs the mixture from the outset. It rejects the possibility that the case involves initial improvement followed by impairment, citing the first clause where all agree it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from the seifa of the Mishnah (wine into lentils, vinegar into grits) that the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon is about a case where the forbidden substance impairs the mixture from the outset.

The Gemara raises the objection that the seifa might be a case of initial improvement followed by impairment, but rejects this because the first clause of the Mishnah (terumah falling first) is unanimously forbidden, proving that initial improvement is not at play here.
The Gemara concludes definitively that the dispute is about a case where the forbidden substance impairs the mixture from the outset.

items.text: Question on the necessity of all three clauses in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Question on the necessity of all three clauses in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes three clauses (reisha, metzita, seifa). It explains that the seifa teaches the dispute about initial impairment, and the middle clause teaches that initial improvement followed by impairment is forbidden by all. It then asks why the first clause is needed, since if the seifa (where there is no improvement at all) is forbidden, the first clause (where there is improvement) should certainly be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs three clauses, since the first clause (terumah falling first) seems redundant given that the seifa already teaches that initial impairment is disputed and the middle clause teaches that initial improvement followed by impairment is forbidden by all.

The Gemara asks why the first clause is needed, arguing that if the seifa (where there is no improvement at all) is forbidden, the first clause (where there is improvement) should certainly be forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's answer: the first clause is needed for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: the first clause is needed for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the first clause is necessary for Rabbi Shimon's position. The Sages argue that the dough, which would have leavened in two hours, leavened in one hour due to the forbidden substance, so it is forbidden. Rabbi Shimon responds that both the permitted and forbidden substances improved together and later impaired together. The Gemara then questions why the forbidden and permitted substances do not combine to forbid, and answers that Rabbi Shimon holds that even two forbidden substances do not combine, as per the Mishnah about orlah and kilayim.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the first clause is needed for Rabbi Shimon, who argues that both the permitted and forbidden substances improved together and later impaired together.
The Gemara asks why the permitted and forbidden substances do not combine to forbid the mixture according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon consistently holds that even two forbidden substances do not combine, as per the Mishnah about orlah and kilayim.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a mouse in beer and the principle of נותן טעם לפגם
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a mouse in beer and the principle of נותן טעם לפגם
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that a mouse fell into a barrel of beer and Rav forbade the beer. The Sages asked Rav Sheishes if this means Rav holds that נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a foul taste) is forbidden. Rav Sheishes explains that Rav actually holds it is permitted, but here it is a novelty: even though the mouse is repulsive and people avoid it, the Torah forbade it, so נותן טעם לפגם is also forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask Rav Sheshet whether Rav's ruling that a mouse that fell into a barrel of beer renders it forbidden implies that Rav holds that נותן טעם לפגם (a forbidden substance that imparts a bad taste) is forbidden.

Rav Sheshet answers that Rav generally holds that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, but here the mouse is a novelty: even though it is disgusting and people avoid it, the Torah forbade it, so by extension any נותן טעם לפגם is forbidden.
Rav Sheishes explains that Rav actually holds נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, but here it is a novelty: since the Torah forbade the repulsive mouse, it follows that נותן טעם לפגם is also forbidden.

items.text: Objection from the laws of impurity and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the laws of impurity and resolution
items.desc_en: The Sages object to Rav Sheishes' reasoning by comparing it to the laws of impurity: if the Torah's decree applies even to repulsive things, then a dead sheretz should impart impurity to dry foods as well. Rav Sheishes responds by analogy to seminal emission, which only imparts impurity when it is fit to fertilize; similarly, the Torah's decree about a carcass applies only when it is like its death (i.e., moist).

sub.desc_en: The rabbis object that if Rav's reasoning is applied consistently, then a mouse should also impart ritual impurity to both wet and dry items, but the Mishnah states it only imparts impurity to wet items; the Gemara resolves this by citing the verse 'במותם' (in their death) which requires the item to be capable of decay, analogous to a dead mouse.
Rav Sheishes counters by analogy to seminal emission, which also only imparts impurity to moist foods, not dry ones.
Rav Sheishes resolves: just as seminal emission only imparts impurity when fit to fertilize, so too the Torah's decree about a carcass applies only when it is like its death (i.e., moist).

items.text: Rav Shimi's challenge: is a mouse really repulsive?
items.text_en: Rav Shimi's challenge: is a mouse really repulsive?
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi from Nehardea challenges the assumption that a mouse is repulsive, noting that it is served on kings' tables. He resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a desert mouse (repulsive) and a city mouse (not repulsive).

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi objects that a mouse is not disgusting, as it is served on kings' tables, and resolves that the difference depends on whether the mouse is from a desert region (disgusting) or a settled area (not disgusting).
Rav Shimi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a desert mouse (repulsive) and a city mouse (not repulsive).

items.text: Rava's ruling: נותן טעם לפגם is permitted
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: נותן טעם לפגם is permitted
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the halakha is that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted. He is uncertain about Rav's reasoning in the mouse case: either Rav held it is forbidden (and the halakha does not follow him) or Rav held it is permitted but the mouse actually improves the beer.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the halacha is that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, and he is uncertain whether Rav's ruling was because he held it was forbidden (which is not the halacha) or because a mouse in beer actually improves the taste.

items.text: A question is raised
items.text_en: A question is raised
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a question was raised (about the mouse in beer), but the text breaks off, indicating the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new unresolved inquiry.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on nullification of forbidden substances
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on nullification of forbidden substances
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of a forbidden substance that fell into a mixture, with various Amoraim offering opinions on the required ratio for nullification. Rav Kahana forbids it, Rav Hillel explains it was stirred, and Ravina suggests a 1:100 ratio like terumah, but Rav Tachlifa objects comparing it to spices. Rav Achai and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Ika give different ratios, and the halakha is set at 1:60 for all Torah prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is if a forbidden substance falls into vinegar (חלא).

sub.text: Rav Hillel's report to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Hillel's report to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Hillel tells Rav Ashi that a case occurred before Rav Kahana, who forbade the mixture.
Rav Ashi objects that the case involved a substance that was stirred (אימרטוטי אימרטט), not a simple mixture.
Ravina thought to measure the nullification at a ratio of 1:100, arguing it is no less stringent than תרומה (priestly portion), which is nullified in 1:100.
Rav Tachlifa bar Gizza objects that the case may be like spices of תרומה in a pot, whose taste is not nullified.
Rav Achai measured the nullification in vinegar at a ratio of 1:50.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Ika's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Ika's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Ika measured the nullification in beer at a ratio of 1:60.
The Gemara rules that both vinegar and beer require a 1:60 ratio, and so too all Torah prohibitions.

items.text: Mishnah: Gentile transporting wine with an Israelite
items.text_en: Mishnah: Gentile transporting wine with an Israelite
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a gentile transports wine with an Israelite. If the Israelite is in a position to guard the wine, it is permitted; if the gentile informs him he will be away long enough to open, seal, and dry the vessel, it is forbidden. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a stricter measure. Various scenarios are listed: leaving wine on a wagon or ship, in a shop, or on a table, with distinctions based on proximity and access.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a gentile transporting wine with an Israelite, stating that if the Israelite is in a position to guard it, the wine is permitted, but if the gentile informs him he will be away long enough to open, seal, and dry the vessel, it is forbidden; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a stricter measure.
The Mishnah lists a scenario where one leaves wine on a wagon or ship and goes to a nearby place or bathes, ruling it permitted.
The Mishnah adds that if the gentile informed him he will be away long enough to open, seal, and dry, it is forbidden, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's stricter measure.

The Mishnah presents the case of leaving a gentile in a shop, ruling that even if the Israelite goes in and out it is permitted, but if informed of absence it is forbidden, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's measure.
The Mishnah concludes with the case of eating together at a table, distinguishing between wine on the table (forbidden) and on a sideboard (permitted), and between open and sealed barrels.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'in the presumption of being guarded'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'in the presumption of being guarded'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes 'in the presumption of being guarded' and cites a baraita about workers transporting pure items. Rav Yitzchak explains the difference between the first and second clauses: the first case involves workers who are pure, while the second involves an am ha'aretz who does not care about impurity. Rava then raises an objection about the logic of the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes 'in the presumption of being guarded' and cites a baraita about workers transporting pure items, distinguishing between when the owner is with them and when he tells them to go ahead.
Rav Yitzchak explains the difference: the first clause deals with workers who are pure (מטהר חמריו ופועליו לכך), so they are trusted.

The Gemara objects: if so, the second clause should also be permitted, and suggests that an am ha'aretz (עם הארץ) does not care about his friend's touch, but then counters that even the first clause could be explained that way.
Rava begins his resolution to the objection, though the text cuts off at this point.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needs to list both the case of leaving a gentile in one's shop and the case of leaving wine on a wagon or ship. Each case addresses a different concern: in the shop, the gentile fears the Jew might return and see him; on the wagon, the gentile might sail away and do as he pleases.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages is specifically about a lime seal, but regarding a clay seal, all agree that the time needed is to open, reseal, and let it dry.

items.text: Challenge and resolution from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues with the Sages, saying the seal is recognizable from above and below. The Gemara resolves that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel misunderstood the Sages' position; he thought they were concerned about both lime and clay seals, but the Sages only worry about lime seals where the top is not noticeable.

items.text: Rava's ruling and support from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and support from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel because an anonymous Mishnah supports his view. The Gemara clarifies that the entire Mishnah is not necessarily from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but the ruling stands.

items.text: Practical question about current practice
items.text_en: Practical question about current practice
items.desc_en: Given that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (who is not concerned about seal tampering) and Rabbi Eliezer (who is not concerned about forgery), the Gemara asks why we do not give wine to gentiles nowadays. The answer is due to שייכא (a concern for pouring libations).

items.text: Rava's leniency regarding a gentile prostitute
items.text_en: Rava's leniency regarding a gentile prostitute
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a gentile prostitute is with Israelites reclining at her house, the wine is permitted, because although they have a strong desire for sin, they do not suspect her of pouring libations.

items.text: Opening principle: wine with a harlot and gentiles
items.text_en: Opening principle: wine with a harlot and gentiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: if an Israelite harlot and gentiles are present, the wine is forbidden because she is degraded before them and follows them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle: when an Israelite harlot and gentiles are present, the wine is forbidden because she is degraded before them and follows them.

items.text: Case 1: Gentile near a breach in the wall
items.text_en: Case 1: Gentile near a breach in the wall
items.desc_en: Rava rules that wine near a breach in the wall is permitted, but wine on either side is forbidden, as the gentile could have accessed it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules on a case where a gentile closed a door with a hole in it, finding wine jars on both sides: wine near the hole is permitted, wine on the other side is forbidden.

items.text: Case 2: Gentile in lower story, noise heard
items.text_en: Case 2: Gentile in lower story, noise heard
items.desc_en: Rava permits the wine because the gentile likely assumed the Israelite came down and saw him.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits wine when a gentile closed the door after a fight, reasoning the Israelite might have returned first and is watching from above.
Rava permits the wine, reasoning that the gentile would assume the Israelite came down first and is watching him from the upper story.

items.text: Case 3: Gentile found among wine barrels
items.text_en: Case 3: Gentile found among wine barrels
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if the gentile is caught like a thief (i.e., he fears being seen), the wine is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a gentile found among wine jars is caught like a thief, the wine is permitted; otherwise it is forbidden.
Rava rules: if the gentile is caught like a thief (fearing discovery), the wine is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.

items.text: Case 4: Gentile standing among barrels, with objection
items.text_en: Case 4: Gentile standing among barrels, with objection
items.desc_en: Rava rules based on whether the gentile could slip away unseen. An objection from a baraita about a locked inn is raised and resolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a gentile found among wine jars has a way to slip away unseen, the wine is forbidden; otherwise it is permitted.
The Gemara objects with a baraita about a locked inn, implying the wine is forbidden even when the gentile has no way to slip away.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining the baraita refers to a case where the gentile does have a way to slip away.

items.text: Cases 5-6: Israelite leaves for synagogue or shofar
items.text_en: Cases 5-6: Israelite leaves for synagogue or shofar
items.desc_en: Rava permits the wine in both cases because the Israelite is expected to remember his wine and return quickly.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits wine when an Israelite left a gentile drinking to go to synagogue, reasoning the Israelite will remember his wine and return.

items.text: Digression: Shabbat and finding a purse
items.text_en: Digression: Shabbat and finding a purse
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a related issue: on Shabbat, Jews might not guard their property, but Rava cites a teaching that they carry less than four cubits, so a found purse is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses to discuss Shabbat observance, citing Issur the Convert and Rabbi Yitzchak about finding a purse on Shabbat.
The Gemara raises an objection: if the Jew left due to Shabbat, why is the wine permitted? Jews do not guard their property on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rava's answer via Issur the convert and Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rava's answer via Issur the convert and Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that Jews carry less than four cubits on Shabbat (following Rabbi Yitzchak), so a found purse is permitted, and similarly the Jew could have returned to guard the wine.

items.text: Case 7: Lion roaring, gentile hides
items.text_en: Case 7: Lion roaring, gentile hides
items.desc_en: Rava permits the wine because the gentile likely thought the Israelite also hid behind him and saw him.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits wine when a gentile hid among jars because of a lion, reasoning the Israelite might also have hidden and is watching.
Rava permits the wine, reasoning that the gentile thought the Israelite also hid behind him and could see him.

items.text: Case 8: Thieves open many barrels
items.text_en: Case 8: Thieves open many barrels
items.desc_en: Rava and Shmuel permit the wine because most thieves are Israelites, so the wine is not considered יין נסך.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits wine opened by thieves because most thieves are Israelites; Shmuel similarly ruled in Nehardea.
Rava permits the wine, reasoning that most thieves are Israelites, so the wine is not considered יין נסך.
A similar incident occurred in Nehardea, and Shmuel also permitted the wine.

items.text: Discussion: Comparing to Rabbi Eliezer's principle of doubt
items.text_en: Discussion: Comparing to Rabbi Eliezer's principle of doubt
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rava and Shmuel follow Rabbi Eliezer's rule that a doubt about entry is pure. It then rejects this, explaining that since some thieves open for money, it is a double doubt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rava and Shmuel's ruling follows Rabbi Eliezer's principle that a doubt about entry is pure.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a doubt about entering a contaminated field is pure, while a doubt about actual contact is impure.
The Gemara rejects the comparison, explaining that since some thieves open barrels for money, the case involves a double doubt (ספק ספיקא), unlike Rabbi Eliezer's single doubt.

items.text: First case: a gentile woman found with a ladle among wine barrels
items.text_en: First case: a gentile woman found with a ladle among wine barrels
items.desc_en: Rava rules the wine permitted because the woman likely took wine from the barrel's top, and even if not, she might have accidentally touched it without intent to pour libation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a gentile woman was found among wine barrels holding a ladle.
Rava rules the wine permitted, reasoning that she took wine from the barrel's top, and even if not, she might have accidentally touched it without intent to pour libation.

items.text: Second case: a military cohort opened many barrels
items.text_en: Second case: a military cohort opened many barrels
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Elazar permitted the wine, but the Gemara is uncertain whether it was because he follows Rabbi Eliezer's view that uncertain access is pure, or because most of the cohort were Jews. The Gemara then clarifies that this is a case of uncertain access (ספק ביאה), not uncertain touch (ספק מגע), since the barrels were opened for money.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a military unit entered Nehardea and opened many wine barrels.

sub.text: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Elazar's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Elazar's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Elazar ruled the wine permitted.
The gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar's leniency was because he follows Rabbi Eliezer's principle that a ספק ביאה (doubtful entry) is pure, or because the majority of the military unit were Jews.
The Gemara objects: if the cohort opened the barrels, this is a case of uncertain touch (ספק מגע), not uncertain access.
The Gemara resolves that since many barrels were opened for money, the soldiers' intent was not to touch the wine but to access the barrels, making it akin to uncertain access (ספק ביאה).

items.text: Third case: a Jewish woman gave her key to a gentile woman
items.text_en: Third case: a Jewish woman gave her key to a gentile woman
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak quoting Rabbi Elazar reports that the academy ruled the wine permitted because she only entrusted the key's guarding. Abaye supports this with a Mishnah about purity: one who gives keys to an am ha'aretz keeps his purity, and the same leniency applies to יין נסך.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak quoting Rabbi Elazar reports that the academy ruled the wine permitted because the Jewish woman only entrusted the guarding of the key to the gentile woman.
Abaye supports the ruling with a Mishnah about purity: one who gives keys to an am ha'aretz keeps his purity, and the same leniency applies to יין נסך (wine used for libation).

items.text: Comparison of stringency: purity laws vs. יין נסך
items.text_en: Comparison of stringency: purity laws vs. יין נסך
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether purity laws are more stringent than יין נסך, citing a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan about a courtyard divided by a partition: Rav rules purity is defiled but a gentile does not make יין נסך, while Rabbi Yochanan rules even purity remains pure.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions whether purity laws (טהרות) are stricter than יין נסך (libation wine).

The gemara answers yes, citing a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan: Rav rules that in a divided courtyard, purity is impure but יין נסך is not made, while Rabbi Yochanan rules even purity is pure.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from a baraita about a habér and an am ha'aretz
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from a baraita about a habér and an am ha'aretz
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a habér may spread produce in an inner courtyard even if the am ha'aretz's hand can reach, contradicting Rav's stricter view. Rav answers that the am ha'aretz is restrained as a thief.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a habér may spread produce in an inner courtyard even if the am ha'aretz's hand can reach, which contradicts Rav's stricter view.
Rav answers that the case is different because the am ha'aretz is restrained as a thief, so he will not touch the produce.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita about roofs
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita about roofs
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a habér may spread produce on his roof above an am ha'aretz's roof only if the am ha'aretz's hand cannot reach, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's lenient view. Rabbi Yochanan answers that the am ha'aretz can slip away and claim he was just leaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a habér may spread produce on his roof above an am ha'aretz's roof only if the am ha'aretz's hand cannot reach, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's lenient view.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case is different because the am ha'aretz can slip away and claim he was just leaning on the roof.

items.text: Second challenge to Rav and his defense
items.text_en: Second challenge to Rav and his defense
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that a habér may spread produce on his roof adjacent to an am ha'aretz's roof even if the hand can reach, challenging Rav. Rav defends himself by citing Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel who supports his position.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites another baraita: a חבר's roof adjacent to an עם הארץ's roof — the חבר may spread produce even if the עם הארץ's hand reaches — challenging Rav.
Rav answers: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel supports my position, and I rule like him.

items.text: Mishnah: a military cohort entering a city
items.text_en: Mishnah: a military cohort entering a city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that in peacetime, open barrels are forbidden but sealed ones are permitted; in wartime, both are permitted because there is no time for libation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: when an invading army enters a city in peacetime, open wine barrels are forbidden.
The Mishnah continues: sealed barrels are permitted in peacetime.
The Mishnah concludes: in wartime, both open and sealed barrels are permitted because there is no time for libation.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction from a baraita about a conquered city
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction from a baraita about a conquered city
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that all priestesses in a city conquered by a legion are disqualified, implying that gentiles have time for intercourse. Rav Mari resolves that they have no time for libation but have time for intercourse.

items.text: Mishnah: Jewish craftsmen and a barrel of libation wine
items.text_en: Mishnah: Jewish craftsmen and a barrel of libation wine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a gentile sends a barrel of libation wine as payment to Jewish craftsmen, they may say 'give us its value' before it enters their domain, but once it enters, it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's ruling on asking a gentile to pay the king's tax
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's ruling on asking a gentile to pay the king's tax
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that one may tell a gentile to go and pay the king's tax for him. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita that forbids saying 'go under me to the tax collector,' and Rav distinguishes between asking the gentile to substitute for him and asking him to rescue him from the tax collector.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling wine to a gentile
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling wine to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one sells wine to a gentile and sets the price before measuring, the money is permitted; but if he measures before setting the price, the money is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Amemar and Rav Ashi debate whether meshikha is effective for a gentile
items.text_en: Gemara: Amemar and Rav Ashi debate whether meshikha is effective for a gentile
items.desc_en: Amemar asserts that meshikha (pulling) is effective for a gentile, citing the practice of Persians sending horses to each other without them being returned. Rav Ashi disagrees, arguing that meshikha is not effective, and the horses are not returned due to a spirit of trust. Rav Ashi supports his view from Rav's instruction to wine merchants to take money from gentiles before measuring, to avoid the wine becoming libation wine in the Jew's domain.

items.text: Initial principle: gentile's pulling acquires the wine, but yayin nesekh requires contact
items.text_en: Initial principle: gentile's pulling acquires the wine, but yayin nesekh requires contact
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that when a gentile pulls a barrel of wine, he acquires it, but the wine does not become yayin nesekh until he actually touches it.

items.text: Clarification: pouring wine into a gentile's vessel and the nitzok issue
items.text_en: Clarification: pouring wine into a gentile's vessel and the nitzok issue
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if the gentile pours wine into a Jewish vessel, the wine is not acquired; but if into a gentile's vessel, the gentile acquires it upon reaching the vessel's airspace. This raises the question of whether nitzok (stream) is a connector, but the Gemara deflects by positing the gentile holds the vessel or it rests on the ground.

items.text: Inference about kinyan: kilyo shel lokeach in reshus mokher
items.text_en: Inference about kinyan: kilyo shel lokeach in reshus mokher
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous case that if a buyer's vessel is in the seller's domain, the buyer does not acquire its contents, but this is challenged.

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanation: wine residue on the funnel
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanation: wine residue on the funnel
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that the buyer does acquire, but the case involves wine residue on the funnel that becomes yayin nesekh immediately. This is then aligned with the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rav's ruling that his halakhah applies to barrels but not to wine mixed with wine.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita on purchasing broken idols
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita on purchasing broken idols
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about purchasing broken idols from gentiles: if the gentile pulled before payment, the Jew returns it; if after payment, he discards it. This challenges the idea that meshikhah by a gentile is koneh. Abaye and Rava offer explanations based on mar'it ayin.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah on selling wine to a gentile
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah on selling wine to a gentile
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda challenges Rav Ashi from a mishnah: if a Jew fixed a price before measuring, the proceeds are permitted; if he measured before fixing, they are forbidden. This seems to assume meshikhah is koneh. Rav Ashi responds that the distinction is whether the gentile relied on the price (samkha da'ateih).

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a Noahide
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a Noahide
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that a Noahide is executed for stealing less than a perutah, implying that meshikhah is koneh. Rav Ashi answers that the Noahide is executed because he caused distress to a Jew.

items.text: Gemara's proof that משיכה in a gentile acquires
items.text_en: Gemara's proof that משיכה in a gentile acquires
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah's phrase 'לא ניתן להישובון' to mean that the wine is not subject to reconsideration. It then questions the Mishnah's ruling about a Jew who takes the wine from the gentile being killed, and concludes that this proves that pulling (משיכה) by a gentile effects acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'לא ניתן להישובון' means, and answers that it means the wine is not subject to reconsideration.
The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah's later clause about a Jew taking the wine and being killed is problematic, questioning what the gentile did wrong.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah proves that pulling (משיכה) by a gentile effects acquisition.

items.text: Case of a promise to sell land and the requirement of price-setting
items.text_en: Case of a promise to sell land and the requirement of price-setting
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that if one says 'If I sell this land, I will sell it to you,' and then sells to another, the first person acquires it. Abaye objects that the price was not set, citing a Mishnah about selling wine to a gentile where price-setting before measuring permits the money. The Gemara questions whether the stringency of יין נסך is unique.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man promised to sell land to another if he sells it, and then sold it to a third party; Rav Yosef rules that the first person acquires it.
Abaye objects that the price was not set, citing a Mishnah about selling wine to a gentile where price-setting before measuring permits the money, but measuring before price-setting forbids it.
The Gemara questions the objection and suggests that the stringency of יין נסך (wine used for libation) may be unique and not applicable to land sales.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about measuring and price-setting
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about measuring and price-setting
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin brings a precedent from Rav Chisda and Rav Huna that resolves the issue from a baraita: if one pulls his donkeys and workers into his house, without unloading, he does not acquire until the wine is measured and the price is set. Only after unloading (פרק) does acquisition occur with price-setting before measuring.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing a precedent from Rav Chisda and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing a precedent from Rav Chisda and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin brings a baraita that resolves the issue: if one pulls his donkeys and workers into his house without unloading, he does not acquire until the wine is measured and the price is set, and both can retract.

items.text: Case of a promise to sell at a specific price and subsequent sale at a higher price
items.text_en: Case of a promise to sell at a specific price and subsequent sale at a higher price
items.desc_en: A man says to another: 'If I sell this land, I will sell it to you for 100 zuz.' He then sells it to someone else for 120. Rav Kahana rules that the first person acquires it. Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod objects that the extra 20 zuz is coercion (אנסוה), and the halakha follows Rav Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: Presents the case: a man promises to sell land to another for 100 zuz, then sells it to a third party for 120.
Rav Kahana rules that the first person acquires the land.
Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod objects that the extra 20 zuz constitutes coercion (אנסוה), invalidating the sale to the first person.
The gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod.

items.text: Laws of appraisal by three or four experts
items.text_en: Laws of appraisal by three or four experts
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between saying 'as three appraise' (even two of three suffice) and 'as three say' (all three must agree). For four, it requires all four. A case arises where one party demands different experts, and Rav Pappa says he can delay, but Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects that the new experts may not be more knowledgeable, and the halakha follows him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the halachic difference between saying 'as three appraise' (even two of three suffice) and 'as three say' (all three must agree), and similarly for four.
Rav Pappa rules that when one party demands different experts, he can delay the appraisal.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects that the new experts may not be more knowledgeable than the original ones.
The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua, rejecting Rav Pappa's position.

items.text: Mishnah: Pouring wine and the law of יין נסך
items.text_en: Mishnah: Pouring wine and the law of יין נסך
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches: If one took a funnel and measured into a gentile's flask, and then into a Jew's flask, if there is a residue of wine on the funnel, it is forbidden. Pouring from one vessel to another: the vessel poured from is permitted, the vessel poured into is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of a funnel used for measuring wine into a gentile's flask and then into a Jew's flask, and the law of pouring from one vessel to another.

items.text: Gemara: The law of ניצוק (pouring stream) as a connector for יין נסך
items.text_en: Gemara: The law of ניצוק (pouring stream) as a connector for יין נסך
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta about ניצוק, קטפרס, and משקה טופח not being connectors for impurity. Rav Huna rules that they are connectors for יין נסך. Rav Nachman challenges this from the Tosefta's end about אשבורן, but the Gemara concludes that no proof can be derived. It then cites the Mishnah's case of the funnel to support Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta stating that a pouring stream (ניצוק), a drip (קטפרס), and a moistening liquid (משקה טופח) are not connectors for impurity or purity.
Rav Huna rules that a pouring stream, a drip, and a moistening liquid are connectors for the purposes of יין נסך (libation wine).
Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna, arguing that the Tosefta's end about אשבורן (a pool) being a connector for impurity implies it is not a connector for יין נסך, undermining Rav Huna's inference.
The Gemara concludes that no proof can be derived from the Tosefta regarding יין נסך.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of the funnel to support Rav Huna's ruling.

items.text: Initial proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's ruling that if there is a wine sediment (עכבות יין) it is forbidden, implying that the stream (ניצוק) connecting the sediment to the wine is considered a connection, making the wine forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah that the wine sediment (עכבות יין) is forbidden only because the stream (ניצוק) connecting it to the wine is considered a connection.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Chiya's baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Chiya's baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya's baraita about a flask that was pressed (פחסתו) is cited. The Gemara questions whether the ruling applies only when the flask was pressed, leaving the status of ניצוק unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita about a flask that was pressed, leaving the status of the stream (ניצוק) unresolved.
The Gemara considers whether the baraita implies that ניצוק (a connected stream) is not a halachic connection, but then rejects this inference.
The Gemara concludes that the case of a pressed flask is resolved as forbidden, but the status of ניצוק (a connected stream) remains an unresolved question (תיבעי).

items.text: Proof from a baraita about pouring
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about pouring
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when pouring from one vessel to another, the stream between them is forbidden, implying ניצוק is a connection. The Gemara objects that if so, the wine in the upper vessel should also be forbidden, but resolves that it is poured in drops (מקטיף קטופי). However, the Gemara then rejects this proof by noting the end of the baraita contradicts the inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about pouring from one vessel to another, inferring that the stream (ניצוק) is a connection.
The Gemara objects that if ניצוק is a connection, the wine in the upper vessel should also be forbidden, but resolves that it is poured in drops (מקטיף קטופי).
The Gemara rejects the proof by noting that the end of the baraita contradicts the inference, concluding that no conclusion can be drawn from it.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a barrel and pit
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a barrel and pit
items.desc_en: A baraita says the stream from a barrel to a pit is forbidden. Rav Sheshet explains it refers to a gentile pouring, where the stream is forbidden due to the gentile's force (כוחו). The Gemara questions why the wine inside the barrel isn't also forbidden, and answers that rabbinic decrees only apply to the outflow, not the interior.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that states the stream from a barrel to a pit is forbidden.
Rav Sheshet explains the baraita refers to a gentile pouring, where the stream is forbidden due to the gentile's force (כוחו).
The Gemara objects that if the gentile's force makes the stream forbidden, the wine inside the barrel should also be forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the rabbinic decree only applies to the outflow, not the interior of the barrel.

items.text: Practical rulings by Rav Chisda and Rava
items.text_en: Practical rulings by Rav Chisda and Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs wine merchants to pour wine in drops (קטופי) or shake it (נפוצי) when measuring for gentiles. Rava warns pourers not to let a gentile assist, lest they pour wine onto him, making it forbidden due to his force.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs wine merchants to pour wine in intermittent streams when selling to gentiles, and Rava instructs pourers not to let a gentile assist, lest the wine become forbidden due to the gentile's force (כוחו).
Rava warns pourers not to let a gentile assist, lest they pour wine onto him, making it forbidden due to his force.

items.text: Case of a gentile touching the pipe
items.text_en: Case of a gentile touching the pipe
items.desc_en: A gentile placed his hand on a pipe (גישתא) through which wine flowed. Rava forbade all the wine. Rav Papa asked if this was due to ניצוק being a connection; Rava distinguished because all the wine was drawn through the pipe.

sub.desc_en: A man drew wine through a pipe (גישתא) and a gentile placed his hand on the pipe; Rava forbade all the wine.
Rav Papa asked Rava whether the prohibition was due to ניצוק (a connected stream) being a חיבור (legal connection), implying that Rava holds ניצוק is a connection.
Rava distinguished the case because all the wine was drawn through the pipe and the pipe's extension, so the gentile's touch affected the entire flow.

items.text: Ruling on a siphon (קנישקנין)
items.text_en: Ruling on a siphon (קנישקנין)
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that a siphon is permitted if an Israelite first breaks the flow, but not if a gentile does. Rabba bar Rav Huna permitted drinking via a siphon at the Exilarch's house.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that wine in a siphon (קנישקנין) is permitted if an Israelite first drew the wine, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna permitted drinking from a siphon at the Exilarch's house.
Rabba bar Rav Huna, visiting the Exilarch's house, permitted drinking via a siphon, providing practical support for the ruling.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabba bar Rav Huna's practice
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabba bar Rav Huna's practice
items.desc_en: An alternative tradition states that Rabba bar Rav Huna himself drank at a place called Kanishkaneen, suggesting a lenient view regarding wine handled by gentiles.

sub.desc_en: An alternative tradition reports that Rabba bar Rav Huna himself drank at Kanishkaneen, implying a lenient view regarding wine handled by gentiles.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: nullification rules for yayin nesekh
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: nullification rules for yayin nesekh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that yayin nesekh is forbidden and prohibits mixtures in any amount when it is of the same type (wine with wine, water with water), but when it is of a different type (wine with water or water with wine), it is prohibited only if it imparts flavor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lays down the rule that יַיִן נֶסֶךְ (wine used for idolatry) prohibits mixtures in any amount when the same type mixes, but when different types mix it is prohibited only if it imparts flavor.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's first ruling: nullification by pouring
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's first ruling: nullification by pouring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one pours yayin nesekh from a barrel into a pit of permitted wine, even if he pours all day, each first drop is nullified as it falls, so the mixture is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, reported by Rav Dimi, states that when one pours יַיִן נֶסֶךְ from a barrel into a pit drop by drop, each first portion is nullified even if this continues all day.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that when one pours yayin nesekh from a barrel into a pit, each first drop is nullified as it falls, even if he pours all day.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's ruling from the Mishnah, which says yayin nesekh prohibits in any amount when falling into permitted wine. Rav Dimi resolves that the Mishnah speaks of permitted wine falling into prohibited wine, not the reverse. He explains the entire Mishnah as dealing with permitted substances falling into prohibited ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's ruling by citing the Mishnah that yayin nesekh (libation wine) is forbidden and prohibits in any amount, implying it falls into permitted wine.
The Gemara initially answers that the Mishnah speaks of permitted wine falling into prohibited wine, not the reverse.
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah's clause 'wine in water — by taste', which seems to describe prohibited wine falling into permitted water.
The Gemara again answers that the Mishnah speaks of permitted wine falling into prohibited water.

The Gemara objects further: if the first clause deals with prohibited water, the last clause 'water in wine — by taste' would also have to be prohibited water, but it says 'by taste', not 'any amount'.

Rav Dimi resolves that the entire Mishnah deals with permitted substances falling into prohibited ones: the first clause is permitted wine into prohibited water, and the last clause is permitted water into prohibited wine.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's second ruling: distinction by vessel size
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's second ruling: distinction by vessel size
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan limits his lenient ruling to a small flask where the stream is thin, but not to a barrel where the stream is thick, because a thick stream might not be nullified drop by drop.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, reported by Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef, refines the rule: pouring from a small flask (צַרְצוּר קָטָן) nullifies each drop because the stream is small, but from a barrel the stream is large and nullification does not apply.
The gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's leniency applies only to a small flask with a thin stream, not to a barrel with a thick stream.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's third ruling: nullification via water bucket
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's third ruling: nullification via water bucket
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules: if yayin nesekh falls into a pit and then a bucket of water falls in, we consider the permitted water as if it were absent, and the remaining water is abundant enough to nullify the wine. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda adds that this applies only if the water fell first; otherwise, the wine and water of the same type combine and the prohibition is not nullified.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if yayin nesekh falls into a pit and then a bucket of water falls in, we consider the permitted water as if it were absent, and the remaining water is abundant enough to nullify the wine.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda adds that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only if the water fell first; otherwise, the wine and water of the same type combine and the prohibition is not nullified.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: Some teach Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's statement as applying to the Mishnah's case of wine with wine: if a bucket of water falls in, we consider the permitted wine as absent and the water nullifies the prohibited wine. The difference between the two versions is whether the water must fall first.

sub.desc_en: Presents an alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's statement, applying it to the Mishnah's case of wine with wine: if a bucket of water falls in, we consider the permitted wine as absent and the water nullifies the prohibited wine.

The Gemara clarifies the difference between the two versions: the version applied to the Mishnah does not require the water to fall first, while the version applied to Ravin's statement requires the water to fall first.

items.text: Beginning of an unresolved discussion
items.text_en: Beginning of an unresolved discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about a case where yayin nesekh falls into a pit and then a bucket of water falls in, but the text is cut off, leaving the conclusion unstated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an unresolved discussion about a case where יין נסך (libation wine) falls into a pit and then a bucket of water falls in, but the text is cut off, leaving the conclusion unstated.

items.text: Opening dispute between Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan
items.desc_en: Ḥizkiyya rules that if produce grew from forbidden material it is forbidden, but if it grew from permitted material it is permitted. Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees, ruling that even if it grew from forbidden material it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Ḥizkiyya rules that produce grown from forbidden material is forbidden, but from permitted material is permitted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees, ruling that even if produce grew from forbidden material it is permitted.

items.text: Attempt to link the dispute to a Tannaitic debate
items.text_en: Attempt to link the dispute to a Tannaitic debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests to Rabbi Zeira that Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan are arguing over the same principle as Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages in a Mishnah about leaven that fell into dough. Rabbi Eliezer says the status follows the last addition, while the Sages say it is forbidden only if there is enough to leaven.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the dispute between Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan parallels the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding leaven that combines to leaven dough.

The Mishnah is cited: leaven of חולין (non-sacred) and תרומה (priestly portion) fell into dough; Rabbi Eliezer says the status follows the last addition, while the Sages say it is forbidden only if there is enough to leaven.

items.text: Rejection of the link and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rejection of the link and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the link because Abaye's qualification about removing the forbidden leaven shows the Mishnah is not analogous. Instead, the dispute is about the principle of 'ro'in' (viewing the permitted as if it were absent). Ḥizkiyya rejects this principle, while Rabbi Yoḥanan accepts it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proposed link between the dispute of Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan and the Mishnah of leaven, citing Abaye's qualification that the Mishnah only applies when the forbidden leaven is removed first, and then asks which Tanna Ḥizkiyya follows.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute between Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan is actually about the principle of רוֹאִין (viewing the permitted portion as if it were absent): Ḥizkiyya rejects this principle, while Rabbi Yoḥanan accepts it.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Yoḥanan accepts the principle of ro'in
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Yoḥanan accepts the principle of ro'in
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yoḥanan actually holds the principle of ro'in, citing a case where he initially did not answer Rabbi Assi about two cups of wine. However, it concludes that he later answered, ruling that we view the permitted as if it were absent, and the remaining water nullifies the forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yoḥanan actually holds the principle of רואין (viewing the permitted as if absent), citing that he initially did not answer Rabbi Assi's question about two mixed cups of wine.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yoḥanan initially did not answer but later ruled that we view the permitted wine as if it were absent, and the remaining water nullifies the forbidden wine.

items.text: General principle and the view of Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: General principle and the view of Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: a forbidden substance of the same type is nullified in any amount, while a different type requires a taste. Rav and Shmuel apply this to all Torah prohibitions. The phrase 'zeh haklal' comes to include all prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a general rule: a forbidden substance of the same type is nullified in any amount (במשהו), while a different type requires a detectable taste (בנותן טעם).
Rav and Shmuel both state that this rule applies to all Torah prohibitions: same type nullified in any amount, different type by taste.
The Gemara asks: what does the phrase 'זה הכלל' (this is the rule) come to include?
The Gemara answers: it comes to include all Torah prohibitions, extending the rule beyond the specific case of the Mishnah.

items.text: View of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: View of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish disagree, holding that all prohibitions are nullified by taste, except for tevel and yeyn nesekh, which in their own kind are nullified in any amount. The phrase 'zeh haklal' comes to include tevel.

sub.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish both rule that all Torah prohibitions are nullified only if they impart flavor, except for טבל (untithed produce) and יין נסך (libation wine), which are prohibited in any amount in their own type, and the rule comes to include טבל (untithed produce).
The phrase 'zeh haklal' in their statement comes to include tevel as an exception.

items.text: Supporting baraitot for both views
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot for both views
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav and Shmuel's position, the other supports Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish's position, confirming that both views have Tannaitic backing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara announces that baraitot support both Rav and Shmuel's view and Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish's view.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rav and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that rules all Torah prohibitions are nullified in their own kind by any amount and in a different kind by imparting flavor, supporting Rav and Shmuel.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that rules all Torah prohibitions are nullified by imparting flavor in both their own and a different kind, except for טבל (untithed produce) and יין נסך (libation wine) which are nullified in their own kind by any amount, supporting Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish.
The gemara asks: granted that יין נסך (libation wine) is stringent due to the severity of idolatry, but what is the reason for טבל (untithed produce) being stringent?

The gemara answers that the stringency of טבל (untithed produce) follows its leniency: just as a single grain exempts an entire heap from tithes, so too a small amount of טבל prohibits a mixture in its own kind, citing Shmuel's principle and a supporting baraita.

items.text: Reason for tevel's stringency
items.text_en: Reason for tevel's stringency
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why tevel is stringent: just as its permission is through a single grain (as Shmuel said), so too its prohibition is in any amount. A baraita confirms that tevel forbids in its own kind in any amount, but in a different kind by taste.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that יין נסך (wine used for idolatry) is stringent due to the severity of idolatry, but what is the reason for tevel (untithed produce)?
The Gemara answers: just as tevel's permission (היתר) is through a single grain (as Shmuel said: one wheat exempts the entire heap), so too its prohibition is in any amount.
A baraita confirms that tevel forbids in its own kind in any amount, but in a different kind by taste.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: list of items forbidden and prohibiting in any amount
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: list of items forbidden and prohibiting in any amount
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates items that are forbidden and prohibit a mixture in any amount, including yayin nesekh, avodah zarah, and others.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are forbidden and prohibit a mixture in any amount.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the Tanna's criteria
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the Tanna's criteria
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Tanna lists items that are a 'davar shebeminyan' or 'issurei hana'ah', and resolves that both criteria apply. It addresses objections about omitted items like neveilah, chametz, and others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what principle the Tanna is counting — items that are a 'דבר שבמנין' (a counted item) or items forbidden for benefit — and challenges that either category would include additional items not listed.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha)
sub.desc_en: The Tanna requires both conditions: the item must be a 'דבר שבמנין' (a counted item) and forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna should also list 'אגוזי פרך' (nuts of Perek) and 'רימוני בדן' (pomegranates of Baddan), which are both a 'דבר שבמנין' and forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara answers that those items are already taught elsewhere in the Mishnah under the categories of ערלה (orlah) and כלאי הכרם (mixed species of the vineyard).
The Gemara objects that the Tanna should also list 'כיכרות של בעל הבית' (loaves of a householder) regarding חמץ בפסח (leaven on Passover), and answers that Rabbi Akiva already adds them elsewhere.

The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הרי אלו' (these are) excludes, and answers that it excludes items that are a 'דבר שבמנין' but not forbidden for benefit, or forbidden for benefit but not a 'דבר שבמנין'.

items.text: Mishnah: yayin nesekh falling into a pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: yayin nesekh falling into a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if yayin nesekh falls into a pit, the entire mixture is forbidden for benefit. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits selling the mixture to a gentile, deducting the value of the yayin nesekh.

sub.text: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if יין נסך (libation wine) falls into a pit, the Tanna Kamma says the entire mixture is forbidden for benefit, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it may be sold to a gentile except for the value of the forbidden wine.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits selling the entire mixture to a gentile, deducting the value of the yayin nesekh.

items.text: Gemara: dispute about nullification of yayin nesekh
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute about nullification of yayin nesekh
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakhah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only for a barrel among barrels, not wine among wine. Shmuel and others permit even wine among wine. Rav Nachman concludes that for yayin nesekh, wine among wine is forbidden, barrel among barrel is permitted, but for stam yayin, even wine among wine is permitted.

sub.text: Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Nachman bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Nachman bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only for a barrel mixed with barrels, but not for wine mixed with wine; Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Nachman bar Avuha all rule that even wine mixed with wine is permitted.
Rav rules that the halakhah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only for a barrel among barrels, not for wine among wine.

Rav Nachman issues a practical ruling: for יין נסך (libation wine), wine mixed with wine is forbidden, barrel with barrel is permitted; for סתם יין (ordinary gentile wine), even wine mixed with wine is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan also permits wine among wine.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Chanina also permits wine among wine.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rabbah bar Avuha also permits wine among wine.
