Rav Nachman issues a practical ruling: for יין נסך (wine used for idolatry), wine among wine is forbidden and barrel among barrel is permitted; for סתם יין (ordinary gentile wine), even wine among wine is permitted.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of a winepress (gat) that a gentile coated with pitch: for a stone press, wiping suffices; for a wooden one, Rabbi says wipe and the Sages say scrape off the pitch; for an earthenware one, even scraping is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of a winepress (gat) that a gentile coated with pitch: for stone, wiping suffices; for wood, Rabbi says wipe and Sages say scrape; for earthenware, even scraping is insufficient.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the Mishnah's case is specifically where the gentile only coated the press with pitch, not where he trod grapes in it; if he trod, wiping is insufficient. Two versions of Rava's statement are presented, both emphasizing the precision of the Mishnah's wording.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's leniency of wiping applies specifically when the gentile only coated the press with pitch, not when he trod grapes in it.
The Gemara objects that Rava's point is obvious, since the Mishnah explicitly says 'coated it with pitch' (זְפָתָהּ).

The Gemara explains that Rava's statement is necessary to counter a possible assumption that the Mishnah's wording 'coated it' is merely describing the typical case, but the same leniency would apply even if the gentile trod grapes.
An alternative version of Rava's statement is presented, adding that if the gentile trod grapes, wiping is insufficient.
The Gemara again objects that the point is obvious from the Mishnah's wording.
The Gemara explains that the alternative version emphasizes that the Mishnah's wording is precise: only coating with pitch allows wiping, but treading requires more.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rav
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rav
items.desc_en: A man comes to Rabbi Chiyya seeking someone to purify his winepress. Rabbi Chiyya sends Rav, who initially thinks wiping suffices but then discovers the press is full of wine, requiring scraping. This illustrates the practical application of the halakha.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi
sub.desc_en: A story is told about a man who came before Rabbi Chiyya asking for someone to kasher his winepress.
Rabbi Chiyya tells Rabbi to go with the man and be careful not to cause him to be shouted at in the study hall.
Rabbi sees that the press is very smooth and initially rules that wiping suffices.
While going back and forth, Rabbi sees a crack underneath the press filled with wine and realizes that scraping is required.
Rabbi concludes that this is what Rabbi Chiyya meant by warning him not to cause shouting in the study hall.

items.text: Baraita dispute and resolution
items.text_en: Baraita dispute and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding the gat, makhatz, and mashpeikh of gentiles: Rabbi permits wiping, Sages forbid. The Gemara reconciles this with the Mishnah by distinguishing cases where the gentile trod grapes (baraita) versus where he did not (Mishnah).

sub.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi (permitting wiping) and the Sages (forbidding) regarding the gentile's winepress, vat, and spout, with additional distinctions for wood and stone vessels.
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah (0) which permits wiping for a stone winepress that was pitched, seemingly contradicting the baraita's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the Mishnah as referring to a case where the gentile did not tread grapes, while the baraita refers to a case where he did tread grapes.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's earthenware case
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's earthenware case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's ruling on earthenware (even scraping is insufficient) aligns with the baraita. Rava explains that the Mishnah's final clause (about earthenware) follows the opinion of the Sages, not Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that Rabbi permits wiping for these vessels while the Sages forbid.
The Gemara asks: but we learned in the Mishnah that an earthenware press is forbidden even after scraping the pitch — this seems to contradict the baraita's leniency for Rabbi.
Rava answers that the end of the Mishnah (the earthenware case) comes to state the view of the Sages, not Rabbi.

items.text: Rava's practice with barrels
items.text_en: Rava's practice with barrels
items.desc_en: Rava taught that an idolatrous vessel (na'avah) must be scalded. When sending barrels to Harpanya, he would cover their openings and seal them, reasoning that the Sages decreed even temporary absorption is treated as permanent.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that a gentile's clay vessel (נעוה) must be boiled with water to be kashered.
Rava's practice when sending jugs to Harpanya: he would invert them over their openings and seal them at their bases.
The Gemara explains that Rava holds that the Sages decreed a prohibition on any vessel stored with wine (מכניסו לקיום), even temporarily.

items.text: Dispute over wiping method
items.text_en: Dispute over wiping method
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah disagree on whether to wipe with water or ash. The Gemara begins to question each position but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: with what substance does one wipe the press?
Rav says: with water.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah says: with ash.
The Gemara asks: does Rav mean specifically water and not ash?
The Gemara asks: does Rabbah bar bar Chanah mean specifically ash and not water?
The Gemara begins to resolve the dispute but the text is cut off.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah on water and ash
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah on water and ash
items.desc_en: Rav says the rule applies to water, and the same applies to ash; Rabbah bar bar Chanah says it applies to ash, and the same applies to water. They do not disagree, as one refers to moist vessels and the other to dry vessels.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the rule applies to water, and the same applies to ash.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah states that the rule applies to ash, and the same applies to water.
The gemara resolves that they do not disagree, as one refers to moist vessels and the other to dry vessels.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the number of immersions
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the number of immersions
items.desc_en: In Sura, they teach that Rav says two or three, and Shmuel says three or four. In Pumbedita, they teach that Rav says three or four, and Shmuel says four or five. They do not disagree, as one counts the final rinsing water and the other does not.

sub.desc_en: Reports the version taught in Sura: Rav says two or three immersions, Shmuel says three or four.
Reports the version taught in Pumbedita: Rav says three or four, Shmuel says four or five.
Resolves the apparent dispute: one version counts the final rinsing water, the other does not, so they do not actually disagree.

items.text: Question about gentile wine presses and Rabbi Abahu's answer
items.text_en: Question about gentile wine presses and Rabbi Abahu's answer
items.desc_en: They asked Rabbi Abahu about gentile wine presses. He replied by citing a mishnah about purifying vessels for terumah: boards, beams, and poles are rinsed; willow and fig-bark ties are wiped; and those of shifah and gemi are left for twelve months. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says they are left from one press to another.

sub.desc_en: They asked Rabbi Abahu about the status of gentile wine-press boards (גורגי).
Rabbi Abahu answered by citing a mishnah about purifying vessels for terumah (תרומה), listing different treatments for different materials, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's dissenting opinion.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma. The difference between them is regarding חוֹרְפֵי וְאַפְלֵי (early and late produce).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement differs from the Tanna Kamma, since they appear identical.
The Gemara answers that the difference between them lies in the case of חוֹרְפֵי וְאַפְלֵי (early and late produce).

items.text: Rabbi Yose's alternative methods and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's alternative methods and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose says one who wants to purify them immediately may scald them in boiling water or steep them in olive brine. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yose says to place them under a spout with flowing water or in a spring with running water. How long? One onah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose states that one who wants to purify vessels immediately may scald them in boiling water or steep them in olive brine.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yose
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yose
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, in the name of Rabbi Yose, adds an alternative: placing the vessels under a spout with flowing water or in a spring with running water.
The stam asks for the required duration, and the answer is given: one onah (a period of time).

items.text: Correction of the mishnah's wording regarding wine libation and purities
items.text_en: Correction of the mishnah's wording regarding wine libation and purities
items.desc_en: The mishnah states 'Just as they said regarding wine libation, so they said regarding purities.' The Gemara objects that we are dealing with purities, so it should say the opposite: 'Just as they said regarding purities, so they said regarding wine libation.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the rules for purities follow the same pattern as those for wine libation.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah's wording is backwards, since the context is purities, not wine libation.
The Gemara corrects the mishnah's wording to read: 'Just as they said regarding purities, so they said regarding wine libation.'

items.text: Dispute about the length of an onah and its resolution
items.text_en: Dispute about the length of an onah and its resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says an onah is either a day or a night. Rabbi Chana She'inah (or Rabbi Chana bar She'inah) in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says it is half a day and half a night. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak says they do not disagree: one refers to the equinoxes of Nisan and Tishrei, the other to the solstices of Tammuz and Tevet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How long is an עונה (a period of waiting for the vessels to become permitted)?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that an עונה is either a full day or a full night.

sub.text: Rabbi Chana She'inah (or Rabbi Chana bar She'inah) in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chana She'inah (or Rabbi Chana bar She'inah) in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chana She'inah (or Rabbi Chana bar She'inah) in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that an עונה is half a day and half a night.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak resolves the dispute: they do not disagree; one refers to the equinoxes of Nisan and Tishrei (when day and night are equal), the other to the solstices of Tammuz and Tevet (when one is longer).

items.text: Rav Yehudah's ruling on various gentile vessels
items.text_en: Rav Yehudah's ruling on various gentile vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah rules: gentile combs of palm-bark are rinsed, of wool are wiped, of linen are left for twelve months, and if there are knots, they are untied. Gentile baskets and nets woven with palm-fiber ropes are rinsed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah rules on the purification methods for various gentile vessels: palm-bark combs are rinsed, wool combs are wiped, linen combs are left for twelve months (with knots untied), and baskets and nets woven with palm-fiber ropes are rinsed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt on winepress purification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt on winepress purification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a gentile's winepress is used, the clusters must be dried, and if there are knots, they must be untied. This sets the stage for the Gemara's discussion on impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a gentile's winepress, clusters must be dried and knots untied, establishing the initial halacha.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya on impurity spread
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya on impurity spread
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: when an am ha'aretz touches grape clusters in a winepress, one opinion holds only the cluster and its surroundings are impure, while the other says the entire winepress is impure. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case of a creeping animal in a mill, where liquids can spread impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya: when an am ha'aretz touches grape clusters in a winepress, one says only the cluster and its surroundings are impure, the other says the entire winepress is impure.

The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that only the cluster and surroundings are impure, why is this different from the case of a creeping animal in a mill where liquids can spread impurity throughout?
The Gemara answers: in the mill case there is no interruption, but here the grape clusters separate and block the spread of impurity.

items.text: Ruling in favor of the lenient opinion
items.text_en: Ruling in favor of the lenient opinion
items.desc_en: The rabbis instructed Rabbi Yirmeya (or his son) to rule in accordance with the opinion that only the cluster and its surroundings are impure, not the entire winepress.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis instructed Rabbi Yirmeya (or his son) to rule in accordance with the lenient opinion that only the cluster and its surroundings are impure, not the entire winepress.

items.text: Mishnah on purifying vessels from gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah on purifying vessels from gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the required purification methods for vessels bought from gentiles: immersion for those used with cold, hag'alah for those used with hot, and libbun for those used with fire. It specifically mentions that a spit and a grill require libbun, while a knife can be sharpened and becomes pure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the purification methods for vessels bought from gentiles: immersion for cold-use, hag'alah for hot-use, libbun for fire-use, with a spit and grill requiring libbun and a knife becoming pure by sharpening.

items.text: Gemara: Source for immersion requirement
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for immersion requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the requirement for immersion in 40 se'ah from the verse "and it shall be purified" and "in the waters of niddah." Bar Kappara teaches that the word "ach" excludes the need for sprinkling on the third and seventh days. The Gemara explains why both verses are necessary: one for any amount of water, the other for the requirement of 40 se'ah and immediate purification.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that all vessels require immersion in 40 se'ah of water.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this requirement.
Rava derives the immersion requirement from the verse 'and it shall be purified,' indicating an additional purification beyond the fire treatment.
Bar Kappara teaches that the word 'אך' (only) excludes the need for sprinkling on the third and seventh days from the phrase 'in the waters of niddah.'
The Gemara asks what the verse 'in the waters of niddah' does teach if not the sprinkling requirement.
The Gemara answers that 'waters of niddah' teaches that the immersion must be in water fit for a niddah's immersion, i.e., 40 se'ah.
The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: 'and it shall be purified' alone would imply any amount of water, so 'waters of niddah' specifies 40 se'ah.
The Gemara adds that 'waters of niddah' alone would imply sunset purification like a niddah, so 'and it shall be purified' teaches immediate purification.

items.text: Debate on which vessels require immersion
items.text_en: Debate on which vessels require immersion
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says even new vessels require immersion, but Rav Sheishes objects that this would include even a garment pin. Rav Nachman limits it to vessels used for meals. Rav Nachman also says the law applies only to purchased vessels, not borrowed ones. A story with Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef shows that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that only metal vessels are included.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha rules that even new vessels require immersion.
Rav Sheishes objects that if even new vessels require immersion, then even a garment pin would be included.
Rav Nachman responds that the law applies only to vessels used for meals.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman further limits the law to purchased vessels, not borrowed ones.

sub.text: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A story with Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef shows that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that only metal vessels are included in the immersion requirement.

items.text: Glass vessels and mortgaged vessels
items.text_en: Glass vessels and mortgaged vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says glass vessels are like metal because they can be repaired. A dispute about a kuniya (a type of vessel) is resolved in favor of the opinion that it is like its final state. The Gemara then questions whether a mortgaged vessel requires immersion, with Mar bar Rav Ashi citing his father's practice but uncertain whether it was because a mortgage is like a sale or because the gentile intended to forfeit it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that glass vessels are like metal vessels because they can be repaired when broken, thus requiring immersion.
A dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about a kuniya (a type of vessel) is recorded, with the ruling following the opinion that it is like its final state.
The Gemara raises a question about whether a mortgaged vessel requires immersion.
Mar bar Rav Ashi cites his father's practice of immersing a mortgaged cup, but is uncertain whether it was because a mortgage is like a sale or because the gentile intended to forfeit it.

items.text: Baraita on purification methods and dispute on nosen ta'am lifgam
items.text_en: Baraita on purification methods and dispute on nosen ta'am lifgam
items.desc_en: A baraita details the purification process for vessels based on their use: immersion for unused, rinsing and immersion for cold use, hag'alah and immersion for hot use, libbun and immersion for fire use. A contradiction about using vessels before purification is resolved by the dispute over whether nosen ta'am lifgam (imparting a foul taste) is permitted or forbidden. The Gemara questions how, according to the lenient opinion, the prohibition of gentile's cooking vessels is ever applicable, and Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna limits the Torah prohibition to a pot used for cooking.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the purification methods for vessels bought from gentiles based on their prior use: immersion for unused, rinsing and immersion for cold use, hag'alah and immersion for hot use, libbun and immersion for fire use.
The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one forbids using vessels before purification, the other permits it.
The contradiction is resolved by attributing the dispute to the broader disagreement over whether נותן טעם לפגם (imparting a foul taste) is forbidden or permitted.
The Gemara asks: according to the lenient opinion that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, how can the Torah's prohibition of gentile's cooking vessels ever apply?

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna answers that the Torah only prohibited a pot used for cooking, where the absorbed taste is beneficial, not foul.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about a one-day-old vessel
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about a one-day-old vessel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a vessel that is not בן יומו (one-day-old) should be prohibited, since its absorbed flavor is פגום (tainted). It answers that there is a decree forbidding a vessel that is not בן יומו because of a vessel that is בן יומו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a vessel that is not בן יומו (one-day-old) should be prohibited, since its absorbed flavor is פגום (tainted) and should be permitted.
The Gemara answers that there is a decree forbidding a vessel that is not בן יומו because of a vessel that is בן יומו.

items.text: Objection: even a one-day-old vessel is tainted
items.text_en: Objection: even a one-day-old vessel is tainted
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even a vessel that is בן יומו is also tainted (פגום), so the decree seems unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even a vessel that is בן יומו (one-day-old) also imparts a tainted flavor, so the decree seems baseless.

items.text: Rabbi Amram's contradiction and Rav Sheshet's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Amram's contradiction and Rav Sheshet's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Amram raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires libbun (burning) for spits and grids used by idolaters, but a baraita about sacrifices requires hag'alah (immersion in hot water). Rav Sheshet answers that the cases differ: here (idolatry) the utensil absorbed permitted food, there (sacrifices) it absorbed forbidden food.

sub.text: Rav Amram's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Amram's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram raises a contradiction to Rav Sheshet: the Mishnah requires libbun (burning) for non-sacred vessels, but a baraita about sacred vessels requires hag'alah (scalding) for the same items.
Rav Sheshet answers that sacred vessels absorb היתירא (permitted substance) while non-sacred vessels absorb איסורא (forbidden substance), so different treatments apply.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that when the utensil emits absorbed flavor, it emits forbidden taste. He suggests that 'hag'alah' in the baraita means merely rinsing and wiping, not full immersion.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that ultimately, when the vessel emits its absorbed substance, it emits forbidden matter, so the distinction is invalid.
Rava reinterprets 'הגעלה' (hag'alah) in the sacred context as merely rinsing and wiping, not scalding.

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that rinsing is done with cold water, while hag'alah requires hot water. He proposes that each source teaches one method, and the other method is implied by analogy (יגיד עליו רעו).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that rinsing is done with cold water while hag'alah requires hot water, so they are not equivalent.
Abaye answers that each source teaches one method, and the other method is implied by analogy (יגיד עליו רעו).

items.text: Rava's rejection of Abaye's analogy
items.text_en: Rava's rejection of Abaye's analogy
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's proposal, arguing that if the two methods were interchangeable, the Mishnah would have stated them together or explicitly indicated the analogy.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if the analogy principle applied, the Mishnah should have taught both cases together or explicitly stated the analogy.

items.text: Rava's final explanation based on Rav Nachman's principle
items.text_en: Rava's final explanation based on Rav Nachman's principle
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case of sacrifices is different because, according to Rav Nachman, each day the utensil becomes 'hag'alah' (purged) for the next day's use. The Gemara then questions this regarding a sin-offering, which is eaten only for one day, and attempts to resolve it, but the difficulty remains.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the case of sacrifices is different because, per Rav Nachman's principle, each day the utensil becomes 'hag'alah' (purged) for the next day's use.
The Gemara objects that for a sin-offering (חטאת), which is eaten only for one day, the utensil would absorb leftover (נותר) from the first day when used for the next day's cooking.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the objection by suggesting that the sin-offering and peace-offering from the previous day are cooked together, so their consumption periods end simultaneously.
The Gemara objects that if the resolution were correct, no 'hag'alah' (purge) would be needed at all, leaving the difficulty unresolved.

items.text: Rav Pappa's and Rav Ashi's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's and Rav Ashi's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa distinguishes between a utensil that is קריד (caked) and one that is not. Rav Ashi returns to the original distinction: here (idolatry) the utensil absorbed permitted food, there (sacrifices) it absorbed forbidden food, and when it emits, the forbidden taste is not in its original state.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa distinguishes between a utensil that is קריד (caked with absorbed taste) and one that is not, explaining the difference in treatment.

Rav Ashi returns to the original distinction: here (idolatry) the utensil absorbed permitted food, there (sacrifices) it absorbed forbidden food, and when it emits, the forbidden taste is not in its original state.

items.text: Practical halakhot of libbun and hag'alah
items.text_en: Practical halakhot of libbun and hag'alah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the extent of libbun (until the outer peel falls off) and how hag'alah is performed (a small pot inside a large pot). It then questions the case of a large pot and brings a supporting story from the house of Rav Akavya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to what extent libbun (scouring with fire) must be performed, and Rabbi Mini answers: until the outer peel falls off.
Rabbi Mini rules that libbun must be done until the outer peel of the utensil falls off.
The Gemara asks how hag'alah (scalding with boiling water) is performed, and Rav Huna answers: a small pot inside a large pot.
Rav Huna explains that hag'alah is done by placing a small pot inside a large pot of boiling water.
The Gemara asks what the rule is for a large pot that needs hag'alah, and then says: come and hear.

sub.text: Supporting story from the house of Rav Akavya
sub.text_en: Supporting story from the house of Rav Akavya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story about a pot in the house of Rav Akavya that was turned over (to serve as a cover) to address the question of a large pot.

items.text: Rava's praise of Rav Akavya's method
items.text_en: Rava's praise of Rav Akavya's method
items.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Akavya for his wisdom in devising a method to purge a knife by inserting it into a dough, filling it with water, and boiling it. Rava explains that the principle is that as the knife absorbs through sparks, it also expels through sparks.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes Rav Akavya's method: inserting the knife into a dough, filling it with water, and boiling it.
Rava praises Rav Akavya as a great sage and explains the principle: as the knife absorbs through sparks (ניצוצות), it also expels through sparks.

items.text: The knife: sharpening and sticking in the ground
items.text_en: The knife: sharpening and sticking in the ground
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a knife can be purified by sharpening it. Rav Ukva bar Chama adds that one must stick it into the ground ten times. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua specifies that the ground must be hard (not tilled), and Rav Kahana adds that the knife must be smooth without notches. A baraita supports this. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua concludes that this is only for eating cold food.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's rule: if one sharpens a knife, it becomes ritually pure (טהורה).
Rav Ukva bar Chama adds that one must also thrust the knife into the ground ten times.
Rav Huna specifies that the ground must be untilled (שאינה עבודה).
Rav Kahana adds that the knife must be smooth (יפה) without notches (גומות).
A baraita supports the ruling: a smooth knife without notches is thrust ten times into the ground.
Rav Huna concludes that this method is only for eating cold food with the knife.

items.text: Story of Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tovi before King Shapur
items.text_en: Story of Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tovi before King Shapur
items.desc_en: A story is told about Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tovi sitting before King Shapur. An etrog was brought, and the king cut a piece and gave it to Bati bar Tovi, then stuck the knife into the ground ten times before giving a piece to Mar Yehuda. Bati bar Tovi questioned why the king did this, suspecting Mar Yehuda was not a Jew. The king replied that he knew Mar Yehuda's status but not Bati's. An alternative version has the king reminding Bati of what he did the previous night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story: Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tovi were sitting before King Shapur; an etrog was brought, the king cut a piece and gave it to Bati bar Tovi, then stuck the knife into the ground ten times before cutting and giving a piece to Mar Yehuda.
Bati bar Tovi questioned the king: is that man (Mar Yehuda) not a Jew (that you treat him differently)?
The king answered: I am certain about Mar Yehuda's status (that he is a Jew), but I am not certain about yours (Bati bar Tovi's).
An alternative version is cited: the king said to Bati bar Tovi, 'Remember what you did last night' (implying Bati's own questionable behavior).
